t: Activated microglia and astrocytes release pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, and TNF-alpha that sensitize neurons and promote central pain amplification in fibromyalgia.
A multiplex protein panel revealed elevated IL-8 levels in cerebrospinal fluid and plasma of fibromyalgia patients relative to healthy controls.

Elevated levels of the chemokine CX3CL1 (fractalkine) were found in cerebrospinal fluid and plasma of fibromyalgia patients, and cathepsin S inhibitors may block its cleavage to reduce microglial activation and hyperalgesia.
Elevated serum amyloid beta 1-42 and tau levels have been reported in fibromyalgia, suggesting glial activation and neuroinflammation may contribute to subtle neurodegenerative processes.
PET studies show neuroinflammation in the left medial frontal, left superior frontal, and left amygdala correlates with psychological stress dysregulation in fibromyalgia.

Fibromyalgia has been reported to develop following viral infections, with post-viral fatigue syndromes such as SARS-CoV-2/long COVID or EBV-associated chronic fatigue syndrome considered a common cause of associated neuroinflammation.

Long COVID symptoms including fatigue, brain fog, anxiety, sleep disturbance, headaches, and orthostatic hypotension have been observed even in patients with mild or asymptomatic acute infection who did not require hospitalization.

Some fibromyalgia patients meet diagnostic criteria for both chronic fatigue syndrome and fibromyalgia, and long COVID complications with widespread pain may also meet fibromyalgia diagnostic criteria.

Neuroinflammation in long COVID is suspected to arise from chronic persistent SARS-CoV-2 infection, activation of autoantibodies and immune cells reactive to the nervous system, and reactivation of latent viruses such as HHV-6, HHV-7, and Epstein-Barr virus.
Patients with fibromyalgia exhibit elevated glutamate concentrations in the right posterior insula, potentially indicating enhanced pain signaling.
Fibromyalgia patients show impaired conditioned pain modulation, suggesting dysfunction of the descending pain inhibitory system.
Fibromyalgia patients have decreased cerebrospinal fluid concentrations of serotonin, noradrenaline, and dopamine, monoamines involved in endogenous pain inhibition.
SNRIs such as duloxetine and milnacipran have demonstrated efficacy in enhancing endogenous pain inhibition and reducing pain intensity in fibromyalgia.
A history of adverse childhood experiences such as emotional abuse and neglect has been reported to be associated with an increased risk of chronic pain, including juvenile fibromyalgia.
Neuroendocrine dysregulation, including HPA axis dysfunction and a flattened cortisol response, may exacerbate fatigue and stress reactivity in fibromyalgia.
Cathepsin S inhibitors are proposed to block CX3CL1 (fractalkine) cleavage, potentially suppressing persistent microglial activation and reducing hyperalgesia in fibromyalgia.
Elevated serum levels of Aβ1–42 and tau have been reported in fibromyalgia patients, suggesting glial activation and neuroinflammation may contribute to subtle neurodegenerative processes.
Oxidative and mitochondrial dysfunction have been implicated as upstream triggers of neuroinflammation in fibromyalgia, linking cellular energy metabolism disorders to central pain amplification.

PET studies show that neuroinflammation localized to the left medial frontal, left superior frontal, and left amygdala regions correlates with psychological stress dysregulation in fibromyalgia patients.
Fibromyalgia has been reported to develop following viral infections, implicating infectious triggers in disease onset.

Post-viral fatigue syndromes such as SARS-CoV-2 infection (long COVID) or Epstein-Barr virus infection-associated chronic fatigue syndrome are increasingly considered common causes of neuroinflammation associated with fibromyalgia symptoms.

Long COVID symptoms including fatigue, brain fog, anxiety, sleep disturbance, headache, and orthostatic hypotension occur even in patients with mild or asymptomatic acute infection, and closely resemble chronic fatigue syndrome/myalgic encephalomyelitis.
Some fibromyalgia patients meet diagnostic criteria for both chronic fatigue syndrome and fibromyalgia, and long COVID-related widespread pain may also satisfy fibromyalgia diagnostic criteria.

Neuroinflammation in long COVID is suspected to arise from chronic persistent SARS-CoV-2 infection, autoantibodies and immune cells reactive to the nervous system, and reactivation of latent viruses such as HHV-6, HHV-7, and Epstein-Barr virus.

Brainstem damage from neuroinflammation can cause dysfunction of the descending pain inhibitory system, autonomic nuclei, and reticular formation, producing hyperalgesia, fatigue, orthostatic hypotension, and brain fog.

Functional MRI studies have demonstrated increased connectivity and activity in the insular cortex, amygdala, and somatosensory cortex in fibromyalgia patients, consistent with CNS neuronal hyperexcitability in pain processing.
Patients with fibromyalgia exhibit elevated concentrations of glutamate, a major excitatory neurotransmitter, in the right posterior insula, potentially indicating enhanced pain signaling.
Fibromyalgia patients show impaired conditioned pain modulation, indicating dysfunction of the descending pain inhibitory system.
Fibromyalgia patients have decreased cerebrospinal fluid concentrations of serotonin, noradrenaline, and dopamine, neurotransmitters involved in endogenous pain inhibition.
Pressure pain threshold can be easily measured in outpatient settings with a pressure meter and may help classify FM patients into low or normal pain threshold subgroups.
Measuring peripheral blood cytokines such as IL-8, IL-10, and TNF-alpha may help infer the presence of neuroinflammation in patients with FM.

Cerebrospinal fluid cytokine measurement or PET imaging would give a more definitive assessment of neuroinflammation in FM than peripheral blood tests, but these are not practical for routine clinical use.
Resting-state functional MRI is non-invasive and may be useful for evaluating FM subtype status in facilities where it is available.

Cognitive behavioral therapy and mind-body therapies such as yoga, meditation, neurofeedback, and expressing gratitude may effectively reduce pain in FM patients whose pain perception is affected by attentional bias.
Exercise and rehabilitation therapy have shown consistent benefits in reducing pain and fatigue and improving mood in FM according to recent RCTs and meta-analyses.

Redox-imbalance-targeting therapies such as ubiquinol, coenzyme Q10, melatonin, glutathione (and glutathione donors), and vitamin D have been proposed for neuroinflammation in FM, but none has yet been clinically established.

SNRIs (duloxetine, milnacipran), amitriptyline, and antiepileptic drugs such as pregabalin have demonstrated efficacy in some FM patients, especially when tailored to individual symptom profiles, comorbidities, and psychosocial factors.

Opioids are not recommended for chronic pain conditions such as FM because they can induce tolerance and, relatively early, opioid-induced hyperalgesia via dysfunction of the descending pain inhibitory system.

ACR diagnostic criteria for FM evolved from examiner-based tender point assessment to later revisions prioritizing patient-reported pain distribution and associated symptoms, improving feasibility but increasing reliance on subjective reporting.
Epidemiological studies report FM prevalence of approximately 5.4% in the UK, 2.1% in Japan, and a pooled global prevalence of 1.78% from a large-scale meta-analysis.
First-degree relatives of FM patients have an up to eightfold increased risk of developing FM, suggesting a genetic component to disease clustering in families.

Small fiber neuropathy, evidenced by reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density on skin biopsy and abnormal corneal confocal microscopy, is detected in up to 40-60% of FM patients, with a recent meta-analysis reporting approximately half of patients showing small fiber dysfunction.
A history of adverse childhood experiences such as emotional abuse and neglect is associated with increased risk of chronic pain, including juvenile fibromyalgia.

Long COVID symptoms, including fatigue, brain fog, anxiety, sleep disturbances, headaches, and orthostatic hypotension, occur even in patients with mild or asymptomatic acute infection who did not require hospitalization.

Neuroinflammation in long COVID is suspected to arise from chronic persistent SARS-CoV-2 infection, autoantibody and immune cell activation against the nervous system, and reactivation of latent viruses including HHV-6, HHV-7, and Epstein-Barr virus.

Some FM patients meet diagnostic criteria for both chronic fatigue syndrome and FM, and widespread pain in long COVID complications may also meet FM diagnostic criteria, suggesting shared pathophysiology across these conditions.

Latent profile analysis of 26 PASC symptoms identified four distinct symptom profiles among Korean adults: low-symptom (23.3%), moderate multisystem (44.1%), fatigue/PEM-dominant (15.9%), and high multisystem burden (16.7%).
Fatigue was the most frequently reported PASC symptom (90.6% of participants) and had the highest mean severity score among the 26 symptoms assessed.

Post-exertional malaise (PEM) was reported by 85.2% of participants with a high mean severity score and defined the fatigue/PEM-dominant symptom profile, overlapping with a hallmark feature of ME/CFS.
Cough was reported by 86.3% of participants with a mean severity of 2.82, making it the second most prevalent PASC symptom.
Mean HRQoL among PASC participants was significantly lower than the general Korean adult population and comparable to levels reported in patients with heart failure or multiple sclerosis.
HRQoL declined in a stepwise manner with increasing PASC symptom burden across the four latent classes, with the high multisystem burden profile showing the lowest scores.
Higher educational attainment (college degree or higher) was an independent predictor of significantly higher HRQoL among PASC patients.
Absence of pre-existing chronic disease was independently associated with higher HRQoL, while presence of chronic disease predicted lower HRQoL, suggesting a 'double burden' effect.
Self-perceived healthy status was independently associated with significantly higher HRQoL compared with perceiving oneself as unhealthy.
Participants who visited a hospital for treatment during the acute phase of COVID-19 had significantly lower HRQoL than those who did not.
Compared with participants whose symptoms persisted at the time of survey, those whose symptoms resolved within 13-24 weeks or 6-9 months had significantly higher HRQoL.
Membership in the high multisystem burden latent class was independently associated with significantly lower HRQoL relative to the low-symptom class, after adjusting for covariates.

Membership in the moderate multisystem latent class was independently associated with lower HRQoL relative to the low-symptom class after adjustment, despite showing the highest unadjusted HRQoL among the four classes.
Contrary to expectation, membership in the fatigue/PEM-dominant latent class was associated with slightly higher HRQoL than the low-symptom class in the adjusted regression model.
Number of COVID-19 vaccine doses received showed a nonlinear association with HRQoL, with those receiving four or more doses having the lowest HRQoL and those with three doses having the highest.
Serum anti-SITH-1 antibody titers were significantly higher in PASC patients compared to healthy controls, with good discriminatory performance by ROC analysis.
Using a titer threshold of 1.43, 62.8% of PASC patients were seropositive for anti-SITH-1 antibodies compared to only 5.6% of healthy controls.
Anti-SITH-1 antibody titers did not differ significantly among PASC patients infected with different SARS-CoV-2 variants (wild-type, Alpha, Delta, Omicron).
PASC patients seropositive for anti-SITH-1 antibodies reported significantly more severe fatigue and depression than seronegative patients.
Mice with nasal expression of SARS-CoV-2 spike (S1) protein showed increased IL-1β mRNA expression in the olfactory bulb compared to vector controls.
Mice with nasal expression of SARS-CoV-2 spike (S1) protein showed increased bFGF mRNA expression in the olfactory bulb compared to vector controls.

Mice transiently expressing HHV-6B SITH-1 in olfactory bulb astrocytes showed markedly reduced ChAT-positive cells in the medial septum and diagonal band of Broca and reduced whole-brain ChAT mRNA compared to controls.
Donepezil treatment reversed the reduction in hippocampal neurogenesis (DCX-positive cells) seen in SITH-1-expressing mice.

Donepezil significantly reduced immobility time in the tail suspension test and increased Y-maze arm entries in SITH-1-expressing mice, indicating improvement of depression-like behavior and spontaneous activity.
Donepezil administration reduced the number of active caspase-3-positive (apoptotic) cells in the olfactory bulb of SITH-1-expressing mice.
In the overall PASC RCT cohort, donepezil did not significantly improve Chalder Fatigue Scale scores at 3 weeks compared to placebo.
In anti-SITH-1 antibody seropositive PASC patients, donepezil significantly reduced HADS depression scores at week 3 and CFS total scores at week 8 compared to placebo.
No significant improvement in PHQ-9 depression scores was observed with donepezil in the anti-SITH-1 seropositive subgroup, despite improvement on HADS depression.
In anti-SITH-1 antibody seronegative PASC patients, donepezil tended to worsen symptoms compared to placebo, possibly due to gastrointestinal side effects.

Anti-SITH-1 antibody positivity rate in PASC patients (62.8%-71.7% across cohorts) markedly exceeds the typical general-population seropositivity rate of approximately 25%, suggesting SARS-CoV-2-triggered HHV-6B reactivation.
Across clinical sites in the RCT subgroup, the proportion of PASC patients positive for anti-SITH-1 antibodies ranged from 63.2% to 100%, with an overall positivity rate of 71.7%.
Transient adenoviral expression of HHV-6B SITH-1 in mouse olfactory bulb astrocytes induced olfactory bulb apoptosis and depression-like behavior, consistent with prior reports.
LC/PASC participants were older on average than FM-only comparators.
LC/PASC participants were less often female compared to FM-only comparators.
Fibromyalgia participants showed greater use of centrally acting medications than LC/PASC participants.
Across symptom and function measures (FIQR/SIQR-equivalent, BDI, CSI, MPQ, VAS pain), LC/PASC and FM showed partial overlap with domain-specific differences.
SF-36 quality-of-life domains showed broad similarity between LC/PASC and FM, with some domain-specific differences.

Senescence-associated SenMayo genes were significantly upregulated in the early post-infection period among individuals who later developed Long COVID symptom phenotypes compared to those who did not.
SenMayo senescence-associated genes were upregulated in participants with long-term cognitive impairment (measured by BRACE) compared to those without.
SenMayo senescence-associated genes were upregulated in participants with persistent dyspnea compared to those without.
The transcription factor gene ETS2 was consistently upregulated across all impairment-related Long COVID phenotypes examined, while other SenMayo genes varied by phenotype.

Aging is associated with autonomic imbalance featuring sympathetic overactivation, reduced parasympathetic tone, and impaired beta-adrenergic signaling in immune cells, contributing to inflammaging and immune dysregulation.
The review describes β2-adrenergic control of the Th17/regulatory T cell balance via cAMP-dependent mechanisms that interact with cytokine-driven STAT signaling.
Chronic sympathetic stimulation and beta-adrenergic receptor desensitization weaken regulatory immune constraints, favoring pro-inflammatory immune trajectories and loss of immune tolerance.

The authors propose Long COVID as a paradigmatic condition in which pre-existing inflammaging and autonomic vulnerability are amplified by viral infection, leading to persistent inflammation, impaired immune regulation, and increased susceptibility to autoimmune manifestations.
Participants with long COVID had markedly worse health-related quality of life on the SF-12 compared with recovered controls.
Depressive symptoms measured by PHQ-9 were significantly higher in long COVID cases than recovered controls.
Fatigue severity as measured by the FSS was significantly greater in long COVID cases than recovered controls.
Sleep quality assessed by PSQI was significantly worse in long COVID cases than recovered controls.
Exercise capacity, measured by the six-minute walk test distance, was significantly shorter in long COVID cases than recovered controls.
Long COVID cases were less frequently actively employed compared with recovered controls.
Long COVID cases had a higher prevalence of post-COVID comorbidity than recovered controls.
Within long COVID cases, active employment was independently associated with better HRQoL in the multivariable model.
Depressive symptoms (PHQ-9) were independently associated with worse HRQoL within long COVID cases in multivariable analysis.
Within long COVID cases, a higher number of post-COVID comorbidities was independently associated with worse health-related quality of life in multivariable analysis.
Fatigue severity showed a borderline, non-significant association with worse HRQoL in the multivariable model among long COVID cases.
The multivariable regression model combining employment, depressive symptoms, comorbidity count, and fatigue explained 48.9% of variance in SF-12 score among long COVID cases.
Exploratory clustering analysis did not identify discrete long COVID phenotypes, instead suggesting a continuous symptom severity gradient across patients.

A descriptive lower-burden stratum (42.3%) and higher-burden stratum (57.7%) of long COVID patients were operationalized and differed across symptom load, fatigue, mood, functional status, exercise capacity, and HRQoL.
A higher total self-reported symptom score was associated with increased odds of having long COVID.
A higher mental impairment questionnaire score, especially memory, concentration, and post-exertional exhaustion, was associated with increased odds of long COVID.
A higher total fatigue impairment score (Daily Fatigue Impact Scale) was significantly associated with increased odds of long COVID.

Female sex was associated with higher odds of long COVID, reflected in higher total symptom, mental impairment, and fatigue impairment scores compared to men, an association not seen in the never-infected group.
A higher number of self-reported respiratory infectious episodes in the year following SARS-CoV-2 infection was associated with increased odds of long COVID.
Total antibiotic use in the preceding year showed only a non-significant trend toward association with long COVID.
In women, total white blood cell (leukocyte) count was lower in the long COVID group than in never-infected controls, and this lower count was associated with increased odds of long COVID.
Neutrophil counts were lower in long COVID women compared to never-infected women, with higher neutrophil counts associated with lower odds of long COVID.
Basophil counts were lower in long COVID women, with an extremely large and unstable odds ratio noted by the authors.
Lymphocyte counts were lower in long COVID women, with higher lymphocyte counts associated with lower odds of long COVID.
No association was found between eosinophil or monocyte counts and long COVID.
In men, no difference in white blood cell counts was found between the long COVID and never-infected groups.
No differences were found in other blood analyses, including acute phase reactants such as thrombocytes, ferritin, or C-reactive protein, between the long COVID and never-infected groups.

A comprehensive clinical and paraclinical evaluation, including ECG, spirometry, neurological examination, smell/taste testing, and MoCA cognitive testing, showed no objective associations with long COVID.

The long COVID group reported markedly higher prevalence of fatigue, headache, sleep problems, concentration and memory problems, and respiratory symptoms compared to never-infected controls, whose most common symptoms were respiratory, joint pain, fatigue, and sleep problems at lower prevalence.

The long COVID group predominantly reported cognitive complaints (concentration and memory difficulty), stress, and post-exertional fatigue, with relatively less impact on emotions, depression, and anxiety compared to the more evenly distributed profile in the never-infected group.

Qualitative research with young people describes Long Covid fatigue and physical impacts as materializing changes in biographical and social relationships, making everyday activities exhausting and contingent.
Social responses that frame the COVID-19 pandemic as a past event contribute to young people feeling their Long Covid experience is discounted and 'out of sync' with prevailing social narratives.
Participants reported slight to moderate overall symptom burden, with the highest scores in respiratory and psychological domains.
Functional impairment across work, social and daily activities was moderate, with a Work and Social Adjustment Scale mean of 17.35.
Disability assessed via the WHO Disability Assessment Schedule 2.0 showed a mean of 16.61, reflecting moderate functional limitation.
Post COVID-19 Functional Status Scale mean was 2.20, indicating moderate functional limitation.
Fatigue was notable, with a Modified Fatigue Impact Scale mean of 43.39, indicating clinically relevant fatigue.
Post-exertional malaise, measured via the DePaul Symptom Questionnaire-PEM, had a mean of 22.47, indicating notable symptom burden.
Cognitive difficulties were commonly reported, with a Perceived Deficits Questionnaire mean of 33.43.
Cognitive difficulties were commonly reported among racialized adults with pre-existing mental health conditions and long COVID, with a mean Perceived Deficits Questionnaire score of 33.43.
Anxiety symptoms were in the mild range among this population, with a mean GAD-7 score of 9.27.
Depression symptoms were in the moderate range among this population, with a mean PHQ-9 score of 11.43, indicating clinically relevant depression.
Low serum selenium alone showed no strong association with persistent fatigue after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Low SELENOP levels alone showed no strong association with persistent fatigue after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Elevated SELENOP-specific autoantibodies alone showed no strong association with persistent fatigue after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
The combination of low serum selenium and elevated SELENOP-autoantibodies was associated with more than twice the prevalence of persistent fatigue compared to the reference group.
The combination of low SELENOP levels and elevated SELENOP-autoantibodies was associated with more than twice the prevalence of persistent fatigue compared to the reference group.
Long COVID patients show sustained elevation of IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β along with chronic activation of the monocyte-macrophage system.
Macrophages in long COVID persistently maintain an M1-dominant, pro-inflammatory polarization state.
Impaired regulatory T cell function is described as further impeding resolution of inflammation in long COVID.
Long COVID patients show reduced high-frequency HRV components and elevated LF/HF ratios, indicating a shift toward sympathetic dominance.

Studies report reduced vagal nerve activity, decreased acetylcholine availability, and downregulated α7nAChR expression in individuals with long COVID, suggesting impaired cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway responsiveness.
Functional neuroimaging studies reveal reduced metabolic activity in brainstem and limbic autonomic centers in long COVID, corroborating autonomic dysfunction findings.

Under persistent inflammatory stimulation in long COVID, immune cells shift from oxidative phosphorylation to aerobic glycolysis, which if prolonged impairs ATP production and causes mitochondrial dysfunction.
Core metabolic regulators AMPK, SIRT1, and PGC-1α are reported to be inhibited in long COVID, leading to impaired mitochondrial biogenesis and reduced antioxidant defense.
WHO estimates that approximately 6 in 100 people with COVID-19 develop post-COVID-19 condition (long COVID), though prevalence varies substantially by population and study design.
In LPS-induced endotoxemia and sepsis-related animal models, EA at ST36 reduced inflammatory cytokine production, improved survival-related outcomes, and attenuated tissue injury.

In sepsis-related lung injury and postoperative ileus animal models, EA restored α7nAChR expression and inhibited NF-κB signaling via JAK2/STAT3 activation, with reduced effects after α7nAChR antagonism or vagotomy, confirming CAP-pathway dependence.

In an acute pancreatitis animal model, EA at ST36 increased vagal activity, reduced pancreatic inflammation, and increased α7nAChR-positive macrophages; the protective effect was weakened by vagotomy or methyllycaconitine.
In a dry eye disease animal model, EA reduced lacrimal gland inflammation, upregulated α7nAChR, and inhibited NF-κB, though vagal dependence was not directly tested.
Clinical studies report that EA intervention is associated with improvements in HRV parameters, selected metabolic indicators, and systemic inflammatory markers.
Long COVID patients receiving EA treatment showed improvements in fatigue, dyspnea, abnormal heart rate, and low energy levels, along with reduced inflammatory marker levels and enhanced HRV.

A registered prospective, randomized, sham-controlled, patient-assessor-blinded trial protocol plans to enroll 150 long COVID patients for 32 EA sessions over 16 weeks plus 8-week follow-up, assessing cognitive, depressive, sleep, fatigue, and quality-of-life outcomes; this is a protocol only, not yet reporting efficacy results.

Excessive sympathetic signaling in long COVID is proposed to amplify proinflammatory pathways via the norepinephrine-β2 adrenergic receptor axis, while diminished vagal activity weakens cholinergic anti-inflammatory feedback.
Fatigue was the most commonly reported symptom among students screening positive for Long COVID.
Cough was among the most commonly reported symptoms in students with Long COVID.
Sleep disturbances were also prevalent among students with Long COVID.
Students with Long COVID reported significantly lower quality of life scores compared to those without Long COVID.
No significant differences in DASS-21 (depression, anxiety, stress) scores were found between students with and without Long COVID.
No significant differences in overall PSQI sleep quality scores were found between students with and without Long COVID, despite prevalent sleep disturbance symptoms.
Number of vaccination doses received differed significantly between students with and without Long COVID.
Number of prior COVID-19 infections differed significantly between students with and without Long COVID.
Fatigue persisted significantly longer among individuals with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection compared to uninfected controls, with infection associated with approximately 50% longer duration.
Sleep disturbance persisted significantly longer among infected individuals than uninfected controls, with infection associated with approximately 50% longer duration.
Respiratory and physical symptoms resolved at similar rates between infected participants and uninfected controls.

Individuals aged 40-59 years showed slower recovery (longer symptom duration) compared to other age groups, while other demographic and clinical factors showed minimal associations with recovery time.
Severe fatigue was reported by 88% of the entire Long COVID sample.
Clinically significant depression was reported by 78% of the entire Long COVID sample.
Long COVID had major negative functional impacts, with 27% of participants unable to return to full-time work since contracting COVID-19.
The biggest perceived barrier to Long COVID treatment and rehabilitation was dismissal of symptoms by healthcare providers, which was worsened by gender identity (being a woman) and race.
Black participants reported more experiences of discrimination compared to White participants, and this discrimination correlated with more severe depression.
Among 177 patients enrolled in an AI-enhanced nurse navigation program after COVID-19, 60 (33%) were identified as having long COVID.
Among long COVID patients identified, the most frequently reported symptoms via text-message NLP analysis were memory loss, dyspnea, cognitive fatigue, and hair loss.

An XGBoost-based machine learning model ('XGBoost-minor'), trained on structured clinical/sociodemographic data and NLP-derived text-message features, achieved 72% accuracy, 38% sensitivity, 88% specificity, 63% PPV, 74% NPV, and an AUROC of 0.59 for identifying long COVID.
Predictive factors for long COVID identification in the machine learning model included age, number of COVID-19 episodes, vaccination status, comorbidities, and respiratory symptoms.
The AI-enhanced nurse navigation platform, delivered via monthly WhatsApp interactions over 16 weeks, achieved a Net Promoter Score of 92, indicating strong user endorsement.
Documented neurologic/autonomic chronic condition burden increased from the pre-infection to post-infection window among patients with clinician-coded long COVID.
Documented respiratory chronic condition burden increased from the pre-infection to post-infection window among patients with clinician-coded long COVID.
Documented hypercoagulable-related chronic condition burden increased from the pre-infection to post-infection window among patients with clinician-coded long COVID.
Documented endocrine/metabolic chronic condition burden increased from the pre-infection to post-infection window among patients with clinician-coded long COVID.
Documented sleep-related chronic condition burden increased from the pre-infection to post-infection window among patients with clinician-coded long COVID.
Documented symptom-based (non-specific) diagnosis burden increased from the pre-infection to post-infection window among patients with clinician-coded long COVID.

Pre-infection, two multimorbidity phenotypes were identified in long COVID patients: low burden (87.9%) and multimorbid (12.1%); post-infection, four phenotypes emerged: low burden (63.3%), multimorbid/systemic (21.0%), respiratory-dominant (4.3%), and high-utilization/low-coded multimorbidity (11.3%).
After infection, increases in chronic disease burden were concentrated in neurologic/autonomic conditions among long COVID patients.
Post-infection increases in coded chronic conditions were also seen in hypercoagulable and endocrine/metabolic domains.
Sleep-related and symptom-based diagnostic domains also showed increased coding burden after long COVID infection.
The high-utilization/low-coded multimorbidity phenotype was characterized by younger age, female predominance, and greater emergency department and outpatient healthcare use.
Statistically significant changes in chronic condition burden after infection were less frequent in children than in adults with long COVID.
Patients with higher baseline (pre-index) multimorbidity had a greater adjusted probability of transitioning to the post-index multimorbid/systemic phenotype.

Respiratory-dominant and high-utilization/low-coded post-index phenotypes emerged from patients with either low-burden or multimorbid pre-index baseline status, unlike the multimorbid/systemic phenotype.

Across the included studies, Long COVID patients showed a consistent long-term decline in health-related quality of life relative to healthy controls, most pronounced in physical functioning, vitality, fatigue, daily activities, pain, discomfort, and respiratory distress.
Elevated inflammatory markers including CRP, hsCRP, IL-6, and TNF-alpha were the most frequently measured biomarkers in Long COVID patients across included studies.
Endothelial dysfunction and coagulation markers such as D-dimer and VCAM-1 were commonly measured and linked to lower HRQoL in Long COVID patients.
Decreased calcium levels were associated with lower health-related quality of life among Long COVID patients in some studies.
Signals from individual autoantibodies were associated with lower HRQoL, indicating phenotype-specific autoimmune heterogeneity in Long COVID.
Neurotoxicity signals were associated with lower health-related quality of life in patients with Long COVID.

Long COVID patients showed the greatest HRQoL deterioration in physical functioning, vitality, fatigue, daily activities, pain, discomfort, and respiratory distress domains compared to healthy controls.
Across included studies, prevalence of long COVID among healthcare workers with prior infection or whole-staff samples ranged from 10% to 74%, with several studies reporting rates above 50%.
Among 13 studies evaluating return to work, 19-63% of healthcare workers with long COVID had resumed work within six months, commonly with restrictions.
In some cohorts, around one in five healthcare workers with long COVID remained unable to work.
Full-time employment among affected healthcare workers decreased markedly from pre-infection levels, e.g. 57% pre-infection versus 31% at follow-up in one study.
Between 16% and 40% of healthcare workers with long COVID required workplace adjustments such as reduced hours, reassignment, or avoidance of night shifts.
Sixteen of the included studies reported diminished work ability among healthcare workers with long COVID compared with their pre-infection status or unaffected peers.
One study estimated that healthcare workers with long COVID took a mean of 223 days to return to their pre-infection level of work ability.
Older age, depression, comorbidity, and acute disease severity were recurrent factors associated with worse return-to-work and work-ability outcomes among healthcare workers with long COVID.
Evidence regarding the influence of gender and job category on return-to-work and work-ability outcomes in healthcare workers with long COVID was inconsistent across studies.
Fatigue (67%) and brain fog (58%) were the most commonly reported symptoms among long COVID participants in this cohort.
Global whole-blood gene expression profiles significantly separated LC cases from controls in multivariate space, with modest effect size.
Differential expression analysis identified 63 genes distinguishing LC cases from controls (BH-FDR < 0.10), with large effect sizes (Cohen's d > 1 for these genes).
S100A8, a monocyte/neutrophil-associated calprotectin-encoding gene, was significantly upregulated in LC cases with fold change greater than 1.5.
S100A8 expression correlated strongly with the neutrophil signature module but showed no significant association with monocyte/macrophage, cytotoxic, or NK function modules.

KIR2DL1 expression correlated positively with NK-cell identity and functional activity, and negatively with S100A8 and the neutrophil signature, indicating divergent regulation of NK versus neutrophil programs in LC.

Hierarchical clustering identified two compartmentalized immune modules in LC: an NK-associated module (NK-cell score, NK function, KIR2DL1) and a neutrophil/inflammatory module (S100A8, neutrophil signature), with weak or negative cross-module correlations.
Eight DEGs exceeded |FC| > 1.5, spanning platelet activation (ITGA2B, THBS1), innate immunity (S100A8, LY96, ANXA1, CD163), NK-cell regulation (KIR2DL1), and protein translation (RPS6).
Serum metabolomic profiles at the post-infection timepoint significantly separated LC cases from controls in multivariate analysis, with within-group dispersions found to be similar.

Limma analysis identified 22 metabolites discriminating LC cases from controls (FDR<0.05), 14 of which had |FC|>1.5, including 1,2-dilinoleoylglycerol, indole-3-acetate, oxoadipate, lauroylcarnitine, N-acetylglucosamine, glutamine, tryptophan, hypoxanthine, and others, all with Cohen's d >1.
Oxoglutarate, a TCA cycle intermediate, significantly increased from pre- to post-infection in LC cases while decreasing in controls, reflecting a robust time-by-LC group interaction.
Oxoadipate and threonine showed nominally significant time-by-group interactions in longitudinal metabolomic analysis, but neither survived FDR correction.

Paired t-tests showed nominal pre- to post-infection increases in deoxyuridine, oxoglutarate, and oxoadipate in LC cases, and decreases in oxoglutarate and threonine with an increase in 2,3-dihydroxybenzoate in controls; none survived FDR correction.
Integrated protein-protein interaction network of DEGs and mapped metabolites identified APP, RELA, ATF2, and HLA-B as the highest-degree hub nodes.
KEGG pathway over-representation analysis identified necroptosis and serotonergic synapse pathways as significantly enriched in both the transcriptomic and metabolomic datasets.

In external Transcriptomic Cohort A (GSE224615, PBMC RNA-seq), all 63 discovery DEGs were represented and 54.0% showed concordant direction of change, but fold-change correlation with the discovery cohort was not significant.

In external Transcriptomic Cohort B (GSE275334, NanoString Immune Exhaustion panel), 24 discovery DEGs overlapped and 45.8% showed concordant directionality, without significant fold-change correlation.

In an external metabolomics cohort, 7 of the 24 significant discovery metabolites were represented and 85.7% showed concordant direction of change, though the fold-change correlation was not statistically significant.

Despite limited statistical replication, several immune-related genes (CD4, IL6R, CD163, LAMP1, NFATC1, HLA-E) showed consistent directionality across the discovery and external cohorts, as did metabolic-inflammatory features contributing to necroptosis and serotonergic synapse pathways.

LC cases exhibited altered (elevated in this serum cohort) tryptophan levels, consistent with dysregulated tryptophan-kynurenine pathway activity, contrasting with a prior meta-analysis reporting decreased circulating tryptophan in LC, possibly due to serum versus plasma differences.
Asparagine levels were elevated in LC cases, consistent with reports that asparagine and aspartate increase during SARS-CoV-2 infection through activation of the integrated stress response.
Deoxyuridine and ureidopropionate, markers of pyrimidine metabolism, were elevated in LC cases, potentially indicating impaired nucleotide turnover or altered pyrimidine salvage pathway activity.

ARG1, a gene expressed in neutrophils and myeloid regulatory populations linked to post-viral immune dysregulation, was also dysregulated in LC cases, further supporting persistent neutrophil-driven inflammation.
HLA-B, a hub gene involved in antigen presentation and NK-cell regulation, was downregulated in the integrated network, potentially indicating impaired immune recognition in LC.

APP, a central network hub, has been linked to neuroinflammation and cognitive symptoms such as brain fog, consistent with reports that SARS-CoV-2 infection upregulates APP expression and perturbs amyloid processing.
ITGA2B, a marker of platelet activation, was among the eight genes with fold change >1.5 distinguishing long COVID cases from controls.
THBS1, another platelet activation marker, was among genes with fold change >1.5 distinguishing LC cases from controls.
ANXA1, an innate immunity gene, was among genes with fold change >1.5 distinguishing LC cases from controls.

CD163, an innate immunity/monocyte marker, was among genes with fold change >1.5 distinguishing LC cases from controls, and showed consistent directionality across independent cross-cohort validation datasets.
RPS6, a protein-translation-related gene, was among genes with fold change >1.5 distinguishing LC cases from controls.
LY96, encoding the TLR4 co-receptor MD-2, was dysregulated in LC and, together with S100A8, HMGB1, and RELA, is proposed to converge on a neutrophil-driven TLR4/NF-κB inflammatory axis.

HMGB1, a damage-associated molecular pattern linked to neutrophil activation and tissue injury, was proposed as a potential trigger sustaining TLR4-mediated inflammatory signaling in LC, and showed concordant directionality across cross-cohort validation.
RELA, encoding the NF-κB p65 subunit, was a central hub (degree 11) in the integrated protein-protein interaction network combining LC transcriptomic and metabolomic data.

APP was the highest-degree hub (degree 16) in the integrated network and its dysregulation was linked to neuroinflammation and brain fog, with SARS-CoV-2 infection previously shown to upregulate APP expression and perturb amyloid processing.
HLA-B, a component of antigen presentation and NK-cell regulation, was downregulated and identified as a central network hub (degree 10), potentially indicating impaired immune recognition in LC.

ARG1, expressed in neutrophils and myeloid regulatory populations and linked to post-viral immune dysregulation, was also dysregulated in LC cases, supporting persistent neutrophil-driven inflammation.
Threonine levels showed a nominal decrease from pre- to post-infection in controls, and a nominally significant time-by-group interaction, though this did not survive FDR correction.
2,3-dihydroxybenzoate increased nominally from pre- to post-infection in controls, but this did not remain significant after FDR correction.
Among the 17 long COVID cases identified in the CORSIP cohort, the most common symptoms were fatigue (67%) and brain fog (58%).
Women comprised 67% of LC cases compared to 40% of controls, consistent with previously reported female predominance in long COVID among healthcare workers and non-hospitalized populations.

In a preclinical post-acute SARS-CoV-2 model cited by the authors, neutrophils showed sustained pro-inflammatory/pro-fibrotic transcriptional programs marked by persistent S100A8/S100A9 upregulation across tissues, and pharmacologic inhibition of S100A8/A9 reduced long COVID incidence.

Elevated asparagine levels were observed in LC cases, consistent with reports that asparagine and aspartate increase during SARS-CoV-2 infection via activation of the integrated stress response, potentially reflecting persistent metabolic stress.
Patients with severe long COVID symptoms had significantly higher D-dimer levels than those without severe symptoms.
Patients with severe long COVID symptoms had significantly higher fibrinogen levels than those without severe symptoms.
Platelet count did not differ significantly between patients with and without severe long COVID symptoms.
Prothrombin time did not differ significantly between patients with and without severe long COVID symptoms.
Activated partial thromboplastin time did not differ significantly between patients with and without severe long COVID symptoms.
Patients with raised D-dimer had approximately threefold higher risk of severe long COVID symptoms.
Patients with elevated fibrinogen had a 2.34-fold higher risk of severe long COVID symptoms.
Elevated D-dimer was the most common baseline coagulation abnormality, found in about a quarter of long COVID patients.
Elevated fibrinogen was found in about a fifth of long COVID patients at baseline.
Elevated CRP was found in 17.26% of long COVID patients at baseline.
Prolonged aPTT was noted in 11.68% of patients at baseline.
Prolonged PT/INR was noted in 10.66% of patients at baseline.
Thrombocytopenia was noted in 5.08% of long COVID patients at baseline.
More than half of the long COVID cohort failed the Six-Minute Walk Test at baseline, indicating impaired functional/exercise capacity.
38.07% of patients reported severe long COVID symptoms that interfered with routine daily activities at baseline.
The proportion of patients reporting severe symptoms decreased from 38.07% at baseline to 19.5% at three-month follow-up.
The proportion of patients failing the 6MWT decreased from 55.84% at baseline to 25.7% at three-month follow-up.
Among patients with baseline abnormalities, D-dimer elevation persisted in about half at three-month follow-up, suggesting delayed normalization of fibrinolytic activity.
Among patients with baseline abnormalities, fibrinogen elevation persisted in nearly half at three-month follow-up.
CRP elevation was uncommon at three-month follow-up among patients with abnormal baseline markers, suggesting resolution of systemic inflammation while coagulation markers remained elevated.
The predominant persistent long COVID symptom was decreased effort tolerance/easy fatigability, present in 76.65% of patients.
Myalgia/body pain was present in 36.55% of long COVID patients.
Breathlessness was present in 34.01% of long COVID patients.
Persistent cough was present in 24.37% of long COVID patients.

Patients with elevated D-dimer or fibrinogen were further evaluated for venous thromboembolism and received anticoagulation when clinically indicated, though treatment efficacy was not a study endpoint.

Patients described the highly specialized US healthcare system as organized into rigid specialty 'silos' that were incompatible with the multisystem nature of Long COVID, leading specialists to decline addressing symptoms outside their subspecialty.
Lack of communication among multiple treating physicians led to oversight of needed tests and required patients to relay their own medical information between providers.

Patients reported that once referred to specialists, no single provider took ownership of overall care or followed up on outcomes, leaving responsibility diffusely distributed and patients feeling abandoned.

Participants reported long wait times to access Long COVID and specialist care, ranging from 3-8 months in general, with an 18-month waitlist reported for a POTS clinic and a two-year wait for psychiatry.
Obtaining a formal Long COVID diagnosis facilitated care coordination, making providers more willing to treat patients and address concerns outside their specialty.
Some patients had to actively fight to have a Long COVID diagnosis documented in their medical records, with providers minimizing symptom severity or omitting the diagnosis entirely.

Women with Long COVID reported a pervasive pattern of their physical symptoms being dismissed or misattributed to anxiety or depression, despite thorough self-advocacy, whereas men more often faced diagnostic uncertainty rather than outright psychological dismissal.
The logistical burden of scheduling multiple appointments was cognitively and physically exhausting for patients experiencing brain fog and fatigue, sometimes described as a 'full-time job.'
Frustration with unresponsive and fragmented care led some patients to discontinue seeking formal medical treatment and instead manage symptoms independently or pursue alternative therapies.

Fatigue and post-exertional malaise compounded the logistical burden of navigating fragmented referrals, consistent with the concept of 'recursive debility' from ME/CFS in which PEM recursively worsens patient debility and limits self-advocacy.

A cited case-control study found that, compared to a control group without Long COVID, patients diagnosed with Long COVID showed a sharper decline in emergency department and hospital visits and a greater increase in outpatient/specialist visits one year after diagnosis.

A cited qualitative study of Veterans Affairs health records for 200 Long COVID patients similarly found care to be siloed and fragmented, with COVID-19 team care often disconnected from primary care.

The study sample's demographic composition (68% women, >70% aged 45+, 30% Black) mirrored broader documented sex and racial patterns in the US Long COVID population, though men and younger adults were underrepresented relative to national estimates.
Patients attending the long-COVID clinic were referred into the service an average of 5.75 months after their initial COVID-19 infection, indicating a substantial delay to specialist care.

The majority (82%) of long-COVID clinic patients required onward referral to other healthcare providers, most commonly pulmonary rehabilitation, chronic fatigue specialists, and a specialist COVID-19 rehabilitation general practitioner embedded within the service.
Long-COVID patients reported rehabilitation needs, moderate depression and anxiety, and difficulty performing usual activities of daily living.

Using the Theoretical Domains Framework, beliefs about capabilities, environmental context and resources, knowledge, and reinforcement were identified as the domains most relevant to successful implementation of the reactive long-COVID care pathway, with leadership, multidisciplinary teamwork, and knowledge exchange as facilitators and funding constraints and rapid emergency-context evolution as barriers.
Long COVID participants scored significantly higher than normative healthy data on the NIH Toolbox crystallized cognition composite, indicating preserved acquired intelligence.
Fluid cognition composite scores in the long COVID sample did not significantly differ from normative healthy data after correction for multiple comparisons.
The discrepancy between crystallized and fluid cognition scores was significantly greater in long COVID patients than in normative data, indicating a within-person pattern of cognitive decline.
Using a definition requiring two or more fluid subtests falling 1.0–1.5 SD below crystallized composite, half of the long COVID sample met criteria for clinically significant cognitive impairment.

Four weeks of 40 Hz vibratory and auditory treatment (VAT) significantly improved performance on the flanker attention/executive function subtest relative to controls, with 80% of treated participants improving versus 20% of controls.
Plasma BDNF increased significantly more in the VAT treatment group than in controls after 4 weeks, with 60% of treated participants showing an increase versus 10% of controls.
The magnitude of increase in plasma BDNF after VAT was strongly correlated with the magnitude of improvement on the flanker attention test.
Baseline resting heart rate in the long COVID sample was significantly higher than normative healthy adult heart rate values.
Heart rate significantly changed acutely immediately before versus after a single 30-minute VAT session, averaged across the 4-week period.
Over 4 weeks, pre-session resting heart rate decreased significantly more in the VAT treatment group compared to controls.

The authors propose that VAT stimulates endothelial release of nitric oxide, which in turn upregulates BDNF and GDNF, providing a plausible neuroprotective/neurotherapeutic mechanism for cognitive improvement.
In the earliest-intervention experimental group (recovered within 3 months), 6 weeks of incentive spirometer training reduced PCFS scores from 1.6 to 0.58.
The waitlist control group, which received no incentive spirometer training, showed no significant change in PCFS scores over the study period.
Incentive spirometer training in participants recovered within 3 months (EG1) markedly reduced D-12 dyspnea scores from 8.3 to 1.84.
The control group did not show a statistically significant reduction in dyspnea scores over the study period.
The control group showed a non-significant decline in 6-minute walk distance without intervention.
In EG1, incentive spirometer training significantly increased 6-minute walk distance alongside a significant decrease in resting heart rate and improved inspiratory ball counts.
EG2 (recovered 3-6 months) showed significant improvements in heart rate and 6MWD but concurrently experienced slight reductions in hemoglobin, hematocrit, and arterial oxygen content.
In later-recovery groups EG3 and EG4, incentive spirometer training significantly improved inspiratory volume, with no other significant physiological or functional changes.

Generalized estimating equation analysis showed that compared with waitlist controls, all four experimental groups had significantly greater reductions in PCFS scores after incentive spirometer training, with the largest effect in the earliest-treated group.
GEE analysis showed significant reductions in dyspnea scores versus control in EG1 and EG4, but not in EG2 or EG3, relative to the control group.
GEE analysis found that only EG2 (recovered 3-6 months) showed a significant relative decline in oxygenation parameters compared with control, despite improved functional status.
GEE analysis showed EG1, EG2, and EG3 had significantly greater improvements in 6-minute walk distance compared with control, while EG4 did not differ significantly from control.

Item-level analysis of the D-12 showed that in EG1 all items improved significantly except item 6 ('My breathing is uncomfortable'), whereas this item did significantly improve in the other, later-treated experimental groups.

Across all groups, physiological dyspnea items (D-12 items 1-6) scored consistently higher than psychological items (items 7-12), both before and after intervention, indicating that Long COVID patients experience greater distress from physiological aspects of dyspnea than psychological aspects.

A bimodal response pattern in dyspnea improvement was observed across recovery-duration subgroups, with the greatest effect in the earliest-treated group (EG1), reduced effect in EG2/EG3, and a resurgence of significant improvement in EG4 (9-12 months post-recovery).

In EG3 (recovered 6-9 months), 58% of participants had taken the traditional Chinese medicine formula NRICM101 during acute COVID-19 infection, which the authors suggest may explain the relatively modest post-intervention gains in this subgroup.
At post-test, the control group exhibited significantly lower pre-activity SpO2 compared with all experimental groups.
6.6%-10.4% of individuals infected with SARS-CoV-2 continue to experience symptoms such as fatigue, palpitations, and cognitive dysfunction that can persist for years.

The elevated risk of multiorgan manifestations in infected people compared to non-infected controls gradually declined over the three years following infection, though contribution to disability-adjusted life years persisted.
Electronic health record-based clustering identified four long COVID sub-phenotypes: cardiac/renal, respiratory/sleep/anxiety, musculoskeletal/neurologic, and digestive/respiratory.

A PASC symptom assessment based on participant-reported symptoms identified four clusters: smell/taste loss; PEM and fatigue; brain fog with PEM and fatigue; and fatigue with PEM, dizziness, brain fog, GI symptoms, and palpitations.
IL-1R2, MATN2, and COLEC12 were associated with cardiopulmonary symptoms, fatigue, and anxiety/depression symptom clusters in long COVID.
MATN2, CSF3, and C1QA were elevated in long COVID patients with gastrointestinal symptoms, and C1QA was also elevated in those with cognitive impairment.
Markers of altered neural tissue repair, SPON-1 and NFASC, were elevated in long COVID patients with cognitive impairment.
Elevated SCG3 indicates a brain-gut axis disorder and is also elevated in patients with GI symptoms.

In the inflammatory cluster of long COVID, IL-6, IL-8, IL-1β, and C-reactive protein were significantly increased compared with the non-inflammatory cluster, alongside high neutrophil activity and active B cell profile.

SARS-CoV-2 viral RNA was detected in 10 solid tissues, plasma, and blood cells in patients recovering from mild COVID-19 (median follow-up 4 months); recovered patients with detectable viral RNA and higher viral copy number had greater risk of developing long COVID.

SARS-CoV-2 spike protein was detectable in plasma in 60% of long COVID patients even one year after infection but not in controls, with more organ systems involved correlating with higher spike protein amounts; detection was inconsistent across two to twelve months post-infection.

Epstein-Barr virus reactivation is more common in patients with long COVID than in those without it, and human herpesviruses are associated with symptoms such as headache, myalgia, neurological disorders, and pulmonary disorders.
Compared to uninfected individuals and those who fully recovered, long COVID patients showed excessive inflammation with persistently elevated IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β.

Severe COVID-19 reprograms hematopoiesis and establishes an epigenetic memory in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells and daughter myeloid cells that persists for up to one year, altering transcription factor activity and increasing myeloid cell numbers.
Elevated D-dimer has been observed in long COVID patients, increasing the risk of thromboembolic disease.
Amyloid deposits were found in plasma samples from long COVID patients, suggesting a role for micro-thrombosis.
Angiogenic markers such as angiopoietin-1 and P-selectin showed high accuracy in identifying individuals with long COVID.
C5bC6 complement levels were elevated during the acute phase and at six-month follow-up in long COVID patients, while C7 complex levels were reduced.
Markers of tissue damage including von Willebrand factor and its regulatory component ADAMTS13 were detected in long COVID patients, indicating extensive vascular injury.
The gut microbiome of long COVID patients was characterized by higher levels of Ruminococcus gnavus and Bacteroides vulgatus and lower levels of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii.

Alpha and beta diversity of the gut microbiota were significantly different in recovered COVID-19 patients compared to uninfected controls at three months after discharge, with gradual restoration among those who did not develop long COVID.

Neuropsychiatric symptoms and fatigue in long COVID were correlated with nosocomial gut pathogens including Clostridium innocuum and Actinomyces naeslundii six months after infection, while persistent respiratory symptoms correlated with opportunistic gut pathogens.
The oral microbiome is also altered in long COVID patients, with higher abundance of Prevotella and Veillonella genera.
Dysbiosis of the gut microbiome in long COVID can also be associated with the toxic metabolite 5-sulfoxymethylfurfural.
The STOP-PASC randomized clinical trial, the first to test Paxlovid for treating long COVID, did not show positive results.
AER002 (P2G3), a long-acting fully human IgG1 monoclonal antibody, can neutralize multiple SARS-CoV-2 variants and the non-replicating spike protein, suggesting potential use in treating long COVID.

Mesenchymal stem cells, which possess immunomodulatory and anti-inflammatory properties and have shown safety and efficacy in treating COVID-19, are proposed as a reasonable anti-inflammatory therapy for long COVID given evidence of persistent inflammation.

Baricitinib, a JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor and the first immunomodulator found to reduce mortality in COVID-19, may merit consideration for treating long COVID although its effectiveness for this condition remains unclear.

BC007 targets harmful functional autoantibodies implicated in autoimmune conditions as a potential treatment for long COVID, following observations that transferring long COVID patient antibodies into mice caused pain sensitivity and dizziness-like symptoms.
In an RCT, vitamin D administered to long COVID patients with fatigue or neuropsychiatric symptoms reduced fatigue, alleviated anxiety, and improved cognitive symptoms.
A systematic review of vitamin treatments for long COVID indicates that the effects of vitamins on treating long COVID require further clarification.
A meta-analysis of 620,221 participants estimated that two doses of vaccine reduce the risk of long COVID by 36.9% and three doses reduce the risk by 68.7%.
Female sex, older age, more severe acute infection, obesity, and being unvaccinated are associated with higher risk of developing long COVID.
In male patients with long COVID, TGFβ1 levels are elevated during the acute infection phase, whereas this is not observed in females, reflecting sex differences in immunity.
The Omicron variant of SARS-CoV-2 is associated with less risk of long COVID than the Delta and pre-Delta variants, attributable to pandemic-era effects and vaccination.
A national survey in Scotland reported long COVID prevalence rates of 6.6%, 6.5%, and 10.4% at 6, 12, and 18 months after infection respectively.

According to CDC data, an estimated 6.9% of noninstitutionalized US adults who previously contracted SARS-CoV-2 experience long COVID; global cumulative incidence was estimated at approximately 400 million people by the end of 2023.

The golden hamster model provides insight into sustained lung, kidney, and olfactory damage, while the K18-hACE2 mouse model is used to study lung fibrosis and neurological damage associated with SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Bioinformatics analysis identified 102 upregulated and 46 downregulated differentially expressed genes in fibromyalgia blood samples compared with normal blood samples.
Differentially expressed microRNAs in fibromyalgia included 206 downregulated and 15 upregulated miRNAs compared with normal blood samples.
CD38 was identified as a candidate hub gene in fibromyalgia through protein-protein interaction network analysis.
GATM was identified as a candidate hub gene in fibromyalgia through protein-protein interaction network analysis.
HDC (histidine decarboxylase) was identified as a candidate hub gene in fibromyalgia through protein-protein interaction network analysis.
FOS was identified as a candidate hub gene in fibromyalgia through protein-protein interaction network analysis.
Candidate hub genes for fibromyalgia were significantly associated with musculoskeletal disease, mental disorder, and immune system disease categories in the Comparative Toxicogenomics Database.
Genes related to metformin therapy showed partial overlap with fibromyalgia-related genes, suggesting metformin as a potential candidate for drug repurposing.
In a randomly selected German general population sample, 3.4% met the modified 2016 ACR fibromyalgia (FM 2016) criteria.
Using the AAPT pain taxonomy criteria, 5.7% of the general population sample met criteria for fibromyalgia.
Agreement between FM 2016 and AAPT criteria classification was moderate-to-substantial (kappa = 0.65).

Compared with AAPT-positive subjects, subjects meeting the FM 2016 criteria had higher multisite pain, Widespread Pain Index scores, Polysymptomatic Distress Scale scores, Symptom Severity Scores, and psychological symptom burden.
Physician-diagnosed FM was reported by 1.1% of subjects, of whom 44.0% met the FM 2016 criteria and 47.5% met the AAPT criteria.
Subjects meeting the FM 2016 criteria had significantly higher multisite pain (MSP) scores than subjects meeting the AAPT criteria.
FM 2016-positive subjects scored higher on the Widespread Pain Index than AAPT-positive subjects.
FM 2016-positive subjects had higher Polysymptomatic Distress Scale scores than AAPT-positive subjects.
FM 2016-positive subjects had higher Symptom Severity Scores than AAPT-positive subjects.
Fibromyalgia prevalence estimated by the AAPT criteria was 73% greater than that estimated by the FM 2016 criteria in the same population.
Among subjects reporting a physician diagnosis of fibromyalgia (1.1% of the sample), 44.0% met the FM 2016 criteria.
Among subjects reporting a physician diagnosis of fibromyalgia, 47.5% met the AAPT criteria.
The FM 2016 criteria, unlike the AAPT criteria, provide a general severity measure for fibromyalgia, while the AAPT criteria select individuals with less symptom severity and fewer pain sites.
Resting heart rate was significantly higher in children with ASD compared with age- and sex-matched healthy controls.
The frontal QRS-T angle, a marker of ventricular repolarization heterogeneity, was significantly wider in children with ASD compared with healthy controls.
QT interval tended to be shorter in the ASD group but did not reach statistical significance compared with healthy controls.
QTc interval and QRS duration were comparable between ASD and healthy control groups.
The systemic immune-inflammation index (SII), a composite hematological inflammatory marker, was significantly higher in children with ASD compared with healthy controls.
The systemic inflammatory response index (SIRI) did not differ significantly between ASD and healthy control groups.
The pan-immune-inflammation value (PIV) did not differ significantly between ASD and healthy control groups.
Lymphocyte counts trended lower in children with ASD compared with healthy controls, without reaching statistical significance.

Hemoglobin, platelet count, leukocyte subsets, metabolic markers, liver enzymes, thyroid function tests, albumin, vitamin B12/folate/D levels, CRP, and ESR did not differ significantly between ASD and healthy control groups.
Behavioral severity, as measured by the Autism Behavior Checklist (ABC), was positively correlated with the systemic immune-inflammation index in the ASD group.
Behavioral severity (ABC score) was more strongly positively correlated with the frontal QRS-T angle than with SII in the ASD group.
Behavioral severity (ABC score) was not significantly correlated with heart rate in the ASD group.
SII showed a significant positive correlation with the frontal QRS-T angle in the ASD group.
SII was not significantly correlated with heart rate.

A fully flexible triboelectric sensor using a liquid-metal electrode network, fabricated via current direct writing technology, maintained stable electrical conductivity under mechanical deformation and temperature variation while detecting subtle touch pressure changes.

A machine-learning-integrated color preference recognition system using the liquid-metal flexible sensors achieved a color selection recognition rate of 98.125% for assessing individualized color preferences in children with autism.
The paper states that appropriate color intervention can regulate autonomic arousal level, improve attention, and mitigate anxiety in children with autism.
Mental health/behavioral disorders were the most common comorbidity category among children diagnosed with orthostatic dysregulation, occurring in 23.6% of patients.
Sleep disorders were the most prevalent specific comorbid condition, present in 10.2% of OD patients.
School non-attendance was recorded as a comorbid condition in 9.3% of OD patients, consistent with the known link between OD and school absenteeism in Japan.
Autism spectrum disorder/attention-deficit hyperactivity was found as a comorbidity in 7.1% of patients diagnosed with orthostatic dysregulation.
Pharmacotherapy was provided to 44.0% of OD patients, with a mean of 1.3 medications prescribed per treated patient.
Midodrine was the most frequently prescribed medication among treated OD patients, used in 78.3% of pharmacotherapy cases.
Midodrine was the most commonly prescribed medication for orthostatic dysregulation, used in 78.3% of treated patients.
Amezinium metilsulfate was the second most prescribed medication for orthostatic dysregulation, used in 6.7% of treated patients.
Propranolol was prescribed in 2.8% of treated patients with orthostatic dysregulation.
Sleep medications were prescribed to 9.4% of treated patients with orthostatic dysregulation.
Blood tests were the most frequent diagnostic medical practice, performed in 48.6% of patients with orthostatic dysregulation.
Diagnostic imaging was performed in 35.9% of patients with orthostatic dysregulation.
Electrocardiograms were performed in 24.2% of patients with orthostatic dysregulation.

Patients with orthostatic dysregulation who were prescribed sleep medications had a higher prevalence of neurodevelopmental disorders, school non-attendance, and depression compared to other treated patients.

In typically developing individuals, autonomic regulation during head-up tilt was best explained by a coupled reciprocal control mode with high sympathetic and low parasympathetic activity, whereas ASD individuals showed convergence of sympathetic and parasympathetic weighting rather than this differentiated pattern.

In ASD individuals, empirical heart rate and blood pressure data during postural challenge extended toward regions of relatively higher parasympathetic weighting, suggesting persistent parasympathetic engagement instead of the expected withdrawal seen in typical development.
Simulated deep respiration enhanced reduction of mean arterial pressure during blood pressure recovery, particularly when sympathetic activity was over-elevated.
PTEN hamartoma tumour syndrome confers high hereditary risk of breast, thyroid, and endometrial cancer, and moderate risk of renal and colorectal cancer and skin melanoma.
Beyond cancer risk, PHTS is associated with benign skin and connective tissue tumours, vascular malformations, and neurodevelopmental disorders including autism spectrum disorders.
The ERN GENTURIS guideline revised cancer surveillance recommendations for breast, thyroid, endometrial, renal, and colorectal cancer and skin melanoma in PHTS based on new evidence since 2020.
VPA-exposed rats showed sustained hyperdefecation during handling compared to saline control rats.
VPA rats had a higher prevalence of defecation during electro-tactile (nociceptive) stimulation than controls, independent of changes in freezing behavior.
During classical fear conditioning, VPA rats showed a delayed onset of freezing but a subsequent enhancement of the freezing response compared to controls.
VPA rats exhibited disrupted temporal coordination between freezing and defecation behaviors during fear conditioning, unlike controls.
22-kHz ultrasonic vocalizations positively correlated with freezing behavior in both VPA and control rats.
In an emotional contagion task, observing a distressed conspecific increased freezing prevalence and suppressed vocalization rates in both VPA and control rats.
In the emotional contagion task, VPA rats exhibited persistent freezing that lasted longer than in control rats after observing a distressed conspecific.
VPA rats showed an earlier reduction in vocalization rate compared to controls during the emotional contagion task after exposure to a distressed conspecific.
Overall, VPA-exposed rats displayed heightened stress reactivity and a habituation deficit, with disrupted coordination of autonomic and behavioral fear responses relative to controls.
Fibromyalgia is described as extremely frequent as a comorbidity in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome in daily clinical practice.
Infections, particularly oral candidal infections, are extremely frequent comorbidities in pSS patients in daily clinical practice.
Preclinical vascular disease studies using various techniques have demonstrated the presence of early atherosclerosis in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome.
Coronary events may be slightly more frequent in pSS patients compared with the general population.
The overall risk of malignancy in pSS patients appears slightly increased, likely largely due to excess lymphoma occurrence.
An association between primary Sjögren's syndrome and thyroid cancer might exist, though it requires confirmation by further studies.
The review describes that chronic fatigue, pain, and depression are common, mutually interacting symptoms in primary Sjögren's syndrome that substantially impact quality of life.

The authors propose that fatigue and pain in Sjögren's syndrome have a genetic foundation and are regulated by deeply conserved neuronal pathways also implicated in other systemic autoimmune diseases, cancer, and neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's disease.
Fibromyalgia patients had a higher rate of comorbid anxiety and depressive disorders than patients with rheumatoid arthritis, spondyloarthritis, or Sjögren's syndrome.
Fibromyalgia patients scored higher on disease impact, physical symptoms, pain, and fatigue than rheumatoid arthritis patients.
Fibromyalgia patients reported more fatigue than patients with spondyloarthritis.
Fibromyalgia patients used the distancing-from-pain coping strategy less than patients with rheumatoid arthritis and spondyloarthritis.
Fibromyalgia patients used the strategy of ignoring pain sensations less than the other rheumatic disease groups.
Fibromyalgia patients used the catastrophizing coping strategy more than rheumatoid arthritis patients.
No significant differences were found between fibromyalgia and Sjögren's syndrome patients on disease impact and psychological adjustment measures.
Children with generalized joint hypermobility had significantly higher visible plaque index scores than healthy controls.
Children with generalized joint hypermobility had significantly higher gingival bleeding index scores than healthy controls.
No significant differences in DMFT/dmft scores were found between children with generalized joint hypermobility and healthy controls.

Temporomandibular disorder-related symptom frequencies were significantly higher in children with generalized joint hypermobility than in healthy controls, with clicking during maximum active mouth-opening being the most common clinical sign.
Combined TMJ symptoms and TMD were observed in approximately one third of children with generalized joint hypermobility.
Individuals with periodontal disease exhibited widespread repression of salivary microRNAs, consistent with persistent immune dysregulation.

Relative to COVID-19-negative/periodontal-disease-negative controls, 32 salivary miRNAs were differentially expressed in COVID-19-positive/periodontal-disease-positive individuals, and all were downregulated.

Pathway analysis showed that the differentially expressed salivary miRNAs regulate Ras, MAPK, and NF-κB signaling, converging on IL-1β- and TNF-centered inflammatory networks relevant to both periodontal disease and COVID-19.
Restoration of miR-30e-3p attenuated NF-κB activation and cytokine release in TLR-stimulated human oral keratinocytes, whereas inhibiting its function potentiated inflammation.
Restoration of miR-106a-3p attenuated NF-κB activation and cytokine release in TLR-stimulated human oral keratinocytes, whereas inhibiting its function potentiated inflammation.
Restoration of miR-652-3p attenuated NF-κB activation and cytokine release in TLR-stimulated human oral keratinocytes, whereas inhibiting its function potentiated inflammation.
miR-30e-3p was predicted and validated by dual-luciferase reporter assay to target SARS-CoV-2 spike and nucleocapsid transcripts.
miR-106-3p was predicted and validated by dual-luciferase reporter assay to target SARS-CoV-2 spike and nucleocapsid transcripts.
miR-652-3p was predicted and validated by dual-luciferase reporter assay to target SARS-CoV-2 spike and nucleocapsid transcripts.
Overexpression of miR-30e-3p, miR-106-3p, and miR-652-3p reduced spike and nucleocapsid protein/RNA expression in Beta- and Omicron-variant-infected epithelial cells.

Functional suppression of miR-30e-3p, miR-106-3p, and miR-652-3p using inhibitors potentiated inflammatory cytokine release in TLR-stimulated oral keratinocytes, opposite to the effect of miRNA restoration.
Capsaicin C2 cough threshold did not differ significantly between children with high versus low anti-Spike IgG titers.
Capsaicin C5 cough threshold (motor response to intense stimulation) was comparable between high and low anti-Spike IgG groups.
Mucosal anti-Spike IgA stratification showed no significant difference in C2 capsaicin threshold between high and low IgA groups.
Mucosal anti-Spike IgA stratification showed no significant difference in C5 capsaicin threshold between high and low IgA groups.
Acute COVID-19 severity (mild/asymptomatic vs moderate/severe) was not associated with differences in capsaicin C2 or C5 thresholds.
Parent-reported nocturnal cough, sleep disruption, and bothersomeness (PCQ) did not differ significantly between high and low IgG groups.
Subjective cough intensity (VAS) did not differ significantly between high and low IgG groups.
Asthma-specific quality of life was preserved and did not differ between high and low IgG groups.
Anti-Spike IgG titer showed no significant Spearman correlation with capsaicin C2 threshold.
Anti-Spike IgG titer showed no significant Spearman correlation with capsaicin C5 threshold.
Parent-reported symptom severity (PCQ, VAS) and quality of life (PedsQL) showed a complete lack of correlation with objective capsaicin-measured airway nerve sensitivity across the whole cohort.
Allergic rhinitis was highly prevalent in the cohort and is proposed as a more likely driver of reported post-COVID cough than a novel viral neuropathy.
Gastroesophageal reflux disease, a known non-asthmatic trigger of neurogenic cough, was present in two-thirds of the cohort.
Parent-reported persistent Long COVID symptoms lasting more than 4 weeks were noted in a minority of the cohort.

The authors hypothesize that near-universal maintenance inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) therapy in the cohort suppressed cytokine-driven TRPV1 upregulation, acting as a 'pharmacological shield' that preserved normal cough reflex excitability despite SARS-CoV-2 infection.

The authors propose that pediatric airway epithelium mounts a rapid, vigorous mucosal interferon response that restricts SARS-CoV-2 replication to superficial layers, limiting cytopathic invasion of subepithelial vagal nerve endings compared to adults.
Nearly half of surveyed university students reported new symptoms lasting three or more months after COVID-19, consistent with Long COVID.
The most commonly reported persistent symptoms among the survey respondents were fatigue, shortness of breath, loss of taste/smell, and headache.
Survey data indicated a higher proportion of female than male respondents reporting musculoskeletal and other Long COVID symptoms.
EBV-transformed lymphoblastoid cell lines were generated with 100% success from LC-19 patient blood samples versus only 72% success from post-C-19 recovered controls.

Post-C-19 recovered controls showed markedly increased NADH production (2-3 fold) across most carbon energy sources compared to pre-pandemic controls, indicating a general metabolic shift from prior SARS-CoV-2 exposure.

Compared with pre-pandemic controls, over half of tested carbon compounds produced higher NADH levels in Long COVID cells, indicating a stimulatory effect of SARS-CoV-2 on major energy-producing pathways.

Glucose, dextrin, glycogen, and mannose showed reduced NADH generation in Long COVID cells relative to pre-pandemic controls, suggesting saturation or exhaustion of high-efficiency glycolytic pathways.

In the >4-symptom LC-19 subgroup, over a third of tested compounds (including galactose, fucose, sorbose, xylitol, α-ketoglutaric acid, acetic acid, and butyric acid) showed reduced energy production compared to pre-pandemic controls, indicating broader exhaustion of energetic pathways with greater symptom burden.

In the officially diagnosed LC-19 subgroup, only 4 compounds (glucose, mannose, fucose, α-ketoglutaric acid) showed decreased energy production versus pre-pandemic controls, fewer than seen in the broader symptomatic subgroup.
Compared to recovered post-C-19 controls, the >4-symptom LC-19 subgroup showed reduced utilization of the large majority of carbon energy sources.
Officially diagnosed LC-19 patients showed reduced energy substrate utilization compared to recovered post-C-19 controls across nearly two-thirds of tested compounds.
