Pathway enrichment analysis of the PM-M1 carbon-source metabolic profile identified four significantly altered pathways in Long COVID: galactose metabolism, pyruvate metabolism, fructose and mannose metabolism, and the citric acid cycle.

Post-C-19 recovered controls showed a diminished NADH response to hormones and metabolic effectors compared to pre-pandemic controls, suggesting reduced cellular signaling sensitivity following COVID-19 exposure.

Long COVID cells across all symptom-based subgroups showed progressively reduced NADH responses to hormones and metabolic effectors compared to pre-pandemic controls, with greatest reduction in officially diagnosed patients.
Compared with recovered post-C-19 controls, Long COVID subgroups with >4 symptoms and official diagnosis showed markedly reduced NADH responses to nearly all hormones/effectors tested.

Post-C-19 recovered controls exhibited lower NADH production in response to cytokines/growth factors (PM-M7 plate) compared to pre-pandemic controls, indicating persistently reduced metabolic reactivity after COVID-19.

Lymphoblastoid cells from LC-19 patients with more than 4 symptoms showed significantly reduced NADH responses at any tested concentration of the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-1β, indicating impaired cytokine responsiveness.
Lymphoblastoid cells from LC-19 patients with more than 4 symptoms showed significantly reduced NADH responses to IL-6 at any tested concentration, suggesting impaired cytokine signaling capacity.

Saliva screening showed sporadic EBV positivity without a consistent pattern across groups and no HHV-6 positivity in any sample, indicating that active latent viral reactivation did not clearly drive the observed metabolic differences in this cohort.

The authors interpret reduced NADH generation and impaired effector responses in LC-19 cells as evidence of mitochondrial dysfunction, consistent with an independent 2025 study linking PBMC mitochondrial dysfunction severity to Long COVID severity.

Authors hypothesize that reduced cellular responsiveness to IL-6 and TNF-α in LC-19 cells may trigger a compensatory increase in cytokine production, potentially explaining elevated circulating IL-6 reported in other Long COVID studies.

Across metabolic assays, individuals with greater Long COVID symptom burden or an official clinical diagnosis exhibited greater dysfunction in cellular energy metabolism compared with those with fewer or no symptoms.

Comparing pre-COVID-19 and post-COVID-19 controls on the PM-M7 plate (cytokines/growth factors), 65 of 90 wells (72.2%) showed significant differences, with post-COVID-19 control cells producing lower NADH in all wells, indicating reduced metabolic response to effectors after pandemic-era exposure.
On the PM-M7 plate, all probable LC-19 patients (LC-19_a) showed significantly lower metabolic response than pre-COVID-19 controls in 65 of 90 wells (72.2%).

LC-19 patients with more than 4 symptoms (LC-19_b) showed significantly reduced cellular energetic response to 58 of 90 chemicals (64.4%) on the PM-M7 plate compared with pre-COVID-19 controls, including markedly reduced responses at any concentration of the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-6.

In the LC-19_c (official diagnosis) subgroup, cells showed less than half the metabolic activity of pre-COVID-19 cells across most PM-M7 wells, but no compound reached statistical significance after adjustment for multiple comparisons.

On the PM-M6 plate, LC-19 patients with >4 symptoms (LC-19_b) showed significantly reduced NADH response compared with post-COVID-19 controls in 75 of 90 wells (83.3%), encompassing all compounds except dibutyryl-cAMP.

On the PM-M6 plate, LC-19 patients with an official diagnosis (LC-19_c) showed significantly reduced NADH response compared with post-COVID-19 controls in 78 of 90 wells (86.7%), including at least three concentrations for each metabolic effector.

On the PM-M1 plate, LC-19 patients with >4 symptoms showed 36 compounds (38.7%) with lower energy production and 15 (16.1%) with higher energy production than pre-COVID-19 controls, with reduced NADH extending beyond glucose/dextrin/glycogen/mannose to galactose, fucose, sorbose, xylitol, the Krebs cycle intermediate α-ketoglutaric acid, and the carboxylic acids acetic acid and butyric acid.

In the LC-19_c (official diagnosis) subgroup, only 9 compounds (9.7%) showed increased energy production and 4 compounds (4.3%: glucose, mannose, fucose, and α-ketoglutaric acid) showed decreased energy production relative to pre-COVID-19 controls on the PM-M1 plate.

On the PM-M1 plate, comparison of LC-19 patients with >4 symptoms versus post-COVID-19 controls showed significant differences in 69 of 93 chemicals (74.2%), and comparison of the officially diagnosed LC-19_c subgroup versus post-COVID-19 controls showed significant differences in 60 of 93 chemicals (64.5%), with decreased metabolite utilization in LC-19 patients across all strata.

Pathway enrichment analysis of the PM-M1 metabolic profile identified four major pathways significantly altered between LC-19 and control groups: galactose metabolism, pyruvate metabolism, fructose and mannose metabolism, and the citric acid cycle.

Glucose, dextrin, and mannose showed significantly reduced energy production in post-COVID-19 control cells compared to pre-COVID-19 control cells, suggesting saturation of high-efficiency energy pathways following pandemic-era SARS-CoV-2 exposure.
Lymphoblastoid cell line generation succeeded in 100% of LC-19 blood samples (12/12) compared to only 72% (13/18) in the control group, an unexpectedly higher efficiency in the LC-19 group.

Saliva screening detected EBV positivity in some samples but with no consistent pattern across the LC-19 and control groups, and no samples tested positive for HHV-6, indicating no evidence of latent viral reactivation driving the observed metabolic differences.

In a cross-sectional survey of Clemson University students and employees, 130 of 266 respondents (49%) reported symptoms lasting three or more months that were not present before COVID-19, potentially attributable to Long COVID.
Sex differences were noted in the survey, with more females than males reporting musculoskeletal symptoms following COVID-19, consistent with published literature.
Among survey respondents, 81.6% had previously received a COVID-19 diagnosis and 91.3% (242 respondents) had received COVID-19 vaccination at the time of sampling.

The authors interpret their PM-M6/PM-M7 findings as indicating that the lack of cellular responsiveness to IL-6 and TNF-α in LC-19 cells could reflect a compensatory host response involving increased cytokine production, potentially explaining elevated circulating IL-6 levels reported in other Long COVID studies.

The authors note that infection with different SARS-CoV-2 variants has been associated with varying patterns of Long COVID symptoms, and acknowledge that their study did not stratify the LC-19 cohort by infecting viral variant, which could have influenced observed metabolic outcomes.
Poly I:C injection produced a significantly elevated, polyphasic febrile response in both chronically stressed and unstressed mice.
At 7 days post-poly I:C injection, chronically stressed mice exhibited persistent fatigue-like behavior not seen to the same degree in unstressed controls.
Stressed mice given poly I:C developed mechanical allodynia measured by von Frey filament testing persisting to 7 days post-injection.
Stressed mice given poly I:C showed depressive-like behavior on the forced swim test persisting to 7 days post-injection.
Stressed mice given poly I:C showed impaired spatial memory on the Morris water maze persisting to 7 days post-injection.
Stressed mice given poly I:C showed increased anxiety-like behavior on the open field test persisting to 7 days post-injection.
Stressed mice given poly I:C showed reduced social interaction persisting to 7 days post-injection.
In chronically stressed mice injected with poly I:C, serum IL-6 remained elevated 7 days post-injection and correlated with the severity of behavioral abnormalities.
In chronically stressed mice injected with poly I:C, serum CXCL10 remained elevated 7 days post-injection and correlated with the severity of behavioral abnormalities.
Pretreatment with minocycline, a microglial activation inhibitor, partially attenuated both the behavioral abnormalities and elevated immune markers induced by poly I:C in chronically stressed mice.
Serum IL-10 was measured alongside IL-6 and CXCL10 but was not reported as persistently altered in stressed poly I:C-treated mice.
Pretreatment with RU486, a glucocorticoid receptor antagonist, failed to attenuate either the behavioral or immune responses to poly I:C in stressed mice.
The partial attenuation of symptoms by the microglial activation inhibitor minocycline implicates microglial-driven neuroinflammation as a mechanism underlying persistent PVFS-like symptoms.
Activation of TLR3 by poly I:C in chronically stressed mice triggers systemic inflammation that produces persistent, multi-domain post-viral fatigue syndrome-like symptoms.

In a cross-sectional survey of 41 patients, a fully remote multicomponent intervention combining ketogenic metabolic therapy, thiamine supplementation, and behavioral strategies met all feasibility and acceptability benchmarks, with 96% of respondents reporting it was helpful and 96% recommending it.

Thiamine supplementation was incorporated as a component of the multicomponent remote intervention alongside ketogenic metabolic therapy and behavioral strategies, targeting proposed underlying biological mechanisms of post-viral illness.

A physiological stress protocol combining a six-minute walk and one-minute sit-to-stand test significantly improved PASC classification performance and reduced model variability compared to resting-state recordings across both vowel phonation and coughing tasks.

Fusion of traditional acoustic features with WavLM and wav2vec 2.0 embeddings from post-exercise sustained vowel phonation achieved a peak F1-score of 82.2% for distinguishing PASC from healthy individuals.
Fusion of traditional acoustic features with WavLM and wav2vec 2.0 embeddings from post-exercise voluntary coughing achieved a peak F1-score of 80.8% for distinguishing PASC from healthy individuals.
A late fusion model aggregating results across both vowel phonation and coughing tasks achieved the highest overall PASC classification performance, with an F1-score of 87.7%.
Incorporating self-supervised learning speech representations alongside traditional acoustic descriptors improved the sensitivity of voice-based screening for respiratory and vocal sequelae of PASC.
Combined autoantibody reactivity to 18 self-antigens was significantly higher in SARS-CoV-2 convalescent, seropositive individuals compared to pre-pandemic seronegative controls.
IgG responses to several individual self-antigens were significantly higher in SARS-CoV-2 convalescent seropositive individuals than in pre-pandemic seronegative controls.
CMV seropositivity was not significantly associated with combined autoantibody reactivity.
EBV seropositivity was not significantly associated with combined autoantibody reactivity.
H. pylori seropositivity was not significantly associated with combined autoantibody reactivity.
T. gondii seropositivity was not significantly associated with combined autoantibody reactivity.

Stronger antibody responses to SARS-CoV-2 spike protein antigens (S, S2, and RBD) in convalescent individuals were significantly associated with greater combined autoantibody reactivity and increased responses to multiple individual self-antigens.

Antibody response intensity to CMV, EBV, H. pylori, and T. gondii antigens in corresponding seropositive subsets was not associated with combined autoantibody reactivity, in contrast to SARS-CoV-2 spike responses.
The prevalence of generalized ligamentous laxity, defined by a Beighton score of 5 or higher, was 13.3% among healthy pediatric orthopaedic clinic patients.

When performed unilaterally, the thumb-to-forearm apposition test had a poor positive predictive value (34%) for detecting generalized ligamentous laxity using the composite Beighton score as gold standard.
The thumb-to-forearm apposition test showed excellent negative predictive value (99%) for ruling out generalized ligamentous laxity.
The thumb-to-forearm apposition test had extremely high sensitivity (99%) for detecting generalized ligamentous laxity.
The thumb-to-forearm apposition test had only modest specificity (67%) for generalized ligamentous laxity.
The likelihood ratio of the thumb-to-forearm apposition test for generalized ligamentous laxity was fair, at +3.3.
Performing the thumb-to-forearm apposition test bilaterally instead of unilaterally did not significantly improve its diagnostic utility for generalized ligamentous laxity.
The prevalence of generalized ligamentous laxity, defined by a Beighton score of 5 or greater, was 13.3% among the pediatric orthopaedic clinic population studied.
Other single upper extremity tests of generalized ligamentous laxity were found to perform similarly to thumb-to-forearm apposition testing in identifying GLL.

The authors conclude that single tests such as thumb-to-forearm apposition can help rule out generalized ligamentous laxity but are unreliable for confirming its presence, so results from single-joint tests should be interpreted cautiously in clinical or research settings.
Women who gave preterm birth had significantly higher total Beighton joint hypermobility scores compared with women who had term births.
Among Beighton subgroup scores, elbow hyperextension had the highest hypermobility score in the preterm birth study group.
Among Beighton subgroup scores, thumb hyperextension had the lowest hypermobility score in the preterm birth study group.

A constellation of radiologic findings—lytic, sclerotic, or mixed bone lesions, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, retroperitoneal or periportal/mesenteric lymphadenopathy, and omental thickening—should raise concern for systemic mastocytosis, particularly alongside skin rash, allergic reactions, GI symptoms, tachycardia, weight loss, bone pain, cytopenias, liver dysfunction, or eosinophilia.
The paper discusses the emerging role of MRI, 18-fluorodeoxyglucose PET, and fibroscan as newer imaging techniques that may aid in the diagnosis of systemic mastocytosis.
Radiologic methods were reviewed for their use in evaluating treatment response and prognostication in systemic mastocytosis.
Patients with POTS and orthostatic-induced vasovagal syncope had no major significant adverse events during surgery with general anesthesia.
One patient with POTS experienced an episode of AVNRT during or after surgery with general anesthesia.
One patient with orthostatic-induced vasovagal syncope experienced bradycardia secondary to a vasovagal reflex during or after surgery.

13 of 190 surgeries (6.8%) were followed by episodes of postoperative hypotension, mostly attributable to bleeding, volume depletion, or sepsis rather than the underlying orthostatic intolerance disorder.
In patients with orthostatic hypotension (OH), the rate of postoperative major adverse cardiac events was 4.7%, which was not significantly different from the calculated risk for patients without OH.
In patients with orthostatic hypotension, the 30-day mortality rate was 6.1%, not significantly different from the calculated risk for patients without OH.
There were no myocardial infarctions or deaths at 30 days among patients with POTS or orthostatic-induced vasovagal syncope who underwent surgery.

The rate of postoperative major adverse cardiac events and 30-day mortality in patients with orthostatic hypotension was not significantly different from the calculated risk for patients without orthostatic hypotension.
No myocardial infarctions or deaths occurred within 30 days after surgery among patients with POTS or orthostatic-induced vasovagal syncope.
The majority of Ponseti-treated clubfoot patients had high Beighton hypermobility scores, supporting a proposed association between generalized joint hypermobility and clubfoot deformity.
Higher Beighton hypermobility scores were associated with a slightly lower, but not statistically significant, probability of clubfoot relapse after Ponseti treatment.

Beighton hypermobility score did not significantly influence patient sex, laterality, initial Dimeglio severity, number of pretenotomy casts, need for tenotomy, relapse, or need for tendon transfer surgery.
Unlike clubfeet historically treated with surgical release, Ponseti-treated clubfeet were not prone to excessive overcorrection regardless of the degree of joint laxity.
One third of adults in this Wichi community reported musculoskeletal pain in the past 7 days.
Mechanical back pain was the most prevalent rheumatic condition, affecting 19.0% of the community.
Rheumatic regional pain syndrome was present in 5.2% of the population.
Osteoarthritis prevalence in this community was 3.2%.
Rheumatoid arthritis prevalence in this Wichi community was 3.2%, among the highest reported using COPCORD methodology in Latin American populations.
Inflammatory back pain was found in 1.2% of the Wichi community sample.
Undifferentiated arthritis was found in 0.3% of the community sample.
Sjögren syndrome was identified in 0.15% of the Wichi indigenous community sample.
Fibromyalgia was identified in 0.15% of the Wichi indigenous community sample.
Among RA patients, 90.5% were women and 42.9% reported a family history of RA.
All identified RA patients in this community were seropositive, and two-thirds showed radiologic erosions.
At the time of diagnosis, RA patients had a mean DAS-28 (ESR) score of 5.1, indicating high disease activity.
Among the rheumatoid arthritis patients identified, 66.7% showed radiologic erosions.
At the time of diagnosis, RA patients had a mean Disease Activity Score (DAS-28 ESR) of 5.1, indicating high disease activity.
RA patients had a mean Health Assessment Questionnaire Disability Index (HAQ-DI) score of 0.8 at diagnosis, reflecting functional impairment.
The mean delay in diagnosis of rheumatic disease in this community was 5.8 years.
Pain and functional capacity were the variables associated with a diagnosis of rheumatic disease and were identified as key factors for early specialist referral.

The authors suggest that the absence of the 'migration health' phenomenon (i.e., lack of population mixing/migration) in this isolated indigenous community may be a social determinant that negatively impacts health, potentially explaining the high RA prevalence.
Patients with vasovagal syncope had a lower prospective risk of motor vehicle collisions than the general driving population.
Patients with arrhythmic syncope had a higher prospective risk of motor vehicle collisions than the general driving population.

Motor vehicle collision risk in patients with syncope not yet diagnosed (NYD) was highly variable across studies, with the largest study showing an almost 2-fold increased risk while smaller studies gave contradictory findings.
Transection of the tibialis anterior tendon at the TMT-1 level in cadaver specimens significantly increased first tarsometatarsal joint instability as measured by the cross-glide test.

The cross-glide test was negative in all healthy controls but positive in 62% of hallux valgus cases and 100% of recurrent hallux valgus cases, indicating widespread TMT-1 instability in HV recurrence.
Inter-observer agreement for the cross-glide test between an experienced surgeon and a resident surgeon was high.
Hallux valgus angle was significantly larger in both hallux valgus and recurrent hallux valgus groups compared to healthy controls.
Intermetatarsal angle was significantly larger in both hallux valgus and recurrent hallux valgus groups compared to healthy controls.
On simulated weight-bearing CT, MT-1 internal rotation was significantly increased in hallux valgus cases compared to healthy controls.
On simulated weight-bearing CT, dorsal angle was significantly increased in hallux valgus cases compared to healthy controls.
In hallux valgus cases, MT-1 internal rotation increased significantly when weight-bearing was simulated compared to the non-weight-bearing CT.
Cases with a positive cross-glide test had significantly greater MT-1 internal rotation and dorsal angle on simulated weight-bearing CT than cross-glide-negative cases.
In cross-glide-test-positive cases, MT-1 internal rotation increased significantly with simulated weight-bearing compared to non-weight-bearing CT.
Within the hallux valgus subgroup, cross-glide-test-positive cases showed significantly greater TMT-1 internal rotation on weight-bearing CT than cross-glide-negative HV cases.
Within the hallux valgus group, HV angle and IMT angle were significantly higher in cross-glide-test-positive cases than in cross-glide-test-negative cases.
In 15 patients with recurrent hallux valgus and clinical TMT-1 instability treated with TMT-1 arthrodesis, no recurrent hallux valgus was observed during follow-up.
Lightheadedness occurred in all 20 subjects pre-operatively, and 75% experienced syncope or pre-syncope.

All 20 subjects had ongoing orthostatic intolerance plus at least one other comorbidity, including mast cell activation syndrome, peripheral neuropathy, Chiari I malformation, fibromyalgia, and GI dysmotility disorders.

Fielding type 1 AAI in the hereditary connective tissue disorder cohort results from alar ligament incompetence, distinct from the transverse ligament failure seen in rheumatoid arthritis and Down syndrome.
An angular displacement between C1 and C2 greater than 41° on rotational CT was used as the pathological diagnostic threshold for AAI.
Karnofsky Performance Scores improved significantly after C1-C2 fusion, with 50% of subjects returning to work.
The SF-36 physical function raw score improved from a mean of 16.6 pre-surgery to 20.4 post-surgery.
Patients reported statistically significant improvement in running, lifting, bending/stooping, and walking after C1-C2 fusion.

Frequency and severity of headache, neck pain, hand and lower extremity numbness, arm weakness, syncope, and pre-syncope improved significantly post-surgery, with milder improvement in joint pain, myalgias, nausea, anxiety, and depression.
Headache pain intensity showed a statistically significant improvement after surgery.
Occipital neuralgia intensity improved significantly post-surgery, paralleling headache improvement.
Neck pain intensity improved with high statistical significance after C1-C2 fusion.
Fatigue, memory, balance, swallowing/choking, leg weakness, and sexual difficulties did not significantly improve after C1-C2 fusion.
65% of subjects reported overall improvement on the Global Clinical Impression of Change scale, while 35% reported no significant improvement.
Global body pain VAS score improved modestly but significantly from 7/10 pre-operatively to 6/10 post-operatively.
90% of subjects said they would repeat the surgery given the same circumstances, and 10% would not, citing ongoing comorbidities.
Four of 20 subjects (20%) reported the surgery did not help their overall quality of life.
Eighteen of 20 fusions were confirmed radiographically by CT; two subjects required revision, one for trauma-related failed fusion and one for a broken screw with otherwise good fusion.
Pre-operatively, depression was present in 17/20 subjects and anxiety in 18/20 subjects, a surprisingly high prevalence.

Anxiety and depression showed highly statistically significant improvement following C1-C2 stabilization, which the authors attribute to reduced brainstem/limbic mechanical stress and decreased disability burden.
Hyperreflexia, especially of the patellar tendons, was present in 12/20 subjects, except in those with peripheral neuropathy due to B12 deficiency (8/20), who showed hyporeflexia instead.
In a prior report of four subjects with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, three had atlanto-axial instability.
All 20 subjects had significant loss of C1-C2 facet overlap (<20%), with four subjects below 10% and two below 5% overlap, confirming rotary subluxation.
The average angular displacement between C1 and C2 on full-neck rotation to each side was 42° in this cohort.
Many subjects in this EDS cohort had vitamin D deficiency and osteopenic bone quality, requiring supplementation prior to fusion surgery.
Less commonly observed neurological exam findings in the cohort included weakness, dysdiadochokinesia, Romberg sign, and impaired tandem gait.
Hypoesthesia to pinprick over most cervical, thoracic, lumbar, and sacral dermatomes was a common physical finding, with preserved proprioception and vibratory sensation.
Down syndrome is associated with an 11-17% incidence of atlanto-axial instability.
Three of four subjects with vascular-type Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in a prior series had atlanto-axial instability.
One-third of children with ligamentous laxity from congenital spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia developed atlanto-axial instability with cervical myelopathy.
Three of eight subjects with Goldenhar syndrome had atlanto-axial instability in a prior report.
Before disease-modifying therapies, most rheumatoid arthritis patients had radiographic C1-C2 involvement, with substantial rates of symptoms, myelopathy, and death.
Failure of the alar ligament permits a 30% increase in contralateral rotation at the C1-C2 segment.
At 35° of C1-on-C2 rotation the contralateral vertebral artery stretches and kinks, and between 40-45° both vertebral arteries become fully occluded.
A cervical spinal canal diameter of less than 14 mm predicts both the development and severity of weakness and should prompt consideration of surgery.
The ponticulus posticus (Kimmerle anomaly) is a common anatomical variant associated with higher risk of vertebral artery injury during C1-C2 surgery.
Extra-dural origin of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery and pro-atlantal arterial variants occur at low but notable frequency, relevant to surgical risk.

A high-riding vertebral artery is present in half to most patients with Down syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis, basilar invagination, Klippel-Feil syndrome, and congenital skeletal anomalies, raising surgical risk.
Vertebral artery injury and stroke risk increase when a dominant left vertebral artery is paired with a hypoplastic contralateral vertebral artery.
A high-riding C2 transverse foramen, complicating pedicle screw placement, was reported in 18% of patients in a prior series.

A prior series of transarticular C1-C2 fixation reported substantial rates of screw malposition, failed fusion, screw breakage, and cranial nerve injury, and pedicle anatomy precluded safe screw placement in one-fifth of patients.
Pedicle screw fixation of C1-C2 across the literature carries risks of vertebral artery compromise, neurological deficit, and death.

Larger published series of C1-C2 fusion report suboccipital numbness in up to half of patients along with low but measurable rates of failed fusion, dural tears, screw breakout, screw fracture, infection, and suboccipital neuralgia.
Many subjects in the EDS cohort were found to be deficient in vitamin D and were treated with high-dose ergocalciferol.
Cadaveric studies establishing rotational CT diagnosis of atlanto-axial rotary subluxation found a mean atlas-axis rotation of 31.1°, increasing to 35° after contralateral alar ligament rupture.
The PODCI Upper Extremity Function (UEF) scale demonstrated high test-retest reliability in adolescents with HSDs.
The PODCI Pain (P) scale showed moderate test-retest reliability in adolescents with HSDs.
PODCI UEF scores correlated strongly with the PROMIS Pediatric Upper Extremity-Short Form, supporting concurrent validity.
PODCI Pain scores showed a moderate inverse correlation with the Numeric Rating Scale for pain, supporting concurrent validity.
Headache was significantly more prevalent among IBD patients (52.3%) compared to control patients (40.6%).
Migraine was significantly more prevalent among IBD patients (34.2%) compared to control patients (20.8%).
Migraine was 2.6 times more common in Crohn's disease patients than in control patients.
Migraine was substantially more common in men with IBD than in male controls, with an even higher relative frequency in men with Crohn's disease specifically.
Headache and migraine were also more common in dyspeptic patients than in controls.
Statistical analyses found no association between peripheral neuropathy and headache or primary headache in IBD patients, indicating these comorbidities affect different subgroups.
Multivariate regression analysis found headaches were more prevalent among women and among those with co-existing psychiatric disease, IBD, CD, and UC.

After matching groups for age, gender distribution, hypertension, and psychiatric disease prevalence, headache and migraine prevalence remained significantly higher in IBD, CD, and UC patients compared with controls.
Young females with joint hypermobility had significantly higher peak plantar pressure in the nondominant foot compared with those without hypermobility.
Young females with joint hypermobility had significantly higher peak pressure gradients in the nondominant foot compared with those without hypermobility.
Within the hypermobility group, the nondominant foot showed significantly higher peak pressure than the dominant foot.
Within the hypermobility group, the nondominant foot showed significantly higher peak pressure gradient than the dominant foot.
Within the hypermobility group, the nondominant foot showed significantly higher total force values than the dominant foot.
Open capsular shift combined with Achilles tendon allograft augmentation restored shoulder stability in 4 of 5 shoulders with EDS-related instability.
Mean pain visual analog scale scores decreased markedly from before surgery to final follow-up after Achilles allograft augmentation surgery.
At final follow-up, patients had a mean subjective shoulder value of 84 and mean ASES score of 77.3, indicating overall functional improvement.
One of five shoulders developed recurrent posterior instability after a subsequent injury 1.6 years after the index Achilles allograft augmentation procedure, requiring revision surgery.
All patients used narcotic pain medication before surgery, but at final follow-up only the one patient with recurrent instability still reported pain.
Vestibular migraine was the most common diagnosis in pediatric patients presenting with dizziness or imbalance, occurring in 35.0% of the cohort.
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) was diagnosed in 21.6% of the pediatric dizziness cohort, making it the second most common diagnosis.
Primary dysautonomia was diagnosed in 15.7% of children and adolescents evaluated for dizziness or imbalance.
Anxiety disorder was a contributing diagnosis in 13.5% of pediatric patients with dizziness or imbalance.
Persistent postural perceptual dizziness (PPPD) was diagnosed in 11.2% of the pediatric vestibular clinic cohort.
Nearly half (44.4%) of pediatric patients with dizziness or imbalance received more than one contributing diagnosis, indicating a multifactorial etiology.
Vestibular migraine frequently co-occurred with BPPV or PPPD, and 22 patients carried all three diagnoses concurrently.
Presence of unilateral pain during a migraine attack was significantly associated with achieving a pain-free response 2 hours after frovatriptan intake.
Presence of phonophobia during a migraine attack was significantly associated with a pain-free response to frovatriptan at 2 hours.

Presence of one or more cranial autonomic symptoms (e.g., lacrimation, nasal congestion, eyelid oedema) during a migraine attack was significantly associated with a pain-free response to frovatriptan.

Presence of one or more premonitory symptoms (e.g., yawning, tiredness, mood changes, neck stiffness) in the 24 hours before an attack was significantly associated with a pain-free response to frovatriptan.
Overall, 35% of the 85 recorded migraine attacks became pain-free within 2 hours after frovatriptan 2.5 mg intake.
Repeated daily restraint stress produced transient cutaneous allodynia that resolved by day 16, whereas repeated umbellulone exposure alone did not.

Restraint stress induced long-lasting priming (latent sensitization) that persisted beyond 16 days, revealed by reinstatement of cutaneous allodynia after a subsequent subthreshold umbellulone challenge.
Pretreatment with propranolol prior to restraint stress prevented both the transient cutaneous allodynia and the development of priming, shown by absence of umbellulone-induced allodynia.
Pretreatment with nor-BNI, a kappa opioid receptor antagonist, prior to restraint stress also prevented transient cutaneous allodynia and the development of priming.
In restraint-stress-primed mice, pretreatment with the CGRP-receptor antagonist olcegepant prevented umbellulone-induced cutaneous allodynia when given prior to challenge.
Once restraint stress priming was established, propranolol failed to prevent umbellulone-induced cutaneous allodynia.
Once restraint stress priming was established, the kappa opioid receptor antagonist nor-BNI failed to prevent umbellulone-induced cutaneous allodynia.
When administered 1 hour after umbellulone challenge, sumatriptan reversed established cutaneous allodynia in restraint-stress-primed mice.

Unlike sumatriptan, olcegepant given 1 hour after umbellulone did not reverse established cutaneous allodynia, indicating CGRP receptor blockade is effective only when given before the triggering challenge.

The authors conclude that CGRP receptor activation plays a time-dependent role in migraine-like pain, contributing to initiation of pain but having a more limited role in maintaining it, supporting the rationale for CGRP antagonists as preventive rather than abortive therapies.
The authors propose that kappa opioid receptor antagonists may represent a novel preventive therapy for stress-related migraine.
Systemic vascular distensibility (alpha) during exercise was significantly lower in CTD patients than in age- and gender-matched healthy controls.
Reduced systemic vascular distensibility was associated with impaired stroke volume augmentation during exercise in CTD patients.
On multivariate analysis, lower systemic vascular distensibility was associated with decreased peak exercise oxygen consumption (pVO2) in CTD patients.
Decreased systemic vascular distensibility was associated with decreased systemic oxygen extraction in CTD patients on multivariate analysis.
Of 1905 successive vertigo/dizziness patients referred from outpatient town clinics, 244 (12.8%) were initially classified as vertigo/dizziness of unknown origin before further hospital-based workup.
Short-term hospitalization with a battery of vestibular and autonomic examinations reduced the proportion of cases remaining unexplained from 12.8% to 2.5%.
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) was the most common final diagnosis among previously unexplained vertigo/dizziness cases, accounting for 107 of 240 hospitalized patients.
Gender, evoked dizziness, and positional nystagmus were identified as supporting factors for a final diagnosis of BPPV.
Orthostatic dysregulation was the second most common final diagnosis, found in 56 of 240 previously unexplained vertigo/dizziness patients.
Evoked dizziness, an abnormal Schellong (orthostatic blood pressure) test, and hypertension were supporting factors for diagnosing orthostatic dysregulation.
Gravity perception disturbance (GPD) was the final diagnosis in 4.2% (10/240) of hospitalized patients with previously unexplained vertigo/dizziness.
Psychogenic vertigo accounted for 4.2% (10/240) of final diagnoses among hospitalized patients with vertigo/dizziness of unknown origin.

The proportion of patients remaining classified as unknown-origin vertigo/dizziness fell sharply from 12.8% (244/1905) at initial referral to 2.5% (6/240) after short-term hospitalization with comprehensive testing.
Gender, evoked dizziness, and positional nystagmus were identified as supporting factors leading to a final diagnosis of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo.
Evoked dizziness, Schellong test (S-test) results, and hypertension were identified as supporting factors for a final diagnosis of orthostatic dysregulation.
Vestibular peripheral disease was supported diagnostically by evoked dizziness, head-shaking nystagmus, abnormal caloric test, and abnormal video head impulse test results.
Vestibular migraine diagnosis was supported by gender, presence of headache, and abnormal Schellong test findings.
Meniere's disease diagnosis was supported by ear fullness and abnormal inner ear MRI findings.
Gravity perception disturbance diagnosis was supported by gender, evoked dizziness, and abnormal subjective visual vertical findings.
Psychogenic vertigo diagnosis was supported by elevated self-rating depression scale scores.
Prevalence of gastrointestinal symptoms was significantly higher in all eight PROMIS symptom domains among FD patients compared with a general US adult population.

Despite higher prevalence, the severity of gastrointestinal symptoms (raw PROMIS scores) was significantly lower in FD patients than in the general population comparison group across nearly all domains.
Abdominal pain severity was the sole PROMIS domain in which FD patients did not differ significantly from the general population comparison group.
Surveys completed by caregivers reported the same burden of gastrointestinal symptoms as those completed directly by patients, supporting caregiver-proxy reliability.
A substantial proportion of FD patients depend on gastrostomy tube feeding, with 25% relying on it as their sole nutrition route and an additional 53% using it for liquid intake only.
HF-HRV, a marker of cardiovagal modulation, was significantly lower in women with chronic pelvic pain than in healthy controls across all postural time points.
Women with CPP showed a blunted decrease in HF-HRV when moving from supine to upright posture compared to healthy controls, suggesting impaired vagal withdrawal during orthostatic challenge.
Women with CPP showed poorer recovery of HF-HRV when returning from upright tilt back to supine posture compared to healthy controls.
Healthy controls showed a trend toward increased tachygastria activity on electrogastrography when moving from pre-upright to upright tilt.
Women with CPP showed no significant change in tachygastria activity from pre-upright to upright tilt, unlike the increase seen in healthy controls.

The parallel impairment in both tachygastria response and HRV decrement upon standing supports a generalized blunting of autonomic/physiological modulation across cardiovascular and gastric systems in women with chronic pelvic pain.
Pre-attack symptoms were reported in 71.3% of Korean patients with cluster headache.
When present, pre-attack symptoms occurred at a median of 20 minutes (range 1-120 minutes) before the cluster headache attack.

Local and painful sensory pre-attack symptoms were the most prevalent category, occurring in 58.8% of patients, followed by general symptoms (30.1%), local and painless sensory symptoms (14.7%), and autonomic symptoms (11.0%).
A higher number of cluster headache bouts was independently associated with a higher prevalence of pre-attack symptoms on multivariable logistic regression.
The frequency of pre-attack symptoms in this Korean cluster headache cohort was consistent with findings from previous Western studies.
Half of the health care providers surveyed had no staff specifically dedicated to delivering patient education.
Among HCPs who did have dedicated patient education staff, the large majority felt that staffing was still insufficient to meet patients' needs.
Most patients with connective tissue diseases surveyed had never heard of patient education programs.
Most surveyed patients expressed interest in participating in a patient education program despite low prior awareness.

A heterozygous missense mutation in COL12A1 (c.8336G>A, p.Arg2779His) was identified in a 14-year-old girl presenting with joint hypermobility, recurrent clavicle dislocation, and mild upper limb muscle weakness.
Average retinal nerve fiber layer thickness declined significantly with age in FD subjects at a rate of -0.861 µm/year before plateauing around age 26.2.
Average macular ganglion cell and inner plexiform layer (GCIPL) thickness declined significantly with age at -0.553 µm/year before plateauing around age 24.8.
Optic nerve head parameters (rim area, average cup-to-disc ratio, cup volume) showed significant linear progression over time except in a subset of subjects lacking a measurable cup.
The authors conclude that ONH parameters may be the most suitable structural measure for longitudinal follow-up in FD, specifically in eyes with a measurable cup.
Mean anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) length measured by ultrasound was significantly different between ankles with and without generalized joint hypermobility.
Resting ATFL height (a measure of ligament looseness) on ultrasound was significantly different between ankles with and without generalized joint hypermobility.
Stress ATFL height on stress ultrasonography was significantly different between ankles with and without generalized joint hypermobility.

The mean difference in ATFL height between resting and stress ultrasound (indicating degree of ligament loosening under stress) was significantly different between ankles with and without generalized joint hypermobility.
Resting and stress ATFL length, height, and the difference in height between resting and stress ATFL showed a positive linear correlation with Beighton scores.
Resting and stress ATFL length, height, and the difference in height between resting and stress ATFL showed a positive linear correlation with manual anterior drawer test (ADT) grades.
Among people with MS and chronic pain, 41.1% screened positive for fibromyalgia/central sensitization using the ACR FM Survey Criteria cut-point of ≥13.
On the painDETECT questionnaire, most MS chronic pain respondents did not show strong evidence of neuropathic pain, with roughly equal proportions scoring unlikely, ambiguous, or likely neuropathic.

Combining painDETECT and FM Survey Criteria scores, the largest MS chronic pain subgroup was nociceptive type (40.5%), followed by mixed neuropathic/nociplastic type (26.8%), nociplastic type (23.3%), and neuropathic type (9.4%).
Pain intensity T-scores differed significantly across pain subtypes, with the nociceptive type reporting the lowest intensity and the mixed neuropathic/nociplastic type reporting the highest.

Migraine was the most common chronic overlapping pain condition among MS patients with chronic pain, and its frequency differed significantly by pain subtype, with the mixed neuropathic/nociplastic type having the highest frequency.

Chronic pelvic pain was the second most common chronic overlapping pain condition, but unlike other conditions, it was least frequent in the neuropathic pain subtype rather than the nociceptive subtype.
NSAIDs were the most frequently used pain medication overall in this MS chronic pain sample, while steroids were the least commonly used.

Participants with high centralized (nociplastic or mixed nociplastic/neuropathic) pain most frequently reported use of centrally-acting medications including cannabinoids, opioids, SNRIs, SSRIs, antispasmodics, and benzodiazepines.
Contrary to typical nociplastic pain treatment expectations, the nociplastic pain type reported using NSAIDs about 10% more frequently than the other pain subtypes.
Anticonvulsant use was approximately 15% lower in the nociceptive pain type compared with the other three pain subtypes.
Steroid use, though uncommon overall, was highest among those with any neuropathic pain component (neuropathic alone or mixed with nociplastic).
Opioid (narcotic) medications received the highest average self-reported pain relief rating of any analgesic class across all pain subtypes.
SSRIs were associated with the least self-reported pain relief of any medication class across all MS chronic pain subtypes.
Self-reported pain relief from cannabinoids was significantly higher in patients with mixed neuropathic/nociplastic pain than in those with purely neuropathic pain.

Self-reported pain relief from NSAIDs was significantly greater in patients with nociceptive pain than in those with nociplastic or mixed pain, and greater in nociplastic than mixed pain, consistent with nociplastic pain being less NSAID-responsive.

Although not statistically significant due to low usage frequency, benzodiazepines showed substantial mean differences in perceived pain relief, rated higher by the neuropathic pain type than by the other three subtypes.
SFN and CM patients had significantly lower quality of life than healthy family members, with SFN patients also lower than CM.
Physical health scores (SF-12) were significantly lower in SFN and CM patients compared with healthy family members.
Total pain catastrophizing scores were significantly higher in SFN and CM patients than in healthy family members, with SFN highest.
Catastrophism as a coping strategy (CSQ) was significantly higher in SFN and CM patients than in HFM.
Helplessness scores were significantly higher in SFN and CM patients than in HFM, with SFN highest.
Rumination scores were significantly higher in SFN and CM patients than in HFM (no significant SFN vs CM difference).
Magnification scores were significantly higher in SFN than in CM and HFM (CM vs HFM not significant).
The chronic migraine group had a significantly higher proportion of females than SFN and healthy family member groups.
SFN patients reported significantly greater worry about being more fragile in case of COVID-19 infection and greater worry about infection consequences than CM patients.
Chronic migraine patients reported greater increases in agitation and anxiety during the COVID-19 lockdown than before, more than SFN and HFM.
SFN patients reported significantly greater feelings of being forgotten or rejected by clinicians during the lockdown than CM patients.
SFN patients were significantly more concerned than CM patients about negative consequences of the COVID-19 emergency on the clinical management of their disease.
SFN patients' pain intensity increased significantly during the COVID-19 lockdown compared with the pre-pandemic period.
The number of pain-related symptoms reported by SFN patients increased significantly during the pandemic compared with before.
SFN patients' pain course shifted toward more constant underlying pain with pain accesses during the pandemic compared with before.
Chronic migraine patients' quality of life decreased significantly during the pandemic compared with before.
Even healthy family members showed a significant decline in quality of life during the pandemic compared with before.
In SFN patients, greater physical disability (lower SF-12 physical health) was associated with greater distress about changes in the neurologist-patient relationship during the pandemic.
In SFN patients, higher pain catastrophizing was associated with greater behavioural changes during the pandemic lockdown.
In CM patients, those who suffered more from changes in clinical management during the pandemic had lower mental health scores.
SFN patients reported significantly higher pain intensity (NRS) during the pandemic study period compared to before the pandemic.
SFN patients reported an increase in the number of pain symptoms during the pandemic compared to before it.
SFN patients reported a shift towards a worse pattern of pain course (more constant underlying pain) during the pandemic compared to before it.
Chronic migraine patients showed reduced quality of life during the pandemic compared to before it.
Healthy family members also showed reduced quality of life during the pandemic compared to before it, despite being pain-free.
In SFN patients, greater physical disability was associated with greater perceived suffering from changes in the neurologist-patient relationship during the pandemic.
In SFN patients, higher pain catastrophizing scores were associated with greater behavioural changes (irritability, agitation, sadness, boredom) during the pandemic.
In CM patients, those suffering more from changes in clinical management during the pandemic had lower mental health scores.
In CM patients, greater behavioural changes during the pandemic were associated with higher feelings of loneliness.
In CM patients, greater behavioural changes during the pandemic were also associated with higher catastrophism.
Across both patient groups, behavioural changes due to COVID-19 lockdown were associated with lower mental health scores.
Catastrophism was the only coping strategy associated with the most severe clinical manifestations in both SFN and CM patients, although this association did not survive Bonferroni correction.
There was a significantly higher proportion of females in the chronic migraine group compared to the SFN and healthy family member groups.
SFN patients were significantly more worried than CM patients that their illness would make them more fragile in case of COVID-19 infection.
Chronic migraine patients reported greater agitation/anxiety behavioural change during the pandemic compared to SFN patients and healthy family members.
SFN patients reported significantly greater feelings of being forgotten or rejected by clinicians during the pandemic compared to CM patients.
SFN patients showed significantly greater concern than CM patients about negative consequences of the COVID-19 emergency on the management of their disease by clinicians.
Ubrogepant 50 mg achieved statistically significant pain relief compared with placebo as early as 1 hour post-dose, the earliest point of separation among the endpoints assessed.
The magnitude of ubrogepant's pain relief benefit over placebo continued to increase after the 1-h onset and reached its maximum at 4 hours post dose.
Ubrogepant 50 mg produced significant improvement over placebo in absence of the most bothersome non-headache migraine symptom beginning at 1.5 hours post-dose.
The benefit of ubrogepant over placebo for absence of most bothersome symptom continued to increase after 1.5 h and peaked at 4 hours post dose.
Ubrogepant 50 mg achieved statistically significant pain freedom over placebo beginning at the 2-hour primary endpoint timepoint.
The pain freedom advantage of ubrogepant over placebo continued to increase after 2 h and was greatest at 8 hours post dose, remaining significant through 48 hours.
A significantly greater proportion of ubrogepant-treated participants achieved sustained pain relief from 2 to 24 hours compared to placebo.
A significantly greater proportion of ubrogepant-treated participants achieved sustained pain freedom from 2 to 24 hours compared to placebo.

Pharmacokinetic sampling of ubrogepant 50 mg showed a mean maximum plasma concentration of 182 ng/mL, average systemic exposure (AUC) of 441 ng·h/mL, and a median time to peak concentration of 1 hour.

Using an EC90 pharmacologically active concentration threshold derived from a human capsaicin-induced dermal vasodilation model, ubrogepant plasma levels reached the active threshold within 11 minutes and remained above it for nearly 12 hours.
Treatment-emergent adverse event rates were similar between ubrogepant 50 mg and placebo groups, with nausea the most commonly reported adverse event in both arms.
A statistically confirmed linear increase in the pain relief treatment effect of ubrogepant over placebo was observed across the 2, 3, and 4-hour timepoints.
A statistically confirmed linear increase in the treatment effect on absence of most bothersome symptom was observed across the 2, 3, and 4-hour timepoints.
Unlike pain relief and absence of most bothersome symptom, the linear trend test did not confirm a continued linear increase in the pain freedom treatment effect across 2, 3, and 4 hours.

Across the individual ACHIEVE trials, ubrogepant 100 mg generally showed greater magnitude and duration of efficacy than ubrogepant 25 mg on pain and symptom endpoints, suggesting a dose-dependent effect.

The intravenous gepant olcegepant showed an efficacy time course with magnitude increasing between 1-2 hours and peaking at 4 hours, a pattern similar to oral gepants despite the different route of administration.
Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy produced a short-term reduction in depressed mood compared with usual care in chronic pain patients.
MBCT was associated with a short-term increase in mindfulness compared with non-MBCT interventions in chronic pain patients.
MBCT showed no significant between-group difference in pain intensity compared with control conditions at either short- or long-term follow-up.
MBCT showed no significant between-group difference in pain interference compared with control conditions at either short- or long-term follow-up.
MBCT showed no significant between-group difference in pain acceptance compared with control conditions at either short- or long-term follow-up.
When compared with active treatments (rather than usual care), MBCT showed no significant differences in outcomes at either short- or long-term follow-up.
Mean pupil size was significantly smaller during migraine attacks compared to the interictal phase in migraine patients.
Accommodative response to accommodative stimuli of 1.5 to 5 diopters was significantly increased during migraine attacks compared with the interictal period.
No significant change in ocular higher-order aberrations (spherical, coma, trefoil, RMS) was observed during migraine attacks compared with the interictal period.
Neither ictal nor interictal measurements of pupil size, accommodation, or HOAs differed significantly from healthy controls.

In migraine patients with unilateral headache, no significant differences in pupil size, accommodation, or HOAs were found between the symptomatic and non-symptomatic sides during either ictal or interictal periods.
Six of 2464 new patients seen at an orofacial pain clinic between 2015-2018 met diagnostic criteria for SUNCT (n=2) or SUNA (n=4), indicating these are rare presentations.
Attacks were located in the V1/V2 trigeminal distributions, and five of six patients reported associated intraoral pain, which is atypical for previously published SUNCT/SUNA presentations.
Pain quality was described as sharp, shooting, and burning, with two patients additionally describing numbness/paresthesia, moderate-severe in intensity and lasting seconds per episode.
Common cranial autonomic features accompanying attacks included lacrimation, conjunctival injection, rhinorrhea, and flushing.
Attacks were frequently triggered by touching the nose or a specific intraoral area.
Lamotrigine and gabapentin were the most commonly used initial pharmacologic therapies for SUNCT/SUNA patients in this cohort.
The authors concluded that differentiating between SUNCT and SUNA diagnoses does not appear to be clinically relevant.
Erenumab is a fully human monoclonal antibody that specifically inhibits the canonical calcitonin gene-related peptide receptor.
During weeks 1-4 of the double-blind treatment phase, monthly reversion from chronic migraine to episodic migraine was significantly higher with erenumab 70 mg and 140 mg than placebo.
During weeks 1-4, erenumab 140 mg was also associated with significantly higher monthly reversion to episodic migraine than placebo.
During weeks 5-8 of the DBTP, monthly reversion rates to EM remained significantly higher with erenumab 70 mg and 140 mg compared with placebo.
During weeks 5-8, erenumab 140 mg reversion rates were significantly higher than placebo.
During weeks 9-12, monthly reversion to EM remained significantly higher with erenumab than placebo.
During weeks 9-12, erenumab 140 mg reversion rates remained significantly higher than placebo.
Over the full 12-week double-blind treatment phase, erenumab 70 mg produced significantly higher CM-to-EM reversion rates than placebo.
Over the full 12-week double-blind treatment phase, erenumab 140 mg produced significantly higher CM-to-EM reversion rates than placebo.
Across all erenumab recipients (pooled doses), just over half achieved reversion to episodic migraine by 12 weeks.

Patients who reverted from chronic migraine to episodic migraine had lower baseline monthly headache days and monthly migraine days, and less prior preventive treatment failure, than patients who remained chronic.
Of patients with 12-week reversion who continued erenumab for 24 weeks total, the large majority maintained persistent reversion to episodic migraine.
Among patients treated with erenumab for the full 64 weeks who had reverted to EM at 12 weeks, nearly all maintained long-term persistent reversion through the end of the study.
Among patients who remained in chronic migraine after 12 weeks of erenumab, over one third achieved delayed reversion to episodic migraine by 24 weeks of treatment.
In the completer analysis, over 40% of patients who remained chronic after 12 weeks achieved delayed reversion to episodic migraine by 24 weeks.
Most patients with delayed reversion to episodic migraine maintained that status through the remainder of the 52-week open-label extension.

Approximately two-thirds of all completers treated with erenumab for the entire 64 weeks maintained episodic migraine status throughout the open-label extension, regardless of reversion status at 12 weeks.
At week 40 of the open-label extension, monthly reversion rates to episodic migraine were numerically higher for patients on erenumab 140 mg than 70 mg.
At week 52 of the open-label extension, monthly reversion rates to episodic migraine remained numerically higher for erenumab 140 mg than 70 mg.
Patients achieving persistent EM reversion over 24 weeks of erenumab treatment had a substantial mean reduction in monthly migraine days from baseline.
Patients achieving long-term persistent EM reversion over 64 weeks had an even greater mean reduction in monthly migraine days from baseline.

In the primary analysis of the parent trial, a significantly greater proportion of erenumab-treated patients achieved at least a 50% reduction in monthly migraine days compared with placebo, with a larger mean reduction in MMDs.
Similar to erenumab findings, reversion from chronic to episodic migraine has also been reported after repeated onabotulinumtoxinA treatment cycles in real-world and PREEMPT pooled analyses.
Preliminary reports suggest galcanezumab and fremanezumab produce similar rates of reversion from chronic to episodic migraine after 12 months of treatment as observed with erenumab.
Heart failure patients had lower mean cerebral tissue oxygen saturation than controls both while supine and after 10 minutes of head-up tilt.
In both HF patients and controls, mean SctO2 decreased significantly during head-up tilt, while DBP and HR increased.
The decline in SctO2 from supine to 10 minutes of head-up tilt was significantly greater in HF patients than in controls.

A higher proportion of HF patients than controls had SctO2 below 65% and below 60% after 10 minutes of head-up tilt, with 15% of HF patients (but none of the controls) exhibiting SctO2 <60%, a level associated with orthostatic symptoms or syncope.
After adjusting for age, sex, smoking, diabetes, supine SBP, and HR, heart failure was independently associated with a 2.457 percentage-point lower SctO2 in the supine position.
Heart failure remained independently associated with a 2.597 percentage-point lower SctO2 after 10 minutes of head-up tilt, after adjustment for age, sex, smoking, diabetes, SBP, and HR.
Among HF patients, older age and a higher supine heart rate were associated with lower SctO2 in the supine position.
Among HF patients, older age, smoking, and lower systolic blood pressure were associated with lower SctO2 after 10 minutes of head-up tilt.
No significant associations were found between SctO2 and age, sex, smoking, diabetes, SBP, or HR among control subjects.
Systolic blood pressure did not change significantly during head-up tilt in either HF patients or controls.

The authors propose that impaired vasomotor reactivity and autonomic dysfunction in heart failure may underlie impaired cerebral autoregulation, offering a possible mechanistic explanation for the abnormal cerebral oximetry response to head-up tilt.
Anxiety was more prevalent among rheumatology patients with Sjogren's syndrome compared to other rheumatic disease groups.
Depression was more prevalent among rheumatology patients with Sjogren's syndrome compared to other rheumatic disease groups.
Sleep disturbance was more prevalent among rheumatology patients with Sjogren's syndrome compared to other rheumatic disease groups.
Obesity (BMI greater than 23) was more prevalent among rheumatology patients with Sjogren's syndrome compared to other rheumatic disease groups.
Fibromyalgia was more prevalent among patients carrying more than one rheumatologic diagnosis (RA, SLE, PsA, SS).
Fibromyalgia was significantly correlated with higher RAPID3 disease activity scores in all patient groups except those with psoriatic arthritis.
Higher BMI was significantly correlated with greater RAPID3 disease activity scores in patients with rheumatoid arthritis.
Higher BMI was significantly correlated with greater RAPID3 disease activity scores in patients with Sjogren's syndrome.

A panel of five circulating microRNAs (miR-130a-3p, miR-130b-3p, let-7a-5p, let-7b-5p, let-7f-5p) accurately distinguished RCVS patients from age- and sex-matched controls across three independent cohorts.
Let-7a-5p, let-7b-5p, and let-7f-5p (but not miR-130a-3p or miR-130b-3p) were significantly elevated in patients with ictal migraine compared with controls and patients with interictal migraine.

Target prediction and pathway enrichment analysis implicated the TGF-beta signaling pathway and endothelin-1, both involved in vasomotor control, as links between the identified miRNAs and RCVS pathogenesis, a finding supported by in vitro experiments in vascular endothelial cells.
miR-130a-3p levels were associated with imaging-proven disruption of the blood-brain barrier in patients with RCVS.
Unlike the let-7 family miRNAs, miR-130b-3p abundance did not significantly differ between patients with ictal migraine and controls or interictal migraine patients.

Target prediction and pathway enrichment analysis suggested that the transforming growth factor-beta signaling pathway and endothelin-1, which are responsible for vasomotor control, link the identified miRNAs to RCVS pathogenesis.

Incubating vascular endothelial cells with cerebrospinal fluid from RCVS patients, or transfecting them with miRNA mimics, reproduced functional vascular effects consistent with the proposed miRNA-mediated mechanism.
Pain scores at rest and during chewing were significantly reduced after treatment in both the prolotherapy-alone group and the prolotherapy-plus-arthrocentesis group.
Locking episode frequency decreased to a greater extent in the group receiving prolotherapy combined with arthrocentesis than in the prolotherapy-alone group, at both short- and long-term follow-up.
Overall, dextrose prolotherapy alone was found effective for managing TMJ hypermobility, but combining it with arthrocentesis appeared superior to prolotherapy alone.
Cluster headache attacks were rated as the most painful of all conditions examined, with a mean intensity of 9.7/10, compared to 7.2 for labor pain, 7.0 for pancreatitis, and 6.9 for nephrolithiasis.
Most cluster headache respondents (72.1%) rated their attack pain as the maximum possible score of 10.0.

Cluster headache patients reporting maximal pain (10/10) had a higher proportion of most cranial autonomic features, were more often female, had higher headache frequency, lower calcium channel blocker effectiveness, and higher HDSQ (hopelessness) scores.
Nasal congestion was the only cranial autonomic feature not significantly associated with maximal cluster headache pain.
Restlessness/agitation was more frequent in the maximal pain group but did not reach statistical significance.
Maximal pain in cluster headache was not associated with migraine-like features such as nausea/vomiting, photophobia/phonophobia, or aggravation by physical activity.
Respondents with maximal cluster headache pain reported lower calcium channel blocker effectiveness than those with less than maximal pain.
Average cluster headache pain intensity was higher in female respondents and differed significantly by country.
Country-level differences in cluster headache pain intensity were confounded by sex, with country differences present only among female respondents.
HDSQ (hopelessness) scores were significantly higher in cluster headache respondents with maximal pain, while BDI depression scores did not reach significance.
Maximal cluster headache pain was more likely in respondents with more attacks per day, but was not associated with headache duration.

Respondents who had also experienced nephrolithiasis, migraine, or arthritis were more likely to rate their cluster headache pain as maximal (10/10) than those without those comorbid pain experiences.
Heritability of PTSD was estimated at 43% in this male twin sample.
Heritability of having any one or more chronic pain condition was estimated at 34% in this sample.
Migraine headache showed the highest heritability among the individual pain conditions examined, at 41%.
Tension headaches had the lowest heritability among the pain conditions studied, at 15%, with a confidence interval spanning zero.
A moderate-to-high genetic correlation was found between PTSD and combined history of any chronic pain condition.
The genetic correlation between PTSD and migraine headache was the lowest among individual pain conditions examined.
The genetic correlation between PTSD and tension headache was estimated at 0.75, the highest among the individual pain conditions examined.
The authors hypothesize that small-molecule migraine drugs act as haptens that bind peptide carriers to form immunogenic hapten-carrier complexes capable of provoking strong immune responses.

The paper proposes that immune reactions to hapten-carrier complexes formed by migraine drugs can generate neutralizing IgG and IgA class anti-drug antibodies, analogous to the anti-drug antibody-induced tolerance seen with biologic therapeutics, and that this underlies refractoriness to migraine drugs.
Medication-overuse headache is described as a secondary disorder that can develop following migraine, considered among the mechanisms of pharmacological refractoriness in refractory migraine.
Lamotrigine produced headache improvement in 76% of patients and was classified as effective (responder) in 56%, with no significant difference between SUNCT and SUNA.
Oxcarbazepine improved headache in 71% of patients with 46% classified as responders, similarly effective in SUNCT and SUNA.
Carbamazepine improved headache in 50% of patients with 26% classified as responders, with SUNA showing a higher improvement rate than SUNCT (though not significant after Bonferroni correction).
Topiramate improved headache in 47% of patients with only 25% classified as responders, and was more effective in SUNCT than SUNA for responder classification.
Gabapentin improved headache in only 33% of patients with 10% classified as responders, lower efficacy than a prior audit reported.
Pregabalin improved headache in 30% of patients with only 11% classified as responders.
Duloxetine, used off-label in refractory patients, improved headache in 49% with 30% classified as responders, and was more effective in SUNCT than SUNA.
Mexiletine, tried in refractory patients, produced headache improvement in 60% but with poor tolerability leading to high discontinuation.
Lacosamide, tried in a very small refractory subgroup, produced headache improvement in 33% of patients with reliable data.
Intravenous lidocaine infusion produced an excellent but often short-lived response, with 90% of patients classified as responders and no significant difference between SUNCT and SUNA.
Greater occipital nerve blocks produced headache improvement in 37% of patients with only 27% classified as responders, a lower rate than seen in cluster headache or in a prior SUNHA audit.
Pooled single-arm meta-analysis of published studies confirmed lamotrigine as the most effective oral treatment, with responder proportions of 64% in SUNCT and 46% in SUNA.
In the pooled meta-analysis, topiramate was the only treatment showing a statistically significant difference in responder proportion between SUNCT and SUNA, being more effective in SUNCT.

The authors cite evidence in trigeminal neuralgia showing downregulation of the sodium channel Nav1.7, proposed as a shared pathophysiological mechanism with SUNCT/SUNA given similar drug response profiles.

The authors cite evidence in trigeminal neuralgia showing upregulation of the sodium channel Nav1.3, proposed together with Nav1.7 downregulation as a possible shared mechanism with SUNHA given the efficacy of sodium channel blockers.

Across fibromyalgia trials, MBSR showed superiority over usual treatment (and in two trials over a multicomponent psychoeducational treatment) in reducing fibromyalgia impact and symptomatology, with large effect sizes maintained at one year.
One fibromyalgia/chronic low back pain trial reported CBT was superior to MBSR for short-term improvement in depression.
In chronic low back pain, one trial found pain improved equally with MBSR and CBT compared to usual care at one-year follow-up, but not at post-treatment.
In a chronic low back pain trial, MBSR and CBT (vs usual care) improved coping, functional self-efficacy, and pain self-efficacy, with effects partly maintained at 6 months.
For headache/migraine, MBSR was reported to be superior to MBCT for pain intensity compared to usual care, but both underlying studies were judged high risk of bias.
In headache/migraine trials, self-efficacy in pain control improved in the short term with both MBSR and MBCT compared to usual care.
In Wells et al. (2014), MBSR improved physical health, mental health, global health, energy/vitality, and emotional health in migraine patients compared to usual care.
In Day et al. (2014), MBCT for migraine improved acceptance and headache control relative to treatment-delayed control, with large effect sizes in both intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses.
In Omidi and Zargar (2015), MBSR reduced tension headache symptoms and bodily pain compared to usual care.

The risk of bias assessment (Cochrane tool) rated fibromyalgia and non-specific chronic pain trials as low risk, headache/migraine trials as high risk, and chronic low back pain trials as variable risk.

The authors hypothesize that mindfulness interventions may be more effective for diagnoses within the Central Sensitization Syndrome spectrum (fibromyalgia, chronic low back pain, headache/migraine), which shared improvement in pain-related symptomatology, whereas non-specific chronic pain showed improvement mainly in less specific outcomes like vitality and mental health.

Across all reviewed diagnoses, mindfulness interventions produced improvements in a greater number of outcome variables compared to usual care, with variable maintenance over time, and MBSR had substantially more supporting evidence than MBCT.

Direct trials comparing mindfulness interventions with CBT were found only for chronic low back pain and were not comparable between themselves; no clear conclusion about superiority of either treatment could be drawn for any diagnosis, including headache/migraine, where no CBT comparison trials were found.
Patients with migraine had a higher adjusted odds of having at least one autoimmune condition than migraine-free controls.
Other pain conditions were more than twice as prevalent among migraine patients compared with controls.

Respiratory conditions, neurological conditions, and cerebrovascular conditions were all significantly more common in migraine patients than controls, while unadjusted cardiovascular disease was more common in controls.
Comorbid neurological conditions other than migraine were substantially more common among migraine patients than controls.
Cerebrovascular disease was significantly more common among migraine patients than controls.
Although raw cardiovascular disease prevalence was numerically higher among controls, after adjusting for demographics migraine patients had significantly higher odds of cardiovascular disease.
Type 1 diabetes was the only autoimmune condition examined that did not differ in prevalence between migraine patients and controls.

Several additional conditions—sleep apnea, irritable bowel syndrome, GERD, deep vein thrombosis, and pulmonary embolism—were also more common among migraine patients than controls, though specific rates were not given in the text.
Among migraine patients, those who consulted a neurologist had a higher prevalence of depression than those treated only in primary care.
Anxiety was more prevalent among neurology-treated migraine patients than primary-care-only migraine patients.
Pain disorders including fibromyalgia, temporomandibular joint disorder, and arthritis were more common among neurology-treated migraine patients than primary-care-only migraine patients.
Respiratory conditions such as asthma and allergies/hay fever were more common in migraine patients treated by neurologists than those treated only in primary care.
Neurology encounter rates showed the largest discrepancy between migraine patients and controls of any care-utilization type examined.
Migraine patients were about twice as likely to have ED encounters and 1.17-1.47 times more likely to have primary care visits than controls.
Among migraine patients, those treated by a neurologist had slightly more encounters per patient-year in every care category than those treated only in primary care.
Most migraine patients received at least one acute migraine medication order, with neurology-treated patients more likely to receive such orders than primary-care-only patients.
Opioids were prescribed to more than half of migraine patients, and were more commonly prescribed to those treated by neurologists than those treated only in primary care.

Opioid prescribing for migraine varied by race/ethnicity and sex: Hispanic and non-Hispanic Asian patients had lower odds of being prescribed opioids than non-Hispanic whites, while women had higher odds than men.
About 61% of migraine patients received at least one preventive medication order, with a substantially higher rate among those treated by neurologists than those treated only in primary care.
Migraine patients treated by neurologists were more likely to have preexisting (prevalent) migraine than those treated only in primary care.

Average medication possession ratio for the three most commonly prescribed preventive medication classes (beta blockers, antidepressants, anticonvulsants) exceeded 75% and did not differ between PC-only and neurology-treated migraine patients.
Two-thirds of patients who started topiramate received only a single prescription order during the 5-year study period, suggesting high discontinuation.
Among migraine patients, Hispanic and non-Hispanic Black patients used the emergency department more than non-Hispanic White and Asian patients, regardless of PC-M or N-M group.
Among frequent consulters with migraine, preventive medication use was higher for neurology-treated patients than PC-only patients, though the gap narrowed compared with the overall migraine sample.
Type 1 diabetes was the only autoimmune condition that did not differ in prevalence between migraine patients and controls.

Antidepressants were the most commonly prescribed class of preventive migraine medication, followed by anticonvulsants, beta blockers, and calcium channel blockers, with onabotulinumtoxinA the least prescribed, and neurologists prescribed all preventive classes more frequently than PCPs with the greatest gap for anticonvulsants and onabotulinumtoxinA.
Migraine patients had a substantially higher rate of neurology encounters compared with controls, the largest discrepancy among the utilization types examined.
Migraine patients were twice as likely as controls to have emergency department encounters and 1.17 to 1.47 times more likely to have primary care visits.

The study identified 94,149 migraine patients (7% of the primary care population) and 1,248,763 controls from Sutter Health's 5-year primary care population, representing one of the largest EHR-based migraine cohorts reported.
Self-reported ecological momentary assessment data were successfully collected on a mean of 88.9% of assigned days and 68.9% of assigned reporting moments over the 28-day monitoring period.
Wearable biosensor data capturing autonomic arousal and physical activity were obtained for a mean of 18.7 hours per day of wear across an average of 20.3 monitoring days.
Reliability of collecting objective environmental and sensory data (e.g., ambient noise and light) from participants' own phones was highly variable, ranging from 16.7% to 73.3% of participants.
Most participants rated the intensive monitoring methodology as acceptable, with 63.3%-100% responding at least 'somewhat agree' on acceptability survey items.
A minority of participants (16.7%-23.3%) reported difficulties with study burden and remembering to wear the sensor.
Almost all participants (96.7%) reported wanting information about when a migraine might occur, supporting interest in predictive monitoring approaches.
Depression/major depressive disorder was the most prevalent comorbidity across reviewed studies, with a sample size-weighted lifetime prevalence of up to 63% among fibromyalgia patients.
Roughly one-third of fibromyalgia patients had current or lifetime bipolar disorder, panic disorder, or post-traumatic stress disorder.
Generalized anxiety disorder, obsessive compulsive disorder, and specific phobias (agoraphobia, social phobia) were reported as less common psychiatric comorbidities in fibromyalgia patients.
Chronic tension-type or migraine headache was among the chronic pain comorbidities found at high prevalence (39%-76%) in fibromyalgia patients.
Irritable bowel syndrome was identified as one of the highly prevalent chronic pain comorbidities in fibromyalgia patients, elevated compared to other conditions in clinic-based studies.
Myofascial pain syndrome and temporomandibular disorders were reported as prevalent chronic pain comorbidities among fibromyalgia patients.
Anxiety-related disorders were reported as much less common comorbidities than depression among fibromyalgia patients in the reviewed studies.
The prevalence of generalized joint hypermobility among college students was found to be 11.0%.
Participants with GJH showed a greater active range of motion in anterior/posterior tibial translation of the knee than those without GJH during treadmill gait.
Participants with GJH exhibited greater knee flexion at the end of the terminal stance phase of gait compared to the normal group.
The GJH group showed greater anterior translation of the tibia during almost the entire gait cycle compared to the normal group.
A greater external rotation angle of the knee was observed in the GJH group during the middle stance phase of gait compared to the normal group.
