Erenumab treatment produced a sustained reduction in monthly migraine days throughout the 5-year open-label treatment phase, with a mean reduction of 5.3 days (62.3%) from baseline at the final 4-week assessment.
A large proportion of patients maintained clinically meaningful reductions in migraine frequency (≥50%, ≥75%, and 100% reduction) throughout the 5-year open-label treatment phase.
Reduction in monthly acute migraine-specific medication (AMSM) use days achieved with erenumab was sustained across the 5-year open-label treatment phase.
HIT-6 total score, reflecting headache impact severity, improved from baseline and remained improved through 5 years of erenumab treatment.
The proportion of patients achieving a clinically meaningful (≥5-point) reduction in HIT-6 score increased over time and was maintained through the end of the 5-year treatment phase.

Migraine-specific quality of life across role function-restrictive, role function-preventive, and emotional function domains improved from baseline and was maintained through week 268 of erenumab treatment.
MIDAS total score, along with presenteeism and absenteeism subdomains, improved from baseline and remained improved through week 268, exceeding the threshold considered clinically meaningful.

Over 5 years of open-label erenumab exposure, the overall adverse event incidence rate was not increased compared with the double-blind pooled placebo/erenumab data, with nasopharyngitis, upper respiratory tract infection, and influenza the most frequent events.

A small proportion of patients discontinued erenumab due to adverse events over the 5-year open-label phase, with rash and depression each reported in two patients and all other events single occurrences.

Serious adverse events occurred in a minority of patients over 5 years of erenumab exposure and were not increased compared with placebo or erenumab rates from the pooled double-blind analysis, generally occurring as isolated events without a clear treatment-related pattern.

Two deaths occurred during the 5-year open-label treatment phase, one from arteriosclerosis/hypertensive heart disease confounded by preexisting cardiovascular risk factors and substance use, and one of unclear cause in a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus; both were assessed by investigators as unrelated to erenumab.
Systolic and diastolic blood pressure showed only minor increases over 5 years of erenumab treatment, comparable to age-related increases reported in the general population.
Hypertension incidence during the open-label treatment phase was lower than that observed with placebo in the pooled double-blind placebo-controlled analysis.
Constipation rates during the open-label extension were lower than those seen with erenumab in the pooled double-blind placebo-controlled analysis and did not lead to any treatment discontinuations.
A small subset of patients developed binding anti-erenumab antibodies over the study, with a much smaller subset developing neutralizing antibodies.
Most anti-erenumab antibody responses were transient, with the majority of patients reverting to seronegative status by end of study, and most antibody formation occurred early in treatment.
No association was found between the presence of anti-erenumab antibodies and safety events.
A majority of patients remained on erenumab throughout the 5-year open-label extension, with especially high retention among those who tolerated the dose increase to 140 mg.

Erenumab was associated with substantially lower rates of discontinuation due to adverse events over 5 years than historically reported for oral migraine preventives such as topiramate over a much shorter open-label period.

Sphenopalatine ganglion nerve block with 4% lidocaine produced a statistically significant mean reduction in pain scores of 2.4 points on the VAS in pediatric patients with migraine or status migrainosus.
All 489 pediatric SPG block procedures achieved 100% technical success under fluoroscopic guidance.
No immediate or acute complications were observed following pediatric SPG nerve block procedures.
Erenumab significantly reduced migraine-related physical impairment (MPFID-PI score) from baseline to Week 12 compared with placebo, which worsened.
Erenumab significantly reduced migraine impact on everyday activities (MPFID-EA score) from baseline to Week 12 compared with placebo.
A significantly higher proportion of erenumab-treated patients achieved a clinically meaningful ≥5-point reduction in MPFID-EA score at Week 12 compared with placebo.
A significantly higher proportion of erenumab-treated patients achieved a clinically meaningful ≥5-point reduction in MPFID-PI score at Week 12 compared with placebo.
Nearly twice as many erenumab-treated patients achieved a ≥5-point reduction in HIT-6 total score at Week 12 compared with placebo.
Erenumab produced a significantly greater mean reduction in HIT-6 score from baseline than placebo at every assessed timepoint (Weeks 4, 8 and 12).

Erenumab treatment led to significant improvements versus placebo in three of four Work Productivity and Activity Index (WPAI) parameters at Week 12, including work impairment and activity impairment due to headache.
More than twice the proportion of erenumab-treated patients achieved a ≥50% reduction in monthly migraine days at Week 12 compared with placebo.
Preliminary registry data suggest that chronic corticosteroid use at doses above 10 mg per day is associated with worse COVID-19 outcomes in patients with rheumatic disease.
Preliminary registry data suggest that use of biologic therapies, especially TNF inhibitors, could be protective against severe COVID-19 in patients with rheumatic disease.
Registry data indicate that conventional DMARDs, including hydroxychloroquine, have a neutral effect on COVID-19 outcomes in patients with rheumatic disease.
Registry data show that paediatric patients with rare connective tissue diseases have a much lower risk of clinically significant COVID-19 infection than patients over 61 years old.

A survey of one European rCTD patient community found that only 44% of patients with on-label hydroxychloroquine use obtained on-the-spot drug delivery in early April 2020, and 6.7% experienced a delay of two weeks or more, reflecting pandemic-related drug supply gaps.
An Italian national survey of rare disease patients found that more than half of respondents reported challenges accessing follow-up care during the pandemic.
EULAR provisional recommendations state there is currently no evidence that patients with rheumatic diseases are at higher risk of contracting SARS-CoV-2 or of having a worse prognosis once infected.
Low-frequency/high-frequency ratio of heart rate variability significantly predicted mortality in moderate to severe traumatic brain injury with an AUC ROC of 0.810.
High-frequency peak of heart rate variability showed excellent predictive accuracy for mortality after traumatic brain injury, with low heterogeneity across studies.
Total power of heart rate variability significantly predicted mortality in traumatic brain injury but with high heterogeneity and evidence of publication bias among included studies.
Higher LF/HF ratio was associated with substantially increased odds of mortality in traumatic brain injury patients.
Higher HF peak was associated with substantially increased odds of mortality in traumatic brain injury patients.
Higher total power was associated with substantially increased odds of mortality in traumatic brain injury patients.
Among episodic migraine (EM) participants treated with fremanezumab, 73.8% met the responder threshold of a ≥2 monthly migraine day reduction.
Among chronic migraine (CM) participants treated with fremanezumab, 56.7% met the responder threshold of a ≥4 monthly migraine day reduction.
EM responders had markedly larger reductions in monthly migraine days with fremanezumab than the overall EM population.
CM responders had markedly larger reductions in monthly migraine days with fremanezumab than the overall CM population.
EM nonresponders showed essentially no benefit, with a slight increase in monthly migraine days over the treatment period.
CM nonresponders showed minimal reduction in monthly migraine days compared with CM responders.
Among EM responders, a majority achieved a ≥50% reduction in monthly migraine days, far exceeding the rate seen in nonresponders.
Among CM responders, over half achieved a ≥50% reduction in monthly migraine days, far exceeding the rate seen in nonresponders.
About a quarter of EM responders achieved a ≥75% reduction in monthly migraine days, higher than the overall EM population.
A subset of CM responders achieved a ≥75% reduction in monthly migraine days, higher than the overall CM population.
EM responders had much larger reductions in acute headache medication use days than EM nonresponders.
CM responders had much larger reductions in acute headache medication use days than CM nonresponders.
EM responders had greater reductions in headache-related disability (MIDAS score) than the overall EM population.
CM responders had greater reductions in headache-related disability (HIT-6 score) than the overall CM population.
EM and CM responders showed larger improvements across all three MSQoL domains than nonresponders and the overall population.
The HIT-6 score reductions observed in CM responders exceeded the established minimal clinically important difference for chronic daily headache.
CM responders shifted from severe to substantial/moderate headache impact categories on the HIT-6 after 12 weeks of fremanezumab.
EM responders showed a 72% reduction in MIDAS score, shifting from severe to mild disability categories after fremanezumab.
EM responders reduced their acute headache medication use from baseline to a level that may lower medication overuse headache risk.
CM responders reduced their acute headache medication use from baseline to a level that may lower medication overuse headache risk.
Maximum cardiovagal baroreflex gain (Gmax) measured supine by the modified Oxford method was smaller in POTS patients than in healthy controls.

The response range of the sigmoidal cardiovagal baroreflex curve was reduced in POTS patients while supine, indicating this is not a simple resetting but a genuine deformation of the baroreflex curve.
In POTS, the centering point of the sigmoidal baroreflex curve (where Gmax occurs) was displaced downward to a smaller RR interval and to the left to a lower systolic pressure compared with control.
Pyridostigmine (and digoxin) increased supine Gmax in POTS patients, restoring it to values similar to healthy controls, whereas Gmax remained unchanged with placebo.

Digoxin fully repaired the supine cardiovagal baroreflex deficit in POTS, correcting the centering point's blood pressure and RR-interval location, normalizing Gmax, and expanding the response range beyond control values, whereas pyridostigmine corrected Gmax and centering-point pressure but not the RR-interval displacement or response range.

Neither pyridostigmine nor digoxin corrected the upright (tilted) cardiovagal baroreflex deficit in POTS; the operating point remained shifted onto the flat portion of the sigmoidal curve because of a persistently reduced response range, despite Gmax and centering point being reasonably sustained.

Spontaneous baroreflex sensitivity indices (alpha index and sequence method) were larger in controls than in POTS, and these indices were increased by pyridostigmine and digoxin to levels comparable with control when supine, but decreased once tilted.
Systemic vascular resistance was decreased in POTS patients compared with control both supine and upright.
Supine heart rate was higher in untreated and placebo-treated POTS patients than in controls, but became similar to control following administration of either pyridostigmine or digoxin.

Sodium nitroprusside produced a greater heart-rate increase in POTS than in controls, consistent with a proposed deficiency in endogenous nitrergic nitric oxide leading to a potentiated response to exogenous nitric oxide donor.
Pyridostigmine blunted the sodium-nitroprusside-mediated heart rate increase in POTS both after supine dosing and during tilt, suggesting ganglionic potentiation of nitrergic parasympathetic nerves.

The relatively reduced bradycardic response to phenylephrine during tilt in POTS (except in the pyridostigmine group) was interpreted as consistent with previously reported anti-alpha-1 adrenergic receptor antibodies in POTS.

POTS patients have normal muscle sympathetic nerve activity while supine but increased muscle sympathetic nerve activity when upright compared with healthy controls, suggesting a reflex response with intact arterial baroreflex afferents.
Low-frequency systolic arterial pressure variability, an indicator of sympathetic activation, increased in POTS patients when upright.
During tilt, cardiac output during the SNP phase of the modified Oxford method was lower in POTS than control, except in the digoxin-treated group where it was similar to control.

In untreated or placebo-treated POTS, the operating point was shifted toward the flat, nonlinear 'knee' region of the sigmoidal baroreflex curve relative to control, where control operating points remained near the linear center, resulting in markedly reduced operating-point slope in POTS.

Gmax and response range remained unchanged with tilt in controls but were reduced in POTS supine and further reduced with upright tilt, along with additional left-lateral and downward shifts of centering and operating points.

Supine systolic arterial pressure was reduced in unmedicated POTS patients compared with control, but increased to control levels following administration of pyridostigmine or digoxin while remaining supine.
Antiepileptic drugs used for headache prevention in pregnancy may be associated with fetal/child adverse effects.
Venlafaxine used for headache prevention in pregnancy may be associated with fetal/child adverse effects.
Tricyclic antidepressants used for headache prevention in pregnancy may be associated with fetal/child adverse effects.
Benzodiazepines used for headache prevention in pregnancy may be associated with fetal/child adverse effects.
Beta-blockers used for headache prevention in pregnancy may be associated with fetal/child adverse effects.
Low-dose aspirin used for headache treatment during pregnancy may not be associated with fetal or child adverse effects, based on indirect evidence.
The systematic review found insufficient evidence to evaluate non-pharmacologic treatments for primary headache during pregnancy, postpartum, or breastfeeding.
No evidence was found addressing the effectiveness of any intervention for preventing primary headaches during pregnancy or postpartum.
One reported pediatric case demonstrated a typical association between migraine and red ear syndrome.
A second pediatric case presented with idiopathic red ear syndrome without an identified underlying trigger.
A third pediatric case had red ear syndrome attacks showing many similarities with trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias.
The authors propose that the different forms of red ear syndrome share a common autonomic pathogenetic mechanism involving parasympathetic hyperactivity and sympathetic inhibition.

The variability in temporal characteristics and frequency of red ear syndrome attacks may reflect activation of distinct physiopathological neuronal modules related to pain circuits, per the modular theory of headache.
Young women are reported to be five times more likely than young men to experience orthostatic intolerance.
Nearly a quarter of ankylosing spondylitis patients met screening criteria for concomitant fibromyalgia syndrome.
Plasma PTX-3 levels were significantly higher in AS patients with concomitant fibromyalgia than in AS patients without fibromyalgia.
PTX-3 levels in AS patients without fibromyalgia did not significantly differ from those in matched healthy controls.
PTX-3 demonstrated moderate diagnostic performance for identifying concomitant fibromyalgia in AS patients, with 62.3% sensitivity and 90% specificity.
Plasma PTX-3 levels were significantly higher in AS patients with concomitant fibromyalgia than in AS patients without fibromyalgia.
AS patients without fibromyalgia showed no significant difference in plasma PTX-3 levels compared to matched healthy controls.
Plasma PTX-3 levels correlated positively with disease duration, functional impairment (BASFI), and quality-of-life impairment (ASQoL) in AS patients.
Age, female sex, switching of biologic DMARDs, ASDAS-CRP, and PTX-3 were significant independent predictors of concomitant fibromyalgia in AS patients.
Plasma PTX-3 demonstrated moderate diagnostic accuracy for identifying concomitant fibromyalgia in AS patients, comparable to clinical features.
The authors state that underlying cavovarus deformity and joint hypermobility must be identified and addressed during revision surgical stabilization for recurrent lateral ankle instability.
The review describes CGRP inhibitors as an emerging preventive therapeutic class for migraine developed after decades of translational research.
CGRP has several known systemic actions beyond its role in migraine that raise concerns about potential off-target effects of CGRP-targeting therapeutics.
African Americans with nOH showed markedly lower upright renin activity than non-Hispanic whites with nOH.
African Americans with nOH showed a blunted upright aldosterone increase compared to non-Hispanic whites.
Baseline autonomic clinical characteristics did not differ significantly between African American and non-Hispanic white patients with nOH.
The findings suggest persistent suppression of the renin-angiotensin system in African Americans with nOH, particularly during upright posture.

A structured pain neuroscience education (PNE) group intervention significantly reduced the total Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (FIQ) score compared with treatment as usual over the 1-year study period.
At 1 month, the PNE intervention produced large effect sizes versus control across nearly all FIQ dimensions, with only anxiety showing a medium effect size.
At 12 months, effect sizes of the PNE intervention versus control remained large for pain, fatigue, morning tiredness, anxiety and total FIQ score, and medium for the remaining FIQ dimensions.
The PNE intervention was more effective than treatment as usual in reducing BPI-SF (severity and interference), HADS (anxiety and depression), HAQ, PCS, and PSD scores.
After 1 month of treatment, effect sizes of the PNE intervention were large across all secondary questionnaires except for a medium effect size on the HADS depression subscale.
At 12 months, the effect size of the PNE intervention remained large across secondary questionnaires except for medium effect sizes on the HADS anxiety subscale and HAQ.
The proportion of patients achieving ≥20% reduction, ≥50% reduction, and FIQ score <39 was significantly higher in the PNE intervention group than in controls at every study time point.
The PNE intervention was associated with an absolute risk reduction of 49.7% and a number needed to treat of about 2 patients to achieve a ≥20% reduction in total FIQ score.

The PNE intervention was associated with an absolute risk reduction of 35.2% and a number needed to treat of 2.83 to achieve a ≥50% reduction in total FIQ score, more favourable than a comparator acceptance and commitment therapy trial's NNT of 46.

The PNE intervention was associated with an absolute risk reduction of 39.5% and a number needed to treat of 2.53 for achieving a total FIQ score below 39 (no worse than moderate functional impairment).
The case series proposes Sjögren's syndrome as an underdiagnosed cause of facial pain, presented alongside a review of neurological manifestations of the disease.

A CDC follow-up of nearly 300 PCR-positive COVID-19 patients found that almost half still had symptoms such as fatigue and cough three weeks after their positive test, particularly older patients or those with chronic disease.
Italian investigators found that 60 days after COVID-19 onset, more than half of 143 patients had multiple persistent bothersome symptoms and 41% reported a worsened quality of life.
Irish investigators found that at a median of 10 weeks after COVID-19 symptom onset, 52% of 128 patients reported persistent fatigue and 31% had not returned to work.
In the same Irish cohort, post-COVID fatigue showed no association with the severity of the acute illness or with routine laboratory markers of inflammation and cell turnover.

An international online survey of 3,762 self-reported COVID-19 patients found that at 7 months, fatigue, post-exertional malaise, and cognitive dysfunction—core ME/CFS symptoms—persisted in 77.9%, 71.2%, and 56.8% of respondents respectively, and 67.5% were unable to work or needed a reduced schedule.
CDC and NASEM estimate that between 836,000 and 2.5 million Americans have ME/CFS, with annual direct and indirect economic costs of $17-24 billion.

The authors project that if 25 million Americans are infected with SARS-CoV-2 by end of 2021 and 10% develop illness meeting ME/CFS criteria, this would roughly double the number of Americans with ME/CFS within a year, and globally could generate over 10 million new ME/CFS cases.

The authors propose that chronic low-grade neuroinflammation, with peripheral inflammation signaling to the brain largely via the vagus nerve, may activate a 'fatigue nucleus' and produce sickness-behavior-like fatigue in post-COVID and ME/CFS patients.
SARS-CoV-2 is reported to be able to infect the brain and cause neuroinflammation, which may underlie chronic fatigue in some long-COVID patients.

The authors note that impaired energy production, oxidative stress, ion channelopathies, and impaired cerebral perfusion have been identified as abnormalities in ME/CFS and could also explain post-COVID fatigue.
Dr. Anthony Fauci stated that some post-COVID-19 patients develop a post-viral syndrome that is strikingly similar to ME/CFS.

Post-infectious fatigue syndromes with symptoms resembling ME/CFS have been documented following diverse pathogens including SARS coronavirus, Epstein-Barr virus, Ross River virus, enteroviruses, HHV-6, Ebola, West Nile virus, Dengue virus, parvovirus, Borrelia burgdorferi, Coxiella burnetii, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and Giardia lamblia.
The NASEM case definition of ME/CFS requires that the illness has lasted at least 6 months, limiting current ability to classify early post-COVID illness as ME/CFS.

Most long-term longitudinal studies of ME/CFS conducted before the pandemic found that the illness had not abated after many years in most patients, though children with ME/CFS may have a somewhat better prognosis.
Patients with hereditary connective tissue disorders showed a higher than expected incidence of atlantoaxial instability.
Atlantoaxial instability was strongly associated with manifestations of dysautonomia, particularly syncope and lightheadedness.
All 20 patients with AAI reported lightheadedness, and 15 of 20 had refractory syncope or presyncope despite maximal medical management and physical therapy.
Surgical stabilization of the C1-C2 motion segment led to a statistically significant improvement in lightheadedness postoperatively.
Surgical stabilization of the C1-C2 motion segment led to a statistically significant improvement in presyncope postoperatively.
Surgical stabilization of the C1-C2 motion segment led to a statistically significant improvement in syncope postoperatively.

Following surgical stabilization of the atlantoaxial motion segment, patients reported statistically significant improvement in the frequency of other autonomic-related symptoms including nausea, exercise intolerance, palpitations, tremors, heat intolerance, gastroesophageal reflux, and sleep apnea.

A patient developed Horner's syndrome as a result of complete occlusion of the internal carotid artery on the same side as the affected eye, attributed to occlusive atherosclerotic carotid disease rather than dissection.
Occlusive carotid disease secondary to atherosclerosis is noted to be a relatively rare cause of Horner's syndrome compared to carotid arterial dissection, which is the most common vascular cause.

Across published natural history studies, annual increases in UMSARS-1 and UMSARS-2 scores showed highly variable standard deviations that often exceeded expected drug effect sizes, undermining statistical power for trials.
In the NHSS cohort, orthostatic symptoms, bowel function, and resting tremor items showed low standardized effect (<0.20), indicating poor ability to detect one-year disease change.
Dressing/hygiene and posture/gait items showed high standardized effect (>0.30), indicating good sensitivity to one-year disease progression.
An abridged 11-item version of the UMSARS showed a higher standardized effect and greater percent annual increase than the full 24-item scale over one year.

Power calculations showed the abridged 11-item UMSARS would require fewer randomized patients than the full UMSARS to detect the same treatment effect, translating into substantial cost savings for trials.

UMSARS-1 and UMSARS-2 scores exhibited an apparent ceiling effect, with no patients exceeding 43 and 49 points respectively despite higher maximum possible scores, suggesting the scale fails to capture change in advanced disease.
Patients with lower baseline UMSARS scores tended to have faster subsequent progression rates, significant for UMSARS-1 and near-significant for UMSARS-2.
UMSARS-1 and UMSARS-2 scores increased annually early in disease but plateaued after about five years of disease duration.
The UMSARS-1 sexual function item was excluded from previous MSA placebo-controlled trials to minimize variability and noise, reflecting difficulty scoring this item.
The UMSARS-2 oculomotor item showed only moderate intra- and inter-rater agreement during initial scale validation.

Orthostatic and bowel symptoms captured by UMSARS-1 can be improved with symptomatic non-pharmacologic and pharmacologic treatments (e.g., for constipation or orthostatic hypotension), which can confound assessment of true disease-modifying effects.
Patients with MSA report more burdensome symptoms when depressed, yet the UMSARS does not include a mood assessment item.

UMSARS-3 measures blood pressure after only 2 minutes of standing, whereas the consensus definition of orthostatic hypotension requires readings within 3 minutes of standing, creating inconsistency for cross-study comparison.
The gait items in UMSARS-1 (history-based) and UMSARS-2 (exam-based) are redundant, inflating internal consistency but increasing administration time.
12 weeks of resistance training produced no significant improvement in maximum voluntary isometric contraction of knee extensors compared to a no-training control group.
Resistance training also did not significantly change maximum voluntary isometric contraction of knee flexors compared to the control group.
Secondary outcomes (RFD, thigh muscle cross-sectional area, mass and density) also showed no significant between-group differences, with small and heterogeneous effect sizes.
Ground reaction force parameters during stair ascent/descent showed no change attributable to training.
The training group showed a non-significant tendency toward increased vastus medialis EMG activity during stair descent.
In the untrained control group, vastus lateralis EMG activity showed a non-significant tendency to increase during stair descent over the 12-week period.
In the untrained control group, biceps femoris EMG activity tended to decrease during stair descent over the 12-week period.
SF-36 subscales showed minimal training effects, with only a tendency toward increased social role functioning in the control group and decreased physical functioning in the training group.
Only the AIMS-2 pain dimension showed a tendency to decrease in the training group, while the hypermobility questionnaire (HM-Q) showed no change with training.
Adherence to the self-guided resistance training program was good, with participants completing on average 19.4 of 24 sessions and 63% completing more than 80% of sessions.

One participant in the training group experienced an exacerbation of low back pain classified as an adverse event, later diagnosed as a lumbar disc herniation requiring surgery, with an unclear causal link to training.
Despite randomisation, the training group had significantly higher baseline knee extensor and flexor strength than the control group, likely due to chance given high inter-subject variability.
The large majority of participants with GJH reported some pain on the hypermobility questionnaire at baseline, suggesting many could be classified as having a hypermobility spectrum disorder.
About 43% of study participants fulfilled the Brighton criteria and might be diagnosed with joint hypermobility syndrome, contributing to sample heterogeneity.
A previous study found normalized rate of force development to be 16.2% higher in hypermobile women compared to women with normal joint mobility, which informed this trial's power calculation.

A prior study (To & Alexander, 2018) reported that persons with joint hypermobility syndrome had about 30% lower knee extensor muscle torque than healthy controls, whereas those with generalized joint hypermobility showed about 30% higher torque than controls.

In an external study, an individualized home-based exercise program produced about 100% improvement in knee extensor muscle torque similarly across JHS, GJH, and control subjects, contrasting with the null training effect found in the present trial.
A feasibility study found that participants with hypermobility spectrum disorder gained about 30% in shoulder strength after a 16-week heavy shoulder strengthening program.
An 8-week supervised spinal stabilization program improved trunk muscle endurance by about 50% in a study with methodological limitations including high drop-out and lack of blinding.
A non-significant tendency toward improved muscle density and cross-sectional area on pQCT was observed after training, though training intensity may have been insufficient to build muscle mass.
Male patients with reflex syncope had lower supine systolic blood pressure than age/sex-matched individuals from the general population.
Male patients with reflex syncope showed markedly lower pulse pressure than the general population, consistent with reduced stroke volume.
Male patients with reflex syncope had higher diastolic blood pressure than the general population, interpreted as a compensatory increase in peripheral vascular resistance.
Male patients with reflex syncope had higher resting heart rate than the general population.
Female patients with reflex syncope had lower pulse pressure than the general population.
Female patients with reflex syncope had higher diastolic blood pressure than the general population.
Female patients with reflex syncope had higher resting heart rate than the general population.
Mean arterial pressure did not differ between male reflex syncope patients and the general population, suggesting preserved overall cardiovascular homeostasis.
Mean arterial pressure did not differ between female reflex syncope patients and the general population.
In patients with reflex syncope, the pattern of age-related SBP increase differed by sex, with a significant sex-by-age interaction.
Rate of antihypertensive drug use was correlated with the average age of the studies but did not confound the syncope-vs-general-population comparison.
Baroreceptor sensitivity has been shown to be elevated in reflex syncope patients, which may explain their more pronounced sympathetic and haemodynamic responses to orthostatic challenge.
The presyncopal phase of circulatory instability in reflex syncope is accompanied by a distinct surge in epinephrine.
The presyncopal phase of circulatory instability in reflex syncope is accompanied by a distinct surge in vasopressin.
The authors hypothesize that female individuals' generally lower circulating blood volume and skeletal mass contribute to their higher heart rate and predisposition to reflex syncope.
The relative frequency of reflex syncope by age and sex tracks with the sex-specific SBP levels, potentially explaining the bimodal age distribution of syncope incidence.
TMD symptom prevalence in the US population is five-fold higher among people with severe headache or migraine than those without.
In the Finland Health 2000 Survey, presence of TMD was associated with greater frequency of migraine attacks.
TMD patients show much higher headache comorbidity than dental patients in both US and Brazilian studies.
In a prospective cohort of TMD-free individuals, migraine (but not tension-type headache) was a major risk factor for first onset of TMD.
Both migraine and TMD are associated with autonomic dysfunction, evidenced by reduced heart rate variability.
Propranolol produced a small reduction in mean facial pain index at week 9 among migraineurs but essentially no difference among non-migraineurs, with a non-significant interaction.
Propranolol's efficacy for achieving ≥30% reduction in facial pain index was substantially greater in migraineurs than non-migraineurs, though the interaction term was not statistically significant.
A similar pattern of greater propranolol efficacy in migraineurs was seen for ≥50% reduction in facial pain index, reflected in a lower number needed to treat.
Odds of a clinically meaningful ≥6-point reduction in HIT-6 score at week 9 were greater in migraineurs than non-migraineurs on propranolol.

Across a cumulative range of clinically meaningful response thresholds (20-70% FPI reduction), the treatment-group difference in area under the response curve was larger for migraineurs than non-migraineurs.
Change in facial pain index and change in headache impact (HIT-6) showed negligible correlation.
Causal mediation analysis showed only a weak indirect effect of propranolol on TMD pain reduction operating through change in headache impact (HIT-6), accounting for just 9% of the total effect.
Causal mediation analysis showed a stronger indirect effect of propranolol on TMD pain reduction operating through reduction in heart rate, accounting for 46% of the total effect.
Migraineurs with TMD had significantly higher TMD pain-related disability and pain intensity, and longer duration since TMD onset, compared with non-migraineurs.
A significantly higher percentage of migraineurs than non-migraineurs used headache medication during the trial.
Migraine prevalence of 52% among this myofascial TMD cohort was comparable to previously reported prevalence of 56% and 55% in other TMD cohorts.

The authors propose that propranolol's greater efficacy in migraineurs may reflect its ability to cross the blood-brain barrier and block chronic central sensitization of descending pain pathways to the trigeminocervical complex.
In a prior RCT in healthy males, propranolol increased heart rate variability but did not affect pressure pain sensitivity or other mechanistic pain biomarkers.
Generalized joint hypermobility (GJH), assessed by Beighton score ≥5/9, was identified in 40.9% (54/132) of young female dancers.
Dancers with GJH had significantly reduced dynamic postural balance in the anterior direction (Y Balance Test) compared with non-GJH dancers.
Dancers with GJH showed significantly lower ankle proprioception ability (AMEDA AUC score) than non-GJH dancers.
GJH dancers did not differ significantly from non-GJH dancers on BMI, YBT posterior-medial/posterior-lateral/composite scores, or knee extensor/flexor strength.
Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, identified via Adams forward-bend test and Magee's skyline view test, was present in 28.8% (38/132) of the dancers.
Scoliotic dancers had significantly weaker knee extensors than non-scoliotic dancers.
Scoliotic dancers had significantly weaker knee flexors than non-scoliotic dancers.
Scoliotic dancers had significantly reduced ankle proprioception ability compared with non-scoliotic dancers.
A quarter of the dancers (25.8%, 34/132) had both GJH and scoliosis together, a proportion significantly lower than dancers with neither anomaly (56.1%, 74/132).
Dancers with both GJH and scoliosis had significantly reduced dynamic postural balance in the anterior direction compared with dancers with neither anomaly.
Dancers with both GJH and scoliosis had significantly reduced proprioception ability compared with dancers with neither anomaly.
Dancers with both GJH and scoliosis had significantly weaker knee extensors than dancers with neither anomaly.
Dancers with both GJH and scoliosis had significantly weaker knee flexors than dancers with neither anomaly.
Bilateral patellofemoral pain was significantly more prevalent in GJH dancers (59.3%) than non-GJH dancers (30.8%), and far fewer GJH dancers had no PFP.
Bilateral patellofemoral pain was significantly more prevalent in scoliotic dancers (71.1%) than non-scoliotic dancers (30.9%).
Almost all dancers with both GJH and scoliosis suffered bilateral patellofemoral pain (73.5%), compared with 29.7% of dancers with neither anomaly.
The paper's discussion cites prior work suggesting GJH may contribute to scoliosis through altered collagen structure and cross-linking that compromises spinal integrity.
A cited non-dancer adolescent study found GJH in 51% of children/adolescents with scoliosis compared with 19% of those without scoliosis.
Of 5236 patients investigated for suspected vasovagal syncope, 60% had a positive tilt test.
Cardioinhibitory tilt test responses were more common in younger patients and decreased in prevalence from age 50-59 onward.
Vasodepressor tilt test responses prevailed in older patients, beginning at age 50-59.
Mixed cardioinhibitory-vasodepressor responses, the most common tilt test pattern overall, declined slightly with increasing age.
Overall tilt test positivity showed a significant age-related trend across the cohort.
Baseline systolic blood pressure was significantly related to tilt test positivity.
Most positive tilt tests occurred during the nitroglycerine-potentiated phase rather than the passive phase.
The positivity rate of the passive phase of tilt testing declined with increasing patient age.
Unlike the passive phase, the positivity rate of the nitroglycerine-potentiated phase of tilt testing remained stable across age groups.
When adjusted for age, the prevalence of cardioinhibitory and vasodepressor responses did not differ significantly between the passive and TNG-potentiated phases of tilt testing.

Age significantly impacts the haemodynamic pattern of tilt test responses beginning at age 50, with vagal hyperactivity dominant in younger patients and a shift toward vasodepressor responses in older patients, independent of tilt test phase once age-adjusted.
Early intravenous sumatriptan reduced the proportion of patients developing a PACAP38-induced migraine attack compared with placebo.
Despite reducing migraine incidence, sumatriptan did not significantly reduce overall headache intensity (area under the curve) compared with placebo.
Sumatriptan significantly constricted the PACAP38-dilated superficial temporal artery immediately after infusion compared with placebo.
The authors propose that sumatriptan prevents PACAP38-induced migraine through modulation of nociceptive transmission within the trigeminovascular system, linked to its early vasoconstrictive action.
Adolescent girls with GJH showed a significantly lower mean knee joint angle during treadmill walking than non-GJH girls, indicating increased knee flexion.
Girls with GJH showed a significantly lower minimum knee joint angle during treadmill walking than non-GJH girls, reflecting greater knee flexion at the flexion peak.
Maximum knee joint angle during treadmill walking did not differ significantly between GJH and non-GJH girls.
Knee joint range of motion during treadmill walking did not differ significantly between GJH and non-GJH girls.
Surface EMG activity of the quadriceps femoris during treadmill walking did not differ between girls with and without GJH.

Surface EMG activity of the hamstrings during treadmill walking did not differ between girls with and without GJH, in contrast to previously reported reduced hamstrings activity during isometric tasks.
Surface EMG activity of the gastrocnemius during treadmill walking did not differ between girls with and without GJH.

The hamstrings-quadriceps co-contraction index during treadmill walking did not differ significantly between girls with and without GJH, unlike prior findings of increased co-activation during isometric tasks.
The gastrocnemius-quadriceps co-contraction index during treadmill walking did not differ significantly between girls with and without GJH.

Permanent pacemaker therapy may be considered in vasovagal syncope patients who do not respond to standard therapy, but its efficacy remains controversial because a vasodepressor component during episodes is difficult to exclude.
There are limited medical therapies for vasovagal syncope that have been proven effective in randomized clinical trials.
At baseline (pre-HUT), NRS scores for pain, fatigue, and concentration difficulty were all significantly higher in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls.

Head-up tilt testing produced a significant increase in NRS pain, fatigue, and concentration scores at all post-HUT time points (immediately, 24h, 48h, 7 days) compared with pre-HUT baseline in both ME/CFS subgroups.
Fatigue and concentration abnormalities peaked immediately post-HUT, whereas pain perception peaked at 24 hours post-test with a further increase from immediately post-HUT to 24 hours.
In ME/CFS patients with and without FM, all three NRS scores remained significantly higher than pre-HUT baseline at 7 days after tilt testing, indicating prolonged post-exertional malaise.
In healthy controls only, NRS fatigue scores decreased significantly by 7 days after tilt testing, in contrast to the persistent elevation seen in ME/CFS patients.
The widespread pain index was significantly higher in FM+ ME/CFS patients than in FM- ME/CFS patients.
The symptom severity (SS) scale score did not differ significantly between FM+ and FM- ME/CFS patients.
NRS pain scores were significantly higher in FM+ ME/CFS patients than FM- patients at all measured time points (pre-HUT through 7 days).
NRS fatigue and concentration scores did not differ significantly between FM+ and FM- ME/CFS patients at any time point.
Among FM+ ME/CFS patients, those taking neuropathic pain medication had significantly higher pre-HUT NRS pain scores than those not taking such medication.
In the FM- ME/CFS group, there was no significant difference in NRS pain scores between those using neuropathic analgesics and those not.
ME/CFS patients, both with and without FM, had higher supine and end-of-HUT heart rates than healthy controls.
In the FM- ME/CFS group (n=104), 31 patients (30%) were classified as having POTS on head-up tilt testing.
In the FM+ ME/CFS group (n=174), 73 patients (42%) were classified as having POTS on head-up tilt testing.
The distribution of hemodynamic HUT classifications (normal, delayed orthostatic hypotension, POTS) did not differ significantly between ME/CFS patients with and without FM.
Muscle pain complaints were reported by 72% of ME/CFS patients without FM versus 100% of ME/CFS patients with FM.
The male/female ratio was significantly lower (i.e., a higher proportion of females) in the ME/CFS group with FM compared with the group without FM.
ME/CFS patients without FM were significantly taller than those with FM, although weight and BMI did not differ between the groups.
No significant relationship was found between the degree of cerebral blood flow reduction during HUT and NRS scores for pain, fatigue, or concentration at any time point.
The overall ME/CFS cohort showed a mean cerebral blood flow decline during tilt testing.
The large majority of ME/CFS participants exceeded normal limits for cerebral blood flow reduction during tilt testing.
Neuropathic pain medication was used by 38% of the overall ME/CFS cohort, with a higher proportion in the FM+ group (49%) than the FM- group (19%).
Topiramate was the most frequently initiated migraine preventive medication in this real-world cohort, used by 42.7% of patients at baseline.
Tricyclic antidepressants were the second most commonly initiated preventive medication class, used by 16.7% of patients.
Beta-blockers were initiated as migraine preventive treatment in 11.1% of patients.
OnabotulinumtoxinA was initiated in 10.3% of patients and was more frequently used among treatment-experienced patients.
NSAIDs were the most commonly used acute migraine medication at baseline, reported by 53.0% of patients.
Triptans were used as acute medication by 44.9% of patients at baseline despite initiation of preventive therapy.
18.4% of patients reported using opioids as acute migraine medication, raising concern given clinical guidelines on appropriate opioid use.
Nearly half of patients (49.6%) modified how they took their preventive medication one or more times without consulting their provider over 6 months.
Side effects were the leading patient-reported reason for permanently discontinuing preventive migraine medication.
Perceived lack of efficacy was a frequent reason given for discontinuing preventive migraine treatment.

Among patients who discontinued topiramate, side effects were cited more often (69.4%) than among the full sample discontinuing any preventive treatment (59.1%), suggesting topiramate-specific tolerability issues.
Patients experienced an average reduction of 3.7 migraine days per month from baseline to Month 6 after initiating preventive treatment.
Patients experienced an average reduction of 5.7 headache days per month from baseline to Month 6.

At baseline, severe migraine-related disability (MIDAS Grade IV) was present in the large majority of patients with chronic migraine (81.0%) and was more common in chronic migraine than in episodic migraine (59.3%).
Despite initiation of preventive treatment, 40.9% of patients continued to experience severe migraine disability at follow-up, indicating persistent unmet need.
At baseline, nearly all patients had severe headache impact on HIT-6, with slightly higher rates among chronic migraine (91.4%) than episodic migraine (85.6%) patients.

Over the 6-month follow-up, 65.4% of patients continued to experience severe headache impact despite preventive treatment initiation, with severe impact more frequent among treatment-experienced patients (72.9%).
At baseline, work productivity loss (53.3%) and daily activity impairment (57.0%) attributable to migraine were substantial among employed patients.
Over the 6-month follow-up, presenteeism (reduced on-the-job effectiveness) was nominally higher in chronic migraine patients (44.6%) than episodic migraine patients (40.0%).
Migraine pain severity was rated as severe at baseline (mean 7.7/10) and improved modestly by approximately 1-1.5 points over 6 months following preventive treatment initiation.

Emotional function was the most impacted MFIQ domain, with higher scores than other functional domains such as usual activities and social function, indicating migraine particularly affects emotional wellbeing.
At screening, treatment-experienced patients had a higher baseline frequency of monthly migraine days than treatment-naive patients.
TMD was identified in about a quarter of patients presenting to a neurology outpatient clinic with headache.
Sleep bruxism was present in nearly a quarter of the headache patient cohort.
TMD occurred more frequently among migraine patients than among the overall headache cohort's baseline rate.
TMD occurred in a smaller proportion of tension-type headache patients compared with migraine patients.
The rate of TMD was statistically significantly higher in migraine patients than in tension-type headache patients.
Among 223 UCPPS participants who underwent cystoscopy, 12.5% had Hunner lesion and 87.5% did not.
UCPPS participants with Hunner lesion were older than those without Hunner lesion.
UCPPS with Hunner lesion had increased nocturia compared with those without HL.
UCPPS patients with Hunner lesion were more likely to report painful urgency than those without Hunner lesion.
UCPPS patients without Hunner lesion reported more intense nonurologic pain than those with Hunner lesion.
UCPPS participants without Hunner lesion reported greater distribution of pain outside the pelvis than those with Hunner lesion.
UCPPS participants without Hunner lesion had a greater number of comorbid chronic overlapping pain conditions than those with Hunner lesion.
UCPPS participants without Hunner lesion had higher fibromyalgia-like symptoms than those with Hunner lesion.
UCPPS participants without Hunner lesion showed greater pain centralization than those with Hunner lesion.
UCPPS participants without Hunner lesion were more likely to report comorbid migraine headache than those with Hunner lesion.
UCPPS participants without Hunner lesion reported higher anxiety, perceived stress, and pain catastrophizing than those with Hunner lesion.

There were no differences between UCPPS with and without Hunner lesion in sex distribution, symptom duration, urologic pain intensity, genital pain distribution, pelvic floor tenderness, quality of life, depression, nociceptive vs. neuropathic pain characteristics, suprapubic mechanical hypersensitivity on quantitative sensory testing, or 3-year longitudinal pain and urinary outcomes.

The authors conclude that Hunner lesion UCPPS displays a more bladder-centric symptom profile, whereas non-Hunner lesion UCPPS displays symptoms suggestive of a more systemic pain syndrome, indicating these are distinct phenotypes.
Brain fog was reported significantly more frequently in patients with vestibular migraine and combined vestibular migraine/Meniere's disease than in patients with Meniere's disease alone.
Chronic fatigue was reported significantly more frequently in patients with vestibular migraine and combined vestibular migraine/Meniere's disease than in patients with Meniere's disease alone.
DHI scores were significantly higher in patients with vestibular migraine and combined vestibular migraine/Meniere's disease compared with those with Meniere's disease alone.
A DHI score of 13 or greater was associated with self-reported brain fog with 47.4% sensitivity and 72.3% specificity.
A DHI score of 15 or greater was associated with self-reported chronic fatigue with 81.5% sensitivity and 57.7% specificity.
The authors concluded that the DHI cannot reliably differentiate between vestibular disorder diagnoses nor detect cognitive impairment in these patient populations.
The proportion of female patients was higher among CIDP patients with concomitant Sjögren's syndrome (52%) compared to CIDP patients without Sjögren's syndrome (28%).
Cranial nerve impairment occurred significantly more often in CIDP patients with Sjögren's syndrome (39%) than in those without (14%).

No significant differences were found between the two CIDP groups in initial symptoms, INCAT disability score, sensory deficits, limb weakness, ataxia, pain, dysautonomia, CSF laboratory findings, or electrophysiological findings.

Degeneration and subsequent laxity of the sacroiliac joint, occurring as adjacent segment disease after long-segment lumbosacral fusion, led to distal construct failure and a progressively worsening leftward coronal spinal imbalance.

The kickstand rod technique was used to correct the sacroiliac-joint-laxity-induced coronal imbalance, reduce pain, and promote sacroiliac joint arthrodesis, with stable coronal balance maintained at 3.5 years follow-up and no significant complications.
CVS affects 1-2% of children, and there has been a recent dramatic rise in diagnosed adult cases.
A large subset of CVS patients, termed migraine-equivalent CVS, display strong clinical and genetic features overlapping with migraine.
The proposed unifying pathophysiologic core of CVS involves neuronal hyperexcitability and aberrant central modulation of autonomic signals.
Mitochondrial dysfunction and cellular energy deficits are proposed as a susceptibility factor increasing vulnerability to CVS triggering events.
Mitochondrial dysfunction and cellular energy deficits are proposed as a susceptibility factor underlying vulnerability to cyclic vomiting syndrome episodes.
A hyper-responsive hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis is described as a susceptibility factor contributing to cyclic vomiting syndrome vulnerability.
Cyclic vomiting syndrome episodes are frequently triggered by stressors and intercurrent illnesses.
An upper gastrointestinal contrast study is recommended as an essential diagnostic test of exclusion to rule out intestinal malrotation in cyclic vomiting syndrome workup.
Abdominal ultrasound is recommended to exclude renal hydronephrosis in children and biliary disease in adults with cyclic vomiting syndrome.
Lifestyle and non-pharmacological interventions are described as playing a pivotal role in successful management of cyclic vomiting syndrome given its frequent triggering by stressors and illness.
A meta-analysis of 55 studies found that tilt testing distinguished patients with unexplained syncope from asymptomatic controls with good overall diagnostic accuracy (AUC 0.84).

Tilt protocols incorporating sublingual nitroglycerine provocation had the highest diagnostic odds ratio and greatest sensitivity among tilt testing methods for diagnosing vasovagal syncope, though pharmacological provocation reduced specificity.

Tilt testing is preferred over active standing for diagnosing postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome because unsupported active standing cannot be tolerated long enough and lacks the capacity for beat-to-beat blood pressure/ECG (and EEG when needed) monitoring.

European guidelines recommend active standing as the initial diagnostic test for patients suspected of having orthostatic hypotension, particularly immediate/classical OH, though it is less useful for delayed OH.

Diagnostic yield of syncope evaluation rises from about 60% among general hospital physicians to 70% when following ESC guidelines, and up to 85% in specialized syncope units employing tilt testing and expert history-taking.

Reproducibility of a positive tilt test declines with repeated testing, falling to about 80% positivity on second and third tests, possibly because patients unconsciously act to avoid the unpleasant outcome (e.g., leg movement).
Tilt testing carries very low procedural risk, with rare transient atrial fibrillation and very rare self-terminating prolonged asystole being the only reported adverse events.

Bradyarrhythmias observed on implantable loop recorders during spontaneous vasovagal syncope are more prominent than those seen during tilt-induced syncope, indicating that tilt-induced events are not identical to spontaneous attacks.

A positive tilt table test prior to pacemaker implantation predicts a substantially higher rate of syncope recurrence after pacing compared with a negative tilt test, despite similarly positive ILR findings of vasovagal syncope.

Up to 42% of patients admitted with syncope are discharged without an established diagnosis, and 23% are readmitted for recurrent episodes, often after non-diagnostic evaluation, reflecting the cost and diagnostic burden of syncope management without adequate use of tilt testing.
The 2018 ESC syncope guidelines assign tilt-table testing a class IIb indication (level of evidence C) for discriminating convulsive syncope from epilepsy.

The European Society of Cardiology and the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association/Heart Rhythm Society guidelines independently arrived at a class IIA recommendation for tilt testing in evaluating unexplained syncope after initial clinical assessment.

The relative timing of tilt-induced asystole to hypotension/loss of consciousness predicts pacing benefit: asystole occurring after transient loss of consciousness suggests pacing is unnecessary, whereas asystole occurring before or coinciding with hypotension is associated with symptomatic improvement from pacing.
A questionnaire-based study found transient visual obscurations were far more common and more frequently daily in IIH patients than in controls.
In the IIH Treatment Trial, 68% of 165 patients reported transient visual obscurations with a median of one episode per day.
Diplopia was reported in 18% of the IIHTT cohort compared with a higher reported incidence of 38% by Guiseffi et al.
Sixth nerve palsy, thought to be the most common cause of diplopia in IIH, was found in 14 of 101 patients in one cohort.
In a cohort of 82 patients with mostly Frisen grade 2 papilledema, an enlarged blind spot was seen in 80% and a nasal defect in 72% of visual fields.

Visual acuity was measurably reduced even in relatively mild IIH, with 17% of eyes having acuity of 0.2 logMAR or worse in one study, and 29% of study eyes in the IIHTT worse than 20/20 despite correction for refractive error.
Visual field testing detected abnormalities far more often than visual acuity testing in IIH patients, suggesting greater sensitivity for detecting visual deficits.
In a large retrospective cohort of 353 IIH patients, only 5.7% presented without papilledema, confirming papilledema as a near-universal feature.
The IIHTT found that 7% of patients had asymmetric papilledema, with a difference of two or more Frisen grades between eyes.
Spontaneous venous pulsations were visible in 12 of 20 IIH patients with mild papilledema, including five with an opening pressure above 30 cmH2O, showing SVP presence does not rule out raised ICP.
The IIHTT and other studies found no correlation between CSF pressure and the presence or intensity of headache in IIH.
IIH-related headache frequently has a migrainous phenotype, complicating its differentiation from chronic migraine.
Headache persists long-term in many IIH patients despite normalisation of CSF pressure after treatment.
In the IIH Treatment Trial, acetazolamide produced significantly greater improvement in perimetric mean deviation than placebo at 6 months.
Acetazolamide produced significantly greater improvement in papilledema grade compared with placebo in the IIHTT.
Patients receiving acetazolamide lost significantly more weight than those on placebo, both groups being on a low-sodium weight-reduction diet.
Acetazolamide showed no significant effect on headache in the IIHTT, with similar headache rates in both treatment arms at 6 months.

In an open-label study of 41 IIH patients, both acetazolamide and topiramate produced significant improvement in visual field grading at 12 months, with no significant difference between the two treatments.
A randomised-controlled trial comparing medical management alone to medical management plus surgical intervention was abandoned due to low enrollment.
A meta-analysis of 435 patients undergoing CSF shunting for refractory IIH found papilledema improved in 70% and visual acuity improved in 54%, with a substantial proportion requiring repeat surgery.
Headache improved in 80% of patients following CSF shunting, though data were only available for a subset of the meta-analysis cohort.
In a retrospective study of 50 patients undergoing CSF diversion surgery, headache remained a problem in 56% of patients, with 42% requiring ongoing headache medication post-shunt.
A small randomised open-label study comparing acetazolamide versus no acetazolamide (25 patients per arm) was underpowered to detect a treatment effect.

In an open-label study comparing acetazolamide and topiramate in 41 patients with IIH, both groups showed significant improvement in visual field grading at 12 months compared with baseline, with no significant difference between the two arms.

Topiramate is discussed as an attractive migraine preventive for IIH-related headache because it also inhibits carbonic anhydrase and frequently causes weight loss, but may induce cognitive side effects and depression which are common comorbidities in IIH.

Medication overuse of acute pain-relief drugs is commonly observed in IIH patients, and given mechanistic parallels with migraine, may plausibly contribute to chronification of IIH-related headache, although no clinical study has proven this.

A randomised-controlled trial comparing medical management alone to medical management plus CSF diversion surgery or ONSF was abandoned due to low enrolment, recruiting only 16 of a planned 180 patients.
A large meta-analysis of 435 patients undergoing CSF shunting for refractory IIH found papilledema improved in 70% of patients and visual acuity improved in 54% post-shunt.

In the same meta-analysis of CSF shunting, headache improved in 80% of the 287 patients for whom headache data were available, but 43% of patients required more than one surgical procedure, most commonly due to shunt obstruction.

In a single-centre retrospective study of 50 patients undergoing CSF diversion surgery for IIH, headache remained a problem for 56% of patients, with 42% requiring ongoing medication for headache management post-shunt.
In a meta-analysis of 712 patients (1153 eyes) undergoing optic nerve sheath fenestration (ONSF) for IIH, visual acuity improved in 59% of eyes and papilledema improved in 80% of patients.
Headache improvement following ONSF was reported in 44% of patients, a lower proportion than seen after CSF diversion surgery (80%).
Unilateral ONSF has been observed to improve the grade of papilledema in both eyes, although the mechanism for this bilateral effect is uncertain.
Patients undergoing ONSF require ongoing monitoring, as visual worsening is possible even after a period of stability, occurring at a rate as high as 45% at 3 years.
In a meta-analysis of 136 patients undergoing venous sinus stenting for refractory IIH, papilledema improved in 97% of patients.
Headache improvement was reported in 83% of patients following venous sinus stenting for refractory IIH.
Episodic migraine patients showed significantly greater SREP (Slowly Repeated Evoked Pain) sensitization than healthy controls, while healthy controls showed essentially no sensitization.

Pain ratings increased progressively across the nine SREP stimuli overall, but this pattern was significantly moderated by group, with progressive increase only in migraine patients and not in healthy controls.
Pressure pain threshold did not differ significantly between episodic migraine patients and healthy controls.
Pressure pain tolerance did not differ significantly between episodic migraine patients and healthy controls.

TSP pain ratings increased with repeated stimuli in both groups but did not differ by group, indicating no evidence of enhanced ascending pain facilitation in episodic migraine relative to controls in this sample.
Episodic migraine patients reported significantly higher pain catastrophizing scores than healthy controls.
A significantly higher proportion of episodic migraine patients used regular analgesics compared with healthy controls, of whom none used regular analgesics.
Current clinical pain intensity (PPI-MPQ) was positively correlated with the SREP sensitization index specifically in episodic migraine patients, but not assessed as correlated in healthy controls.
Neither catastrophizing nor current clinical pain intensity (PPI-MPQ) were correlated with the TSP index, in contrast to their association with SREP.
In logistic regression, only the SREP index (and not static pain threshold, tolerance, or TSP) significantly discriminated episodic migraine patients from healthy controls.
SREP showed markedly higher overall diagnostic accuracy for distinguishing episodic migraine from healthy controls than pain threshold+tolerance or TSP.
ROC analysis confirmed excellent discriminatory power of the SREP index for distinguishing episodic migraine patients from healthy controls.

Three candidate SREP cut-off values (0.50, 0.65, 0.90), each yielding 75% overall accuracy, were identified via Youden index, with the 0.50 cut-off maximizing sensitivity and the 0.90 cut-off maximizing specificity for identifying episodic migraine patients.

Despite SREP sensitization differences, there was no significant group difference in overall perceived intensity of individual evoked stimuli, initial pain ratings, or calibrated stimulus pressure, indicating the SREP effect reflects a distinct temporal sensitization phenomenon rather than generalized differences in pain sensitivity.
Daytime heart rate increased significantly after pulmonary vein isolation, stabilizing at a mean of 9.6 bpm above baseline.
Nighttime heart rate increased significantly after ablation, stabilizing at a mean of 7.4 bpm above baseline after an initial transient spike.
Heart rate variability (SDANN) decreased significantly after ablation and remained lower than baseline throughout follow-up.
There was no difference in daytime heart rate, nighttime heart rate, or SDANN between patients treated with radiofrequency ablation versus cryoballoon ablation at any time point.
Cryoablation lesion duration (2 vs 4 minutes) also did not influence the observed autonomic nervous system effects.
Women had lower SDANN than men both before and after ablation at all time points, although the magnitude of change did not differ by sex.
Women in the ablation cohort had a substantially higher prevalence of thyroid dysfunction than men.

Older patients had significantly lower baseline daytime and nighttime heart rates than younger patients, and this age-related difference was amplified after ablation with a smaller relative rise in heart rate.
SDANN did not differ between age categories at any time point, unlike heart rate measures.

Patients free of atrial tachyarrhythmia recurrence after ablation had a significantly larger rise in daytime and nighttime heart rate than those with documented recurrence, despite similar HRV reduction.
SDANN did not differ between patients with and without atrial tachyarrhythmia recurrence, unlike heart rate measures.

Patients who later had documented atrial tachyarrhythmia recurrence had a lower baseline daytime heart rate but similar nighttime heart rate and SDANN compared with those who remained arrhythmia-free.

Circumferential pulmonary vein isolation frequently destroys the ganglionated plexi because of their close anatomical proximity to the pulmonary venous-left atrial junction, providing the likely mechanistic basis for the observed autonomic changes.
The authors hypothesize that the post-ablation rise in heart rate and fall in HRV may reflect elevated sympathetic activity, reduced parasympathetic activity, or both.
Cutaneous application of 660 nm red light has been shown to reduce pain in neuropathies and complex regional pain syndrome-I.
Visual (ocular) exposure to the same 660 nm red light exacerbates migraine headache in patients and induces functional pain in animal models.
Visual exposure to green light has been reported to reduce pain in a variety of pain conditions, including migraine and fibromyalgia.
Cutaneous phototherapy exposures are typically on the order of minutes, whereas visual (ocular) phototherapy exposures are typically on the order of hours.
Both cutaneous and visual photobiomodulation elicit changes centrally in the brainstem and spinal cord, and peripherally in the dorsal root ganglia and nociceptors.
Anti-NMDAR antibodies were detected in 18 of 158 patients with suspected autoimmune encephalitis, more frequently in females and children.
Anti-LGI1 antibodies were detected in 2 of 158 patients with suspected autoimmune encephalitis.
Anti-GAD antibodies were detected in 2 of 158 patients with suspected autoimmune encephalitis.
Behavioral disorder, epileptic seizures, movement disorder, and altered level of consciousness each had greater than 75% sensitivity for identifying anti-NMDAR-positive patients.
Language disorder, psychosis, hypoventilation, altered wake and sleep cycle, and cognitive impairment had greater than 55% sensitivity for anti-NMDAR positivity.
Two of the 158 patients tested positive for anti-LGI1 antibodies.
Two of the 158 patients tested positive for anti-GAD antibodies.
Brain MRI findings suggestive of encephalitis were observed in 7 of the 18 anti-NMDAR positive cases.
Abnormal CSF findings were reported in 12 anti-NMDAR positive patients, giving a sensitivity of 70.6% for detecting NMDAR-positive autoimmune encephalitis.
A predictive model using 7 clinical symptoms achieved 70% sensitivity and 81% specificity for the presence of anti-NMDAR antibodies, with an ROC area of 82%.

Clinical manifestations including movement disorder, behavioral disorder, hypoventilation, dysautonomia, and altered wake and sleep cycle predicted an autoimmune cause in patients with subacute encephalitis.
Children with autoimmune encephalitis were significantly more likely than adults to experience chorea and status epilepticus.
Joint hypermobility, assessed via Beighton (Bayton) criteria, was significantly more prevalent in the younger age subgroup (22–35 years) than in the older subgroup (36–47 years).
The asthenic body type, identified via Quetelet, Varga, and Pignet indices, was more common in the younger group and its diagnostic value decreased with age.
Dolichostenomelia (increased bone length, assessed via foot length/height ratio) was diagnosed in more than half of all subjects and was much more prominent in the older age group.
Frequent ligament sprains/ruptures and spinal pain were reported by all respondents regardless of age group.
The older age group had a significantly higher prevalence of joint crunching, arthralgia, fractures, flatfoot, valgus deformity, and kyphosis than the younger group.
Gothic palate, temporomandibular joint crunching, scoliosis, altered leg shape, malocclusion, and chest deformity were found in over half of subjects with an age-independent distribution.
Thin elastic skin, keloid scars, and soft curling auricles (ectodermal dysplastic stigmas) were more common in the younger age group.
Atrophic striae, hair fragility, alopecia areas, skin hyperpigmentation above the spine, rectus muscle diastasis, and recurrent hernia were more typical for the older age group.
Mitral valve prolapse was found in about one third of Group 1 participants and its prevalence decreased significantly with age.
Biliary dyskinesia and vascular dystonia, along with mitral valve prolapse, were more frequent in the younger group.
Lower-limb varicosity, hemorrhoids, gastroesophageal reflux, asthenic syndrome, and chronic esophagitis were more prevalent in the older age group.
The older age group had significantly higher systolic and diastolic blood pressure than the younger age group.
The total score for dysplastic (connective tissue dysplasia) signs was higher in the older age group than the younger group, reflecting accumulation of dysplastic changes over ontogenesis.
The older age group had a lower quality-of-life score than the younger age group, corresponding to their greater dysplastic sign burden.
Vascular dystonia, with complaints of palpitations, headaches, poor exercise tolerance, fatigue, and sweating, was very common in the younger subjects.
Persons with frequent post-exercise injuries had a high prevalence of average myopia, considered a manifestation of connective tissue changes in ocular tissue.

Functional biomechanical disorders from spine/chest pathology and altered motor stereotype manifested as spine pain in all respondents and shoulder ptosis with shoulder-blade/pelvic asymmetry in most participants, regardless of age.
17 of 89 TMD patients met criteria for fibromyalgia diagnosis and these FM-positive patients had significantly greater disease burden across numerous measures than FM-negative TMD patients.
Higher fibromyalgia-ness (FM-ness) scores were positively associated with greater orofacial pain at rest in TMD patients.
Higher FM-ness scores were positively associated with more negative mood in TMD patients.
Higher FM-ness scores were positively associated with greater tenderness to palpation in TMD patients.
Higher FM-ness scores were positively associated with greater perceived jaw functional limitation in TMD patients.

Higher FM-ness scores were negatively associated with comfortable pain-free jaw opening in TMD patients.
The relationship between fibromyalgia-ness and both perceived jaw functional limitation and pain-related disability was statistically mediated by the level of spontaneous, ongoing orofacial pain.

Students who reported being athletically active had higher rates of self-reported musculoskeletal injuries than those who were not athletically active.

Respondents with generalized joint hypermobility did not report higher rates of musculoskeletal injuries compared to those without it, in either sex.
Respondents with localized joint hypermobility did not report higher rates of musculoskeletal injuries compared to those without it, in either sex.
Gray matter cerebral blood flow was significantly higher in patients with pure autonomic failure compared to healthy controls.
Venous hyperintensities from major dural sinuses, indicative of abnormal capillary flow, were more prevalent in PAF patients than in healthy controls.
The presence and degree of venous hyperintensities was associated with higher mean cerebral blood flow.
In PAF participants, cerebral blood flow was inversely correlated with supine systolic blood pressure.
Across 23 studies with 3593 patients, the weighted mean proportion of vasovagal syncope patients with a history of injury due to syncope was 33.5%.
Nine of the included studies reported major injuries specifically, with a weighted mean rate of 13.9%.
Likelihood of injury from vasovagal syncope increased with the population's age, showing a moderate positive correlation.
Studies enrolling older vasovagal syncope patients had a significantly higher injury rate (43.4%) than studies enrolling younger patients (25.7%).
Injury likelihood from vasovagal syncope did not significantly correlate with patient sex, tilt test positivity, or presence of hypertension.

Abnormal alpha-synuclein deposits underlie the most severe forms of neurogenic orthostatic hypotension seen in multiple system atrophy, Parkinson's disease, Lewy body dementia, and pure autonomic failure.
The goal of NOH treatment is not to normalize blood pressure but to improve quality of life and prevent syncope and falls by reducing symptoms of cerebral hypoperfusion.
Patients who cannot recognize symptoms of NOH are at higher risk for falls, making patient and provider education about high-risk situations and triggering medications the first management step.
Conservative countermeasures such as dietary changes and compression garments should always be tried before pharmacologic therapies for NOH.
Volume expanders such as fludrocortisone and desmopressin are used to treat NOH but should be used with caution.
Drugs that enhance residual sympathetic tone, such as pyridostigmine and atomoxetine, are more effective in patients with mild disease and in MSA patients with spared postganglionic fibers.
Norepinephrine replacement therapy, including midodrine and droxidopa, is more effective in patients with neurodegeneration of peripheral noradrenergic fibers, as seen in pure autonomic failure.

Perceived judgement, including judgement from EMS personnel and negative self-evaluation, emerged as the core category driving patients' decisions about whether to call EMS after a syncopal episode.

Individual patient factors, including age and medical history, were identified as a theme influencing decisions to seek EMS care after syncope.
Attitudes and beliefs, such as not wanting to burden the healthcare system and perceiving syncope as 'not serious,' were identified as a theme discouraging EMS calls.
Contextual factors, including the influence of important others and symptom severity, were identified as a theme affecting patients' decisions to call EMS for syncope.

The authors theorize that previous experiences of feeling judged and unfavorable beliefs about syncope may interfere with patients' receptiveness to traditional EMS protocols designed to risk-stratify syncope in the field.
The 1-year prevalence of migraine in Europe is 22% overall, but is markedly higher in women than men.

Migraine attacks are more frequent, last longer, and are more severe in women than men, with associated symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and light/noise sensitivity also more prevalent and severe in women.

Premenstrual fluctuations in sex hormones are associated with an increased risk of migraine attacks in female migraineurs, while pregnancy (with high, stable hormone levels) is generally associated with improved migraine frequency and menopause has variable effects.
Monoclonal antibodies targeting CGRP (erenumab, galcanezumab, fremanezumab) were approved by the FDA and EMA for migraine prevention in patients with more than four migraine days per month.
Gepants, small-molecule CGRP receptor antagonists, were newly approved by the FDA for acute treatment of migraine.
OnabotulinumtoxinA, administered with a specific 31/39-injection protocol, is used to treat chronic migraine.

A review of RCTs suggests nutritional supplementation with magnesium, riboflavin, niacin, coenzyme Q10, vitamin D, vitamin B12, and alpha-lipoic acid may have a role in migraine prevention and is generally well tolerated.
Episodic migraine progresses to chronic migraine at a rate of approximately 3% per year.
Fibromyalgia prevalence is eight- to nine-fold higher in women than in men.
Approximately 40-50% of fibromyalgia patients show signs consistent with small-fiber neuropathy, including allodynia and hyperalgesia.

In a German cohort of 2,435 RA patients evaluated using 2016 fibromyalgia criteria, women accounted for 58.7% of fibromyalgia cases and had more symptoms, more generalized pain, and higher polysymptomatic distress scores than men.
Testosterone deficiency is linked to increased risk of nociceptive nervous system inflammation and chronic pain, and transdermal testosterone gel therapy has been suggested to reduce pain severity.

Preclinical studies show sex-specific immune mediation of chronic pain: microglia and toll-like receptor 4 activation mediate neuropathic pain in male mice, whereas T cells drive neuroinflammation and pain in female mice.

In an Italian cross-sectional study of 292 RA patients, those with comorbid fibromyalgia had higher tender joint counts and DAS28 scores than RA patients without fibromyalgia, despite similar inflammatory disease activity (ESR, swollen joint count).

In a cross-sectional study of 102 women with early RA, one-third also met criteria for widespread pain, and this subgroup reported more fatigue, anxiety/depression, more tender joints, more intense pain, and worse global health despite similar inflammation levels to those without widespread pain.
Women are more likely than men to develop adverse effects from opioid analgesics such as morphine, including nausea, dysphoria, headache, and vomiting.
