Bladder pain syndrome shows a strong female predominance (5:1 to 10:1) with prevalence estimates ranging widely from 1.8 to 45-51 per 10,000 inhabitants across studies.
Bladder pain syndrome patients with ulcerative disease have a significantly increased number of mast cells, which release inflammatory mediators implicated in pain and urinary frequency.

A systematic review of 16 quantitative studies found a bidirectional association between pain and sleep in fibromyalgia: increased pain was linked to poorer sleep quality, efficiency, and duration, more disturbed sleep, and depressive symptoms.

Resistance exercise is safe in RA patients with moderate or low disease activity and can significantly and clinically improve most RA-related pain and disability outcomes without increasing pain or disease activity.
Emerging evidence shows exercise can provide a clinically significant reduction in menstrual pain intensity and can reduce the frequency of low back pain and associated sick leave in pregnant women.
Fibromyalgia is frequently comorbid with chronic fatigue syndrome, mood disorders, tension-type headache, migraine, and irritable bowel syndrome.

In a study of 500 children aged 6-12 using an extended joint mobility protocol, those classed as hypermobile by the Beighton Score showed significantly increased range of motion in other joints (ankle, hip, shoulder) and association with pes planus, supporting BS validity in children.
A study of 160 individuals aged 16-35 found no correlation between the Beighton Score and measures of shoulder laxity, with low sensitivity and low positive predictive value even at a raised cutoff.
Another study found no relationship between a Beighton Score of ≥6 and shoulder instability, suggesting the BS does not necessarily reflect joint instability.

Among over 100 patients with strong suspicion of EDS, 45 had a negative Beighton Score yet still showed mean glenohumeral abduction 20° higher than normal, showing the BS can miss clinically relevant shoulder hypermobility.

Instrumented measurements of knee and ankle laxity in over 50 individuals (mean age 21) showed non-significant correlation with a positive Beighton Score, suggesting joint laxity is joint-specific rather than generalisable.
A study of over 140 children aged 13-15 found no correlation between the Beighton Score and ankle dorsiflexion.
In contrast to other studies, a smaller study of over 30 adults found a weak but significant association between the Beighton Score and instrumented knee laxity and instability.
One study found individuals with a Beighton Score ≥6 had a statistically significantly higher ankle dorsiflexion range by 4°, though the clinical significance is questionable.
In a study of over 60 individuals, those with a Beighton Score ≥4 demonstrated significantly increased spinal intervertebral mobility on functional radiographs.
A study in men found shorter hamstring length was associated with decreased pelvic and lumbar angle range of motion, restricting the forward flexion of trunk manoeuvre used within the Beighton Score.

In over 200 hypermobile patients aged 2-70 (BS≥5), 87.5% had muscle retractions preventing the forward flexion manoeuvre, and 84.2% were unable to perform it, meaning they were denied an additional point on the Beighton Score.
In over 400 children aged 6-11, 86% of those classified hypermobile (BS≥5) could not perform the forward flexion manoeuvre.

In over 200 children aged 10-13, 84% of hypermobile males and 78% of hypermobile females could not perform the forward flexion manoeuvre, with no difference from non-hypermobile children in trunk/hip-complex flexibility ability.
The forward flexion manoeuvre was found to have high specificity (93.7%) but such low sensitivity (13.8%) that it adds no additional diagnostic value to the Beighton Score.
A study of 60 TMD patients found no significant correlation between a positive Beighton Score and TMJ hypermobility measured by lateral X-rays, a finding echoed by other imaging studies.
In contrast, a study of over 30 women with TMD found a significant positive correlation between mandibular range of motion and a positive Beighton Score.
A study of over 160 individuals found the Beighton Score correlated moderately and significantly with thumb laxity measured via stress view radiograph.
A study in 50 women found a low but significant correlation between the Beighton Score and assessments of wrist laxity.
Across multiple reliability studies, kappa values consistently ranged between 0.4 and 0.8, indicating moderate intra- and inter-examiner reliability of the Beighton Score in adults and children.

A COSMIN-based best-evidence synthesis systematic review rated the overall strength of evidence for the reliability of a positive Beighton Score as limited to conflicting, despite it being the best-performing GJH assessment method reviewed.
Caucasian populations have consistently shown lower prevalence of generalised joint hypermobility compared with Asian, African, and Arab populations.
The prevalence of generalised joint hypermobility has consistently been shown to be higher in females across the lifespan, with sex differences becoming more pronounced around age 14.

The probability of being classified with generalised joint hypermobility decreases by 5.5% for every one-year increase in age, and in a study of 200 individuals over age 70 no one scored higher than 2 on the Beighton Score.
Studies show a general trend of lower generalised joint hypermobility prevalence in Caucasian populations compared with Asian, African, and Arab populations.
A study in a West African population found no increase in articular symptoms associated with generalised joint hypermobility.
A study of Indian schoolchildren found an association between higher Beighton Score and musculoskeletal pain.
A study of Iraqi university students found a significant correlation between generalised joint hypermobility and both articular symptoms and syndromic features.

Prevalence of hypermobility is consistently higher in females across the lifespan, with the sex difference becoming more pronounced around age 14, while the post-adolescent decline in hypermobility is more pronounced in males.

The probability of classification as generalised joint hypermobility decreases with increasing age, dropping 5.5% for every year of age increase, and among individuals over 70 years none scored above 2 on the Beighton Score.
Prevalence of generalised joint hypermobility in children declines sharply with age, from 64.6% at ages 4-7 to 11.7% by ages 13-19.

The natural history of hypermobility within the hypermobile population has been delineated into three phases: a first-decade 'hypermobility' phase with marked joint sprains/strains in ~40% of patients, a second-decade 'pain' phase with widespread chronic pain and increasing instability, and a third 'stiffness' phase with dramatic loss of hypermobility and diminished quality of life.

A cut-off age of 33 has been established after which most diagnosed hypermobile patients will no longer reach the diagnostic Beighton Score cutoff of 4, questioning the tool's suitability for adult diagnosis.
In a cohort of over 380 children aged 10-12, a Beighton Score of ≥6 was an independent predictor of musculoskeletal pain recurrence at 4-year follow-up.
In children presenting with lower limb pain, hypermobility (BS≥6) was associated with a threefold increased risk of lower limb pain recurrence after 4 years.

Symptomatic hypermobile children showed significantly higher skin extensibility and joint hypermobility degree, alongside significantly elevated urinary hydroxyproline (a collagen degradation product) and reduced ultrasound-measured bone density compared with asymptomatic hypermobile children.
Symptomatic hypermobile children had a significantly lower diastolic blood pressure than asymptomatic hypermobile children.

A case study of a patient and her mother with molecularly confirmed classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome due to a COL5A1 splice mutation found both patients scored negatively on the Beighton Score (3 and 4 out of 9), despite the mother's marked skin hyperextensibility, illustrating that a negative BS can miss genuine connective tissue disorder diagnoses.
Several studies show that joint hypermobility is diminished on the dominant side of the body compared with the non-dominant side.

Stretching and warming up increase joint range of motion, while both heat and cold temperature affect the flexibility of tendons and ligaments and thus joint range of motion, meaning circumstantial factors can influence an individual's Beighton Score.
Hormonal fluctuations during the menstrual cycle are thought to affect laxity of the knee joints.

Some researchers propose adjusting the Beighton Score cut-off to a value 2 standard deviations above the mean, or the upper 5%, within each age, sex, and race category to reduce overdiagnosis, though the review argues this may inappropriately exclude genuine GJH cases.

The higher prevalence of generalised joint hypermobility in females is associated with an increased symptomatic presentation, suggesting it likely represents increased penetrance of an underlying heritable connective tissue disorder rather than overdiagnosis.

The validity and reliability of alternative generalised joint hypermobility scoring systems, the Hospital Del Mar criteria and the Rotès-Quérol system, are difficult to establish because published data on these aspects are scarce.
Two hours of local passive heat (40-42°C) applied to the abdomen/pelvis acutely lowered supine systolic blood pressure compared with sham control.
Local passive heat also produced a sustained reduction in diastolic and mean arterial blood pressure compared with sham.
Pulse pressure decreased significantly during acute local heat exposure, suggesting the blood pressure reduction was driven by decreased stroke volume.
Cardiac output and stroke volume decreased significantly during acute local heat exposure compared with sham, while systemic vascular resistance and heart rate were unchanged.
Systemic vascular resistance did not change significantly with local heat compared with sham, an unexpected finding not fully explained by the authors.
Local skin blood flow and cutaneous vascular conductance increased in the heated abdominal area but not in the unheated calf, indicating a localized rather than reflex vasodilatory response.

Core body temperature increased slightly during acute local heat exposure, but this increase occurred after, not before, the drop in systolic blood pressure, indicating the hypotensive effect was not core-temperature dependent.

Overnight application of local passive heat (38°C, 10pm-6am) significantly lowered nocturnal supine systolic blood pressure compared with placebo, with a maximal reduction at 2am comparable to pharmacologic antihypertensives previously tested in this population.
Mean arterial pressure and pulse pressure also decreased significantly during overnight heat therapy compared with placebo.
During overnight heat therapy, diastolic blood pressure showed a similar downward trend to systolic pressure but did not reach statistical significance versus placebo.
Heart rate decreased similarly during both overnight heat and placebo trials, with no treatment effect.

Overnight local heat therapy did not significantly alter sublingual (core) temperature compared with placebo, and did not prevent the normal nocturnal decrease in body temperature, supporting the safety of the approach.
Overall, overnight heat therapy did not significantly reduce nocturnal urine volume compared with placebo across the study population.
Morning orthostatic tolerance, measured as area under the curve of standing systolic blood pressure, did not differ overall between overnight heat and placebo.
In a post hoc analysis, patients with a larger blood-pressure-lowering response to overnight heat tended to have lower nocturnal urine volume, though this trend did not reach significance.
Patients with greater nocturnal blood pressure reduction from overnight heat therapy showed significantly greater improvement in morning orthostatic tolerance in a post hoc analysis.
Both acute and overnight local passive heat therapy were well tolerated in patients with autonomic failure, with no adverse events, burns, or skin irritation reported.
The majority of patients with autonomic failure and supine hypertension reported a history of worsening orthostatic symptoms in hot environments prior to study participation.
A substantial minority of patients had a history of essential hypertension that preceded their diagnosis of autonomic failure.

The magnitude of nocturnal blood pressure lowering achieved by overnight local heat therapy was comparable to that of pharmacologic antihypertensive agents (nitroglycerin, clonidine, losartan, nebivolol, sildenafil, nifedipine, eplerenone) previously tested in the same patient population.
Biallelic pathogenic variants in ZNF469 cause brittle cornea syndrome, a connective tissue disorder within the Ehlers-Danlos syndrome spectrum.
Biallelic pathogenic variants in PRDM5 cause brittle cornea syndrome, a connective tissue disorder within the Ehlers-Danlos syndrome spectrum.

The authors reviewed the literature and identified a total of 85 reported patients with pathogenic variants in ZNF469 (n=53) or PRDM5 (n=32), enabling a genotype- and phenotype-oriented overview of brittle cornea syndrome.

Musculoskeletal findings are often the main reason for referral in brittle cornea syndrome and frequently raise suspicion of other heritable connective tissue disorders such as kyphoscoliotic EDS, osteogenesis imperfecta, or Marfan syndrome, particularly before a corneal rupture has occurred.
Beyond corneal fragility and hearing loss, BCS patients show signs of generalized connective tissue fragility, supporting placement of the disorder within the Ehlers-Danlos syndrome spectrum.
Musculoskeletal findings are often the primary reason patients with BCS are referred for evaluation, especially before a corneal rupture has occurred.

Musculoskeletal features of BCS frequently lead to misdiagnosis or diagnostic confusion with other heritable connective tissue disorders such as kyphoscoliotic EDS, osteogenesis imperfecta, or Marfan syndrome.
The authors conclude that the multisystemic clinical features observed support formally including brittle cornea syndrome within the Ehlers-Danlos syndrome classification.

The authors recommend that diagnostic gene panels for heritable connective tissue disorders should include ZNF469 and PRDM5 to enable timely diagnosis and preventive measures for brittle cornea syndrome.

The study reports nine novel BCS families, with four families harboring ZNF469 variants and five harboring PRDM5 variants, alongside a literature overview of 85 previously reported patients (53 with ZNF469 variants and 32 with PRDM5 variants).
The efficacy advantage of ubrogepant 50 mg over placebo for 2-hour pain freedom did not differ significantly according to participants' historical triptan responder status.
The efficacy advantage of ubrogepant 50 mg over placebo for absence of most bothersome migraine-associated symptom (MBS) at 2 hours did not vary significantly by triptan historical experience.

For pain relief at 2 hours, the treatment-by-subgroup interaction was nonsignificant based on OR and RD but reached significance based on RR, although the direction of benefit for ubrogepant over placebo remained consistent across all triptan subgroups.
Among triptan-insufficient responders due to insufficient efficacy, ubrogepant 50 mg produced significantly higher rates of 2-hour pain freedom than placebo.
Among triptan-insufficient responders due to insufficient efficacy, ubrogepant 50 mg produced significantly higher rates of absence of most bothersome migraine symptom at 2 hours than placebo.
Among triptan-insufficient responders due to insufficient efficacy, ubrogepant 50 mg produced significantly higher rates of pain relief at 2 hours than placebo.

The incidence of treatment-emergent and treatment-related adverse events with ubrogepant did not differ appreciably across triptan historical experience subgroups, and no serious adverse events occurred in any subgroup.
The triptan-insufficient responder subgroup had the highest percentage of treatment-related TEAEs among ubrogepant-treated participants.
No serious adverse events were reported in any triptan-experience subgroup in either the placebo or ubrogepant treatment arms.

Placebo response rates for pain freedom, absence of MBS, and pain relief were higher in triptan-naive participants than in triptan-experienced subgroups (triptan responders and triptan-insufficient responders).
Calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) is described as an endogenous proinflammatory and pronociceptive neuropeptide with an important role in migraine pathogenesis.
A pharmacy claims study found that almost 54% of triptan users did not receive a consecutive refill of their index triptan, indicating high discontinuation rates.
Among current and past triptan users, the 25% who discontinued use most commonly cited lack of therapeutic effect and side effects as reasons.
An estimated over 95% of people with migraine taking an oral acute prescription medication for headache report at least one unmet acute treatment need.
Nearly half of episodic migraine patients screened positive for right-to-left shunt using contrast-enhanced transcranial doppler.
Among migraine patients with RLS, small shunts (Grade 1) occurred in 29.0% and mid-large shunts (Grade 2-4) in 18.1% of the cohort.
Nausea was the most common non-headache symptom reported by episodic migraine patients.
Headache aggravation with physical activity was reported in over half of episodic migraine patients.
Dizziness occurred in over half of episodic migraine patients as a non-headache symptom.
Vomiting was reported by nearly half of episodic migraine patients.
Phonophobia was reported in about 43% of episodic migraine patients.
Yawning during the premonitory phase was significantly more common in migraine patients with mid-large right-to-left shunt (Grade 2-4) than those without shunt (Grade 0).

Migraineurs with grade 2-4 (mid-large) right-to-left shunt had a higher rate of headache aggravation with physical activity than those with grade 0 shunt.

Twins of individuals diagnosed with syncope had a significantly increased risk of syncope themselves, with an odds ratio of 2.39.
Siblings of individuals diagnosed with syncope had significantly increased odds of syncope, with an odds ratio of 1.81.
Half-siblings of individuals diagnosed with syncope had significantly increased but more attenuated odds of syncope, with an odds ratio of 1.28.
Cousins of individuals diagnosed with syncope had a small but statistically significant increase in odds of syncope, with an odds ratio of 1.13.
Tetrachoric correlation coefficients for syncope between relative pairs decreased progressively with decreasing genetic resemblance, from twins to siblings to half-siblings to cousins.

An interaction term between genetic resemblance and family history of syncope was statistically significant, indicating that higher genetic relatedness was associated with greater familial odds of syncope.
A higher proportion of female than male individuals were affected by syncope across all relative-pair types, and female sex was independently associated with higher syncope probability.

Among female twin pairs, familial risk of syncope was also significantly elevated, with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.13, though lower than in male twin pairs.
Across all types of family relationships, familial odds ratios for syncope were highest among younger individuals, supporting a genetic basis for early-onset reflex syncope.

Syncope-free survival curves differed significantly between individuals with and without an affected relative for every relationship type (twins, siblings, half-siblings, cousins), with the degree of separation tracking genetic resemblance.

A sensitivity analysis excluding families with concurrent definite nonreflex syncope/TLOC diagnoses did not substantially change the estimated familial syncope risk, supporting the use of the nonspecific syncope code as a proxy for reflex syncope.

Higher educational attainment was associated with higher probability of a syncope diagnosis, which the authors interpret as possibly reflecting greater symptom awareness and reporting rather than a biological effect.
Across included studies, interrater reliability of the Beighton score was substantial to almost perfect for the majority of reported ICC and kappa values.

Generalized joint hypermobility is described as a risk factor for multiple musculoskeletal instability conditions, including shoulder, hip, and knee pathology.

Bachelor Dance students had significantly higher mean Beighton hypermobility scores than Bachelor Dance teacher students.

Patients with mastocytosis have a much higher incidence of severe anaphylactic reactions to hymenoptera venom than the general population.
Severe allergic reactions to foods and drugs have been reported in a subset of mastocytosis patients, though allergy testing is sometimes negative.

In a study of 28 mastocytosis patients, SARS-CoV-2 infection was not associated with increased COVID-19 mortality or clinical mast cell activation symptoms.

There is no evidence that antiviral drugs or drugs used to treat SARS-CoV-2 infection induce or aggravate mast cell activation in patients with mastocytosis or allergies.
A literature search and expert working group experience found no evidence for an increased number of vaccine reactions in adults with mastocytosis.

Two health care workers with cutaneous and systemic mastocytosis and prior MC mediator-related symptoms had no problems after mRNA COVID-19 vaccination with antihistamine and leukotriene receptor antagonist premedication.
ECNM/AIM experts concluded there is presently no evidence that the incidence and severity of reactions to available COVID-19 vaccines is higher in mastocytosis patients than the general population.

Higher migraine pain intensity (VAS) correlated with lower HRV parameters, predominantly during the migraine attack.
Psychological evaluation of anxiety and depression showed no statistically significant differences between migraine patients and controls.
Dysphagia occurring within 5 years of motor onset is considered an additional diagnostic feature of multiple system atrophy.
Dysphagia in MSA can lead to aspiration pneumonia, which is a recognized cause of death in this disorder.
Abnormalities of the oral and pharyngeal phases of swallowing, esophageal dysfunction, and aspiration occur in MSA and worsen as the disease progresses.

The consensus recommends investigating dysphagia via screening questionnaires plus clinical and instrumental assessment (videofluoroscopy, fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing, and manometry) at MSA diagnosis and periodically thereafter.

The consensus recommends that dysphagia in MSA be investigated with screening questionnaires plus clinical and instrumental assessment (videofluoroscopy, fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing, and manometry) at diagnosis and periodically thereafter.
Compensatory strategies including diet modification, swallowing maneuvers, and specific head postures are recommended for managing dysphagia in MSA.
Botulinum toxin injection may be effective for dysphagia management in MSA in specific conditions.
Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy may be performed in MSA patients with severe risk of malnutrition and pulmonary complications, but its effect on survival is undetermined.
Despite the association of dysphagia with poor survival in MSA, effective treatments for dysphagia are currently lacking.

A 48-year-old woman with exclusive nocturnal bilateral occipital hypnic headache achieved near-complete resolution of headaches after eight weeks of escalating topiramate dosed to a target of 100 mg nightly, with only rare mild breakthrough headaches and no side effects.
A voxel-based morphology study of 14 hypnic headache patients found reduced posterior hypothalamus volume compared to what would be expected, supporting hypothalamic involvement in the disorder.
Topiramate acts through sodium channel blockade, GABA potentiation, glutamate antagonism, and carbonic anhydrase inhibition.
Topiramate may reduce neuropeptide-Y and the fat/mass-obesity associated protein in the ventromedial nucleus of the hypothalamus, part of the posterior hypothalamus implicated in hypnic headache.
In inflammatory animal models, topiramate reduced hyperalgesia through central GABA-A and opioid agonism and peripheral alpha-2 adrenergic agonism.

fMRI evidence shows that a single 100 mg dose of topiramate reduces thalamocortical pain pathway activity by decoupling the thalamus from the somatosensory cortex, posterior cingulate cortex, and precuneus.
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, including topiramate, reduce intracranial pressure, act as vasodilators, and reduce neuropathic pain and cerebral ischemia, with broad use across neurological diseases.
Hypnic headache shows sexual dimorphism, with approximately two-thirds of patients being women and one-third men.
Three-quarters of hypnic headache patients achieve remission with caffeine, lithium, melatonin, or indomethacin.
Melatonin and indomethacin both contain an indole backbone, an aromatic heterocyclic ring, which may explain their similar action in pain modulation for hypnic headache.
REM sleep, during which hypnic headaches typically occur, is associated with sympathetic discharge linked to the posterior hypothalamus.
Contrary to the older view that hypnic headache is exclusively a REM sleep disorder, recent studies show hypnic headaches can also occur during non-REM sleep.
Fewer than 10% of hypnic headache patients present with occipital-predominant headache pain, as in the reported case.

The case patient presented with a four-month history of exclusive nocturnal bilateral occipital pressing pain awakening her nightly at 11pm after falling asleep at 8pm, lasting up to three hours and associated with nausea but no photophobia, phonophobia, or autonomic symptoms.
Pregnant women with generalized joint hypermobility (Beighton score ≥5/9) had similar evening pain intensity at gestation week 30 as women without hypermobility.

Among pregnant women with generalized joint hypermobility, those who also had a pre-pregnancy BMI ≥25 kg/m2 reported substantially higher evening pain intensity than women with normal joint mobility and BMI <25 kg/m2, suggesting BMI modifies the hypermobility-pain association.
A missense mutation in the SCN1A sodium channel alpha 1 subunit pore region was identified in all affected family members and in four unaffected relatives.
Post-ictal migraine was a common feature, occurring in 83% (five of six) of the epilepsy patients in this SCN1A-mutation family.

Seizure semiology in most patients included cognitive, autonomic, and emotional symptoms that evolved into visual sensory phenomena, with some patients also experiencing focal vestibular seizures and altered body perception.
Among 581 subjects (1162 feet), 56.3% had normal feet, 18.9% pronated, 7.1% hyperpronated, 10.8% supinated, and 6.9% hypersupinated foot posture.
Women had a higher prevalence of pronated (21.0%) and supinated (11.7%) foot postures than men (16.8% and 10.3% respectively), a significant gender difference.
FPI scores differed significantly between right and left feet across all foot posture groups.
Height, weight, and BMI were all significantly higher in men than women in this cohort.
Foot posture group had a large effect on near-tandem balance performance, accounting for 81% of variance.
Gender had a small but statistically significant effect on balance, accounting for 1.5% of variance.
Foot posture group had a very large effect on stair ascent performance, accounting for 97% of variance.
Gender had a small but significant effect on stair ascent performance, accounting for 3% of variance.
Foot posture group had a very large effect on stair descent performance, accounting for 98% of variance.
Gender had a substantial effect on stair descent performance, accounting for 28% of variance.
Overall ANOVA showed that foot posture group and gender had a nonsignificant effect on hypermobility (Beighton) scores.
A separate partial eta-squared analysis indicated foot posture group significantly accounted for 49% of variance in hypermobility scores, while gender contributed only 0.2%.
The hyperpronated foot group showed a moderate positive correlation between FPI and joint hypermobility scores.
Across the whole sample, total FPI scores showed a moderate positive correlation with joint hypermobility.
Total FPI scores showed a high positive correlation with balance performance across the sample.
The supinated foot group showed a strong positive correlation between FPI and functional mobility (stair ascent and descent) and a moderate correlation with balance.
The hypersupinated foot group showed a moderate positive correlation between FPI and BMI.
Overall, no significant association was found between BMI and FPI in the whole sample despite significant gender differences in BMI.
Joint hypermobility was reported to be more common in women than men, attributed to differences in the collagen type I/III ratio.
The Saudi Arabian sample's overall foot posture (neutral with slight pronation, men scoring higher than women) was similar to normative FPI values previously reported in Spain and Taiwan.

Participant knowledge and understanding of chronic overlapping pain conditions significantly increased following exposure to electronic educational materials and this improvement was retained at 3-month follow-up.
The number of diagnosed chronic overlapping pain conditions per participant was found to be inversely related to age.
Pain-related symptoms and engagement in self-management strategies did not significantly change over the 3-month follow-up period after education.
Of 216 enrolled individuals, 181 (84%) completed both the baseline and 3-month follow-up assessments, indicating feasibility of electronic delivery of pain education.
A systematic search identified 153 primary headache research articles from Southeast Asia through June 10, 2020.
The majority of the identified publications were epidemiologic studies, followed by case reports/case series.
Migraine was identified as the most frequently studied primary headache subtype among Southeast Asian research output.
Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand were the leading contributing countries to primary headache research output in Southeast Asia.
Among the socioeconomic factors examined, only the percentage of gross domestic product spent on research and development showed a significant correlation with headache research productivity.
Despite the high global disease burden of headache, overall research productivity on primary headache was low in Southeast Asia.

Pooled across 12 cohorts, a negative electrophysiology study (His-to-ventricle interval criterion ≥70 ms) had a negative predictive value of 0.71 for later complete heart block in patients with syncope and bundle branch block.
Continuous monitoring with an implantable cardiac monitor detected a substantially higher rate of complete heart block after a negative EPS than intermittent surface ECG follow-up.
In a US insurance claims database of ~27 million patients, the overall prevalence of Hymenoptera venom allergy was 167 per 100,000 (0.167%).
The overall prevalence of mastocytosis in the US claims database was 10 per 100,000 (0.010%).
Among patients with Hymenoptera venom allergy, mastocytosis prevalence was substantially higher (97 per 100,000, 0.097%) than in the general population, representing a 9.7-fold increase.
In a retrospective University of Michigan cohort of 161 patients undergoing venom immunotherapy between 2015-2018, 2.6% had mastocytosis.
Serum tryptase level did not correlate with the severity of venom reactions in patients undergoing VIT.
Baseline tryptase was higher in patients who experienced systemic reactions during venom immunotherapy compared to those who did not.
The observed prevalence of Hymenoptera venom anaphylaxis in the US insurance claims database was lower than previously reported in prior studies, largely from Europe.
Tryptase levels were higher in patients who experienced systemic reactions during venom immunotherapy compared to those without systemic reactions.
Athletes with joint hypermobility had over three times greater odds of shoulder injury compared with athletes without joint hypermobility across six pooled studies.

The strength of the association between hypermobility and shoulder injury differed significantly by exposure definition, with localised shoulder joint hypermobility showing a much stronger association than generalised joint hypermobility (GJH).
Studies with low risk of bias showed a significantly stronger association between joint hypermobility and shoulder injury than studies with high risk of bias.
Excluding the two studies with the most extreme effect estimates lowered heterogeneity without substantially changing the overall pooled association.

Using shoulder external rotation as an alternative exposure definition instead of the Hospital Del Mar criteria in one study resulted in a slightly lower but still significant association with shoulder injury.
Excluding fractures from one study's shoulder injury outcome increased the strength of the association between joint hypermobility and shoulder injury and reduced heterogeneity.

A post hoc sensitivity analysis excluding the Myklebust et al. handball study, which reported the strongest association among included studies, did not substantially change the overall pooled estimate.
Subgroup analyses found no significant differences in the hypermobility-shoulder injury association based on type of activity, level of sport, study type, or sex.

When accounting for the observed range of shoulder injury prevalence in non-hypermobile athletes, the true relative risk of shoulder injury with joint hypermobility is likely lower than the pooled odds ratio suggests, ranging from about 1.94 to 2.65 depending on assumed baseline prevalence.

Impaired collagen synthesis is proposed to cause laxity of the connective tissue matrix, affecting joint capsule stability and the extensibility of ligaments, tendons, and skin, thereby increasing demand on active muscular stabilisers in hypermobile individuals.
Three of 180 pediatric patients with suspected autoimmune encephalitis tested positive for anti-GAD65 antibodies in both serum and CSF, with evidence of intrathecal synthesis.

One pediatric patient with GAD65-Ab-associated encephalitis developed autonomic dysfunction, including cardiac dysrhythmia, temperature dysregulation, and hyperhidrosis, that was refractory to immunotherapy.

Higher anti-GAD65 antibody titer in one patient did not correspond to lower seizure frequency or severity compared with another patient, suggesting titer level does not predict seizure severity across individuals.
In one patient, CSF GAD65-Ab titer decreased alongside full clinical recovery and MRI improvement after immunotherapy.

Across nine reported pediatric GAD65-Ab encephalitis cases, patients with limbic lobe involvement tended to have worse long-term outcomes, including refractory focal epilepsy, cognitive impairment, and hippocampal sclerosis, compared with extralimbic-only cases.
One patient with GAD65-Ab encephalitis also had elevated thyroid peroxidase antibody, consistent with co-occurring autoimmune thyroiditis.

In a prior comparison of laboratory assays for GAD65 antibodies, cell-based assay (CBA) was reported to be positive in 100% of high-concentration samples and negative in 96% of low-concentration samples, indicating high specificity of CBA testing.
Among nine reported pediatric GAD65-Ab encephalitis patients, seizures, memory loss, and loss of consciousness were the most common clinical symptoms, with autonomic symptoms occurring in a minority.
Patients with fibromyalgia had approximately double the risk of subsequently developing Sjögren's syndrome compared with non-fibromyalgia controls after adjustment.
The incidence rate of Sjögren's syndrome was substantially higher in fibromyalgia patients than in non-fibromyalgia controls.
Women had a substantially higher risk than men of developing Sjögren's syndrome overall.
Comorbid chronic urticaria, osteoporosis, ankylosing spondylitis, depression or sleep disorder were each associated with increased risk of developing Sjögren's syndrome.
In the 20-49 year age subgroup, fibromyalgia patients had roughly triple the risk of developing Sjögren's syndrome compared to non-fibromyalgia controls of the same age.
Among female patients, fibromyalgia was associated with a 1.90-fold increased risk of Sjögren's syndrome relative to females without fibromyalgia.
Among male patients, fibromyalgia was associated with a 2.88-fold increased risk of Sjögren's syndrome relative to males without fibromyalgia, a larger relative risk than in females.
In patients with no other comorbidities, fibromyalgia raised the risk of Sjögren's syndrome more than three-fold.
In patients with any one comorbidity, fibromyalgia was still associated with an increased, though smaller, risk of Sjögren's syndrome.
In patients with comorbid depression, fibromyalgia increased the risk of subsequent Sjögren's syndrome development.

Fibromyalgia patients who were not using systemic steroids had a higher risk of developing Sjögren's syndrome than non-fibromyalgia patients who used steroids, suggesting steroid use may attenuate the excess risk.
The increased risk of Sjögren's syndrome associated with fibromyalgia was present regardless of whether patients used NSAIDs, indicating NSAID use did not modify the association.
IV magnesium sulphate (2 g) produced a significant reduction in migraine pain from VAS 8 to 0 at 2 hours compared with IV caffeine in 70 patients.
IV magnesium sulphate (1 g in saline) significantly reduced migraine pain from VAS 8/10 to 0.66 at 2 hours in 70 patients (Shahrami et al.).
In patients with migraine and aura, 1 g IV magnesium sulphate reduced pain more than placebo at 1 hour (VAS 4/10 vs 6/10).
Demirkaya et al. found a qualitative benefit of IV magnesium sulphate versus placebo for migraine pain over 2 hours in 30 subjects.
Corbo et al. found no beneficial effect of adding IV magnesium sulphate to metoclopramide for migraine pain versus metoclopramide plus placebo.
Cete et al. found no significant effect of 2 g IV magnesium sulphate on migraine pain at 0, 15 and 30 minutes in 113 subjects.
Ginder et al. found no significant effect of 2 g IV magnesium sulphate on migraine pain over 4 hours in 36 subjects.
Three double-blind RCTs of oral magnesium (oxide, pyrrolidone carboxylic acid, citrate) reduced migraine pain intensity as measured by TBI, HIT-6 and VAS.
Five double-blind RCTs of oral magnesium supplementation reduced migraine frequency by about 4.4 days over 6 months.
A single-blind RCT of magnesium oxide 500 mg significantly reduced migraine frequency per day in 139 subjects over 12 weeks.
Two double-blind RCTs found oral magnesium (citrate or oxide) shortened migraine duration from 49 hours to 16 hours over 24 weeks.
Three RCTs of oral magnesium (dicitrate, u-aspartate-hydrochloride-trihydrate, oxide) found no significant reduction in migraine headache/frequency.
Maizels et al. found no effect of magnesium oxide 300 mg on number of migraine days in 99 subjects over 3 months.
Two RCTs showed magnesium supplementation reduced analgesic consumption in migraine patients.
In fibromyalgia, magnesium citrate (with or without amitriptyline) for 8 weeks reduced tender point count, tender point index, depression score and fibromyalgia impact score.
Magnesium acts as a physiological, constitutive antagonist of the NMDA receptor, controlling its excitability and thereby modulating pain signaling.
Central sensitization and long-term potentiation of pain are linked to NMDA receptor hyperexcitability, implicating the receptor in pain chronicization.
Bioavailability studies show that magnesium citrate is absorbed better than magnesium oxide.
Twenty-nine of 44 post-operative RCTs showed a significant decrease in VAS pain after IV magnesium sulphate, ranging from −2/10 to −4/10 at 12 hours versus placebo/conventional treatment.
Sixteen post-operative RCTs found no efficacy of magnesium on pain reduction, across dosing regimens from simple infusion to 50 mg/kg bolus with infusion.
In renal colic, magnesium sulphate significantly reduced pain (VAS) at 30 and 60 minutes in 2 of 5 double-blind RCTs.
In chronic neuropathic pain and CRPS, 2 of 6 RCTs showed pain reduction with magnesium (IV or oral), while 4 showed no effect.
A machine-learning model using questionnaire data alone classified individual patients as having migraine or persistent post-traumatic headache with an average accuracy of 71.9%.

Adding structural and diffusion MRI features to the questionnaire-based model improved overall classification accuracy to 78%, with 97.1% accuracy for identifying migraine patients but only 64.6% accuracy for identifying persistent post-traumatic headache patients.
Questionnaire items related to anxiety and decision-making were the most important clinical features contributing to correctly distinguishing migraine from persistent post-traumatic headache.

Cortical structural and diffusion tensor fibertract features from bilateral superior temporal, inferior parietal, and posterior cingulate regions, and right lateral occipital cortex, uncinate fasciculus, and superior longitudinal fasciculus contributed most to distinguishing migraine from persistent post-traumatic headache.

Compared with incorrectly classified persistent post-traumatic headache patients, correctly classified persistent post-traumatic headache patients had more severe physical, autonomic, anxiety, and depression symptoms, were more likely to have PTSD, and were more likely to have had mild traumatic brain injury attributed to blast exposure.
Questionnaire items related to anxiety and decision-making were the clinical features that contributed most to distinguishing migraine from persistent post-traumatic headache patients.

Structural and diffusion imaging features from bilateral superior temporal, inferior parietal, and posterior cingulate regions, and right lateral occipital cortex, uncinate fasciculus, and superior longitudinal fasciculus were the brain features most contributing to distinguishing migraine from persistent post-traumatic headache.

Persistent post-traumatic headache patients who were correctly classified by the model had more severe physical, autonomic, anxiety, and depression symptoms than those who were incorrectly classified.
Persistent post-traumatic headache patients correctly classified by the model were more likely to have comorbid post-traumatic stress disorder than those incorrectly classified.

Persistent post-traumatic headache patients correctly classified by the model were more likely to have had their mild traumatic brain injury attributed to a blast mechanism than those incorrectly classified.

The authors suggest that lower classification accuracy for persistent post-traumatic headache relative to migraine may reflect greater heterogeneity in the PPTH cohort regarding injury mechanism and physical, emotional, and cognitive symptoms.
NSAID use (scheduled or as-needed) was significantly more common among participants with hypermobile, painful knees than in either control group.

Knees with hypermobility and pain were significantly more likely to show any positive finding on musculoskeletal ultrasound compared to both control groups, although all groups had high rates of positive findings.
The quantitative synovial effusion/hypertrophy score did not differ significantly among the three knee groups.
Patellar tendon hyperemia on Doppler ultrasound was significantly more common in knees with hypermobility and pain than in either control group.
Quadriceps tendon edema was more frequently noted in hypermobile, painful knees than in control knees, though the difference did not reach statistical significance.
Tendon thickness of the quadriceps and patellar tendons did not differ significantly between hypermobile-painful, hypermobile-painless, and non-hypermobile knees at any measured location.
Cartilage thickness of the distal femur did not differ between the hypermobility-with-pain, hypermobility-without-pain, and no-hypermobility groups.
In multivariable analysis, knee hypermobility itself was not associated with an increased risk of synovial effusion or higher synovial effusion/hypertrophy quantitative score.
Scheduled NSAID use was associated with an 83% greater risk of synovial effusion on ultrasound after adjusting for knee group, NSAID use frequency, and BMI.
Scheduled NSAID use showed a trend toward a 77% greater risk of a higher synovial effusion/hypertrophy quantitative score, though this did not reach conventional statistical significance.

Across all three groups, effusion was most frequently located in the lateral parapatellar synovium, followed by medial parapatellar and suprapatellar spaces, suggesting a common anatomical distribution independent of hypermobility status.
Distal patellar tendon thickness across the whole study cohort was larger than values previously reported for healthy children in other studies, whereas proximal tendon thickness was similar.

The frequency of synovial effusion in the study's case group was similar to the frequency of asymptomatic synovial effusion reported in a healthy German pediatric cohort, suggesting that positive MSUS findings do not necessarily indicate pathology.

As expected by study design, knees with no hypermobility had significantly lower Beighton scores and less knee hyperextension by goniometry than knees in either hypermobility group, with no difference between the two hypermobility groups.
Joint hypermobility was found in 10% of children with functional GI disorders, which was not significantly different from healthy controls.
Joint hypermobility was found in 8% of children with Crohn's disease, which was not significantly different from healthy controls.
Joint hypermobility was found in 30% of children with ulcerative colitis, a higher rate than healthy controls though not reaching statistical significance.
Joint hypermobility prevalence was significantly higher in children with ulcerative colitis compared to those with functional GI disorders.
Joint hypermobility prevalence was significantly higher in children with ulcerative colitis compared to those with Crohn's disease.
Latent class analysis of Somatic Symptom Scale-8 items identified five distinct somatic symptom profiles in a representative sample of the general German population.
The majority of the general population sample (40.9%) belonged to a symptom profile characterized by the absence of bothering somatic symptoms.
A somatic symptom profile marked by considerable bothering back and extremity pain, fatigue, and sleep problems was found in 5.9% of the general population sample.

The severe 'considerable bothering' somatic symptom profile was associated with older age, self-reported disabling somatic disease, greater psychological symptom burden, illness worries, and fair to poor self-perceived general health.
Among individuals meeting the 2016 fibromyalgia diagnostic criteria, 63.2% belonged to the severe 'considerable bothering' somatic symptom profile.
A moderate somatic symptom profile characterized by little perturbation from multiple somatic symptoms and good to fair general health was identified in 17.8% of the sample.
The 'considerable bothering' somatic symptom profile (5.9% of the population) was associated with a higher prevalence of self-reported disabling somatic disease.
Higher psychological symptom burden was associated with the 'considerable bothering' somatic symptom profile linked to fibromyalgia-consistent symptom patterns.
The severe fibromyalgia-consistent symptom profile was associated with fair to poor self-perceived general health, contrasting with the milder profile's good to fair health.
The milder 'little perturbation' symptom profile, which contained 36.8% of persons meeting FM 2016 criteria, was characterized by good to fair general health rather than poor health.
The study concludes that two distinct somatic symptom profiles in the general population map onto the 2016 FM diagnostic criteria and support the existence of differing severities of fibromyalgia.
Ever use of medical cannabis was more prevalent among fibromyalgia patients than among non-fibromyalgia rheumatology patients.
Among fibromyalgia patients who had ever used medical cannabis, the majority continued using it at the time of the survey.
Fibromyalgia patients who had ever used medical cannabis tended to be younger than those who had not, though the difference approached but did not reach statistical significance.
Fibromyalgia patients who had ever used medical cannabis were more likely to be unemployed or disabled than nonusers.
Fibromyalgia patients who had ever used medical cannabis used a greater number of different medication types than nonusers.
Fibromyalgia patients who had ever used medical cannabis used a greater number of different medication types than nonusers.
Fibromyalgia ever users of medical cannabis did not differ from nonusers in symptom severity parameters.
Cigarette smoking was more common among fibromyalgia patients who used medical cannabis than among nonusers.
Recreational cannabis use was more common among fibromyalgia patients who used medical cannabis than among nonusers.
Fibromyalgia patients using medical cannabis reported substantial global symptom relief on a visual analogue scale.

Symptoms of anxiety, measured with the HADS, were present in 61% of the sample and more common in females than males.
16.7% of participants reported suffering from a musculoskeletal injury at the time of screening.
Adolescents/young adults with both GJH and anxiety had significantly higher fatigue scores than those without GJH or anxiety.
Adolescents/young adults with both GJH and anxiety had significantly higher pain catastrophizing scores than those without GJH or anxiety.
Adolescents/young adults with both GJH and anxiety had significantly lower composite muscle strength than those without GJH or anxiety.
Adolescents/young adults with both GJH and anxiety had significantly lower exercise workload (steep ramp test) than those without GJH or anxiety.

After adjustment for age, gender, and BMI, participants with combined GJH and anxiety still showed significantly increased fatigue scores.
After adjustment for age, gender, and BMI, participants with combined GJH and anxiety still showed significantly increased pain catastrophizing scores.
After adjustment, adolescents/young adults with anxiety alone (no GJH) still showed significantly increased fatigue, whereas those with GJH alone did not.
Adolescents/young adults with GJH alone (without anxiety) had no increased risk of elevated fatigue after adjustment.
Pain vigilance (PVAQ) was positively associated with age in the regression model.
Pain vigilance (PVAQ) was negatively associated with BMI in the regression model.
After adjustment for age, gender, and BMI, participants with combined GJH and anxiety showed significantly decreased exercise workload.
Adolescents/young adults with GJH alone (without anxiety) had no increased risk of decreased workload after adjustment.

Two siblings (I-4 and I-5) from the first family were compound heterozygous for a frameshift variant (c.907_908delCT, p.L303Dfs*115) and a missense variant (c.688G>A, p.D230N) in CHRNA3, the gene encoding the neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptor alpha3 subunit.
A participant (II-3) from a second, unrelated family was homozygous for the same CHRNA3 frameshift variant (p.L303Dfs*115) found in the first family, and presented with the same autonomic phenotype.
All three affected individuals had low circulating norepinephrine levels consistent with diffuse panautonomic failure.

CHRNA3 encodes a critical subunit of the neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptor responsible for fast synaptic transmission in the autonomic ganglia, and its disruption is proposed as the mechanism underlying the panautonomic failure observed in these patients.

The p.D230N missense variant is predicted to be damaging by SIFT and probably damaging by PolyPhen2, and structural modeling suggests it lies at the interface between the CHRNA3 subunit and other nAChR subunits, destabilizing the pentameric receptor complex.
In population studies of over 100,000 people, migraine affected 12% of the population and was the most disabling primary headache disorder.
Tension-type headache affected 38% of the population studied, making it more prevalent than migraine though less disabling.
Triptans, which are 5-HT1B/D receptor agonists, eliminate migraine pain in 20% to 30% of patients within 2 hours of use.
Triptan treatment is accompanied by adverse effects such as transient flushing, tightness, or tingling in the upper body in about 25% of patients.

Gepants such as rimegepant and ubrogepant, which are calcitonin gene-related peptide receptor antagonists, can eliminate headache symptoms for 2 hours in 20% of patients.

Lasmiditan, a 5-HT1F agonist used for acute migraine treatment, appears safe in patients with cardiovascular risk factors.

Baseline resting-state functional connectivity of the left posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) seed with the whole brain differentiated pregabalin responders from milnacipran responders with 77% classification accuracy using an SVM model.

Baseline resting-state functional connectivity of the right lateral dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) seed with the whole brain differentiated pregabalin responders from milnacipran responders with 77% accuracy.

A combinatorial SVM model using connectivity maps from both the left PCC and right lateral DLPFC classified pregabalin responders versus milnacipran responders with 92% accuracy, outperforming either seed alone.
Predrug clinical pain ratings alone (VAS scores) failed to predict differential response to pregabalin versus milnacipran, achieving only 62% accuracy in logistic regression.

The PCC and DLPFC connectivity classifiers that successfully distinguished pregabalin from milnacipran pain responders did not significantly classify anxiety or depression responders, confirming specificity to pain.
In an exploratory analysis restricted to the milnacipran group, connectivity of the perigenual anterior cingulate cortex classified depression responders versus nonresponders with 73% accuracy.

When the drug-responder classification model was applied to nonresponders from both trials, classification accuracy fell below chance, confirming the model's specificity to true drug responders rather than a general study-group artifact.
The drug-responder classification model did not distinguish high-motion from low-motion subject groups, indicating that head motion did not confound the classification results.

Comparing baseline placebo scans between the pregabalin and milnacipran studies (rather than drug responders) did not yield high classification accuracy for any seed, indicating the classifier was not simply detecting differences in scanner/sequence or study cohort.

In the discovery cohort, alpha-synuclein concentrations in putative oligodendroglial and neuronal exosomes increased in the order control < PD < MSA, with MSA showing the highest levels.
The ratio of oligodendroglial to neuronal exosomal alpha-synuclein concentration distinguished PD from MSA with high accuracy in the discovery cohort.

In an independent validation cohort, the oligodendroglial:neuronal exosomal alpha-synuclein ratio again separated PD from MSA, with slightly lower discriminative accuracy than in the discovery cohort.
Alpha-synuclein concentration in putative oligodendroglial exosomes distinguished healthy controls from MSA with high accuracy in the discovery cohort.
Putative neuronal exosomal alpha-synuclein poorly distinguished PD from healthy controls in both cohorts.
A multivariable logistic model combining neuronal exosomal alpha-synuclein, oligo:neuro ratio, and serum/plasma exosome concentration achieved strong discrimination of PD from MSA in both cohorts.
None of the exosomal alpha-synuclein biomarkers correlated with clinical disease severity measures.
The oligodendroglial:neuronal exosomal alpha-synuclein ratio did not correlate with disease duration, suggesting it is detectable early in disease course.
Presence of neurogenic orthostatic hypotension does not discriminate MSA from PD because it can occur in all synucleinopathies.
Abnormal thermoregulatory sweat testing has high specificity for distinguishing MSA from PD or dementia with Lewy bodies.
Elevated post-void bladder residual volume, particularly in early disease stages, is highly indicative of MSA.

Protein misfolding cyclic amplification of CSF alpha-synuclein separated PD from MSA with high overall sensitivity.
A retrospective post-mortem study found that about one in four patients clinically diagnosed with PD by a general neurologist were actually misdiagnosed and had MSA or progressive supranuclear palsy.
An autopsy study of 134 patients diagnosed with MSA found diagnostic accuracy of 71% for probable MSA and 60% for possible MSA.
