Patients with the parkinsonian subtype of MSA (MSA-P) or mixed diagnosis had higher serum/plasma alpha-synuclein levels than those with the cerebellar subtype (MSA-C).

Samples collected from the NYU Dysautonomia Center showed significantly higher putative neuronal and oligodendroglial exosomal alpha-synuclein concentrations than samples from UCLA, indicating a site/collection effect.
In a small cross-over RCT of people with diabetes, fludrocortisone was associated with a smaller drop in systolic and diastolic blood pressure on standing compared to placebo.
In a small cross-over RCT of people with Parkinson disease, fludrocortisone produced a smaller diastolic BP drop than pyridostigmine.
In people with Parkinson disease, fludrocortisone and domperidone showed no change in orthostatic BP drop after treatment.
In people with diabetes, most participants on fludrocortisone showed improvement in orthostatic symptoms compared to placebo.
In people with Parkinson disease, orthostatic symptoms were unchanged with fludrocortisone compared to pyridostigmine.
In people with Parkinson disease, fludrocortisone and domperidone produced similar improvement on the COMPASS-OD orthostatic symptom scale.
Evidence on adverse events with fludrocortisone in diabetes and Parkinson disease populations was very low-certainty but suggested minimal side effects.
Very low-certainty evidence on adverse events indicated that fludrocortisone's side effects were minimal in both the diabetes and Parkinson disease populations studied.

A retrospective cohort study of 341 people with familial dysautonomia found that long-term fludrocortisone use may not be harmful, though it is unclear whether this translates into meaningful long-term improvement in blood pressure drop or orthostatic symptoms.
Participants reporting any dizziness had a significantly higher prevalence of hypertension compared to those without dizziness.
Participants reporting any dizziness had significantly higher blood pressure medication use compared to those without dizziness.
Participants reporting any dizziness had significantly higher BMI compared to those without dizziness.
Individuals with an orthostatic dizziness profile showed significant differences in prevalence of hypertension compared to those without this profile.
Individuals with an orthostatic dizziness profile showed significant differences in BMI compared to those without this profile.
Among the 1,314 Jackson Heart Study participants screened, 317 (about 24%) reported dizziness and went on to complete a follow-up Dizziness History Questionnaire.
Participants who reported dizziness had a significantly higher prevalence of a history of noise exposure compared to those without dizziness.
Participants who reported dizziness had a significantly higher prevalence of hearing loss compared to those without dizziness.
Participants who reported dizziness had a significantly higher prevalence of tinnitus compared to those without dizziness.

A 20-year-old woman with previously diagnosed POTS developed persistent sinus bradycardia with heart rates in the 30s-40s that did not respond to positional changes, after withdrawal of rate-controlling agents.
The patient's intractable bradycardia was treated with a dual-chamber pacemaker, resulting in significant symptomatic improvement with atrial pacing at a 60%-70% burden.
A 53-year-old woman with long-standing POTS developed new profound sinus bradycardia (20-39 bpm) detected by implantable loop recorder after 12 years of stable disease.
Dual-chamber pacemaker placement in this patient led to near-complete resolution of symptoms and near-normal quality of life, requiring 60%-70% atrial pacing.

A 49-year-old woman with Sjögren's syndrome, mitochondrial myopathy, and hypermobility syndrome progressed from tachycardic episodes to frank chronotropic incompetence with an average heart rate of 40 bpm despite pyridostigmine and dextroamphetamine.
Dual-chamber pacemaker placement in this patient produced significant symptomatic improvement, requiring 80% atrial pacing burden and cessation of prior tachycardic episodes.

A 32-year-old man with small-fiber neuropathy and Sjögren's syndrome showed a postural tachycardia response on tilt-table testing, rising from a baseline of 60 bpm to 144 bpm, with the test halted early due to hypotension.

The same patient later progressed from POTS-related tachycardia to extreme bradycardia with rates in the 30s, documented by implantable loop recorder, roughly coinciding with a diagnosis of early-onset Parkinson's disease.

The authors note that autonomic dysfunction preceding neuromuscular symptoms (as in this patient's near-simultaneous diagnosis of early-onset Parkinson's disease and progressive bradyarrhythmia) is a recognized phenomenon.

Primary neurogenic POTS is proposed to result from an immune-mediated response involving serum autoantibodies against α1-adrenergic receptors, muscarinic M4 receptors, and α3 acetylcholine receptors on peripheral ganglia.

Hyperadrenergic POTS, often genetically predisposed, is characterized by increased norepinephrine levels combined with impaired clearance or decreased uptake, producing anxiety, tremulousness, and elevated diastolic blood pressure.

In vitro studies have reported circulating anti-β-adrenergic receptor antibodies causing persistent, incremental production of cyclic AMP in inappropriate sinus tachycardia, implicating autoimmunity in disease development.
A single point mutation causing norepinephrine transporter deficiency has been identified, leading to impaired NE clearance and excessive sympathetic activation.
Ivabradine, a funny sodium channel (If) blocker, has been reported to reduce heart rate and provide symptomatic relief in POTS and IST without significant drops in blood pressure.
Low-dose propranolol has demonstrated efficacy in reducing tachycardia and achieving symptomatic control in POTS.
Pacemaker implantation, particularly devices responsive to blood pressure variation, has demonstrated efficacy in orthostatic intolerance syndromes refractory to medical treatment.
Abnormal autonomic modulation featuring elevated sympathetic and diminished parasympathetic tone has been shown to be a component of both POTS and inappropriate sinus tachycardia.
POTS has been reported to be inducible following successful slow-pathway atrioventricular nodal ablation.
Patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome had a significantly lower employment rate than healthy controls.
Patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome had significantly higher rates of work disability than healthy controls.
SF-36 and WHOQOL-BREF scores were significantly lower in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome than in healthy controls, except in the WHOQOL-BREF environment domain.
Pain, as measured by ESSPRI, was an independent predictor of poorer quality of life in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome.
Fatigue, as measured by FACIT-Fatigue, was an independent predictor of poorer quality of life in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome.
Antinuclear antibody (ANA) positivity was an independent predictor of quality of life in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome.
Anti-Ro/SSA antibody positivity was an independent predictor of quality of life in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome.
Unlike other SF-36 and WHOQOL-BREF domains, the WHOQOL-BREF environment domain did not differ significantly between pSS patients and healthy controls.
Pain, measured by the ESSPRI, was an independent predictor of poor quality of life in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome.
Fatigue, measured by FACIT-Fatigue, was an independent predictor of poor quality of life in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome.
Antinuclear antibody (ANA) positivity was an independent predictor of quality of life in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome.
Anti-Ro-SSA antibody positivity was an independent predictor of quality of life in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome.
Economic class, as assessed by the Brazilian Economic Classification Criteria (CCEB), was an independent predictor of quality of life in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome.
Auriculotemporal nerve decompression was the most frequently performed trigger-site procedure, used in 91 of 154 patients (59.09%) with refractory chronic migraine.
Supraorbital nerve decompression was performed in 27 of 154 patients (13.63%) with refractory chronic migraine.
Greater occipital nerve decompression was performed in 15 of 154 patients (9.74%) with refractory chronic migraine.

At 1-year or latest follow-up, 62.2% of patients undergoing trigger-site nerve decompression were considered cured and 18.83% reported symptomatic improvement, for an overall success rate of up to 80.5%, while 3.25% reported no change or failed treatment.

Chronic migraine trigger areas are hypothesized to arise from peripheral nerve entrapment due to surrounding connective tissue adhesions and vascular conflicts, which surgical decompression aims to relieve.
Across women with persistent pain, a one standard deviation increase in pain catastrophising was associated with 27% additional pain areas.
A one standard deviation increase in generalised anxiety corresponded to only 7% additional pain area in women, falling short of the pre-specified clinical significance threshold.
Fear of pain showed a negligible negative association with pain spread (-1% additional pain areas per SD increase) in women.
A one standard deviation increase in pain catastrophising corresponded to a 1.1-point increase in pain intensity (0-10 scale) among women overall.
The pre-specified clinical significance criterion (a 30% shift in the pain variable per SD increase in a psychological variable) was not met overall across the whole sample of women.
In the migraine subgroup, pain catastrophising met the 30% clinical significance criterion for association with pain spread.

When pooled across all women with persistent pain, the pre-specified 30% clinical-significance threshold for the effect of a one-SD increase in anxiety-related variables on pain spread or intensity was not met overall.
In the low back pain subgroup, the relationship between pain catastrophising and pain spread met the pre-specified 30% clinical significance criterion.
In the neck pain subgroup, the relationship between pain catastrophising and pain spread met the 30% clinical significance criterion.
In the migraine subgroup, the relationship between pain catastrophising and pain spread met the 30% clinical significance criterion.

In the migraine subgroup, a one standard deviation increase in pain catastrophizing was associated with an increase in the anatomical spread of pain that met the study's pre-defined 30% clinical significance criterion.
In the migraine subgroup, a one standard deviation increase in pain catastrophizing was associated with an increase in pain intensity that met the study's 30% clinical significance criterion.

For fibromyalgia and other subgroups not named among those meeting criteria, the relationship between catastrophizing and pain spread/intensity did not reach the study's clinical significance threshold.

The Bayesian structural equation model that fit women's data generally showed low goodness-of-fit when applied to men's pain and anxiety-related data, suggesting the psycho-sensory relationships may be moderated by sex.
Pain spread and intensity were assessed using the McGill pain chart and a Numerical Rating Scale, respectively, as the outcome measures in the structural equation model.

Nociplastic pain is proposed as a third mechanistic category of pain distinct from nociceptive and neuropathic pain, arising from augmented CNS pain/sensory processing and altered pain modulation rather than tissue or nerve damage.

Nociplastic pain can present in isolation (e.g., fibromyalgia, tension-type headache) or as part of a mixed-pain state combined with ongoing nociceptive or neuropathic pain, as in chronic low back pain.
Nociplastic pain shows decreased responsiveness to peripherally directed therapies such as anti-inflammatory drugs, opioids, surgery, or injections, compared with nociceptive pain.
Lifetime incidence of syncope in the general population is estimated to be at least 32-35%.
Women have a consistently higher incidence of syncope than men, and elderly patients have worse outcomes than younger patients.
Vasovagal syncope and orthostatic hypotension together account for up to two-thirds of ED syncope presentations, while cardiac causes account for about 7-10%.
In a multicenter prospective study of 5000 ED syncope patients followed for one month, presumed discharge diagnosis was vasovagal syncope in 53.3% and cardiac syncope in 5.4%.
Overall mortality after ED syncope presentation is estimated at under 2% at 10 days and 8.4% at one year, with morbidity of 6.9% at 10 days and 25.2% at 2 years.
A Canadian study found low mortality among ED-discharged syncope patients (0.4% at 30 days, 3.0% at one year), whereas hospitalized patients had 3-4 times higher mortality at both time points.

An Italian study found hospitalized syncope patients had 14.7% mortality compared to 1.8% among those discharged from the ED, with nearly half of admitted patients over 65 with significant cardiac comorbidities.
A propensity score analysis of 8864 ED patients admitted within 48 hours found neither short- nor long-term mortality was reduced by hospitalization compared to a matched cohort.

Classic orthostatic hypotension carries a 1.5-fold mortality risk due to later major adverse cardiovascular events compared to patients without OH, with a more pronounced risk in those under 65 years old.
Mortality risk is not increased in vasovagal syncope, unlike other causes of syncope, which vary considerably with underlying comorbidities.
About 15% of syncopal events lead to injuries, 30% of syncope patients are injured at some point, and 33% of vasovagal syncope patients are injured during a faint despite warning signs.
A point score developed by the authors' group distinguished syncope from epileptic seizures with 94% sensitivity and specificity.
A preliminary diagnosis can be established in almost two-thirds of syncope patients using a standardized history, physical exam, and ECG, with 88% diagnostic accuracy.
History of heart disease, male gender, age over 40, lack of prodromes, and no more than two prior spells are major predictors of cardiac syncope, with heart disease being an independent risk factor.

In patients with known structural heart disease, a structured evidence-based history identifies ventricular tachycardia as the cause of syncope with 99% sensitivity, 68% specificity, and 96% negative predictive value.
Non-sinus rhythm and left bundle branch conduction abnormality on ECG carried threefold odds of significant cardiac outcomes in patients over 35 with syncope or near syncope.
Prolonged QTc in patients over 60 years old in sinus rhythm without conduction abnormalities was not an independent risk marker for 30-day serious adverse outcomes.

In smaller retrospective studies with over 30 months mean follow-up, QTc greater than 450 ms in men and 460 ms in women carried a 2.2-fold hazard ratio for long-term mortality, and QTc greater than 500 ms in patients over 65 was associated with a 3.5-fold hazard ratio for mortality.

The Basel IX ECG-based ALERT-CS tool showed high diagnostic accuracy (AUC 0.8) for cardiac syncope in patients over 40, outperforming EGSYS and SFSR, with 30-day major adverse cardiac events 37.5 times higher in the rule-in group than the rule-out group.
The San Francisco Syncope Rule performed poorly in external validation studies due to high miss rates.

A meta-analysis of individual patient data found no additive value of the OESIL, EGSYS, and SFSR scores beyond clinical judgement for predicting serious adverse outcomes in the ED or at 10 and 30 days.

In a matched cohort of 3388 patients from five prior trials, attribute matching for personalized 10-day risk prediction was inferior to a regression model and required a much larger cohort to match all variables.
The Canadian Syncope Risk Score, derived from 4030 adult ED syncope patients, had 99.2% sensitivity for predicting 30-day serious events at a score of -2 or higher.

In a nine-center validation, the observed 30-day risk of serious events was 0.3% in the very-low-risk CSRS cohort versus 51% in the very-high-risk group, with 97.8% sensitivity and 44.3% specificity at a threshold of -1.

An Australian single-center validation study in 283 patients found a lower sensitivity (71.4%) for CSRS at threshold -1, though a threshold of 1 maintained similar sensitivity with improved specificity (72.8%) and 99% negative predictive value.
CoQ10 deficiency is implicated in the pathogenesis of migraine, particularly in pediatric and adolescent patients.
The American Academy of Neurology guidelines recommend CoQ10 supplementation for migraine prevention at level of evidence C.

In a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial of 45 migraine patients, CoQ10 400 mg/day for 3 months significantly reduced migraine attack frequency, severity, and duration compared to placebo.
In the same migraine RCT, serum TNF-alpha was lower in the CoQ10-treated arm compared to placebo, alongside higher CoQ10 levels.
Serum CGRP levels were lower in migraine patients treated with CoQ10 compared to placebo.
A systematic review and meta-analysis of four RCTs found that CoQ10 supplementation significantly reduced migraine attack frequency but had no significant effect on attack severity or duration.
Other studies found a non-significant reduction in migraine frequency and severity with CoQ10, potentially due to heterogeneity in dosing and patient characteristics.
Combining CoQ10 (400 mg/day) with other migraine-prophylaxis nutraceuticals such as curcumin, magnesium, feverfew (Tanacetum parthenium), or riboflavin produced encouraging results.
Oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are associated with ME/CFS pathogenesis, with a reduced rate of ATP synthesis reported in patients.

In a Spanish RCT (NCT02063126) of 73 CFS patients, combined CoQ10 (200 mg/day) plus NADH (20 mg/day) significantly reduced Fatigue Impact Scale scores versus placebo, with improved NAD+/NADH ratio, citrate synthase activity, ATP levels, and reduced lipoperoxides in mononuclear blood cells.

A follow-up RCT of 80 CFS patients found that CoQ10 + NADH supplementation significantly reduced maximum heart rate at week 8 versus baseline during a cycle ergometer test and decreased perceived fatigue versus placebo, though pain and sleep were unchanged.
Fukuda et al. found that 8 weeks of CoQ10 supplementation (150 mg/day) did not improve clinical symptoms in CFS patients.

A 12-week treatment with CoQ10 (150 mg/day) improved sleep quality, autonomic nervous system dysfunction, and arithmetic-task performance in CFS patients versus placebo, and decreases in fatigue and depression levels correlated with increases in ubiquinol concentrations.
AMPK, a key regulator of cellular energy homeostasis, is downregulated in fibromyalgia patients, and CoQ10-induced AMPK activation is associated with improved clinical symptoms.
A quasi-experimental study of 35 female fibromyalgia patients found that CoQ10 300 mg/day for 3 months significantly reduced fibromyalgia-related fatigue as measured by FIQ and VAS.
A RCT of 20 female fibromyalgia patients treated with CoQ10 300 mg/day for 40 days replicated the fatigue-reducing effect seen in the earlier quasi-experimental study.
In juvenile fibromyalgia, 3 months of treatment with ubiquinol 100 mg/day significantly reduced Chalder's Fatigue Scale scores compared to control.
Two additional studies in female fibromyalgia patients using CoQ10 doses of 300-400 mg/day reported significant improvements in FIQ and VAS scores.
A meta-analysis of RCTs found that CoQ10's therapeutic effects on fatigue were greater in statin-related fatigue and fibromyalgia compared with fatigue related to other diseases.
Vestibular migraine was the single most common diagnosis in children referred to a pediatric neurology clinic for dizziness/vertigo, accounting for 21.7% of cases.
Orthostatic hypotension was the second most common diagnosis, found in 20% of children presenting with dizziness.
Among all children referred for dizziness, 40% had an underlying neurological disorder (vestibular migraine 21.7%, epilepsy 10%, benign paroxysmal vertigo 8.3%).
Headache was the most frequent symptom accompanying vertigo/dizziness, reported in 31.7% of children.
Nausea and/or vomiting accompanied vertigo/dizziness in 30% of children.
Vitamin B12 deficiency (≤200 pg/mL) was found in 12 of 44 tested children with dizziness, and B12 replacement improved symptoms in 11 of those 12 patients.

Children with neurological causes of dizziness had significantly earlier age at onset and longer attack duration compared with children with non-neurological causes, with no significant difference in gender, attack frequency, or vitamin B12 levels.
At 12-month follow-up, ongoing symptoms were detected in 31% of children diagnosed with vestibular migraine.
At 1-year follow-up, 28% of children with psychogenic dizziness still had ongoing symptoms.

Only 2 of 13 vestibular migraine patients were treated with topiramate as preventive therapy, and both had good prognosis, but the authors could not draw firm conclusions on its efficacy given the small numbers.
Seven patients had benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) whose only symptom was positional vertigo triggered by head position change.
Cranial MRI performed in all patients showed abnormal but incidental findings (arachnoid cyst, pineal gland cyst) in 8.4% of children, unrelated to their dizziness etiology.
EEG performed in 44 patients showed epileptiform discharges in 4 patients, localized to occipital, central, and temporal regions.

About one-fourth of patients in this pediatric neurology clinic were diagnosed with cardiogenic vertigo (orthostatic hypotension, vasovagal syncope, hypertension, or arrhythmia), typically presenting as dizziness rather than true vertigo during postural change.
A history of motion sickness was most frequently reported among children with vestibular migraine (8 of 13 motion-sickness patients), followed by psychogenic dizziness, BPPV, and BPV.
The authors classified benign paroxysmal vertigo (BPV) as a migraine equivalent and grouped it with vestibular migraine and epilepsy under neurological disorders.
Sedentary mice exposed to neonatal maternal separation (NMS) showed a significantly higher percentage of degranulated dural mast cells than sedentary naive mice.
Voluntary wheel running attenuated the NMS-induced increase in dural mast cell degranulation, with NMS-exercised mice showing significantly lower degranulation than NMS-sedentary mice.
Total dural mast cell counts showed only a non-significant increase in NMS-sedentary mice compared to naive-sedentary and NMS-exercised mice.
NMS significantly increased dural PAR2 protein levels compared to naive mice, with no significant effect of exercise.
Exercised NMS mice had significantly lower dural TRPA1 protein levels compared to exercised naive mice, reflecting a significant NMS/exercise interaction.

Voluntary wheel running unexpectedly increased mouse grimace scores after dural saline/inflammatory soup application, with naive-Ex-Saline, NMS-Ex-Saline, and NMS-Ex-IS mice scoring higher than their sedentary counterparts.
Application of inflammatory soup to the dura significantly lowered forepaw mechanical withdrawal thresholds (increased allodynia) across all groups regardless of NMS or exercise status.

Nitroglycerin injection significantly increased grimace scores across all groups, with exercised naive mice showing the highest increase compared to sedentary naive, saline-treated naive-Ex, and NMS-Ex-NTG mice.

There was a significant overall effect of NMS and a significant NMS/exercise interaction on hindpaw mechanical withdrawal thresholds after saline or NTG injection, with naive-sedentary-saline mice having higher thresholds than naive-exercised-saline and NMS-sedentary-saline mice.
NMS-sedentary mice given NTG showed a non-significant trend toward lower hindpaw withdrawal thresholds compared to naive-sedentary-NTG and NMS-exercised-NTG mice.
In mice with no dural stimulation or NTG, exercised naive mice had significantly higher grimace scores than sedentary naive mice, following brief isoflurane anesthesia.

After nitroglycerin treatment, NMS-sedentary mice spent significantly less time in the light compartment of a light/dark box compared to naive-sedentary mice, indicating increased photophobia-like behavior.
NMS significantly increased the magnitude of change in time spent in the light (from second baseline) after NTG treatment, indicating a greater photophobia response relative to baseline.
Voluntary wheel running significantly decreased CGRP protein levels in the dura in both naive and NMS mice 2 hours after NTG injection.
No significant differences in CGRP levels were found between NMS and naive groups, or between exercise groups, in the trigeminal ganglia or serum.
Serum corticosterone levels measured 2 hours after NTG injection were not significantly different between NMS and naive mice, nor between exercised and sedentary groups.
Naive and NMS mice singly housed with running wheels from 8-12 weeks of age ran similar weekly distances, indicating NMS did not impair voluntary exercise capacity.
In pair-housed mice given running wheels from 4 weeks of age, NMS mice showed a slight but non-significant decrease in weekly running distance compared to naive mice.

Mistreatment during childhood was the strongest psychosocial predictor distinguishing rheumatic disease type and was more strongly associated with fibromyalgia than with rheumatoid arthritis, spondyloarthritis, or Sjögren's syndrome combined.
The agreeableness personality trait was the second most important predictor of rheumatic disease type and was more strongly associated with fibromyalgia than with the inflammatory RMD group.
Somatic disorder was the third most important psychopathological predictor of rheumatic disease type in the random forest model.

Overall, adverse childhood experiences were relatively more important than personality traits, psychopathological variables, or demographic variables in predicting rheumatic disease type, suggesting that childhood trauma may contribute to adulthood psychopathology that underlies fibromyalgia development.
Sixty-one point five percent of pSS patients (80/130) had an ESSPRI score of 5 or higher, indicating an unsatisfactory symptom state.
Patients with ESSPRI ≥5 had a significantly higher prevalence of depression compared to those with lower ESSPRI scores.
Lower non-stimulated whole salivary flow (NSWSF) was associated with ESSPRI scores of 5 or higher.
The overall median ESSPRI score was 6, with subdomain medians of 6 for fatigue, 4 for pain, and 8 for dryness.

Among patients with a second ESSPRI assessment, most had a clinically meaningful change in score over time, but none of the demographic, clinical, or treatment variables studied (including changes in prednisone or immunosuppressant use) were associated with this variation.
Duo exome sequencing identified a novel homozygous missense mutation in SDR42E1 that co-segregated with disease in a family with a brittle-cornea-like syndrome plus genital abnormalities.
In silico structural analysis predicted that the p.Arg154Gln substitution destabilizes the SDR42E1 protein.
Endocrinological investigation revealed that both affected patients had low serum cholesterol levels, consistent with a defect in steroid biosynthesis.

The two affected boys presented with corneal thinning, blue sclera, keratoconus, skin hyperelasticity, joint hypermobility, muscle weakness, hearing loss, dental abnormalities, micropenis, hypospadias and cryptorchidism, defining a novel oculocutaneous genital syndrome.
Karyotyping showed a normal 46,XY karyotype in both boys, excluding chromosomal rearrangements as a cause of their disorder of sex development.

Patients with generalized joint hypermobility (Beighton score ≥4) had significantly thinner hip labra at the indirect rectus (11:30 o'clock) position on MRI compared with matched controls with normal Beighton scores.
Patients with generalized joint hypermobility had significantly thinner hip labra at the anterosuperior (1:30 o'clock) position compared with matched controls.
There was no significant difference in labral width at the Psoas U (3 o'clock) position between the high Beighton score group and controls.
Linear regression showed that higher Beighton score was significantly negatively associated with hip labral width at the indirect rectus position.
Linear regression showed that higher Beighton score was significantly negatively associated with hip labral width at the anterosuperior position.
Beighton score was not significantly associated with hip labral width at the Psoas U position.

Patients with generalized joint hypermobility had a significantly higher rate of diagnosed connective tissue disorders (Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Marfan syndrome, Raynaud disease, or systemic lupus erythematosus) compared with controls.

Among patients undergoing hip arthroscopy for femoroacetabular impingement in this cohort, approximately 12% met criteria for generalized joint hypermobility, a lower rate than the 20% and 32.7% reported in prior studies.
Girls with generalized joint hypermobility showed no statistically significant differences in any measured sagittal spinal curvature compared to girls without GJH.
Boys with generalized joint hypermobility showed no statistically significant differences in any measured sagittal spinal curvature compared to boys without GJH.
Regardless of GJH status, children aged 8-14 adopted an improper kyphotic alignment of the sacral slope and lumbar lordosis when sitting, deviating from standard standing reference values.
Thoracic kyphosis values remained within the normal standing reference range across all subgroups regardless of gender or GJH status.

Regardless of GJH occurrence, the upper part of the thoracic spine showed higher kyphosis values than the lower part, suggesting a tendency toward greater inclination that may lead to head protraction.
Generalized joint hypermobility results from alterations in connective tissue, including impaired function of collagen proteins.
The authors recommend the Beighton score as the most commonly used method to measure knee generalized joint hypermobility.
For patients with ACL injury and generalized joint hypermobility, the authors recommend using a patellar-tendon or quadriceps tendon autograft for ACL reconstruction.
The authors recommend always considering a lateral extra-articular tenodesis in ACL reconstruction for patients with generalized joint hypermobility.

The authors recommend that patients with generalized joint hypermobility pass a return-to-sport test battery including strength, hop performance, subjective knee function, and movement quality before returning to sport.
Return to sport after ACL reconstruction may be delayed by as much as 1 year in patients with generalized joint hypermobility.
35% of patients with rheumatologic diseases reported at least one ophthalmological symptom, most commonly dry eye sensation.
Dry eye sensation was the single most common ophthalmological symptom across the entire cohort of rheumatologic disease patients, similar to prior reports.

21.45% of the total sample had one or more ophthalmologic diagnoses, with keratoconjunctivitis sicca being the most prevalent and the single common pathology among the four most prevalent rheumatologic diseases.
Keratoconjunctivitis sicca was the most frequent ocular diagnosis overall (15.93%), followed by cataract and uveitis.
Nearly 75% of patients with Sjögren syndrome reported ophthalmological symptoms, the highest proportion among rheumatologic diseases studied besides a few rare conditions.
78.34% of Sjögren syndrome patients had an ophthalmological diagnosis, the second highest proportion after celiac disease and neuromyelitis optica (100%).
Keratoconjunctivitis sicca was the most common ophthalmologic diagnosis in Sjögren syndrome patients, present in 77.07% of cases, followed by keratitis and scleritis.
Keratoconjunctivitis sicca and keratitis were statistically significantly associated with Sjögren syndrome.
Dry eye symptom showed a statistically significant association with Sjögren syndrome.
Photophobia was statistically significantly associated with systemic lupus erythematosus.
Ocular pruritus was statistically significantly associated with fibromyalgia.

Rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren syndrome, psoriatic arthritis, and psoriasis were statistically associated with ocular symptoms, while Sjögren syndrome and polyautoimmunity were significantly associated with ophthalmological diagnosis.
Among fibromyalgia patients, 34.8% had ocular manifestations, with dry eye most frequent (31.49%) and keratoconjunctivitis sicca present in a significant proportion (15.46%).

Some fibromyalgia patients presented uveitis, maculopathy, and optic neuritis as ocular manifestations, which the authors state have not been previously reported in fibromyalgia, though not statistically significant.
24.05% of patients with systemic lupus erythematosus had some form of ophthalmic manifestation, compared to 18.42% of RA patients.
20.25% of SLE patients had a keratoconjunctivitis sicca diagnosis, 2.5% had keratitis and optic neuritis, and 1.26% had conjunctivitis and cataract.
In RA patients, the most common ocular diagnoses were keratoconjunctivitis sicca (12.78%) and scleritis (2.25%), followed by cataract, uveitis, and maculopathy.
Among RA patients, 30.08% reported at least one ocular symptom, with dry eye being most common (27%), followed by red eye, ocular pain, decreased visual acuity, floaters, burning, and tearing.
Polyautoimmunity was present in 6.9% of the population; among these patients, almost 44% reported ocular symptoms (most commonly dry eye) and 42% had an ophthalmological diagnosis.
Among patients with polyautoimmunity, keratoconjunctivitis sicca was the most common ocular diagnosis, found in 33.36% of the subgroup.
All patients in the cohort with celiac disease and neuromyelitis optica presented at least one ophthalmological diagnosis.
Overall uveitis prevalence in the cohort was 1.38%, with anterior uveitis at 0.88%, posterior uveitis at 0.13%, and panuveitis at 0.13%, lower than uveitis-focused prior reports.
Meta-analysis of 10 studies found a pooled odds ratio of 3.27 for joint hypermobility in functional somatic syndromes compared with controls.
Nine of the 11 studies included in the qualitative review reported increased rates of joint hypermobility in functional somatic syndromes compared to controls.
GJH was present in 57.14% of screened university students, and was more common among females than males.
Adiposity parameters (BMI, waist, hip, WHR, WHtR) showed no significant association with GJH.
Physical activity, including VO2max, BMR, TEE, and PA scores, was significantly reduced in students with GJH compared to controls.
Pain intensity measured by VAS was significantly higher in students with GJH than in controls.
Serum prolidase enzyme activity (SPEA) was significantly higher in students with GJH compared to controls.
Serum hydroxyproline levels were significantly higher in students with GJH compared to controls, indicating altered collagen metabolism.
Total antioxidant capacity (TAC) was significantly reduced in GJH students compared to controls.
Total oxidant activity (TOA) was significantly elevated in GJH students compared to controls.
Oxidative stress index (OSI) was significantly higher in GJH students compared to controls.
Beighton score correlated positively with pain intensity, prolidase activity, hydroxyproline, TOA, and OSI, and negatively with physical activity and TAC.

Females with GJH exhibited lower physical activity and total antioxidant capacity, and higher serum prolidase activity, hydroxyproline, total oxidant activity, oxidative stress index, and pain intensity compared to males.
Among 626 individuals tested for autoimmune/paraneoplastic antibody panels in 2017, 20.1% had more than one panel requested.
290 of 768 total panels (35.7%) were requested as part of overlapping or repeat evaluations.
Only 10.1% of individuals underwent a paired serum and CSF evaluation, comprising 64 paired evaluations and 128 panels (15.7% of total).
Overlapping antibody panel evaluations (multiple panels ordered <14 days apart, excluding paired serum/CSF) occurred in 7.3% of individuals, comprising 47 evaluations and 98 panels (12.1% of total).
36% of overlapping evaluations consisted of identical antibody panels, suggesting a substantial proportion may represent accidental reordering.
8.6% of individuals underwent repeat antibody evaluations (obtained ≥14 days apart), with an average of 350 days between evaluations (median 200 days, range 140-1,941 days).
The vast majority (86%) of repeat antibody evaluations showed no change in antibody status compared to the prior evaluation, and 97% of initially negative evaluations remained negative.
Eight repeat evaluations (11.4%) showed a transition in antibody status from positive to negative.
Two repeat evaluations (2.8%) transitioned from negative to positive antibody status, both involving a different panel than the initial evaluation.
In one patient with LGI1 antibody-associated seizures, anti-seizure medications were stopped after the LGI1 antibody panel transitioned from positive to negative on repeat testing.
In a second case, immunotherapy was started for a patient with encephalopathy after a new positive GAD-65 antibody result on repeat testing.

GAD-65 antibodies can be present at low, clinically insignificant levels in healthy controls, other systemic inflammatory/autoimmune disorders, and unrelated neurologic diseases, and represented the majority of antibody status conversions in this study.

After excluding clinically insignificant GAD-65 antibody results, four repeat evaluations transitioned from positive to negative and zero transitioned from negative to positive, suggesting initial negative evaluations are generally sufficient for surveillance.
No cases were found in which new antibody panel results correlated with a change in clinical diagnosis or prompted malignancy screening.

Mandl et al.'s 1997 study found significantly lower systolic blood pressure in pSS patients compared to age-matched controls, both at rest and during tilt table testing.
A 2001 follow-up study validated the earlier finding of impaired blood pressure response to postural change in pSS patients compared to controls.

Kovács et al. found that most pSS patients had restricted heart rate variability and blood pressure variability with significantly lower median heart rate and diastolic BP responses across multiple cardiovascular reflex tests, despite normal resting HR/BP.
Brunetta et al. found pSS patients had significantly lower LF and higher HF components of heart rate variability, resulting in a significantly lower LF/HF ratio compared to controls.

Tumiati et al. observed a lower LF/HF ratio in heart rate variability among pSS patients compared to age-matched controls.

Cai et al. found pSS patients had significantly larger increases in brachial systolic BP and attenuation in the RR ratio, along with relative tachycardia, when standing compared to age- and sex-matched controls.

Koh et al. found pSS patients had a significantly lower HF component but no difference in LF, resulting in a significantly higher LF/HF ratio compared to controls, contrary to earlier studies by Brunetta and Tumiati.
Niemela et al. found no evidence of cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction in pSS patients using 24-hour ECG monitoring and cardiovascular reflex tests compared to matched controls.

In an edrophonium challenge study, 4 of 21 pSS patients but none of the healthy controls showed an abnormally reduced sweat response, indicating sudomotor autonomic dysfunction in a subset of patients.
More than half of pSS patients in the edrophonium challenge study showed delayed gastric emptying, consistent with parasympathetic cholinergic dysfunction affecting the gastrointestinal system.

In a large UK Primary Sjögren's Syndrome Registry cohort, COMPASS autonomic symptom scores were significantly higher in pSS patients than in age-matched controls, and nearly 55% of pSS patients scored above the threshold suggesting autonomic dysfunction.

Koh et al. found a higher prevalence of Raynaud's phenomenon and higher ESSPRI fatigue scores in pSS patients with HRV-defined autonomic dysfunction compared to those without.
