A history of oncological disease increased the risk of secondary headache 2.7-fold in logistic regression analysis.
A history of head trauma was associated with a markedly increased, 41.4-fold risk of secondary headache, the strongest predictor identified.
Among patients with a final primary headache diagnosis, migraine was the most frequent subtype (73.4%), followed by tension-type headache (17.2%) and trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias (7.7%).
Trigeminal neuralgia was the most common type of facial pain among ED headache patients, occurring in 3.1% of the total sample.

Secondary headaches were attributed to infection (17.2%), electrolyte dyshomeostasis (17.2%), vascular disorders (16.2%), non-vascular disorders (15.2%), trauma (5.7%), intoxication/substance withdrawal (7.4%), and psychiatric disorders (11.1%).
Among vascular-cause secondary headaches, acute cerebral ischemia (20.8%), subarachnoid hemorrhage (12.5%), subdural hematoma (14.6%) and arterial vessel dissection (6.3%) were identified.
Almost a quarter of headache patients (24.7%) received no final headache diagnosis, which the authors link to incomplete phenotypic documentation.
Patients with secondary headache were significantly older than those with primary headache.
Within primary headaches, migraine was significantly more frequent in women while trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias were significantly more frequent in men.
Stabbing headache character occurred significantly more often in patients in the neuropathies and facial pain diagnostic group compared to other headache groups.
Pain intensity did not differ significantly between the individual headache diagnostic groups.
A history of cardiovascular disease was significantly associated with a diagnosis of secondary headache.
Patients with primary headache had a higher risk of having a history of CNS disease, including known migraine.
A positive history of cerebral infarction was associated with patients not receiving a final headache diagnosis.
Patients who self-presented to the ED were more likely to be diagnosed with trigeminal neuralgia and facial pain.
A diagnosis of secondary headache was significantly associated with inpatient admission of the patient.
Logistic regression showed the risk of secondary headache increased 1.03-fold with every additional year of patient age.
Patients aged 50 years or above were 2.85 times more likely to have secondary headache than those under 50.
A medical history of respiratory disease was associated with a 3.6-fold increased risk of secondary headache.
A medical history of cardiovascular disease was associated with a 3.0-fold increased risk of secondary headache in the regression model.
A history of oncological disease was associated with a 2.7-fold increased risk of secondary headache.
A history of trauma was associated with a strikingly increased, 41.4-fold risk of secondary headache, the strongest risk factor identified.
A previous neurological condition (including migraine) reduced the risk of secondary headache by 0.39-fold.
Concomitant fever increased the risk of secondary headache by 9.93-fold.
Headache aggravation by sneezing, coughing, or Valsalva maneuver increased the risk of secondary headache by 7.57-fold.
Nausea, photophobia, phonophobia and visual disturbances were each associated with a significantly lower risk of secondary headache, i.e., they were markers favoring a primary headache diagnosis.
No significant association was found between secondary headache and pain character, pain intensity, suddenness of onset, headache duration, or previously experienced headache.
No association was found between the type of referral/presentation to the ED and diagnosis of secondary headache.
Patients with refractory epilepsy treated with a fully implanted vagus nerve stimulator incidentally reported improvement in their migraine and cluster headache.
In a controlled study, transcutaneous cervical vagus nerve stimulation (tcVNS) produced a significant but limited effect when used for acute treatment of migraine attacks.
tcVNS showed no significant prophylactic effect in episodic migraine.
tcVNS showed a clear beneficial effect in prophylaxis of chronic cluster headache.
tcVNS was clearly beneficial in the acute attack treatment of episodic cluster headache.
In a small controlled clinical trial, transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) had a significant effect in preventing chronic migraine.
Less well-defined clinical studies suggest taVNS may provide some benefit for chronic back pain.
Preliminary clinical observations suggest taVNS may help unspecific gastrointestinal pain in adolescents.
The authors conclude it is probable that vagus nerve stimulation has a clinically meaningful effect on pain syndromes overall, though key parameters remain unresolved.
Hypermobility Joint Syndrome (HJS) was confirmed in 8.1% (26 of 322) of patients presenting with temporomandibular disorders.
Among patients with HJS and TMD, 61.5% had disc displacement with reduction co-occurring with myofascial pain, while 38.5% had purely myogenic TMD.
Among HJS patients, maximum mouth opening was normal in 57.7% and increased beyond the individual physiological norm in 42.3%.
Patients with HJS+TMD were characterized by an increased range of mouth opening, whereas the TMD-only control group's main problem was limitation of mouth opening.
Deviation-type mandibular movement dysfunction occurred at similar rates in the HJS group (73.1%) and the TMD-only control group (69.8%).
Three weeks of stomatognathic physiotherapy significantly increased maximum mouth opening in both the HJS+TMD group and the TMD-only control group.
Physiotherapy significantly decreased myofascial pain in all assessed masticatory and neck muscles in both HJS+TMD and TMD-only groups.
After physiotherapy, visual improvement in mandibular movement coordination occurred in 10 of 19 HJS patients with deviation and 26 of 37 control patients with deviation.
The HJS+TMD group was significantly younger (mean age 27.1±9.4 years) than the TMD-only control group (mean age 37.4±9.2 years).
The HJS+TMD study group consisted predominantly of women (92.3%, n=24 of 26).
Tilt testing induced reflex syncope in 60% of the 5236 patients investigated for unexplained syncope, with 40% remaining tilt-negative.
Tilt test positivity rates were similar between males (61%) and females (59%), indicating no major overall sex difference in test positivity.
Patients who developed reflex syncope during tilt testing had significantly lower resting systolic blood pressure than tilt-negative patients.
Patients who developed reflex syncope during tilt testing had significantly lower resting diastolic blood pressure than tilt-negative patients.
Patients who developed reflex syncope during tilt testing had significantly lower resting heart rate than tilt-negative patients.
In gender-stratified analysis, baseline SBP was similar between sexes, but males had higher DBP and females had higher HR than the opposite sex.
Univariate analysis found a significantly higher rate of tilt-test-induced reflex syncope in patients younger than 30 years.
Univariate analysis found that patients without a history of hypertension had a significantly higher rate of tilt-test-induced reflex syncope than hypertensive patients.
In multivariable-adjusted logistic regression, younger age independently predicted tilt-test positivity, with each 10-year decrease in age slightly increasing the odds.
In multivariable-adjusted logistic regression, a resting SBP below 128 mmHg independently predicted tilt-test positivity.
In multivariable-adjusted logistic regression, a resting heart rate below 69 bpm independently predicted tilt-test positivity.
Absence of a hypertension diagnosis independently increased the probability of a positive tilt test by over 50% in multivariable analysis.
The rate-pressure product, a marker of cardiovascular fitness and myocardial oxygen consumption, was significantly lower in tilt-positive patients across most age and sex strata.
Center-specific analysis showed the association between blood pressure and tilt positivity was weaker in the Florence cohort, reaching significance only for diastolic blood pressure.
In a sensitivity analysis, the independent association between low SBP and tilt-test positivity was attenuated to non-significance in the multivariable model after excluding the Lavagna cohort.
Among 357 patients hospitalized for vertigo/dizziness, 111 (31.1%) had an abnormal head-upright subjective visual vertical (HU-SVV) test result.
The modified head-tilt SVV (HT-SVV) test detected abnormal results in 132 of 357 patients (37.0%).
Combining the HU-SVV and HT-SVV tests identified abnormal gravity-perception results in 185 of 357 patients (51.8%).
Adding the HT-SVV test to the standard HU-SVV test significantly improved detection of gravity perception disturbance compared with the HU-SVV test alone.

The abnormal HU-SVV rate was significantly higher in patients with peripheral vestibular diseases (Meniere's disease, unilateral vestibular disease, BPPV, bilateral vestibular disease) than in those with vestibular migraine, orthostatic dysfunction, central dizziness, vestibular schwannoma, or psychogenic dizziness.

The abnormal HT-SVV rate was significantly higher in patients with peripheral vestibular diseases than in those with vestibular migraine, orthostatic dysfunction, central dizziness, vestibular schwannoma, or psychogenic dizziness.

The combined HU-SVV and/or HT-SVV abnormality rate was significantly higher in patients with peripheral vestibular diseases than in those with vestibular migraine, orthostatic dysfunction, central dizziness, vestibular schwannoma, or psychogenic dizziness.
The authors defined normal reference ranges of absolute HU-SVV (<2.5°) and HTPG (0.80-1.25) in the sitting position, which were then used to classify abnormality in each vertigo/dizziness subtype.
Two cohort studies found approximately a two-fold increase in risk of systemic sclerosis among breast implant users compared to non-users.
Three case-control studies found no increased risk of systemic sclerosis among breast implant users.
Three cohort studies did not find an increased risk of incident and confirmed Sjogren's syndrome among breast implant users.
Despite no increased risk of confirmed Sjogren's syndrome, breast implant users reported sicca symptoms, myalgia and fatigue more frequently than non-users.
A meta-analysis of heterogeneous studies found a less than two-fold increase in risk of rheumatoid arthritis among breast implant users.
Studies did not support an association between breast implants and systemic lupus erythematosus.
Implant rupture detected on imaging was not clearly associated with incident rheumatic disease, though no studies specifically examined acute or traumatic rupture.
Explantation of breast implants often led to a temporary improvement in symptoms.
Removal of breast implants (explantation) often led to temporary improvement in reported rheumatic-type symptoms among breast implant users.
Evidence was insufficient to determine whether breast implants are associated with other rheumatic disorders beyond SSc, SS, SLE, RA, and autoimmune myositis.
Joint hypermobility is estimated to affect approximately 20% of the general population.
Individuals with hypermobility are more likely to experience severe chronic widespread pain and have comorbid rheumatic conditions, reported in 60% of cases.
Hypermobility is reported to co-occur with dysautonomia.
Hypermobility is described as a risk factor for both the development and presence of anxiety and panic, with reported odds ratios of 4.39 and 6.72.

Symptomatic hypermobility is under-recognised relative to inflammatory arthritides yet accounts for up to 45% of general rheumatology outpatient referrals, an estimated 900,000 attendances in England in 2014-2015.

A pilot multidisciplinary rehabilitation programme combining physical and cognitive-behavioural therapy in 12 people with Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome/Joint Hypermobility Syndrome produced significant improvements in perceived performance of daily activities and self-perceived pain, though its impact on anxiety was not assessed.

Prior experimental data used for sample size calculation reported a mean Beck Anxiety Inventory score of 24.5 (SD 9.36) in hypermobile subjects, indicating clinically significant anxiety burden in this population.
Serum levels of l-kynurenine, kynurenic acid, 3-hydroxykynurenine, 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid, 5-HIAA, and quinolinic acid were decreased in chronic migraineurs compared with controls.

Serum concentrations of l-tryptophan, anthranilic acid, and xanthurenic acid were significantly higher in migraineurs than controls, suggesting l-kynurenine is preferentially shunted to anthranilic acid at the expense of kynurenic acid and 3-hydroxykynurenine.
Similar decreases in kynurenine pathway metabolites observed in migraine were also found in patients with episodic or chronic cluster headache.

In rats, peripherally administered kynurenic acid poorly crossed the blood-brain barrier under normal conditions, but in animals with KCl-induced cortical spreading depression it significantly shortened the CSD wave half-amplitude duration.

Systemic administration of l-kynurenine (alone or with probenecid) increased cortical kynurenic acid concentration and decreased cortical spreading depression frequency in rats, with females more sensitive to this inhibitory effect than males.

Plasma concentrations of l-tryptophan and its metabolites (l-kynurenine, anthranilic acid, kynurenic acid, 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid, 5-HIAA, picolinic acid, melatonin) were decreased in the interictal period of episodic migraineurs, especially in those without aura, while 3-HAA, 5-HIAA, and melatonin rose during the ictal phase.
A negative correlation was observed between interictal levels of 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid or melatonin and migraine attack frequency.

Male IBS patients showed increased serum l-kynurenine and l-kynurenine/l-tryptophan ratio compared with healthy controls, while kynurenic acid levels and the KYNA/l-kyn ratio were decreased, interpreted as reflecting increased IDO activity.
Female IBS patients with diarrhea-predominant subtype had a lower melatonin/l-tryptophan ratio than IBS-constipation and control groups, associated with poorer sleep quality.

IBS patients had lower duodenal mucosal but higher systemic (plasma) concentrations of kynurenic acid and serotonin than controls, with mucosal (not plasma) KYNA and 5-HT correlating positively with psychological state.

Whole blood from IBS patients cultured with TLR1-9 agonists showed a higher l-kynurenine/l-tryptophan ratio than controls, with a distinct downstream kynurenine production profile involving TLR1/2, TLR2, TLR3, TLR5, TLR7, and TLR8.
TLR4 signaling via MyD88 was shown to be important for initiating and maintaining migraine-like behavior and nucleus caudalis neuronal activation in mice.
The 4896 A>G polymorphism of the TLR-4 gene was suggested to be a risk factor for migraine.

Diarrhea-predominant IBS patients had higher serum l-tryptophan and lower tryptophan dioxygenase activity/total l-tryptophan oxidation than expected, indicating inhibited kynurenine-pathway catabolism in this subtype.
A dairy-free diet did not change kynurenine pathway metabolite levels or reduce IBS symptoms in diarrhea-predominant IBS patients.

A positive correlation was observed between IBS occurrence/symptom intensity and cerebrospinal fluid levels of l-tryptophan and l-kynurenine in subjects with depression and unexplained neurological symptoms including headache, contradicting earlier studies based on blood measurements.
A population-based study found a positive association between the occurrence of migraine and functional GI disorders including GERD, IBS, and dyspepsia.

Children and adolescents with migraine had a substantially higher rate of functional GI disease (32%) than controls (18%), with significant associations to functional dyspepsia, IBS, and abdominal migraine, but a negative correlation with functional constipation.
Children with functional constipation had a markedly higher headache prevalence than controls, though the association was significant only for mild, nonmigraine headache subtypes.
Migraine prevalence was higher in patients with dysmotility-like dyspepsia than in those with ulcer-like or reflux-like dyspepsia, and higher still in patients with isolated nausea/vomiting.
A meta-analysis of five case-control studies found higher H. pylori infection rates in migraineurs than controls, with stronger association in Asian than European populations.
A large-scale cohort study found 60% higher odds of migraine, fibromyalgia, and depression in an IBS cohort compared with a non-IBS population.
Mendelian randomization analysis in the UK Biobank found a weak but statistically significant causal association between IBS and migraine.
In a Norwegian population-based cohort, migraine occurred about twice as frequently in the IBS subpopulation than in controls.
A meta-analysis of six studies found that 25-50% of IBS patients had coexisting migraine/headache versus only 4-19% of controls, with an odds ratio of 2.66 for migraine in the IBS population.
A meta-analysis of 11 studies with over 28,000 migraineurs and 1.5 million controls found a 42% higher pooled prevalence of IBS in migraineurs compared with controls.
IBS was more likely among migraine patients with a long headache history, recurrent episodic headache attacks, and comorbid anxiety.
Migraine was found to be a risk factor for future development of IBS in patients without comorbid anxiety or depression, but did not add risk in patients who already had those comorbidities.
A strong positive correlation was observed between migraine severity and fecal microbiota dysbiosis in IBS patients.
About half of young female migraineurs without aura had gut microbiota dysbiosis, which was associated with early signs of atherosclerosis and severe migraine disability.
Migraine was positively correlated with higher levels of nitrate-, nitrite-, and nitric oxide-reducing oral microbes in a large gut microbiome cohort.

In mice, antibiotic depletion of gut microbiota prolonged nitroglycerin-induced migraine-like pain via TNFα upregulation in the trigeminal nucleus caudalis, an effect blocked by TNFα deletion or receptor antagonism.
Germ-free mice showed markedly enhanced nitroglycerin-induced migraine-like pain compared to wild-type mice, and this enhancement was reversed by fecal microbiota transplantation from wild-type mice.
Probiotic administration inhibited the antibiotic-induced prolongation of migraine-like pain in the mouse model.
A metagenome-wide association study in elderly women found that the gut microbiota functional module for l-kynurenine synthesis was enriched in migraineurs compared with controls.
Some earlier reports indicated that probiotic treatment had a beneficial effect on the frequency and severity of migraine headache attacks.
Georgescu et al. found a strong positive correlation between migraine severity and the degree of dysbiosis in the fecal microbiota of IBS patients.
About half of young female migraineurs without aura showed gut microbiota dysbiosis, which was associated with early signs of atherosclerosis and more severe migraine disability.

Gonzales et al. showed that migraine occurrence was positively correlated with higher levels of nitrate-, nitrite-, and nitric oxide-reducing oral microbes in a large cohort from the American Gut Project.

In mice, antibiotic-induced depletion of gut microbiota prolonged nitroglycerin-induced migraine-like pain via upregulation of TNFα in the trigeminal nucleus caudalis, and this effect was blocked by TNFα gene deletion or local TNFα receptor antagonism.

Germ-free mice exhibited markedly enhanced nitroglycerin-induced migraine-like pain compared with wild-type mice, and colonization with fecal microbiota from wild-type mice reversed this enhanced pain response.
A metagenome-wide association study found that the functional gut microbiome module for l-kynurenine synthesis was enriched in elderly women with migraine compared with controls.
Prior reviewed evidence suggested probiotic treatment could beneficially reduce the frequency and severity of migraine headache attacks.

A pooled analysis of randomized controlled trials by Parohan et al. concluded that probiotic supplementation had no significant effect on the frequency or severity of episodic migraine attacks, contradicting earlier reports of benefit.
Lasmiditan, a selective 5-HT1F receptor agonist, dose-dependently reduced dural-evoked trigeminovascular activation at the trigeminocervical complex in a preclinical migraine model.
Lasmiditan reduced superior salivatory nucleus-evoked activation of the trigeminal-autonomic reflex, a model relevant to cluster headache.
Lasmiditan had no effect on cranial autonomic activation measured via anterior choroidal blood flow alterations despite reducing the trigeminal-autonomic reflex.
mRNA profiling of human post-mortem tissue showed 5-HT1F receptor expression in several structures relevant to migraine and cluster headache pathophysiology.

The authors conclude that lasmiditan's proven translational efficacy in the preclinical trigeminal-autonomic reflex model supports its potential as a therapeutic option for acute treatment of cluster headache attacks.
PET imaging with [C]PBR28 showed elevated regional TSPO binding in multiple system atrophy patients compared to Parkinson's disease patients, indicating increased glial activation.
TSPO binding hotspots localized to the lentiform nucleus were identified as a distinguishing regional pattern in MSA relative to PD.
TSPO binding was also elevated as a hotspot in cerebellar white matter of MSA patients compared to PD patients.
Visual reading of [C]PBR28 PET images discriminated MSA from PD with 100% specificity and 83% sensitivity.
A machine learning approach applied to TSPO PET imaging data improved diagnostic sensitivity for MSA versus PD to 96%.
TSPO binding patterns differed between MSA subtypes, showing subtype-specific distributions between cerebellar and parkinsonian variant MSA.

A case series of 8 migraine patients (7 women, 1 man) developed new or exacerbated systemic inflammatory/autoimmune disease following treatment with CGRP monoclonal antibodies, with de novo cases arising at a median of 88 days post-exposure.

A 56-year-old man with distant rheumatoid arthritis history developed biopsy-proven autoimmune hepatitis 14 days after a single dose of erenumab for chronic migraine, stabilising with prednisolone/azathioprine and erenumab cessation.

A 67-year-old woman with no prior inflammatory disease developed ocular-limited Susac's syndrome (branch retinal artery occlusion) after 12 months of erenumab for chronic migraine, stabilising with IVIg, prednisolone and mycophenolate after erenumab cessation.

A 44-year-old woman with no significant past medical history developed biopsy-proven DRESS syndrome 26 days after a single 70 mg dose of erenumab for chronic migraine, improving with steroid treatment.

A 32-year-old woman developed granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) with unilateral hearing loss and granulomatous paranasal disease after erenumab for 6 months followed by fremanezumab for chronic migraine, managed with prednisolone and methotrexate after fremanezumab cessation.

A 20-year-old woman with pre-existing IgG4 disease on stable prednisolone developed severe generalised polyarthralgia 4 days after her first galcanezumab injection for chronic migraine, which improved after CGRP mAb cessation; autoantibody and inflammatory testing were negative.

Two patients (cases 6 and 7) with pre-existing psoriasis or psoriatic arthritis experienced severe disease flares after only 1-2 doses of a CGRP monoclonal antibody, improving after drug cessation with steroid therapy and, in one case, a change in biological therapy.

A 46-year-old woman developed severe urticarial eczema of unknown other cause 16 months after starting a CGRP monoclonal antibody for chronic migraine, improving with topical steroids, emollients and UVB therapy after cessation.

CGRP signalling activates cAMP/protein kinase A, inhibiting NF-κB and ICER, thereby negatively regulating pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-12, IFN-γ, TNFα, IL-23) while increasing IL-1 and MHC class II expression, so CGRP inhibition may reverse this immune dampening.

CGRP inhibits platelet aggregation in vitro by increasing platelet cyclic AMP concentrations, suggesting CGRP inhibition could promote platelet aggregation and thrombus formation, a proposed mechanism for the Susac's syndrome case.
CGRP influences differentiation of CD4 T cells away from the Th1 and Th17 pathways, implying that CGRP inhibition could promote Th1/Th17-driven inflammatory disease.

In studies of Moraxella catarrhalis, CGRP has been shown to decrease leukocyte migration and recruitment in the lung, suggesting CGRP inhibition may increase leukocyte recruitment in disease states such as GPA, contributing to hyperactivation seen in the disease.

In several cases, remission of the inflammatory complication was maintained after tapering of immunosuppressive therapy concurrent with withdrawal of the CGRP monoclonal antibody, which the authors state supports a causative relationship between CGRP inhibition and the complications.

Three of the eight cases had a history of previously well-controlled or quiescent rheumatological or dermatological disease prior to starting CGRP monoclonal antibody therapy, raising the possibility of an unrecognised 'at-risk' subgroup for immunological complications.
Systemic mastocytosis (encompassing AdvSM, ISM, and SSM) is a mast cell neoplasm driven by the KIT D816V mutation.

In concept elicitation interviews, AdvSM patients most frequently reported vomiting, abdominal pain, skin spots, diarrhea, nausea, tiredness/fatigue, itching, flushing, and weight loss as disease symptoms.
All interviewed clinical experts identified bone pain, diarrhea, itching, and weight loss as cardinal symptoms of AdvSM.

In concept elicitation interviews, ISM/SSM patients most frequently reported skin spots, itching, diarrhea, tiredness/fatigue, flushing, abdominal pain, bone pain, cognitive issues/brain fog, and nausea.
All interviewed clinical experts identified anaphylaxis, brain fog, diarrhea, flushing, and itching as the most common ISM/SSM symptoms.
Fibromyalgia was a reported comorbid condition in a subset of ISM patients participating in both the concept elicitation and cognitive debriefing interviews.
Migraine headaches were reported as a comorbid condition by over a quarter of ISM patients in the concept elicitation interviews.
Depression/anxiety was a commonly reported comorbid condition among ISM patients, reported by over half of concept elicitation participants and 70% of cognitive debriefing participants.

The AdvSM Symptom Assessment Form (AdvSM-SAF), a 10-item, 24-hour recall electronic daily diary assessing abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, spots, itching, flushing, and fatigue (plus vomiting and diarrhea frequency), was found to be content valid based on cognitive debriefing interviews with AdvSM patients.

The ISM Symptom Assessment Form (ISM-SAF) was developed as a 24-hour recall daily diary and found content valid via cognitive debriefing, with the joint pain item ultimately removed due to regulatory feedback and redundancy with bone pain, and the mental confusion item removed due to poor interpretability.

Existing patient-reported outcome tools for mastocytosis have notable limitations: the Memorial Symptom Assessment Scale (MSAS) was developed without input from AdvSM patients despite use in AdvSM trials, the Mastocytosis Quality of Life Questionnaire (MC-QoL) focuses on quality-of-life impact rather than symptom severity and uses a two-week recall period, and the Mastocytosis Activity Score (MAS), while prospective, is not considered consistent with FDA regulatory guidelines.
Sodium handling mechanisms that normally couple natriuresis to dietary salt intake and maintain blood pressure via pressure natriuresis are impaired in autonomic failure.
When salt intake is restricted, autonomic failure patients cannot appropriately reduce renal sodium excretion, and this worsens their orthostatic hypotension.
Although clinical guidelines recommend high salt intake (6-10 g/day) for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, there is no empirical evidence supporting this recommendation, only expert opinion.
Increased dietary salt intake has been shown to improve conditions such as syncope and postural tachycardia syndrome (POTS), unlike its unproven use in orthostatic hypotension.
Fludrocortisone is often added to a high salt diet to improve sodium retention and increase plasma volume, though these effects are transient.
Fludrocortisone is contraindicated in patients with heart failure and should be used with caution, if at all, when supine hypertension is present.
In patients with supine hypertension, blood pressure substantially increases while supine, triggering pressure natriuresis and extensive sodium loss.
Fludrocortisone is often combined with a high-salt diet to promote sodium retention and expand plasma volume, but this effect is not sustained.
Fludrocortisone should be avoided or used cautiously in patients with heart failure or supine hypertension.
In patients with supine hypertension, blood pressure rises substantially while supine, which triggers pressure natriuresis and extensive sodium loss.
Avoiding the supine posture may be as important as increasing dietary salt intake in managing orthostatic hypotension in patients with supine hypertension.
A high salt diet has been shown to improve syncope and postural tachycardia syndrome, unlike its unproven use in orthostatic hypotension.
Sectioning of the intermetacarpal ligament significantly increased translation of the first carpometacarpal joint under applied loads compared to the intact specimen.
Sectioning of the dorsal radial ligament significantly increased translation of the first carpometacarpal joint under applied loads compared to the intact specimen.
Sectioning of the anterior oblique ligament alone was not associated with a significant increase in first CMC joint translation, implying IML and DRL are the primary stabilizers.
Sectioning of the ulnar collateral ligament alone was not associated with a significant increase in first CMC joint translation, implying IML and DRL are the primary stabilizers.
During dose escalation, the proportion of blood pressure responders (≥10 mmHg increase in seated systolic BP vs placebo) was highest at the 5 mg and 10 mg doses, with no additional benefit at 20 mg.
In the double-blind, placebo-controlled Part B, seated systolic BP increased 4 hours after ampreloxetine while it decreased after placebo, yielding a statistically significant treatment difference.
Standing systolic BP at 3 minutes was numerically higher 4 hours after ampreloxetine than after placebo, but the confidence interval crossed zero.
In Part B, a higher proportion of ampreloxetine-treated participants reported symptomatic improvement in dizziness/lightheadedness than placebo-treated participants.
In symptomatic participants, four weeks of open-label ampreloxetine treatment produced a clinically meaningful decrease in dizziness/lightheadedness scores.
A majority of symptomatic participants achieved clinically meaningful reductions in dizziness/lightheadedness scores by week 4 of ampreloxetine treatment.
The symptomatic improvement from ampreloxetine treatment was sustained through 20 weeks of open-label treatment.
Withdrawal of ampreloxetine after 20 weeks led to loss of symptomatic benefit, with symptoms returning toward baseline despite most participants resuming alternative pressor agents.
Standing time improved with 20 weeks of ampreloxetine treatment and reverted to baseline after drug withdrawal.
The pressor response to standing after ampreloxetine was related to plasma norepinephrine levels, a biomarker of residual sympathetic tone in autonomic failure.
In the dose-escalation study, ampreloxetine was well tolerated with no serious adverse events; the most common AEs were headache, urinary tract infection, and constipation.
In the 20-week open-label extension, the most common adverse events were urinary tract infection, hypertension, and headache, considered unrelated to ampreloxetine.
Five of 21 participants in the open-label extension experienced a serious adverse event, none considered related to study drug.

No difference in clinical benefit from ampreloxetine was detected between participants with a central preganglionic phenotype of autonomic failure (MSA) versus those with predominantly postganglionic Lewy body disorders (PD and PAF).
The pressor effect of ampreloxetine was greater and more durable on standing systolic BP than on supine systolic BP, suggesting a favorable safety profile regarding supine hypertension.
Based on similar efficacy at 5-10 mg and comparable safety/tolerability, the 10 mg once-daily dose of ampreloxetine was selected for phase 3 trials.
The ISM-SAF Total Symptom Score demonstrated adequate internal consistency reliability, with Cronbach's alpha of 0.86, 0.85, and 0.86 at Baseline, C3D1, and C4D1 respectively.
The Gastrointestinal Symptom Score showed acceptable but declining internal consistency across visits (alpha 0.83, 0.73, 0.72).
The Skin Symptom Score demonstrated adequate internal consistency reliability across timepoints (alpha 0.82, 0.76, 0.76).
Test-retest reliability of the ISM-SAF Total Symptom Score between Baseline and C1D15 was excellent (ICC=0.956) among patients with unchanged PGIS ratings.
Test-retest reliability of the Gastrointestinal Symptom Score was adequate (ICC=0.858).
Test-retest reliability of the Skin Symptom Score was excellent (ICC=0.981).
The ISM-SAF Total Symptom Score at C4D1 was moderately-to-strongly correlated with the Patient Global Impression of Severity, supporting construct validity.
The ISM-SAF Total Symptom Score at C4D1 correlated strongly with the MC-QoL Symptoms domain, consistent with expected construct validity relationships.
The ISM-SAF Total Symptom Score at C4D1 was negatively correlated with the EQ-5D-5L VAS, indicating higher symptom scores associated with worse general health status.

The ISM-SAF Total Symptom Score clearly distinguished patients grouped by PGIS severity category, with significantly different mean scores across Absent/Minimal, Moderate, and Severe/Very Severe groups.
The ISM-SAF Total Symptom Score decreased from Baseline to C4D1 with a moderate effect size, indicating sensitivity to change.
The Gastrointestinal Symptom Score decreased from Baseline to C4D1 with a moderate effect size.
The Skin Symptom Score decreased from Baseline to C4D1 with a moderate effect size.
Distribution-based methods estimated candidate clinically important differences for ISM-SAF biweekly scores of 7-10 points for TSS, 2-4 for GSS, and 3-4 for SSS.

A 30% individual percentage decrease on the ISM-SAF Total Symptom Score was selected as the clinically important response threshold, based on an anchor-based estimate of 29.4% decrease among PGIS-defined improvers.

At Baseline, mean ISM-SAF severity item scores ranged from 3.0 (diarrhea) to 7.2 (fatigue), with mean TSS, GSS, and SSS of 54.2, 10.9, and 16.2 respectively, indicating substantial and variable symptom burden.

Removing the diarrhea severity item increased Cronbach's alpha for the GSS and removing the spots item increased alpha for the SSS, but the diarrhea item was retained given its established relevance from qualitative patient interviews despite many patients scoring zero for diarrhea at each timepoint.

In concept elicitation interviews, 75% of ISM patients identified diarrhea as a symptom of ISM and 90% of cognitively debriefed patients reported experiencing diarrhea due to their disease, supporting retention of the diarrhea item despite psychometric limitations.
ISM-SAF gastrointestinal items (abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea) were moderately to strongly correlated with one another at Baseline, as were skin items (spots, itching, flushing).
ISM-SAF diarrhea frequency and diarrhea severity items were strongly correlated at Baseline, as expected given they assess the same underlying symptom.
Syncope is common, accounting for a substantial fraction of emergency department visits and affecting a large proportion of the general population over a lifetime.
Non-cardiac syncope, though generally less feared than cardiac syncope, is more common and can cause severe injuries and quality-of-life impairment, especially in older adults.

A mechanism-based classification of non-cardiac syncope proposes two main phenotypes: a hypotensive/vasodepressive phenotype in which hypotension predominates, and a bradycardic phenotype in which cardioinhibition predominates.
Identifying whether a patient's syncope is bradycardic or hypotensive/vasodepressive in mechanism is proposed as the first step toward personalized, customized preventive management.

Pure autonomic failure associated with intraneuronal alpha-synuclein aggregates (Lewy bodies) and degeneration of postganglionic sympathetic neurons can phenoconvert to Parkinson disease or dementia with Lewy bodies, but not to multiple system atrophy.
Pure autonomic failure lacking intraneuronal synucleinopathy and postganglionic sympathetic denervation may represent a premotor stage of multiple system atrophy.

Prior longitudinal studies classified patients as having pure autonomic failure based solely on neurogenic orthostatic hypotension without evidence of motor/cognitive impairment, thereby lumping together two pathologically and neurochemically distinct nOH syndromes (Lewy body-type versus MSA-type).
CGRP is released during the headache phase of migraine attacks and its intravenous administration induces migraine-like headache, implicating it as a key mediator of migraine pathophysiology.
Across pooled trials, CGRP monoclonal antibodies reduced monthly migraine days by an average of 1.9 days versus placebo in episodic migraine.
Across pooled trials, CGRP monoclonal antibodies reduced monthly migraine days by an average of 2.2 days versus placebo in chronic migraine, the largest reduction among all agents studied.

In patients with difficult-to-treat migraine (failure of two to four prior preventive treatments), four randomized placebo-controlled trials of CGRP mAb showed relatively high MMD/MHD reduction versus placebo in two of three completed trials, partly attributable to a low placebo response.
Candesartan (8-16 mg) reduced monthly migraine days by a weighted average of 0.9 days versus placebo, the lowest efficacy among all agents compared.
Topiramate (50-200 mg) reduced monthly migraine days by 1.2 days versus placebo in episodic migraine across eight placebo-controlled trials.
One episodic migraine trial of topiramate 200 mg daily did not reach its primary efficacy endpoint.
Valproate (250-1500 mg) reduced monthly migraine days by 1.7 days versus placebo across six trials including 436 episodic migraine patients.
Propranolol (80-160 mg) reduced monthly migraine days by 0.7 days versus placebo, based on data from two of eighteen included trials.
Metoprolol (100-200 mg) reduced monthly migraine days by 1.6 days versus placebo, based on data from two of four included trials.
Amitriptyline (25-100 mg) treated patients (n=59, from one trial) showed a monthly migraine day reduction of 1.1 days versus placebo.

In a 20-week trial including episodic and chronic daily headache patients, amitriptyline reduced headache frequency significantly versus placebo only at 8 weeks, not at 12, 16, or 20 weeks, and was considered a negative result.
OnabotulinumtoxinA (155-195 U) reduced monthly migraine days by 2.0 days versus placebo in chronic migraine, based on the PREEMPT 1 and 2 trials (688 patients).
The PREEMPT 1 trial of onabotulinumtoxinA for chronic migraine did not reach its primary endpoint, while PREEMPT 2 did.
The real-world development or worsening of hypertension due to erenumab is an evolving safety concern that requires further elucidation.

Among standard prophylactics, amitriptyline, valproate and topiramate had the highest dropout rates compared to placebo, consistent with real-world adherence data showing higher discontinuation with topiramate and amitriptyline than propranolol.

CGRP mAb trials studied markedly larger patient populations (3191 in CM, 4632 in EM) than standard prophylactics such as candesartan (132 patients), and recent meta-analyses found CGRP mAb trial quality to be more homogeneous with overall low risk of bias compared to standard prophylactics.
At initial presentation, the patient's neurological exam was notable for dysautonomia, irritability, choreoathetosis, and severe oro-facial dyskinesias.
Longitudinal quantitative MRI analysis showed reversible cycles of regional cortical volume loss and gain that were greatest in the frontal and occipital lobes and smallest in the temporal lobes.
Despite cycles of reversible change, the net effect across the full 14-month period was stable cortical volume loss, most prominent in the frontal and occipital lobes.

Periods of clinical decline preceded cortical volume loss, while periods of clinical improvement preceded cortical volume gain, indicating volume changes tracked treatment response and clinical status.
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed inflammatory pleocytosis and positive antibodies against the GluN1 subunit of the NMDA receptor, confirming the diagnosis of anti-NMDAR encephalitis.
The patient did not improve after first-line therapy consisting of high-dose IV methylprednisolone followed by IVIG, prompting escalation to second-line immunotherapy.

Repeated escalation of immunotherapy, including high-dose steroids and rituximab, during a presumed relapse of autoimmune epileptic encephalopathy led to dramatic improvement in inter-ictal EEG and resolution of seizures.

Patients with de novo mutations in GRIN1, the gene encoding the GluN1 NMDA receptor subunit, experience a chronic encephalopathy with motor, cognitive, and visual symptoms similar to those seen in acquired anti-NMDAR encephalitis.

Prior literature reported medial occipital lobe hypometabolism on FDG-PET/CT in patients with acute anti-NMDAR encephalitis and visual symptoms, suggesting visual impairment as an under-recognized specific clinical feature.

An association between Lennox-Gastaut Syndrome and cerebral volume loss has been previously described, raising the possibility that the volume changes observed in this patient could partly reflect seizure activity rather than the underlying autoimmune encephalopathy.

Corticosteroid treatment has been associated with reversible short-term decreases in brain volume, possibly due to loss of intracellular water, with volume loss in multiple sclerosis patients resolving within 30-60 days.
Patients with interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome (IC/BPS) have a higher prevalence of comorbid migraine than the general population.
Patients with IC/BPS have a higher prevalence of comorbid fibromyalgia than the general population.
Patients with IC/BPS have a higher prevalence of comorbid irritable bowel syndrome than the general population.
Patients with IC/BPS have a higher prevalence of comorbid chronic fatigue than the general population.

A multiple regression model using ankle plantar flexion angle, BMI, and generalised joint laxity explained 38% of the variance in knee flexion angle at initial contact of single-leg drop landings.
Ankle plantar flexion angle was the only significant predictor of knee flexion angle, showing an inverse relationship at initial contact during single-leg drop landings.
Generalised joint laxity was included in the regression model but was not found to be a significant predictor of knee flexion angle.
Body mass index (BMI) was included in the regression model but was not a significant predictor of knee flexion angle.
External validation of the regression model on a separate data set showed it explained 26% of the variance in knee flexion angle, with a large effect size.

Of five patients with refractory autoimmune encephalitis, three met criteria for definite anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis while two had probable NMDARE acutely but were ultimately classified as seronegative autoimmune encephalitis.
One of five patients with severe refractory autoimmune encephalitis developed autonomic failure severe enough to require pacemaker placement.

All five patients with severe refractory autoimmune encephalitis who received intrathecal methotrexate as an add-on therapy improved and returned to at or near their premorbid baseline at last follow-up.

Prior to intrathecal methotrexate, patients had already failed combinations of methylprednisolone, IVIG, plasma exchange, and rituximab, illustrating the treatment-refractory severity of their autoimmune encephalitis.
All five patients received methylprednisolone as part of initial immunosuppressive treatment for refractory autoimmune encephalitis.
Three of five patients received a course of IVIG prior to escalation to intrathecal methotrexate.
Four of five patients underwent plasma exchange (PLEX) before intrathecal methotrexate was administered.
Four of five patients received rituximab prior to receiving intrathecal methotrexate for refractory disease.
Three of five patients required mechanical ventilation at the time intrathecal methotrexate was administered, reflecting severe disease refractory to conventional therapy.
Two of five patients ultimately had seronegative autoimmune encephalitis despite initially meeting criteria for probable NMDARE in the acute setting.
Intrathecal methotrexate was well tolerated by all patients with no adverse events precluding continued use.
Among 11 patients with hypnic headache, 8 (72.72%) were male and 3 (27.27%) were female, indicating a male predominance in this Indian cohort.
The age of patients with hypnic headache ranged from 53 to 78 years with a mean of 63.36 years, consistent with the typical late-onset presentation of this disorder.
The frequency of hypnic headache attacks per month ranged from 5 to 46, with a mean of 20.36 attacks.
Each hypnic headache episode lasted between 30 minutes and 4 hours, with a mean duration of 1.93 hours.
Hypnic headache attacks occurred predominantly during the nocturnal hours of 0.00-2.00am (38%) and 2.00-4.00am (36%), reflecting its characteristic sleep-related timing.
The pain quality in hypnic headache was dull in the majority of patients, 7 out of 11 (63.63%).
None of the hypnic headache patients in the cohort exhibited trigeminal autonomic features such as lacrimation, ptosis, or rhinorrhea.
Motor activity during headache episodes was noted in the majority of the hypnic headache cohort.
A subset of hypnic headache patients had co-occurring migraine headaches.
A subset of hypnic headache patients had co-occurring tension-type headache.
No patients in the hypnic headache cohort had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
A substantial proportion of hypnic headache patients had comorbid systemic hypertension.
One hypnic headache patient had comorbid diabetes mellitus.
Trigeminal autonomic features such as lacrimation, ptosis, or rhinorrhea were not observed in any patient with hypnic headache in this cohort.
None of the patients with hypnic headache in this Indian cohort had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
Routine blood examinations were normal in all hypnic headache patients studied.
Three patients (27.27%) showed nonspecific MRI abnormalities including lacunar infarcts and T2-weighted hyperintensities.
The authors suggest that MRI voxel-based morphometry demonstrating gray matter loss in the posterior hypothalamus may become a reliable diagnostic test for primary hypnic headache in the future.
Two of 47 examined patients (4%) fulfilled inclusion criteria for temporomandibular joint hypermobility (TMJH), a subtype of joint hypermobility not captured by standard RDC/TMD classification.

Time-frequency (spectrogram) analysis of TMJ acoustic signals shows TMJH is characterised by periods of spectral equilibrium separated by high-amplitude double-peak waveforms, distinguishing it from pathological clicking (continuous crackle noise) and healthy joints (smooth, low-amplitude signal).
Prior literature (Nosouhian et al.) reports that TMJH occurs much more frequently in women than men.

Prior literature (Pasinato et al.) found that generalised joint hypermobility (GJH) is a predisposing factor for temporomandibular disorders (TMD), with 64.71% of TMD patients also exhibiting GJH, including TMJH.
Prior MRI research (Mehndiratta et al.) linked TMJH to an anatomic variant of the articular eminence with a steep, short posterior slope and a longer anterior slope.
Literature estimates that hypermobile joint syndrome affects 5-10% of populations and is more prevalent among women.
Prior literature (Chang et al.) found that only 9.52% of a hypermobile-joint-syndrome group also had TMD, with 90.48% otherwise healthy.
Prior literature (Collinge et al.) reports hypermobility prevalence of 21-42% depending on the criteria and score used on the Beighton scale.

Prior literature (Hirsch et al.) found generalised joint hypermobility in 6.9% of subjects among a broader hypermobile group representing 2.8-14.8% of examined patients, more prevalent in women, with discrepancies attributed to differing diagnostic criteria.
Both confirmed TMJH patients in this study had hypermobility of the temporomandibular joints confirmed by functional X-ray showing condylar translation.
One TMJH patient also met RDC/TMD criteria for myofascial pain and bilateral arthralgia, illustrating comorbidity between TMJH and other temporomandibular disorders and associated facial/muscle pain.
Prior literature (Kirk et al.) notes that hypermobility is widespread but its symptoms are typically mild and ambiguous, making diagnoses unreliable.
Because TMJH predisposes patients to temporomandibular disorders, affected patients may require occlusive splints, muscle relaxation, or speech therapy exercises.
Nausea was the most commonly reported visceral autonomic symptom across all phases of migraine, occurring in 52.9% of participants.
About half of migraineurs reported at least one visceral autonomic symptom during the premonitory (pre-attack) phase.
During the headache attack phase, 71% of participants reported visceral autonomic symptoms.
In the postdrome phase (after the headache resolves), 36% of participants reported visceral autonomic symptoms.
Migraineurs with visceral autonomic symptoms had significantly longer headache attack duration than those without such symptoms.
Migraineurs with visceral autonomic symptoms reported more severe premonitory-phase symptoms than those without visceral symptoms.
Migraineurs with visceral autonomic symptoms reported more severe during-attack symptoms than those without visceral symptoms.
In the Piedmont Plateau region, Moist Tropical and Moist Moderate synoptic weather types were often associated with the highest rates of emergency department visits for pain conditions.
Polar synoptic weather types were frequently associated with the fewest emergency department visits for pain in the Piedmont Plateau region.
In the mountainous Appalachian region, most pain types showed weather-type associations similar to the Piedmont Plateau, but migraine and fibromyalgia were notable exceptions with different patterns.
Migraine-related emergency department visits in the mountain region did not follow the same weather-type pattern seen for other pain conditions, representing a geographic exception.
Fibromyalgia-related emergency department visits in the mountain region did not follow the same weather-type pattern seen for other pain conditions, representing a geographic exception.
In the Coastal Plain region, few statistically significant relationships were found between synoptic weather type and emergency department visits for pain.
Chronic headache patients reported significantly higher pain severity than healthy controls.
Chronic headache patients reported significantly higher pain interference on daily activity than healthy controls.
Chronic headache patients showed significantly higher pain catastrophizing than healthy controls.
Chronic headache patients exhibited significantly lower heart rate variability at rest compared to healthy controls, indicating reduced autonomic flexibility.
Pain catastrophizing statistically mediated the relationship leading to pain severity in chronic headache patients.
Pain catastrophizing statistically mediated the relationship leading to pain interference on daily activity in chronic headache patients, while HRV did not emerge as a mediator.
Both pain catastrophizing and heart rate variability were associated with pain interference on daily activity, though only catastrophizing held as a mediator.
The interaction between resting RMSSD (a time-domain HRV metric) and self-critical rumination significantly predicted somatic symptom distress at baseline.
Lower resting HRV was associated with greater somatic symptom distress, particularly among individuals with higher levels of self-critical rumination.

Among participants with high resting HRV, somatic symptom distress was largely unaffected by the level of self-critical rumination, suggesting high HRV may buffer against rumination-related somatic distress.
The interaction between resting HRV and self-critical rumination did not significantly predict somatic symptom distress six months later, unlike the baseline finding.
Self-critical rumination was negatively related to subjective well-being, independent of resting HRV.
The activating KIT D816V mutation found in mastocytosis is proposed to influence susceptibility to severe anaphylaxis via intrinsic mast cell abnormalities.
The genetic trait hereditary alpha-tryptasemia is proposed to influence susceptibility to severe anaphylaxis.
There is strong evidence linking severe anaphylaxis, particularly that induced by hymenoptera (insect) venom, with underlying mast cell disorders.
Pooled incidence of any adverse event after ED presentation for syncope was 5.1% at 24 hours, rising over time.
By 1 year after ED presentation for syncope, the pooled cumulative incidence of any adverse event reached 21.3%.
Pooled all-cause mortality after ED presentation for syncope was low at 24 hours (0.2%).
Pooled all-cause mortality rose to 5.9% by 1 year after ED presentation for syncope, in contrast to other outcomes that plateaued after 72 hours.
Arrhythmia (ventricular, supraventricular, bradyarrhythmia) was the most common adverse event after syncope, occurring in 3.1% of patients at 24 hours.
Pooled arrhythmia incidence rose only modestly after the first 3 days, reaching 9.9% by 1 year.
Pooled rate of pacemaker or ICD implantation after syncope rose from 0.6% at 24 hours to 3.6% at 1 year.
Across the nine included studies, the pooled hospital admission rate for ED syncope patients was 32%, with wide variability between studies.
The proportion of syncope patients with adverse events did not increase significantly between 72 hours and 7-10 days after ED presentation, suggesting most events occur within the first 72 hours.
The 1-year mortality rate of 5.9% found in this pooled analysis is consistent with previous systematic reviews reporting mortality rates of 8.4% and 7%.
Fatigue, measured only in one study using the PedsQL Multidimensional Fatigue Scale, was found to be an independent predictor of functional deterioration in children with GJH and associated symptoms.
A greater number of systemic symptoms (e.g., orthostatic intolerance, functional gastrointestinal disorders, stress incontinence) is associated with worse functional disability in children with GJH.
Children with the poorest functional status among those with hypermobility and associated symptoms experience worse fatigue and higher pain intensity than their peers.
Gastrointestinal involvement and stress incontinence reported by children and parents are associated with poorer quality of life in relation to hypermobility.
The Beighton score has been found to be a valid method for assessing generalised joint hypermobility in children, despite not being originally intended as a diagnostic tool.

The 2017 International Classification of the Ehlers-Danlos syndromes recommends age-specific Beighton score cut-offs of ≥4/9 for adults over 50, ≥5/9 for pubertal children and adults ≤50, or ≥6/9 for prepubertal children.

Across the six included studies, 20 distinct outcome instruments (15 patient/parent-reported and 4 clinician-reported) were used to measure pain, function, quality of life and fatigue, indicating substantial heterogeneity in outcome measurement.
Pain was the most commonly measured construct across included studies, most frequently assessed with the patient-reported Visual Analogue Scale.

In Bale et al. (2019), pain scores improved by a similar magnitude in both the tertiary physiotherapy/occupational therapy intervention group and the standard-care control group at 12 months, showing no between-group difference.
In Kemp et al. (2010), combined physiotherapy groups showed a significant reduction in pain (VAS) at 5 months follow-up.

In Scheper et al. (2017), children classified as having severe hypermobility-related impairment showed a greater decline in 6-minute walk test distance over 3 years than those classified able/moderate.

In Hsieh et al. (2018), children receiving physical therapy plus customised orthotic insoles showed greater improvement in PODCI transfer and basic mobility scores than those receiving physical therapy and podiatry without customised insoles.
In Kemp et al. (2010), parents rated a greater reduction in perceived impact of hypermobility for children receiving targeted physiotherapy than those receiving general physiotherapy.
Children with GJH and associated symptoms commonly report chronic pain, fatigue and functional difficulties that negatively impact quality of life.

Chronic joint pain in children with GJH is often exacerbated by physical activity, with lower limb pain being the most commonly reported location, alongside joint instability episodes and frequent soft tissue injuries.
Functional difficulties in children with GJH include motor development challenges, muscle torque deficits and poor proprioception, negatively affecting school and social activity participation.
A random 5% sample of survey respondents was interviewed and the diagnosis of cluster headache was confirmed in 97.5% of those interviewed, validating the survey's ICHD-based diagnostic criteria.
Pediatric onset of cluster headache was found in 27.5% of participants, higher than previously appreciated in clinic-based studies.
Among those with pediatric-onset cluster headache, only 15.2% were actually diagnosed before age 18, indicating substantial diagnostic delay.
Men were more likely than women to have episodic cluster headache between ages 10 and 50, but the sex ratio was approximately equal outside this age range.

The sex distribution pattern of cluster headache onset is the inverse of migraine, since in migraine women (rather than men) predominate between ages 10 and 50 with an approximately equal ratio otherwise.
Nearly all cluster headache respondents reported restlessness during attacks.
About half of cluster headache respondents reported migraine-like features of photophobia or phonophobia.
Nearly a third of cluster headache respondents reported pain aggravated by physical activity, a migrainous feature.
About a quarter of cluster headache respondents reported nausea and vomiting, a migrainous feature.
Oxygen, the first-line acute treatment for cluster headache, was rated as significantly less effective by respondents with chronic cluster headache than by those with episodic cluster headache.

Calcium channel blockers, the first-line preventive treatment for cluster headache, were rated as significantly less effective by respondents with chronic cluster headache than by those with episodic cluster headache.

Chronic cluster headache appears less responsive not only to first-line treatments but also to newer treatments such as noninvasive vagus nerve stimulation and galcanezumab, according to the discussion of participant data.
Urgency was the most frequently reported urinary symptom, affecting 97% (n=65) of children with symptomatic joint hypermobility.

People with joint hypermobility syndrome (JHS) stood for a significantly shorter time before their pain increased by two points compared to hypermobile (GJH) and normal-flexibility (NF) controls.
JHS participants reported significantly higher baseline joint pain before standing began compared to both GJH and NF groups.

Although JHS participants tended to show a higher median number of fidgets at all bodyweight thresholds during prolonged standing, this difference from GJH and NF groups was not statistically significant.
During quiet standing periods, JHS participants showed significantly greater anteroposterior sway than the NF group, though the effect size was small and not clearly different from GJH.
No significant differences were found between JHS, GJH, and NF groups in mediolateral sway, sway area, or sway velocity during quiet standing periods.
Joint hypermobility syndrome (JHS) prevalence is much higher in healthcare settings than in the general population, with 39% prevalence reported at a UK pain clinic.
In a West-London general rheumatology clinic, JHS prevalence was reported as 58% in females and 29% in males, indicating a sex difference in clinical prevalence.
A prior study found that generalised joint hypermobility (GJH) was a risk factor for developing venous insufficiency, based on long-term impact of prolonged standing.
People with JHS have been reported to experience central fatigue during tasks that do not fatigue people with normal flexibility.

People with JHS are reported to have several features that could explain standing difficulty, including muscle weakness, fatigue, impaired balance, impaired proprioception, venous insufficiency/varicose veins, and knee/lower-back pain.
Chronic pain in hypermobile individuals may lead to changes in neuromuscular control, which has been reported in hypermobile cohorts and could affect balance control.
Vasovagal syncope remains a common presentation across the lifespan including in older adults, generally has a favorable prognosis, and usually requires only conservative management.
In elderly patients, vasovagal syncope and carotid sinus syndrome may be misdiagnosed as accidental falls and are frequently associated with injury.
Head-up tilt testing and carotid sinus massage retain their diagnostic accuracy and safety when used in elderly patients with syncope.
Implantable loop recorders provide important diagnostic information in many elderly patients presenting with unexplained falls and syncope.

In elderly patients with non-cardiac syncope, the initial management step is withdrawal of unnecessary vasoactive and psychotropic medications, which are often a major modifiable contributing factor via polypharmacy.
Both non-pharmacologic and pharmacologic therapies for syncope in the elderly have limited efficacy and raise safety concerns in this population.
In selected elderly patients, pacemaker therapy may provide symptomatic relief from syncope despite lacking proven efficacy when the vasodepressor component is prominent.

In chronic migraine patients without a history of aura, erenumab 70 mg and 140 mg reduced monthly migraine days versus placebo.

Inappropriate sinus tachycardia (IST) is prevalent in about 1% of the middle-aged population and occurs predominantly in females.

IST has also been mechanistically linked to muscarinic receptor autoantibodies or muscarinic receptor hyposensitivity.
Impaired baroreflex control is proposed as a contributing mechanism to IST.
Depressed efferent parasympathetic/vagal function is proposed as a mechanism contributing to IST.
Impaired baroreflex control has been proposed as a possible mechanism underlying inappropriate sinus tachycardia.
Depressed efferent parasympathetic/vagal function is cited as a possible contributing mechanism to inappropriate sinus tachycardia.
Nociceptive stimulation and central autonomic overactivity are described as additional possible mechanisms of inappropriate sinus tachycardia.
Patients with IST commonly experience palpitations, chest pain, fatigue, shortness of breath, presyncope, and syncope.
Despite its distressing symptoms, IST has not been associated with tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy or increased major cardiovascular events.
Ivabradine, beta-adrenergic blockers, calcium channel blockers, psychiatric evaluation, and exercise training are listed as treatment options for IST.
Endocardial radiofrequency ablation targeting the sinus node has been used for treatment-refractory IST but with dismal results.

Other ablation-based modalities for refractory IST include endocardial modification of the sinus node, combined endo/epicardial ablation, thoracoscopic epicardial ablation, and sinus node sparing thoracoscopic/endocardial hybrid ablation.

Among 11,510 rheumatoid arthritis patients, 20.1% reported moderate or severe subjective cognitive dysfunction (CS+).
Increasing severity of subjective cognitive dysfunction was associated with younger age, with mean age falling from 62.0 years in CS-F=0 to 54.1 years in CS-F=3.
Female sex was associated with higher odds of being CS+ (moderate/severe subjective cognitive dysfunction), with proportion of women rising from 78.7% at CS-F=0 to 88.3% at CS-F=3.
Self-reported work disability increased sharply with increasing cognitive dysfunction severity, from 8.6% at CS-F=0 to 41.9% at CS-F=3.
Opioid use increased with increasing cognitive dysfunction severity, from 20.4% at CS-F=0 to 47.4% at CS-F=3.
Fibromyalgia (per 2016 criteria) was present in 21.7% of the 11,510 RA patients studied.
In the NDB clinical cohort, 43.0% to 52.3% of fibromyalgia cases met the CS+ (moderate/severe subjective cognitive dysfunction) definition, depending on which fibromyalgia criteria were used.
In two German general population studies, 42.3% to 52.0% of fibromyalgia cases satisfied the CS+ definition, similar to the clinical RA cohort.

In the clinical (RA) setting, the ratio of CS+ cases was reversed compared with the general population: for every fibromyalgia-negative CS+ case there were 1.29 to 1.94 fibromyalgia-positive CS+ cases.
Nearly half (43.6%) of CS+ cases in the RA cohort did not satisfy fibromyalgia 2016 criteria, arguing against SCD ('fibrofog') being specific to fibromyalgia.
Among patients negative for cognitive dysfunction (CS-C negative), only 12.9% satisfied FM 2016 criteria, versus much higher rates in CS+ patients.
Among patients with a Polysymptomatic Distress Scale (PSD) score ≥12, 84.5% were fibromyalgia-positive, and no fibromyalgia-positive cases occurred below a PSD of 12.
The adjusted symptom severity score (cognitive item omitted) was a strong predictor of cognitive dysfunction status, with a correlation of 0.608, ROC AUC of 0.855, and 83.7% correct classification.
The full Symptom Severity Score (SSS) was the strongest predictor of subjective cognitive dysfunction status, with a correlation of 0.773, ROC AUC of 0.932, and 88.5% correct classification.

The Widespread Pain Index (WPI), a pure measure of pain extent, was a much weaker predictor of subjective cognitive dysfunction than symptom-based scales, with a correlation of 0.391, ROC AUC of 0.724, and 79.9% correct classification.

A symptom scale of items unrelated to pain or fibromyalgia (NONPNONS) was moderately predictive of subjective cognitive dysfunction, with a correlation of 0.476, ROC AUC of 0.768, and 81.5% correct classification, and each of its 26 component symptoms was significantly associated with CS+.

Fibromyalgia (2016 criteria) prevalence rose stepwise with cognitive dysfunction severity, found in 53.1% and 68.5% of patients with CS-F scores of 2 and 3 respectively, with widespread pain in 60.2% and 70.0% of the same groups.

In the transition from fibromyalgia-negative/CS-negative to fibromyalgia-negative/CS-positive groups, WPI did not increase stepwise, while symptom severity score, anxiety, and self-reported disability increased disproportionately, indicating CS status tracks more with symptom burden than with pain extent.

In a separate cited study, fibromyalgia patients scored significantly higher on self-report measures of dyscognition than healthy controls, and perceived dyscognition was most strongly associated with fatigue and mood.

The authors conclude that 'fibrofog' is a misnomer, since fibromyalgia and subjective cognitive dysfunction are correlated but appear to represent different parts of a shared symptom-severity continuum rather than cognitive dysfunction being a defining feature specific to fibromyalgia.
