Endothelin-1 levels did not significantly differ among participants with migraine with aura, migraine without aura, and controls.
There was no significant association between endothelin-1 levels and headache intensity (mild, moderate, severe) in migraine participants.
Endothelin-1 was not significantly associated with headache frequency per month among participants with episodic and chronic migraine.
A history of migraines or headaches was associated with a substantially increased risk of reflex syncope in soldiers performing ceremonial duties.
A history of antihistamine prescription was associated with a reduced risk of reflex syncope in soldiers.
Non-white ethnicity was associated with a markedly reduced risk of reflex syncope.
Male sex was associated with a reduced risk of reflex syncope compared with female sex in this military cohort.
Among soldiers who had fainted, orthostasis was the most common precipitating factor for reflex syncope.
Heat exposure was a common precipitating factor for reflex syncope, second only to orthostasis.
Maintaining hydration was the most commonly used self-management intervention among soldiers who had fainted.
Purposeful movements were a commonly used self-management intervention among soldiers who had previously fainted.
Male sex was associated with a reduced risk of reflex syncope compared with female sex among soldiers performing State Ceremonial and Public Duties.
Meta-analysis of 27 studies from 20 low- and middle-income countries estimated the overall pooled prevalence of chronic pain among children and adolescents at 8%.
Pooled prevalence of general/multi-site/any chronic pain in pediatric LMIC populations was estimated at 20%.
Pooled prevalence of chronic musculoskeletal/back pain in pediatric LMIC populations was 9%, lower than the 25% reported in adults in LMICs.
Pooled prevalence of chronic abdominal pain in pediatric LMIC populations was estimated at 7%.
Pooled prevalence of any chronic headache (chronic daily headache, chronic migraine, or chronic tension-type headache) in pediatric LMIC populations was 4%.
Pooled prevalence of juvenile fibromyalgia syndrome in pediatric LMIC populations was 3%, comparable to adult LMIC and pediatric HIC estimates.
A single eligible study reported a 15% prevalence of chronic temporomandibular disorder pain in a pediatric LMIC population.
A sensitivity analysis excluding the one moderate-risk-of-bias study did not materially change the pooled chronic pain prevalence estimate (7%).
Restricting analysis to studies using a consistent ≥3-month chronic pain definition (excluding ≥6-month or 1-year definitions) did not change conclusions, yielding a prevalence of 5%.
Chronic headache was 1.65 times more prevalent in girls compared with boys in pediatric LMIC populations.
Chronic abdominal pain was 1.36 times more prevalent in girls compared with boys in pediatric LMIC populations.
General/multi-site/any chronic pain was 1.54 times more prevalent in girls compared with boys in pediatric LMIC populations.
Unlike other pain types, musculoskeletal pain prevalence did not differ significantly between boys and girls.

The 4% prevalence of chronic headache found in this review's pediatric LMIC population was comparable to the 5.5% migraine prevalence reported for LMICs in the Global Burden of Disease 2013 Study on Children and Adolescents.

Empiric permanent pacemaker implantation reduced the composite of cardiovascular death, syncope, bradycardia requiring pacemaker, and device complications compared with an implantable cardiac monitor-guided strategy.
Rates of syncope recurrence were similar between patients randomized to pacemaker versus implantable cardiac monitor, indicating pacing did not prevent syncope itself.
The authors suggest that recurrent syncope in pacemaker recipients is likely caused by vasodepressor (reflex-mediated) syncope rather than bradyarrhythmia.

Patients with moderate levels of nociplastic pain features (as measured by the Fibromyalgia Survey Questionnaire) were less likely to show clinically significant improvement on the Neck Disability Index after physical therapy.
Patients with moderate levels of nociplastic pain features were less likely to show clinically significant improvement on the PEG score (pain, enjoyment, general activity) after physical therapy.
Patients with moderate levels of nociplastic pain features were less likely to show clinically significant improvement in pain catastrophizing after physical therapy.

Patients with higher levels of nociplastic pain had a similar chance of showing improvement from physical therapy as those with lower levels, except regarding pain catastrophizing, where higher nociplastic pain was associated with less improvement.
Significant improvements from physical therapy were independent of the type or amount of therapy received.
The degree of nociplastic pain in patients with myofascial pain appears to be inversely related to the magnitude of improvement obtained from a peripherally based treatment such as physical therapy.
Each 1-point increase in Beighton score was associated with a 1.69-fold increased odds of developing iliopsoas tendinitis after hip arthroscopy for FAI.
Patients with a high Beighton score (≥4) had nearly 10-fold greater odds of developing iliopsoas tendinitis compared with those with a low score (<4).
Higher Beighton scores were not associated with a greater likelihood of patients receiving corticosteroid injection therapy.
Having a family member diagnosed with Chiari malformation type I was the strongest independent contributor to poorer patient-reported surgical outcome in the regression model.
Having a family member diagnosed with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome was significantly associated with patient-reported surgical impact on symptoms.
Having a family member diagnosed with migraines was significantly related to patient-reported surgical symptom outcome after Chiari decompression surgery.
Duration of symptoms greater than 2 years prior to surgery was significantly associated with patient-reported surgical impact on symptoms.
A history of multiple prior surgeries was significantly related to patient-reported surgical symptom outcome.
Presurgical symptom severity was significantly related to patient-reported surgical impact on symptoms.
Depression showed the strongest correlation with negative patient-reported surgical outcome among all factors tested.
Presurgical depression was the strongest independent correlate of a negative (worse) patient-reported surgical outcome in adult women with Chiari malformation type I.
Presurgical anxiety was significantly associated with worse patient-reported surgical outcome.
Presurgical stress was significantly related to patient-reported surgical outcome.
Presurgical loneliness was significantly related to patient-reported surgical outcome.

A forward selection regression model combining significant presurgical factors accounted for more than a third of the variance in patient-reported surgical outcome, with five factors contributing significant unique variance.

In the multivariable regression model, having a family member diagnosed with Chiari malformation type I contributed the largest unique variance to predicting worse postsurgical outcome, suggesting hereditary CMI may represent a distinct patient subset with poorer outcomes.

The authors suggest that presurgical screening and treatment of psychological conditions such as depression and anxiety may improve postsurgical symptom outcomes in Chiari malformation type I patients.
Across all patients, fractal dimension (FD) values of the mandibular condyle significantly decreased from baseline (T0) to six months after prolotherapy (T1).
The magnitude of the FD change over time differed significantly between prolotherapy treatment groups and the untreated control group.
Paired comparisons showed FD values significantly decreased between T0 and T1 in the prolotherapy treatment groups, whereas no significant change occurred in the untreated control group.
The number of prolotherapy injections (one, two, or three) had no significant effect on the degree of FD change in the mandibular condyle.
Sex had no significant effect on FD values of the mandibular condyle.
There was no significant difference in FD values between the right and left temporomandibular joint sides.
All patients receiving 20% dextrose prolotherapy for TMJ hypermobility achieved positive clinical outcomes, though specific clinical measures were not quantified in this study.

The authors interpret the post-treatment decrease in FD as reflecting reduced trabecular bone complexity in the condyle, potentially resulting from inflammation-mediated hard-tissue remodeling induced by hypertonic dextrose over the six-month follow-up.
Young women with generalized joint laxity showed faster X-axis (rotational) angular velocity of the tibia during active knee extension than women without generalized joint laxity.
Beighton score for joint laxity was positively correlated with the X-axis (rotational) angular velocity of the tibia during knee extension.
X-axis (rotational) angular velocity of the tibia was positively correlated with Z-axis (anterior-posterior) acceleration during knee extension.
X-axis (rotational) angular velocity was positively correlated with Y-axis (extension) angular velocity of the tibia during knee extension.

Most acceleration and angular velocity parameters other than X-axis angular velocity showed no significant differences between the GJL and non-GJL groups, and no other significant correlations among parameters were found.
In female college athletes, knee hyperextension (a marker of joint laxity) was associated with a 4.78-fold higher risk of ACL injury, per a cited study.
A left-right difference in anterior-posterior knee translation motion was associated with a 4.03-fold higher risk of ACL injury in female college athletes, per a cited study.
In men, generalized joint laxity was associated with unilateral ACL injury, with an odds ratio of 1.3 according to a cited systematic review.

Women with generalized joint laxity have been reported to show instability in head extension and rotation while standing, increasing their risk for musculoskeletal injuries in sports requiring these movements.
Pyridostigmine harnesses residual sympathetic tone to preferentially improve standing blood pressure in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension without worsening supine hypertension.
Atomoxetine harnesses residual sympathetic tone to preferentially improve standing blood pressure in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension without worsening supine hypertension.
An automated abdominal binder device targets the inappropriate splanchnic venous pooling that causes orthostatic hypotension.
Nighttime supine hypertension induces natriuresis and volume loss, which in turn worsens daytime orthostatic hypotension.
Local heat application can control nighttime supine hypertension, reduce nocturia, and improve orthostatic hypotension.
A patient with Tolosa-Hunt syndrome presented with a headache phenotype mimicking hemicrania continua, a trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia, rather than the classic presentation.
The patient's diagnosis was revised to hemicrania continua based on a favorable response to indomethacin, then later revised back to chronic migraine.
Serial MRI studies showed a stable enlarged pituitary gland throughout the patient's disease course.
The patient's final diagnosis of Tolosa-Hunt syndrome was confirmed after she developed a left cavernous sinus syndrome four years into her disease course.
The case illustrates that Tolosa-Hunt syndrome may present with a non-side-locked headache and delayed development of clinical signs, warranting clinical suspicion despite incidental MRI findings.
Total Fibromyalgia Survey Criteria scores declined significantly from baseline to 3 weeks after initiation of a very low-energy diet (VLED).
Widespread Pain Index scores decreased significantly from baseline to week 3 of the VLED.
Symptom Severity subscale scores (fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive difficulty, depression) decreased significantly from baseline to week 3.
72% of participants (n=140) achieved at least a 30% reduction in fibromyalgia survey scores within the first 3 weeks of the VLED, and 89% showed at least one point of improvement.
Improvement in fibromyalgia symptoms at week 3 was strongly correlated with improvement at week 12, suggesting early responders continue to improve.
Baseline BMI was higher among patients who showed little or no improvement in fibromyalgia symptoms at week 3 compared with those showing moderate or high improvement.
A higher proportion of female patients achieved moderate (30-50%) improvement in fibromyalgia symptoms compared with other groups.
Physician-diagnosed depression was more common among patients who showed little or no improvement in fibromyalgia symptoms after 3 weeks of VLED, suggesting improvement is not driven by mood change.

There was no significant difference in the magnitude of BMI change or percentage weight loss at week 3 between patients with little/no, moderate, or high symptom improvement, indicating symptom improvement was not simply proportional to weight loss.

In the authors' prior study, the anti-inflammatory cytokine interleukin-10 increased substantially following 12 weeks of VLED, though its increase was not associated with degree of symptom improvement.

A cited study found that 4 weeks of calorie restriction in women with obesity substantially reduced markers of inflammation including high-sensitivity C-reactive protein and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein.

A cited study found that a 2-week period of VLED did not result in significant reductions of inflammatory markers in individuals with overweight, and pain/somatic symptoms were not addressed in that study.

Short-term calorie restriction increases expression of neuropeptide Y (NPY) in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus, and centrally expressed NPY has substantial analgesic properties, suggesting a possible mechanism for VLED-induced pain relief.

Baseline central mu-opioid receptor (MOR) availability is decreased in men with obesity compared with lean controls, a pattern also previously observed in patients with fibromyalgia, and MOR availability increased in several brain regions after calorie-restriction-induced weight loss.
Navicular height measured before and after exercise in ballerinas was significantly different from the value obtained in the sitting position.
Navicular height values obtained in the three measurement positions (sitting, pre-exercise, post-exercise) differed significantly from one another in the non-dancer control group.
Posterior tibial vein diameter measured before and after exercise differed significantly from the reference (baseline) value in both ballerinas and non-dancer controls.
In the non-dancer control group, venous flow velocity in the posterior tibial vein significantly decreased following the cycling warm-up exercise.
Venous flow volume values measured after exercise differed significantly between the ballerina and non-dancer groups.
Generalized joint hypermobility was found to have no distinctive effect on foot mobility or plantar venous pump activity in ballerinas.
The presence of generalized joint hypermobility did not influence the effect of a short-term warm-up cycling exercise on foot mobility or plantar venous pump activity.
At one-year follow-up, generalized joint hypermobility was present in 28.7% of all dancers, with higher prevalence in females than males.
Anxiety prevalence did not change significantly over the one-year follow-up, remaining present in 52.3% of dancers overall.
Both male and female dancers showed a significant increase in total muscle strength between baseline and one-year follow-up.
Fatigue levels increased significantly in both male and female dancers between baseline and one-year follow-up.
Pain coping scores decreased significantly in both male and female dancers over the one-year follow-up.
Dancers with both GJH and anxiety at baseline had significantly lower odds of participating in the follow-up assessment one year later.
55% of dancers with both GJH and anxiety at baseline dropped out before the second year, compared with 34%, 29%, and 33% in the no-GJH/no-anxiety, GJH-only, and anxiety-only groups respectively.
Dancers who missed the follow-up assessment had significantly higher baseline anxiety and pain-vigilance scores than those who were assessed at follow-up.
Dancers who dropped out of the academy (due to performance or injury) had significantly higher fatigue scores at baseline than those who remained enrolled at follow-up.
Dancers who transferred to a different academy had significantly lower body weight and BMI at baseline than those who remained enrolled at follow-up.

Dancers with GJH alone (without anxiety) scored comparably to the reference group without GJH or anxiety on physical and psychosocial parameters, indicating GJH alone had no negative impact on functioning.
Dancers with both GJH and anxiety weighed significantly less and had less muscle strength than the reference group without GJH or anxiety, and this subgroup had almost twice as many females.
Within the GJH-only subgroup, Beighton score and pain complaints decreased significantly while fatigue increased significantly between baseline and one-year follow-up.
Within the anxiety-only subgroup, muscle strength and fatigue increased significantly between baseline and one-year follow-up.
Within the combined GJH and anxiety subgroup, muscle strength, workload, and fatigue all increased significantly between baseline and one-year follow-up.
Within the reference subgroup without GJH or anxiety, muscle strength and fatigue increased significantly between baseline and one-year follow-up.
Classification of dancers into GJH/anxiety subgroups showed only moderate absolute agreement between baseline and one-year follow-up.
At one-year follow-up, 40% of all dancers were at serious risk for sick leave and work disability due to fatigue, with a higher incidence among those with both GJH and anxiety.
Trial sphenopalatine ganglion stimulation produced a favorable analgesic effect in 7 of 10 patients tested, and 6 of these went on to permanent pulse generator implantation.

Among 11 patients who underwent permanent implantation of a stimulation device, nearly half experienced device-related complications such as lead migration or system infection, and only 54% continued to use stimulation.
Patients with cluster headache showed significant improvement at long-term follow-up after sphenopalatine ganglion stimulation.

Facial proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation and connective tissue massage produced statistically similar posttreatment pain scores and pressure pain threshold values, with no significant difference between the two groups.

Both the facial proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation group and the connective tissue massage group showed significant within-group improvement in pain-related outcomes after 6 weeks of treatment.
This is a clinimetrics article discussing the Beighton score as a tool for assessing generalised joint hypermobility, with no title/abstract text available describing specific study findings.
KIT-activating mutations, particularly p.D816V, are strongly linked to the pathogenesis of mastocytosis.
KIT p.D816V is the most frequently encountered mutation in systemic mastocytosis and its detection constitutes a minor diagnostic criterion.
Allele-specific quantitative PCR and droplet digital PCR are described as the most sensitive current techniques for detecting and quantifying the KIT p.D816V mutant allele.
Presence of KIT p.D816V across multiple non-mast-cell hematological lineages is associated with worse prognosis in systemic mastocytosis.
In advanced forms of systemic mastocytosis, mutations in genes other than KIT are frequently identified and negatively affect disease outcome and response to therapy.

Combined quantitative/sensitive KIT mutation analysis and next-generation sequencing of recurrently involved myeloid genes better characterize the affected cellular compartments and molecular aberrations underlying the clinical heterogeneity of systemic mastocytosis.

Combining sensitive quantitative KIT mutation analysis with next-generation sequencing of other recurrently mutated myeloid genes allows better characterization of the affected cellular compartments and molecular aberrations underlying the clinical heterogeneity of systemic mastocytosis.
The overall average CSI Part A score across 164 migraine patients was 34.2, corresponding to a mild degree of central sensitization on average.
Nearly 29% of migraine patients had moderate-to-severe central sensitization and 3.7% had extreme central sensitization by CSI classification.
CSI score was numerically higher in chronic migraine than episodic migraine but the difference did not reach statistical significance.
CSI score did not differ significantly between migraine patients with and without medication overuse headache.
Migraine patients whose maximum attack lasted longer than 72 hours had significantly higher CSI scores than those with attacks lasting less than 24 hours.
Patients with maximum attack pain severity NRS ≥8/10 had significantly higher CSI scores than those with NRS <8.
Over half (52.4%) of migraine patients reported at least one cranial autonomic symptom during headache attacks.
Lacrimation was the most commonly reported cranial autonomic symptom, occurring in 20.1% of the migraine cohort.
Migraine patients with three or more cranial autonomic symptoms had moderate central sensitization severity, significantly higher than those with none.
Migraine patients with at least one conspicuous cranial autonomic symptom had significantly higher CSI scores than those without such symptoms.
Migraine patients with highly consistent (>80%) or unilateral cranial autonomic symptoms trended toward higher CSI scores but the differences were not statistically significant.
Lacrimation was significantly more frequent in migraine patients with CSI ≥40 than those with CSI <40.
Aural fullness was significantly more frequent in migraine patients with CSI ≥40 than those with CSI <40.
Nasal blockage was significantly more frequent in migraine patients with CSI ≥40 than those with CSI <40.
Rhinorrhea was significantly more frequent in migraine patients with CSI ≥40 than those with CSI <40.
Interictal photophobia was significantly more common in migraine patients with CSI ≥40 than those with CSI <40.
Phonophobia was significantly more frequent in migraine patients with CSI ≥40 than those with CSI <40.
Osmophobia was significantly more frequent in migraine patients with CSI ≥40 than those with CSI <40.
Cutaneous allodynia was significantly more frequent in migraine patients with CSI ≥40 than those with CSI <40.
Temporomandibular joint disorder and irritable bowel syndrome were the most common comorbid central sensitivity syndrome diagnoses among migraine patients.
Anxiety/panic attacks and depression were reported in 11.0% and 18.9% of migraine patients, respectively, as comorbid diagnoses assessed by CSI Part B.
CSI score did not differ significantly between male and female migraine patients.

Headache specialists reported that patients with chronic headache commonly have multiple comorbidities and frequently experience stigmatization after having seen many doctors and tried numerous unsuccessful treatments.

All interviewed headache specialists believed that multidisciplinary care—incorporating adequate specialist staffing, structured intake/follow-up protocols, newest medications, neuromodulation devices, botulinum toxin injections, monoclonal antibodies, nerve blocks/infusions, and health psychology—is essential to a comprehensive headache center.

Specialists identified additional essential services for a comprehensive headache center, including behavioral health (cognitive behavioral therapy, mindfulness, biofeedback, pain management), autonomic neurology, neuropsychology, vestibular audiology, sleep medicine, physical/occupational/speech therapy, exercise physiology, nutrition, and complementary integrative health.
Cervical joint position error was significantly larger in the GJH group with non-specific neck pain compared to the asymptomatic GJH group across all tested directions.
The joint position error in the extension direction was the largest of all directions tested, with much greater error in the NSNP group than the asymptomatic group.
Cervical flexor muscle endurance holding capacity was significantly lower in the NSNP group than in the asymptomatic GJH group.
Cervical extensor muscle endurance holding capacity was significantly lower in the NSNP group than in the asymptomatic GJH group.
In the NSNP group, higher Beighton hypermobility scores were moderately correlated with greater cervical joint position error in the flexion direction.
In the NSNP group, higher Beighton hypermobility scores were moderately correlated with greater cervical joint position error in the left rotation direction.
In the NSNP group, higher Beighton hypermobility scores were correlated (good/moderate strength) with greater cervical joint position error in the right rotation direction.
In the asymptomatic GJH group, there was no significant correlation between Beighton hypermobility score and cervical joint position error.
In the NSNP group, higher Beighton hypermobility scores were moderately negatively correlated with cervical flexor muscle endurance.
In the NSNP group, higher Beighton hypermobility scores were moderately negatively correlated with cervical extensor muscle endurance.
In the asymptomatic GJH group, higher Beighton hypermobility scores were mildly-to-moderately negatively correlated with cervical flexor muscle endurance.
In the asymptomatic GJH group, higher Beighton hypermobility scores were moderately negatively correlated with cervical extensor muscle endurance.

There was a significant interaction between group (NSNP vs asymptomatic) and Beighton score for both cervical joint position error and cervical muscle endurance, such that hypermobile NSNP individuals showed the largest errors and lowest endurance.
There was a significant gender interaction, with females showing greater joint hypermobility than males in both the NSNP and asymptomatic groups.
Mutations in genes coding for connective tissue proteins including collagen, elastin, and tenascin are associated with general joint hypermobility.

At least one-third of migraine patients experience bilateral headache, and bilateral presentation occurs more frequently in those with near-daily attacks (≥25 headache days/month) than other chronic migraineurs.
In fibromyalgia patients, M1-targeted tDCS produced greater pain relief and quality-of-life benefit than DLPFC-targeted tDCS, with clinical efficacy lasting up to 1-2 months.

Ten sessions of tDCS treatment significantly reduced pain intensity and migraine episode length in chronic migraine patients, with continued reduction in pain levels up to 120 days after treatment ended.
tDCS significantly decreased patient-controlled opioid usage compared to sham stimulation after total knee arthroplasty or lumbar surgery.
Clinical application of 4x1 HD-tDCS to fibromyalgia patients has been shown to reduce pain intensity across different studies.

In a 5-day, 2x2 HD-tDCS trial targeting M1 contralateral to the worst pain side in chronic TMD patients, the active group had more responders (>50% VAS pain relief) at 1-month follow-up than placebo, with improvement seen only in contralateral, not ipsilateral, sensory-discriminative pain measures.

In a single case of central dysesthetic pain and intentional tremor, bilateral motor cortex stimulation eliminated most pain-evoked phenomena and improved steady burning pain and tremor two months after permanent electrode placement.
A single case study showed pain relief with bilateral motor cortex stimulation applied for deafferentation pain following spinal cord injury.
In 23 diabetic neuropathic pain patients, 5 days of active bilateral H-coil rTMS produced significantly greater pain reduction than sham stimulation, with effects lasting 3 weeks.
Five daily sessions of H-coil rTMS reduced lower-limb neuropathic pain 1 hour post-stimulation, but this analgesic effect did not last more than 2 weeks.
Bilateral anodal tDCS over tongue motor cortex in healthy individuals induced greater enhancement of cortical excitability and tongue motor function than unilateral stimulation.

In healthy individuals, multifocal tDCS with bilateral M1 anodes reversed experimentally induced inhibition of corticomotor excitability and impaired conditioned pain modulation caused by topical pain.

Neuroimaging evidence indicates that conventional-montage M1 tDCS modifies μ-opioid receptor availability, consistent with engagement of the endogenous opioid system similarly to motor cortex stimulation.
Conventional-montage M1 tDCS has been shown by neuroimaging to modulate Glx (glutamate and glutamine) levels in brain regions associated with pain processing.

The authors' prior work showed HD-tDCS targeting M1 reduced contralateral TMD pain, hypothesized to act through direct/indirect modulation of the ipsilateral hemisphere via highly focused stimulation.
A home-based neurostimulation study in fibromyalgia demonstrated feasibility and effectiveness of extending treatment up to 60 sessions with associated reduction in pain levels.
In older adults with knee osteoarthritis, 10 home-based tDCS sessions with real-time monitoring reduced pain severity and sleep disturbances.

Finite element modeling showed that the main source of variability in peak electric field between lab-based (12 mm disk) and home-based (4 cm x 1 cm strip) bilateral HD-tDCS montages was electrode dimension rather than tissue conductivity.
HD-tDCS was reported to be more efficient than conventional tDCS at inducing longer-lasting neuroplasticity.
Diagnostic criteria for chronic cluster headache were updated to define it by remission periods lasting less than three months, replacing the previous threshold of less than one month.
Galcanezumab is described as a recent advance in the treatment of episodic cluster headache.
Non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation is described as a recent advance in the treatment of episodic cluster headache.
High flow oxygen gas is noted as one of the most effective treatments for cluster headache, though it is rarely used for other headache disorders and is underused due to diagnostic delay.
Cluster headache is associated with a high rate of suicidal ideation and attacks are suspected to be among the most painful human experiences.
Cluster headache is typically diagnosed with a delay of years, often because it is confused with migraine and trigeminal neuralgia, and secondary causes may be overlooked.
BPPV was detected during the interictal period in 12.3% of vestibular migraine patients.
Ten percent of patients had hearing loss on audiometry, with 8.7% showing unilateral low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss below 2000 Hz consistent with Meniere's disease.
Tinnitus was reported in 94.4% of patients with combined vestibular migraine and Meniere's disease.
Aural fullness was present in 83.4% of patients with combined vestibular migraine and Meniere's disease.
Nausea was present in 72.2% of patients with combined vestibular migraine and Meniere's disease.
Vomiting occurred in 30.5% of patients with combined vestibular migraine and Meniere's disease.
More than half of vestibular migraine patients reported a past history of motion sickness.
A family history of migraine was present in nearly three-quarters of the vestibular migraine cohort.
Patients with a family history of migraine had an earlier age of onset of migraine headaches than those without.
Patients with a family history of migraine had an earlier age of onset of vertigo attacks than those without.
The overall median attack severity for headache, rated on a 0-10 visual analog scale, was 8.
The overall median attack severity for vertigo, rated on a 0-10 visual analog scale, was 7.
The mean age of onset of headache was 25 years in the vestibular migraine cohort, notably earlier than the mean age of onset of vertigo at 39 years.
Erenumab treatment was associated with a decrease in median monthly migraine days from baseline to weeks 9-12 in the overall real-world cohort.
Migraine-related disability measured by HIT-6 decreased significantly from baseline to weeks 9-12 of erenumab treatment in the overall cohort.
Patients achieving a ≥75% relative reduction in MMDs almost universally had a low absolute residual migraine burden.
Patients with a 50-74% relative response still frequently had a substantial residual monthly migraine burden.
Among patients with only a 30-49% relative response, most still had a high absolute residual migraine burden similar to non-responders.
High migraine-related disability (HIT-6 ≥60) remained common across all relative response categories, including among high responders.
Women had a less favorable HIT-6 (migraine-related disability) distribution than men in the lowest relative response categories.
Residual monthly migraine days after erenumab treatment did not differ between men and women.

Most patients classified as 50-74% responders still exceeded the clinical threshold of 4 residual monthly migraine days, with a substantial minority meeting high-frequency episodic or chronic migraine criteria.
The authors conclude that a 30% reduction in monthly migraine days should not be considered an acceptable clinical response to migraine prevention, even in chronic migraine patients.
SPECT imaging showed increased Gallium-67 uptake in the cavernous sinus region during in-bout periods of cluster headache, which faded during out-of-bout periods.

A SPECT study using 99mTc-HSA in six episodic CH patients found no difference in cavernous sinus uptake during vs. outside nitroglycerin-triggered attacks, failing to support a cavernous sinus inflammatory mechanism.
High-resolution T2-weighted MRI found no structural differences in cavernous sinus or surrounding structures between CH patients and healthy controls, refuting a narrow-cavernous-sinus hypothesis.
CH patients showed a larger left-to-right transcranial diameter at the temporal fossa level compared with healthy controls, suggesting wider skulls.
133-Xenon SPECT showed no global CBF change but a significant regional CBF increase in central, basal, and part of the right parietotemporal regions during CH attacks.

MR angiography showed vasodilatation of the major basal arteries during both triggered and spontaneous CH attacks, similar to that seen in healthy subjects after experimental capsaicin-induced forehead pain, suggesting vasodilation is a nonspecific pain epiphenomenon rather than the primary cause of CH.

Plasma CGRP is elevated in the jugular vein ipsilateral to CH attacks, normalizes in out-of-bout periods and after sumatriptan, and CGRP can induce attacks in CH patients, supporting the trigeminovascular model.
Plasma VIP, a marker of parasympathetic activation, is elevated in the jugular vein ipsilateral to CH attacks and normalizes during out-of-bout periods and after sumatriptan.

PET imaging demonstrated increased regional cerebral blood flow within the hypothalamus ipsilateral to attacks in chronic CH patients compared with out-of-bout episodic CH patients during nitroglycerin-induced attacks, the landmark finding establishing hypothalamic involvement in CH.
fMRI showed higher ipsilateral hypothalamic activation during CH attacks compared with outside attacks, with activation tracking pain resolution after subcutaneous sumatriptan rescue treatment.

Resting-state fMRI showed increased functional connectivity between the right hypothalamus and ipsilateral cortical regions (angular gyrus, supramarginal gyrus, insula, superior temporal gyrus, precuneus) during spontaneous CH attacks compared with outside attacks in the same patients.

In an fMRI study using kinetic oscillation stimulation of the nasal mucosa in 26 healthy controls, painful trigeminal stimuli activated the anterior hypothalamus, locus coeruleus, thalamus, and insula, whereas nonpainful stimuli activated brainstem pontine nuclei and cerebellar lobule VIII but not the hypothalamus.
Proton MR spectroscopy showed a decreased NAA/creatine ratio, a marker of neuronal/mitochondrial dysfunction, in the hypothalamus of CH patients compared with healthy controls.
Reduced hypothalamic NAA/Cr persisted across episodic (in-bout and out-of-bout) and chronic CH subgroups, suggesting a permanent hypothalamic neuronal dysfunction fingerprint of CH.

In a study of 47 episodic CH patients versus 21 healthy controls and 16 chronic migraine patients, hypothalamic NAA/Cr was confirmed reduced, along with reduced choline/Cr ratios, suggesting both neuronal dysfunction and membrane lipid changes as a CH hallmark.
A voxel-based morphometry study found an isolated increase in gray matter volume in the inferior-posterior hypothalamus in CH patients compared with healthy controls.

ROI/manual segmentation studies found increased gray matter volume in the anterior hypothalamus (mirrored to the headache side), centered on the supraoptic nucleus, in episodic and chronic CH patients compared with healthy controls and migraine patients.
Hypothalamic structural volume abnormalities identified in earlier VBM studies were never replicated in subsequent studies, even with the same VBM approach.

A VBM study found decreased gray matter volume in multiple pain-processing regions (posterior cingulate cortex, caudate nucleus, thalamus, inferior parietal lobe, middle temporal gyrus, insula, precentral gyrus, frontal gyrus) in chronic CH patients.

A larger cohort study confirmed reduced frontal gray matter volume in CH patients while also finding increased gray matter volume in anterior cingulate cortex, insula, and fusiform gyrus, interpreted as correlates of dysfunctional descending pain modulation.

In the largest CH cohort studied to date, VBM changes in pain-processing brain areas were positively correlated with the severity of structural abnormalities and the burden of disease experienced by patients.

Exclusive structural alteration of anterior cingulate cortex, amygdala, and secondary somatosensory cortex was observed in chronic (but not episodic) CH, implicating these structures in disease chronification.

ROI-based resting-state fMRI showed increased functional connectivity between the ipsilateral posterior hypothalamus and midbrain dopaminergic-related structures (ventral tegmental area, dorsal raphe, substantia nigra, subthalamic and red nuclei) in chronic CH patients outside attacks compared with healthy controls.

A longitudinal resting-state fMRI study showed decreased hypothalamic functional connectivity with the medial frontal gyrus, precuneus, and cerebellar areas during in-bout compared with out-of-bout periods in episodic CH patients.

Diffusion tensor imaging showed increased mean, axial, and radial diffusivity in widespread white matter of the frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes in patients with cluster headache, with axial diffusivity positively correlating with attack frequency.
Fractional anisotropy was reduced in the corpus callosum and several frontal and parietal white matter tracts, predominantly contralateral to the pain side, in patients with cluster headache.
Connectome analysis revealed a significant hub reorganization, with increased strength and closeness centrality of the cingulate gyrus, in patients with cluster headache.

Seed-based resting-state fMRI showed increased functional connectivity between the ipsilateral posterior hypothalamus and diencephalic-mesencephalic structures of the midbrain dopaminergic system (ventral tegmental area, dorsal raphe nuclei, substantia nigra, subthalamic and red nuclei) outside attacks during in-bout periods in chronic cluster headache compared with healthy controls.

In episodic cluster headache outside attacks during in-bout periods, the right hypothalamus showed higher functional connectivity with multiple cortical pain-processing regions (cingulate cortices, frontal and temporal gyri, inferior parietal lobule, parahippocampal gyrus, amygdala) compared with healthy controls.

A longitudinal resting-state study found decreased hypothalamic functional connectivity with the medial frontal gyrus, precuneus, and cerebellar areas during in-bout compared with out-of-bout periods, and annual bout frequency correlated negatively with hypothalamus-cerebellar (culmen/declive) connectivity.

Regional anatomic connections between cerebellar areas and the hypothalamus differed between in-bout and out-of-bout periods in cluster headache, supporting a role for cerebellohypothalamic circuits in pathophysiology.

Using hypothalamic and thalamic seeds, increased functional connectivity with the sensorimotor and primary visual resting-state networks was observed in cluster headache patients compared with healthy controls.

A decreased functional connectivity between the hypothalamus (bilaterally) and the salience network was found in episodic cluster headache patients outside attacks during in-bout periods compared with healthy controls.

Increased frequency-specific activity was found between the hypothalamus and the attention network ipsilateral to the headache side, and the cerebellar network contralateral to the headache side, in episodic cluster headache outside attacks during in-bout periods versus healthy controls.

Whole-brain resting-state analysis revealed functional connectivity abnormalities in the default mode, temporal, frontal, salience, somatosensory, dorsal attention, and visual networks in patients with episodic cluster headache during in-bout periods.

Patients with cluster headache showed higher short-range functional connectivity than healthy controls and migraine patients within the working memory network and executive control network, mapped ipsilaterally to the pain side.

Comparison between in-bout and out-of-bout scans showed altered functional connectivity in the frontal and dorsal attention networks, and lower frontal network connectivity correlated with longer cluster headache disease duration.

Tractography studies suggest that deep brain stimulation for refractory cluster headache acts not on the posterior hypothalamus itself but on the dorsal longitudinal fasciculus and mammillotegmental fasciculus, two fascicles involved in autonomic response modulation, via orthodromic and antidromic neuromodulation.

A voxel-based morphometry study found gray matter atrophy in thalamus, caudate nucleus head, posterior cingulate cortex, middle frontal gyrus, precuneus, middle temporal gyrus, and precentral gyrus in cluster headache patients compared with healthy controls, with middle frontal gyrus atrophy correlating with disease duration and no hypothalamic volume abnormality.

In a larger cohort, reduced frontal gray matter volume was confirmed alongside increased gray matter volume of the anterior cingulate cortex, insula, and fusiform gyrus, interpreted as correlates of dysfunctional descending pain-modulatory systems in cluster headache.

In the largest cohort of cluster headache patients studied to date, gray matter volume abnormalities in pain-processing brain areas were confirmed and positively correlated with the severity of the patients' disease burden.

Exclusive structural alteration of the anterior cingulate cortex, amygdala, and secondary somatosensory cortex was found specifically in patients with chronic (versus episodic) cluster headache, implicating these structures in disease chronification.
Human provocation studies confirmed that CGRP can trigger migraine attacks, establishing it as a key mechanistic target.
Rimegepant shows very high binding affinity/specificity for the CGRP receptor with weaker but notable cross-reactivity at the amylin-1 (AMY1) receptor.
In an adaptive-dose phase II RCT of 799 participants treating a single migraine attack, rimegepant 75, 150, and 300 mg doses were all efficacious versus placebo.

Rimegepant 75 mg was superior to placebo for freedom from the most bothersome symptom at 2 hours in phase III trials.
Study 303 confirmed the rimegepant orally disintegrating tablet significantly improved 2-hour pain freedom versus placebo without hepatotoxicity.
Rimegepant ODT showed a superior sustained pain response rate compared to placebo when assessed at 48 hours.
In the pivotal preventive RCT, the primary endpoint reduction in monthly migraine days at weeks 9-12 with rimegepant did not reach statistical significance versus placebo.

Ubrogepant combined with the CGRP monoclonal antibodies galcanezumab or erenumab showed similar AUC and side effect profile compared to controls, supporting combination safety.
Atogepant has affinity for the AMY1 receptor, though approximately 100-fold weaker than its affinity for the CGRP receptor.

Like olcegepant, ubrogepant also has moderate affinity and antagonist activity at the AMY1 receptor.
Ubrogepant dose-dependently inhibited capsaicin-induced dermal vasodilation, a pharmacodynamic marker of CGRP blockade.
In the phase II trial, only the 100 mg ubrogepant dose achieved statistically significant pain freedom at 2 hours compared to placebo.

In a preclinical medication-overuse headache model, ubrogepant reversed sumatriptan-induced allodynia dose-dependently without inducing sensitization itself upon repeated dosing.
A phase I hepatic safety trial of ubrogepant 100 mg in 516 healthy participants found similar adverse events and hepatic enzyme elevations between drug and placebo groups.
The most frequently reported adverse events with ubrogepant within 48 hours were nausea, dry mouth, and somnolence, occurring more with the 100 mg dose.

Atogepant 60 mg showed no pharmacokinetic interaction with sumatriptan 100 mg, though it could delay Tmax and lower Cmax of sumatriptan.

Intranasal zavegepant 10 mg and 20 mg were both superior to placebo for pain freedom at 2 hours in a phase IIb/III RCT.
Dysgeusia was the most common adverse event with intranasal zavegepant, occurring more frequently in active dose arms than placebo.
An azepinone-based analog of zavegepant showed similar CGRP receptor affinity but markedly improved oral bioavailability compared with zavegepant in rats.
Blood pressure was not affected when subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg was combined with rimegepant 75 mg compared to sumatriptan alone.

Nausea and other gastrointestinal adverse events were reported infrequently and at similar rates between fremanezumab and placebo groups.
Serious adverse events and adverse events leading to discontinuation occurred in a small, similar proportion of patients across all treatment groups.
Two deaths occurred during the trials (intentional diphenhydramine overdose and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), and study drug intake was not considered causal for either.
Among patients with a prior cardio-/cerebrovascular medical history, the incidence of cardio-/cerebrovascular adverse events (CVAEs) with fremanezumab was low and comparable to placebo.
Hypertension was the most commonly reported CVAE among patients with CV medical history but occurred at low, similar rates across fremanezumab and placebo groups.
CVAEs occurred in low, similar proportions of patients without CV medical history across all treatment groups.
CVAEs were infrequent in patients with two or more, or three or more, cardiovascular risk factors, with no meaningful difference between fremanezumab and placebo.

Hypertension was the most frequently reported CVAE among patients with two or more or three or more cardiovascular risk factors but occurred at low, similar rates across fremanezumab and placebo groups.
Patients with both two or more cardiovascular risk factors and a CV medical history had a modestly higher but low overall incidence of CVAEs, without a clear treatment-related pattern.
No CVAEs were reported in any treatment group among patients with four or more cardiovascular risk factors.

In a 12-month long-term extension cohort, mean systolic and diastolic blood pressure remained stable or decreased from baseline through up to 15 months of fremanezumab treatment in patients with hypertension history, baseline hypertension, or antihypertensive medication use.

Among patients receiving concomitant cardiovascular medications at baseline, overall adverse event incidence was somewhat higher with fremanezumab than placebo, similar to the total pooled population pattern.
Injection-site induration occurred substantially more often with fremanezumab than placebo among patients receiving concomitant cardiovascular medications.
CVAEs were low and similar across treatment groups in patients receiving cardiovascular medications at baseline, with no CVAE occurring in more than one patient per group.
In patients using concomitant triptans, CVAEs occurred in low, similar proportions across all treatment groups.
Increased heart rate was among the most commonly reported CVAEs in triptan users but occurred in fewer than 1% of patients in each treatment group.
Hypertension was among the most commonly reported CVAEs in triptan users but occurred in fewer than 1% of patients in each treatment group.
CVAEs were also infrequent in patients not using triptans, occurring in a small proportion of patients in each treatment group.

A pooled analysis of three phase 3 galcanezumab trials found no increased incidence of CVAEs or changes in blood pressure, pulse, or ECG features compared with placebo, including in triptan users.
The most common cardiovascular risk factors in the pooled migraine population were obesity, history of cardiovascular disease, and hormonal birth control pill use.
Ultrasound-guided stellate ganglion block significantly reduced MIDAS disability scores from baseline to 3-month follow-up in migraine patients.

The frequency of analgesic (NSAID) use over 3 months decreased substantially after stellate ganglion block treatment.
Minor, transient side effects including hoarseness, local bruising, and upper limb numbness occurred after ultrasound-guided stellate ganglion block, with no serious complications observed.
In two patients, a single stellate ganglion block treatment triggered worsening headache/migraine attack, leading them to discontinue further treatment.
A 6 mL dose of ropivacaine was used for ultrasound-guided stellate ganglion block, consistent with prior reports that this volume is sufficient for successful SGB with fewer complications.
The title reports a case (or cases) of indolent systemic mastocytosis undergoing remission without receipt of any targeted (e.g., KIT-inhibitor or anti-mast-cell) therapy.
Offspring of parents with substance use disorder had a 2.48-fold higher risk of bipolar disorder compared to offspring of unaffected parents.
Offspring of parents with substance use disorder had a 2.22-fold higher risk of depressive disorder compared to controls.

Offspring of parents with substance use disorder had a 1.43-fold higher risk of alcohol use disorder compared to controls.

The majority of patients with systemic mastocytosis carry somatic mutations in the KIT gene.

Patients with indolent systemic mastocytosis generally have a normal to near-normal life expectancy, while advanced systemic mastocytosis (including aggressive SM and mast cell leukemia) carries a poor prognosis.

Mediator-related symptoms occurring across mastocytosis types can range from mild to severe or even life-threatening, and severe acute presentations may warrant a diagnosis of mast cell activation syndrome.
IgE-dependent and IgE-independent allergies are relevant comorbidities in patients with severe mast cell activation symptoms.

Individuals in the lowest decile of median-based expiration-inhalation difference (E-Imedian), reflecting low respiratory sinus arrhythmia during deep breathing, had significantly higher odds of a coronary artery calcium score ≥100 after adjustment for cardiovascular risk factors.
Low E-Imedian in the lowest decile was also significantly associated with the higher coronary calcium threshold of CACS≥300 after full risk-factor adjustment.
Each 1-SD reduction in E-Imedian was associated with increased odds of CACS≥100 after adjustment for cardiovascular risk factors.
Each 1-SD reduction in E-Imedian was also associated with increased odds of the higher-severity CACS≥300 threshold.
The unadjusted proportion of participants with CACS≥100 was roughly twice as high in the lowest decile of E-Imedian compared with those with higher E-Imedian.
A similar unadjusted relationship was observed for the higher-severity CACS≥300 threshold across E-Imedian deciles.
Unlike other RSA/HRV measures, RMSSD modeled as a continuous per-1-SD-decrease variable was not significantly associated with high coronary calcium score.
SD of heart rate (SDHR) and mean circular resultant (MCR), both measures of heart rate variability, were similarly significantly associated with high coronary calcium score as the RSA measures.

The association between reduced RSA/HRV measures and coronary calcium was strongly present in individuals with diabetes, while it was weaker (though still significant for E-Imedian and E/I on CACS≥100) in individuals without diabetes.
There was a statistically significant interaction between diabetes status and SDHR with respect to the risk of CACS≥100.

Individuals with low E-Imedian were older, more often men, more often smokers, and had higher systolic blood pressure, higher CRP levels, and a higher prevalence of diabetes than those with higher E-Imedian.

The association between low E-Imedian and high coronary calcium score remained significant even after excluding participants with a self-reported history of myocardial infarction or angina pectoris, suggesting the finding was not driven by pre-existing clinical coronary disease.

One-year reproducibility testing in a subset of 84 participants showed moderate intraclass correlation coefficients for RSA and HRV measures, comparable to other commonly used population biomarkers such as CRP.

The paper cites prior mouse studies indicating that the vagal anti-inflammatory pathway acting via the α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor modulates atherosclerotic disease development, with receptor deficiency accelerating and receptor stimulation decreasing atherosclerosis.

In this atypical case of recurrent painful ophthalmoplegic neuropathy, contrast-enhanced inflammation of the oculomotor nerve was located in the cavernous sinus region rather than at the nerve root, which is the typical site in RPON.

The order of onset of headache and oculomotor nerve palsy differed in each recurrence, suggesting that both autoimmune and vascular mechanisms may be involved in disease onset.
In migraine patients, 51.1% (23/45) of those receiving intravenous lidocaine infusion achieved a 50% or greater reduction in pain, after a mean of 4.5 days.
31.1% of migraine patients receiving lidocaine infusion achieved complete pain freedom over a mean 6.2-day infusion.
In migraine patients receiving ketamine infusion, 34.4% achieved a 50% or greater reduction in pain after a mean of 3.4 days.
15.6% of migraine patients receiving ketamine infusion achieved pain freedom over a mean 5.1-day infusion.
The mean percentage reduction in VAS pain score in migraine patients was greater with lidocaine (53%) than with ketamine (31.6%).

After adjusting for comorbidities and number of failed preventative treatments, lidocaine infusion produced a significantly greater estimated marginal mean percentage reduction in VAS pain score (62%) than ketamine (33.4%).
The overall adverse event rate of intravenous lidocaine infusion was 32%, lower than the 42.4% seen with ketamine infusion.
10% of lidocaine infusions and 12.1% of ketamine infusions were ceased due to an adverse event.
In status migrainosus, lidocaine infusion achieved a ≥50% pain reduction in 43.8% of patients compared to 20% with ketamine infusion.

Ketamine's anti-nociceptive effect in headache is postulated to relate to NMDA receptor antagonism, which in turn inhibits glutamate implicated in cortical spreading depression propagation, central sensitization, and nociceptive neuron activation.
The 30-day re-admission rate following infusion was 6.7% for lidocaine and 3.1% for ketamine in the migraine cohort.

Women who joined the intervention group reported a history of significant pain during infancy far more often than those in the control group at baseline.
Headache was the cardinal presenting symptom in 9.1% of patients seen in the neurological emergency department.
Among headache patients, primary headaches accounted for 40.1% and secondary headaches for 29% of cases, per the group's prior study.
No single doctor's note contained documentation of all identified red flags for secondary headache.

Some red flags, such as recent headache onset or change in pattern, fever, and age, were documented more frequently than other items, with 'recent onset or change' recorded in 49.8% of notes.
A complete set of headache characteristics essential for ICHD-3 diagnosis was never fully recorded in any patient's chart.
When headache localization was excluded, a full set of the remaining ICHD-3 characteristics was documented in 22.7% of patients.
Headache localization, a core ICHD-3 diagnostic item, was not reported in any patient chart.
Headache duration was documented in 68.4% of patients, more frequently than most other ICHD-3 items.
Pain intensity was documented in 43.2% of patients with headache.
Headache character (quality of pain) was documented in 42.1% of patients.

A cited external study (Locker et al.) similarly found a complete headache history was documented in only 0.3% of ED cases (1 of 353), corroborating the present study's finding of poor documentation.
Other cited ED studies reported considerably higher rates of patients discharged without a specific headache diagnosis, up to 33.9% and 59%, compared to 24.7% in the present cohort.

The authors' prior study found a high correlation between a history of cardiovascular disease and secondary headache, prompting its inclusion as an additional red flag in their proposed structured headache interview.
Patients who ultimately received an ILR were older, had more syncope episodes, more fall trauma, and were more often hospitalized than patients who did not receive an ILR.
Patients who received an ILR had less frequent prodromal symptoms (nausea, cold sweat) before syncope than those who did not receive an ILR.

The proportion of abnormal CAT results did not differ significantly between patients with normal versus abnormal ILR monitoring results, indicating CAT findings do not predict ILR outcome.
The frequency of abnormal ILR findings did not differ significantly between patients stratified by normal versus abnormal CAT results, indicating CAT results do not predict ILR outcome.
Only a minority of the unexplained syncope registry underwent ILR implantation.

The discussion cites the SPRITELY randomized trial in patients ≥50 years with bifascicular block, in which empiric permanent pacing failed to reduce syncope recurrence compared with an ILR-guided strategy, supporting that much of the syncope recurrence after pacing is vasodepressor (reflex) in origin.

Heterozygous pathogenic variants in FBN1 cause Marfan syndrome, characterized by thoracic aortic aneurysm/dissection, mitral valve defects, tall stature, arachnodactyly, scoliosis, muscle hypoplasia, and ectopia lentis.

Heterozygous pathogenic FBN2 variants cause congenital contractural arachnodactyly (CCA/Beals-Hecht syndrome/Distal Arthrogryposis type 9), featuring tall stature, arachnodactyly, progressive scoliosis, joint contractures, and crumpled ears.

Pathogenic FBN1 variants also cause acromelic dysplasias (Weill-Marchesani syndrome, geleophysic dysplasia, acromicric dysplasia), sharing short stature, brachydactyly, joint stiffness, contractures, and thick skin - phenotypically opposite to Marfan syndrome.
Early-onset carpal tunnel syndrome occurs in an estimated 25-66% of patients with FBN1-related acromelic dysplasias.

A newly identified FBN2-related disorder presents with brachydactyly, early-onset carpal tunnel syndrome, short palpebral fissures, relative short stature, and short Achilles tendons causing toe walking, caused by the variant c.5009T>G p.(Phe1670Cys) in cbEGF23.
Studies in Marfan syndrome mouse models demonstrated that increased TGF-β signaling plays a key role in driving aortic aneurysm progression.
Studies of iPSC-derived chondrocyte pellets from Marfan syndrome patients suggest that increased TGF-β signaling promotes linear growth in growth plates, contributing to tall stature.

In contrast to other short fibrillinopathies, normal TGF-β signaling was found in fibroblasts of Weill-Marchesani syndrome patients and a WMS mouse model carrying an FBN1 exon 9-11 deletion, and in acromicric/geleophysic dysplasia patients with LTBP3 variants.

Heterozygous pathogenic LTBP3 variants cause geleophysic dysplasia phenotypically indistinguishable from FBN1-related GD, with diminished and disorganized microfibril networks observed in patient tissue.

Heterozygous variants in THSD4 (encoding ADAMTSL6) predispose to hereditary thoracic aortic aneurysms, with haploinsufficiency causing reduced FBN1 microfibril assembly and increased TGF-β signaling in patient and mouse aortic tissue.

A pediatric MFS cohort study found dominant-negative FBN1 variants in exons 26-49 result in a more severe aortic phenotype than haploinsufficient variants or dominant-negative variants elsewhere, contradicting earlier reports that haploinsufficiency confers greater aortic risk.

A clear gradient in ectopia lentis prevalence was found according to dominant-negative FBN1 variant location, with the highest prevalence of lens dislocation associated with N-terminal region variants.
Skeletal features including pectus excavatum and tall stature are more pronounced in Marfan syndrome patients carrying haploinsufficient FBN1 variants compared to dominant-negative variants.
A study in adult Marfan syndrome patients found an association between premature stop codon FBN1 variants and a higher risk of severe scoliosis and tall stature.

Pathogenic FBN1 variants in exon 64, clustered around the C-terminal furin cleavage site, cause marfanoid-progeroid-lipodystrophy syndrome via reduced levels of the cleavage hormone asprosin, leading to abnormal adiposity and metabolic dysregulation.
The stiff skin syndrome-causing variant p.(Trp1570Cys) in the TB4 domain of FBN1 inhibits FBN1-integrin (α5β1, αvβ5, αvβ6) interactions, affecting normal cell adhesion and cell spreading.
Fbn2 knockout mice display syndactyly, muscle weakness, and transient contractures, along with reduced bone mass and shortened bone length, but do not fully recapitulate the human CCA phenotype.
Autosomal recessive ADAMTSL2 variants cause geleophysic dysplasia, and Adamtsl2 knockout mice show increased Fbn2 staining in the lungs without altered Fbn2 transcriptional regulation.
FBN1 RGD-integrin interaction upregulates miR-503, which downregulates TGF-β2 and reduces pSMAD2 activity, representing a mechanism by which fibrillin-1 inhibits TGF-β signaling.
Multiple studies report a strong association between cysteine-creating or -replacing FBN1 variants and ectopia lentis in Marfan syndrome.

Autosomal recessive truncating variants in LTBP1 cause cutis laxa type IIE, characterized by generalized cutis laxa, inguinal hernias, craniofacial dysmorphology, short stature, brachydactyly, and mild cardiac defects.

Biallelic pathogenic variants in the FBN1-binding region of LTBP2 cause an autosomal recessive form of Weill-Marchesani syndrome (WMS3) and impair LTBP2 secretion and/or its ability to bind FBN1, destabilizing fibrillin microfibrils.

In the eye of a mouse model with truncated Adamts10, excessive fibrillin microfibrils were observed that were primarily composed of Fbn2.

Adamtsl2 knockout mice, modeling geleophysic dysplasia, showed increased Fbn2 staining in the lungs, but unlike ADAMTS17 loss, Fbn2 transcriptional regulation was not altered.

Limb-specific (Prx1-Cre) Adamtsl2 knockout mice failed to confirm the chondrocyte-specific growth plate abnormalities seen in Col2a1-Cre knockouts, contradicting the chondrocyte-dysfunction hypothesis for short stature in geleophysic dysplasia.

Tendon- and ligament-specific (Scx-Cre) Adamtsl2 knockout mice showed impaired skeletal growth, suggesting the growth impairment in geleophysic dysplasia may arise secondary to shortened tendons/ligaments rather than intrinsic chondrocyte or growth plate defects.
Tendon- and ligament-specific (Scx-Cre) Fbn1 deletion in mice, as a model for Marfan syndrome, results in increased longitudinal bone growth.

Heterozygous THSD4 variants (encoding ADAMTSL6) predispose to hereditary thoracic aortic aneurysms with limited skeletal involvement; in transfected HEK293 cells these variants caused haploinsufficiency or reduced FBN1 microfibril assembly, and Thsd4+/- mice developed progressive thoracic aortic aneurysms with increased TGF-β signaling.
One geleophysic dysplasia patient with a compound heterozygous ADAMTSL2 variant developed several arterial aneurysms including a thoracic aortic aneurysm.
Studies in Marfan syndrome mouse models that recapitulate the human phenotype demonstrated that increased TGF-β signaling plays a key role in the progression of aortic aneurysm.
Elevated TGF-β signaling has been found in the mitral valves of Marfan syndrome mice.
Studies of iPSC-derived chondrocyte pellets from Marfan syndrome patients suggest that increased TGF-β signaling promotes linear growth in the growth plates of tubular bones.

Reduced bone mass and reduced bone length in Fbn2-/- mice was attributed to elevated TGF-β signaling.

Fibrillin-1 RGD-integrin interaction inhibits expression of miR-1208, an inhibitor of noncanonical TGF-β signaling.

The FBN2 cbEGF23 variant p.(Phe1670Cys) causing the short fibrillin-2-opathy altered cell adhesion and cell spreading to mutant FBN2 protein fragments in vitro.
Early-onset carpal tunnel syndrome occurs in an estimated 25%-66% of patients with acromelic dysplasia (Weill-Marchesani syndrome, geleophysic dysplasia, and acromicric dysplasia).

KIT p.D816V is the most common activating mutation and key molecular driver in adults with cutaneous mastocytosis or indolent systemic mastocytosis.

A 2-hour infusion of VIP significantly increased plasma CGRP levels in migraine patients relative to baseline, with post-hoc increases seen at T30 and T60 compared to T180.
Among migraine patients who developed a VIP-induced migraine attack (n=6), plasma CGRP changes did not differ significantly from placebo days in the same individuals.

In healthy individuals, plasma CGRP did not significantly change during either VIP infusion or placebo, though a post-hoc analysis of T0 vs T120 approached significance.
A 2-hour infusion of VIP induced migraine-like attacks in 71% of migraine patients during the 12-hour observational period, compared with only 5% after placebo.
VIP infusion caused headache in 67% of healthy individuals compared to 8% after placebo, and 25% of healthy individuals experienced a migraine-like attack after VIP.

Plasma VIP was significantly elevated during VIP infusion relative to baseline in healthy individuals, while no change occurred during placebo infusion.

A de novo heterozygous missense variant (c.2330G>A, p.G777E) in ZMIZ1 was identified in a 5-year-old Chinese girl and classified as pathogenic (PS2+PM1+PM2+PP2+PP3), making this the first reported ZMIZ1-related NEDDFSA case in a Chinese patient.
The proband exhibited excessive joint mobility along with short fingers/toes and conical fingers, part of the distal skeletal anomalies characteristic of NEDDFSA.

NEDDFSA, caused by ZMIZ1 pathogenic variants, is characterized by global neurodevelopmental delay, hypotonia, poor growth, speech/language impairment, and additional features including eye anomalies, joint hypermobility, and distal skeletal anomalies of the hands and feet.

Among 54 Chinese NEDD/ID patients screened by array-CGH and whole-exome sequencing, pathogenic variants were identified in 33 (61.11%), comprising 5 microdeletions and 28 protein-coding gene variants.
The p.G777E variant lies within the highly conserved MSX-interacting zinc-finger (zf-MIZ) domain and was predicted deleterious/damaging by multiple in-silico tools (SIFT, PROVEAN, PolyPhen-2).
ZMIZ1 has a probability of loss-of-function intolerance (pLI) value of 1.000, indicating it is a haploinsufficient gene consistent with autosomal dominant disease mechanism.
Four additional rare ZMIZ1 variants were detected in four other patients within the NEDD/ID cohort and classified as variants of uncertain significance, though pathogenicity could not be excluded.

Among ZMIZ1 amino-acid-changing variants compiled from DECIPHER, published literature, and this cohort, the majority clustered in the highly conserved alanine-rich low-complexity region, with six of nine such variants (66.67%) located there, suggesting this region is a mutational hotspot.

Compiling this study with the DECIPHER database and prior published articles, a total of 32 patients with ZMIZ1-related neurodevelopmental disorder have now been reported globally (29 protein-coding variants, 3 chromosomal translocations), nearly all previously of Caucasian or one Thai origin prior to this Chinese case.
ZMIZ1 mRNA expression across 79 human tissues was detected in heart, thyroid, immune cells, ovary, retina, and brain, with the highest expression level found in the pineal gland.

STRING protein-protein interaction analysis showed ZMIZ1 interacts with SMAD3, SMAD4, MYC, NOTCH1, RBPJ, SMARCA4, ETS1, and UBE2I, with GO enrichment for mesenchyme morphogenesis, hypoxia response, tube morphogenesis, transcriptional regulation, endocardium development, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and cardiac left ventricle morphogenesis, forming MAML1-RBPJ-ICN1 and SMAD nuclear protein complexes.
The proband's full-scale intelligence quotient (WPPSI-IV) was 75, placing her at the borderline/edge level of intellectual development consistent with mild intellectual disability.
Visual evoked potential testing showed prolonged latency of the P100 and N145 waves bilaterally, indicating mild abnormality of the visual pathway in the proband.
Hip X-ray imaging showed left and right acetabular angles of approximately 22° and 25° respectively, consistent with congenital hip dysplasia in the proband.

The ≥20/10 mmHg systolic/diastolic blood pressure drop criterion for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension within 3 minutes of standing has better sensitivity than the older ≥30/15 mmHg criterion for diagnosing MSA, with similar specificity.
An elevated post-void residual urine volume is the most specific sign distinguishing MSA from Parkinson's disease, though not from progressive supranuclear palsy.
Post-void residual urine volume progressively increases with disease duration in MSA, nearly doubling from year one to year two.
Urinary urge incontinence is a more sensitive but less specific marker than PVR for diagnosing MSA.
In the majority of men later diagnosed with probable MSA, erectile dysfunction preceded urinary symptom onset.
A meaningful minority of MSA patients show beneficial levodopa response, more often in the parkinsonian than the cerebellar subtype, with the response typically waning after a few years.
Early postural instability, especially within the first year of motor onset, is a specific marker distinguishing MSA from Parkinson's disease.
Patients with MSA fall much earlier in the disease course than patients with Parkinson's disease.
Early and severe autonomic failure within 3 years of symptom onset increases the likelihood of an MSA diagnosis over progressive supranuclear palsy.

Urinary urgency/incontinence, erectile dysfunction, neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, and RBD are highly specific non-motor markers suggestive of the cerebellar subtype of MSA at initial assessment.
Conventional structural brain MRI has good but imperfect overall accuracy for radiological MSA diagnosis when validated against postmortem-confirmed cases.
Increased diffusivity in the putamen shows excellent accuracy for distinguishing MSA from Parkinson's disease.
Increased diffusivity of the middle cerebellar peduncle combined with normal superior cerebellar peduncle diffusivity separates MSA from progressive supranuclear palsy.
Laryngeal motion abnormalities detected during a swallowing task are far more common in MSA than in Parkinson's disease.
Cardiac sympathetic imaging with 123I-MIBG scintigraphy typically shows normal uptake in MSA, in contrast to reduced uptake indicating postganglionic sympathetic denervation in Parkinson's disease.

Plasma norepinephrine levels are relatively preserved in MSA but reduced in Parkinson's disease with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension and in autoimmune or Lewy body isolated autonomic failure, distinguishing preganglionic from postganglionic autonomic failure.
Supine plasma norepinephrine above 100 pg/mL is the most sensitive and specific predictor of phenoconversion to MSA among patients with isolated autonomic failure.
Prolonged motor unit potential duration on external anal sphincter EMG is suggestive of MSA-related sphincter denervation, though it also occurs in other neurodegenerative diseases.

Protein misfolding cyclic amplification detects distinct alpha-synuclein conformational strains that distinguish MSA from Lewy body disease based on different aggregation kinetics and fluorescence intensity.
Elevated CSF neurofilament light chain levels distinguish MSA from Lewy body disease with high accuracy.
CSF neurofilament light chain is already elevated at the isolated autonomic failure stage in patients who go on to phenoconvert to MSA, unlike those who do not phenoconvert.
A substantial minority of patients with isolated autonomic failure eventually phenoconvert to MSA, with several clinical and biochemical predictors identified.
Among patients with idiopathic RBD who develop a neurodegenerative disease after several years, a minority are eventually diagnosed with MSA.
The previously widely-used second consensus criteria for MSA diagnosis show suboptimal diagnostic accuracy against postmortem confirmation, especially early in disease, motivating the new criteria.
Erenumab treatment led to significant reductions in monthly migraine days at both 3 and 6 months compared to baseline in a real-world chronic migraine cohort.
At 3 months, 53% of patients achieved a ≥30% reduction in monthly migraine days and 36% achieved a ≥50% reduction with erenumab.
Monthly headache days, rescue medication use days, and HIT-6 scores significantly improved after 3 months of erenumab treatment.
The number of previous preventive treatment classes tried was inversely correlated with degree of MMD improvement at 3 months, though the relationship explained only a small amount of variance.
Half of patients evaluated at 6 months (21 of 42) had their erenumab dose escalated from 70mg to 140mg monthly because they did not meet criteria for initial response at 3 months.
Disability measures (MIDAS) showed sustained significant improvement at 6 months of erenumab treatment, alongside sustained headache variable improvement.

Patients with medication overuse had a significantly longer duration of chronic migraine compared to those without medication overuse, the only baseline difference surviving correction for multiple comparisons.
There was no significant difference in erenumab response (MMD change, 30% responder rate, or secondary outcomes) at 3 months between patients with and without medication overuse.
41% of patients (38/92) reported adverse events with erenumab; constipation was the most common, affecting about half of those with AEs, with no serious AEs reported.
No serious adverse events were reported in this real-world erenumab cohort over the audit period.
Seven patients (8%) discontinued erenumab due to lack of efficacy, four after three injections and three others after six injections.
A cited head-to-head trial found erenumab had more favorable dropout rates due to side effects and better efficacy compared to topiramate.
The NFF tool showed higher concordance, kappa, and AUC than the modified ACR 2011 and 2016 criteria when compared against the study's own rheumatologist-based gold standard diagnosis.
The Ghavidel-Parsa et al. study site ('Bidari') showed markedly lower ACR criteria diagnostic sensitivity than the average across 14 other studies.
Fibromyalgia patients at the anomalous study site had a substantially lower widespread pain index than the overall mean/median across other studies.

In the current Ghavidel-Parsa et al. study, the mean WPI and PSD were even lower than in the same group's 2013 study.
A separate general-population study in Germany found higher WPI and PSD values among fibromyalgia patients than seen in the Ghavidel-Parsa et al. cohorts.

The letter authors conclude that because the gold-standard fibromyalgia diagnosis used by Ghavidel-Parsa et al. was anomalous and less severe than standard rheumatology/epidemiological diagnoses, the study's conclusions about relative agreement among diagnostic criteria are untenable and should be rejected.
Hypermobility of the first CMC joint can impair hand function and predispose to osteoarthritis later in life.
CMC joint instability occurs more commonly in younger women with generalized joint hypermobility or in postmenopausal women with early-stage arthritis.
