Among females with long-COVID, the prevalence of restless legs syndrome significantly increased from before to after COVID-19 infection.
Post-COVID-19 RLS prevalence in females with long-COVID was more than double that seen in female controls who never had overt COVID-19 symptoms.

A logistic regression found that hospitalization, sleep apnea, neuropathic pain severity, and antihistamine or antidepressant use did not significantly predict development of post-COVID-19 RLS among females with long-COVID.
The severity of restless legs syndrome symptoms was moderate and similar between the long-COVID and control groups.
The baseline (pre-COVID-19) prevalence of RLS in females with long-COVID was similar to that of the general population and to rates reported in epidemiological studies.

Patients who underwent combined ACL reconstruction with anterolateral ligament internal bracing had significantly less anteroposterior knee laxity on KT-1000 arthrometry than those who had isolated ACL reconstruction.

Combined ACL reconstruction with ALL internal bracing resulted in a lower rate of positive pivot-shift test (12.9%) compared with isolated ACL reconstruction (43.2%), indicating better rotational stability.
Although Group 2 (ALL-IB) had a numerically lower graft failure rate than Group 1, the difference between groups was not statistically significant.
Postoperative functional outcome scores did not differ significantly between patients who had isolated ACL reconstruction and those who had combined ACL reconstruction with ALL internal bracing.
Three patients (8.8%) who received ALL internal bracing had transient lateral knee discomfort lasting up to 3 months postoperatively without affecting rehabilitation.
Generalized joint hypermobility, arising from abnormal soft tissue structures, is described as a risk factor for both ACL injury and subsequent ACL graft failure.
In a prospective study of 1558 athletes, knee hyperextension beyond neutral was associated with a five-fold higher risk of ACL injury when accounting for GJH measurements.
A higher hypermobility index was associated with greater residual postoperative knee instability and lower Lysholm and IKDC functional scores after ACL reconstruction.
Patients with hypermobility had a 25% failure rate for hamstring autograft ACL reconstruction.

Female athletes with joint hypermobility showed a positive pivot-shift rate of 57.1%.
A biomechanical study showed that concurrent ACL and ALL reconstruction significantly improves knee rotatory stability compared with isolated ACL reconstruction.
Approximately 90% of anterolateral ligament injuries are associated with ACL tears, reflecting a strong anatomical/biomechanical relationship between the two structures.
Ligamentous hypermobility is associated with poorer Lachman, anterior drawer, and pivot-shift test results in individuals with ACL injury.
Knee recurvatum of more than 5° was identified as a significant independent predictor of ACL graft failure in a multicenter study.
Joint hypermobility is more common in patients with ACL injury than in control groups.
Patients with knee recurvatum showed more anteroposterior instability both preoperatively and postoperatively.

Avapritinib is described as one of the two most effective and well-studied tyrosine kinase inhibitors active against KIT D816V in ISM.
Imatinib is less effective or noneffective against KIT D816V and is recommended only for patients with non-codon-816 KIT mutations or wild-type KIT.
Masitinib is less effective or noneffective against KIT D816V and is recommended only for patients with non-codon-816 KIT mutations or wild-type KIT.

Patients with chronic migraine showed a significantly longer time to reach maximum pupillary gradient recovery at 2 and 5 minutes after the cold pressor test compared with healthy controls, suggesting delayed parasympathetic withdrawal.
No significant differences were found between CM and HC groups in pupil diameter, contraction velocity, latency, or amplitude of the pupillary light reflex at any time point of the cold pressor test.

Heart rate and blood pressure did not significantly differ between CM and HC groups at any time point during the cold pressor test, suggesting cardiovascular autonomic innervation was not differentially affected.

Confirming prior knowledge, type 2 diabetes was found to be more common among people with HS.
Confirming prior knowledge, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease was found to be more common among people with HS.

Watad et al.'s cross-sectional study reported an increased odds of Sjögren's syndrome diagnosis in breast implant recipients.

Knee implant recipients with osteoarthritis showed an increased risk of Sjögren's syndrome compared with osteoarthritis patients without knee implant surgery.
In a large cohort study, knee implant recipients had a significantly increased standardized incidence ratio for any autoimmune or connective tissue disorder compared to the general population.
Hip implant recipients also showed a modestly increased standardized incidence ratio for any autoimmune or connective tissue disorder relative to the general population.
In a case-control study, women with undifferentiated connective tissue disorder were significantly more likely to have silicone-containing devices than matched controls.
Women with undifferentiated connective tissue disorder were also significantly more likely to have artificial joint implants than matched controls.
Women with undifferentiated connective tissue disorder were also more likely to have orthopedic metallic fixation devices than matched controls.
A questionnaire study found that women with breast implants reported significantly higher anxiety and more anxious personality traits than both healthy controls and medical/surgical inpatients.
Women receiving cosmetic breast implants show increased rates of mental illness and psychiatric hospital admission, including prior to surgery.
Silicone particulates have been detected in the liver, spleen, and mediastinal, axillary, and internal mammary lymph nodes after breast implant rupture.

Peripheral blood mononuclear cells from women with silicone breast implants showed increased frequency and intensity of cellular immune reactivity against collagen I, collagen III, fibrinogen, and fibronectin compared to age-matched controls.
The same study found no significant difference in cellular immune reactivity to silicone antigens (silicon dioxide, D4, silicone gel) between silicone breast implant recipients and controls.
A study of 90 women found no statistically significant difference in clinical complaints between those with MRS-confirmed silicone in the liver and those without detectable hepatic silicone.
A study of 238 women found no difference in occurrence of self-reported diseases or symptoms between women with ruptured versus intact silicone breast implants.

A large retrospective cohort study of osteoarthritis patients found increased rates of Sjögren's syndrome and systemic lupus erythematosus in patients who received hip implants, and increased Sjögren's syndrome rates in knee implant recipients, compared with osteoarthritis patients without implants.
Signorello et al. found an increased risk of any autoimmune or connective tissue disorder diagnosis in both knee implant and hip implant recipients compared to the general population.

A case-control study found that women with undifferentiated connective tissue disorder had significantly greater exposure to silicone-containing devices, artificial joints, and orthopedic metallic fixation devices compared with age- and ethnicity-matched controls, even after adjustment for confounders.

Peripheral blood mononuclear cells from women with silicone breast implants showed increased frequency and intensity of cellular immune reactivity against collagen I, collagen III, fibrinogen, and fibronectin, but no significant difference in reactivity against silicone antigens, compared to age-matched controls.

A study of 90 women found no statistically significant difference in complaints between those with MRI-confirmed silicone in the liver and those without, concluding that implant integrity has little impact on clinical symptoms.

In a study of 238 women, there was no difference in self-reported symptoms or in serum levels of antinuclear antibodies and rheumatoid factor between women with ruptured versus intact breast implants.
Ahern et al. found that women with breast implants had significantly higher anxiety scores than both healthy controls and medical/surgical inpatients, and scored higher on anxious personality traits.

In a study of 50 women with breast implant illness symptoms, positive bacterial cultures (most commonly Cutibacterium acnes and Staphylococcus epidermidis) from explanted implants and capsules were identified in a higher proportion of the BII cohort than controls.
In cultures obtained during explantation, positive culture results associated with breast implant illness symptoms were most commonly linked to Staphylococcus genus organisms.
Biofilm-forming Staphylococcus epidermidis on breast implants has been reported to result in host immune activation.

Systemic symptoms including myalgias, arthralgias, fatigue, neuropathy, or cognitive impairment in breast implant patients were a major risk factor for eventual explantation surgery, with a risk ratio of 5.6.
A systematic review of 23 studies found that explantation of silicone breast implants improved complaints in 75% of patients (469/622).

In patients with autoimmune disease and breast implant illness, only 16% (3/18) improved after explantation without additional immunosuppressive therapy, whereas 56% (10/18) improved when immunosuppressive therapy was added.
The FDA reported receiving 2,497 medical device reports of breast implants causing symptoms consistent with breast implant illness between November 2018 and October 2019.

Breast implant illness symptoms have been recorded to arise many years after surgery, in some patients developing more than 20 years after the operation, which argues against a purely psychosomatic, post-surgical-stress etiology.
Women who underwent breast implant explantation reported decreased appearance satisfaction and decreased confidence in their appearance compared with prior implant status.

The 1999 Institute of Medicine report concluded there was insufficient evidence to support an association between silicone breast implants and connective tissue or rheumatic disease, or a novel syndrome.

A case series of 45 women with various biomaterial implants or injections (medical grade silicone, polyalkylimide, poly-L-lactic acid, hyaluronic acid) found largely consistent symptoms—arthralgias, general weakness, and myalgias—regardless of implant material.
Symptoms consistent with breast implant illness/ASIA were also observed in populations with polyacrylamide hydrogel implants, further supporting a biomaterial-independent mechanism.
Bacterial biofilm formation by C. acnes and S. epidermidis has been established as playing a positive causative role in the pathogenesis of capsular contracture in breast implant patients.

Two placebo-controlled trials demonstrated that inhaled oxygen was significantly more effective than room air for aborting cluster headache attacks, with 78% of oxygen-treated patients pain-free at 15 minutes compared with 20% on room air.
Two double-blind clinical trials found no significant difference in cluster headache outcome according to oxygen flow rate or type of delivery mask, though sample sizes were small.

In a migraine trial, oxygen therapy via simple face mask showed no difference in pain scores at 15 minutes versus room air, but a higher proportion of oxygen-treated patients achieved pain intensity ≤1 at 60 minutes.
Oxygen therapy reduced migrainous visual symptoms such as photophobia, blurred vision, and scotomata compared with room air.

A trial comparing dry oxygen, dry air, and humidified oxygen via high-flow nasal cannula found humidified oxygen produced the greatest reduction in migraine pain scores at 2 hours relative to humidified air control.
In an RCT of headache patients (mostly tension-type and migraine) treated in the emergency department, oxygen via non-rebreather mask improved VAS pain scores more than room air at 15 minutes.
In the same ED headache trial, fewer patients needed rescue analgesics at 30 minutes when treated with oxygen compared with placebo.
Oxygen therapy is a first-line abortive treatment for cluster headache, with more than 70% of patients likely to respond.

Approximately 20% of cluster headache patients do not respond to oxygen therapy, with poor response associated with being a nonsmoker, longer attack duration, photophobia/phonophobia, nausea/vomiting, restlessness, chronic cluster headache, and interictal headache.
In Kudrow's pivotal cluster headache study, inhaling oxygen at 7 L/min showed the same efficacy in male and female patients.

In the United States Cluster Headache Survey, roughly equal proportions of male and female patients reported oxygen as effective, but response was slower in females, possibly reflecting the lower oxygen flow rates typically used in women.
In a study of 246 patients with cluster headache, oxygen therapy efficacy was numerically higher in females than males, but this difference did not reach statistical significance.

Experimental recordings showed that 100% oxygen inhalation inhibited superior salivary nucleus-evoked effects, suppressed neuronal firing in the trigeminocervical complex, and reduced increases in corneal and lacrimal blood flow, suggesting inhibition of the cranial parasympathetic/trigeminoautonomic reflex as a mechanism of action.

Oxygen inhalation did not affect meningeal vasodilation or trigeminocervical complex activation induced by dural electrical stimulation, suggesting OT may not act at trigeminal afferents or be effective in typical migraine.

Hyperoxia was found to suppress cortical spreading depression and reduce brain injury, suggesting a possible mechanism by which oxygen therapy could alleviate migraine, particularly migraine with aura.
Two double-blind clinical trials found no significant difference in primary outcomes between different oxygen flow rates or mask types for treating cluster headache.

Oxygen inhalation did not affect meningeal vasodilation or trigeminocervical complex activation induced by dural electrical stimulation, suggesting OT may not act at trigeminal afferents in typical migraine.

Hyperoxia induced by 100% oxygen administration causes vasoconstriction, and its cooling effect may attenuate activation of the trigeminovascular system, potentially benefiting cluster headache and migraine treatment.
In Kudrow's pivotal cluster headache study, oxygen inhalation at 7 L/min showed equal efficacy in male and female patients.

The United States Cluster Headache Survey found that similar proportions of male and female patients considered oxygen effective, but women had a slower response to oxygen therapy than men, possibly related to lower flow rates used in women.
In a study of 246 patients with cluster headache, oxygen therapy efficacy was numerically higher in females than males, but this difference was not statistically significant.

A single published case reported partial efficacy of oxygen therapy in chronic paroxysmal hemicrania, though OT does not appear generally effective for trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias other than cluster headache.
In a survey of 20 German patients with hypnic headache, only 1 of 4 patients who used 100% oxygen inhalation as abortive therapy found it effective.
Daily oxygen therapy (every hour for 3 minutes) was reported to relieve withdrawal headache in patients with medication-overuse headache, presumably via a vasoconstrictive effect.

Ten of 12 patients with postdural puncture headache who received inhaled oxygen at 12 L/min via a non-rebreather mask reported improvement in headache intensity even before receiving adjuvant intravenous metoclopramide.

A case report described a migraineur with ipsilateral cranial autonomic symptoms who became pain-free with 100% oxygen inhalation for 15 minutes but experienced headache recurrence 30 minutes after OT discontinuation.

Although high-flow oxygen therapy can generate oxygen free radicals causing tissue damage, the short exposure duration (15-60 minutes) used for headache treatment carries little risk of oxygen toxicity.
Cluster headache is associated with cigarette smoking, and patients undergoing home oxygen therapy should be counseled about fire risk from smoking during OT.

The United States Cluster Headache Survey found that 16% of patients reported oxygen was unaffordable, and 12% purchased non-medical welder-grade oxygen as an economical alternative, risking contamination with toxic gases.

During the 52-week open-label extension, erenumab produced sustained mean reductions in monthly migraine days (MMD) from parent study baseline across all treatment-failure subgroups, with the largest reduction in patients who had never failed a preventive treatment.
Erenumab also produced sustained reductions in monthly acute migraine-specific medication days (MSMD) at Week 52 across all subgroups.
The proportion of patients achieving a ≥50% reduction in MMD from baseline at Week 52 was highest in never-failed patients and decreased with increasing number of prior treatment failures.
Among completers, erenumab 140 mg produced numerically greater reductions in MMD and MSMD than 70 mg across most subgroups at Weeks 40 and 52.

High-threshold response rates (≥75% and 100% MMD reduction, i.e., migraine-free) were achieved by a subset of patients with erenumab treatment, with higher 100% response in never-failed patients versus treatment-failure subgroups.
Exposure-adjusted adverse event incidence rates during the OLTP increased with the number of prior preventive treatment failures.

Despite higher AE rates with increasing treatment failures, AE incidence during the long-term OLTP in each TF subgroup was lower than rates observed in either the erenumab or placebo arms during the double-blind period, with no new safety signals and no fatal adverse events.
During the double-blind treatment period of the parent study, erenumab (70 and 140 mg) showed greater mean reductions in MMD and MSMD compared with placebo across all treatment-failure subgroups.
At parent study baseline, monthly migraine days and the proportion of patients using acute migraine-specific medication both increased with increasing numbers of prior preventive treatment failures.
Patients in whom prior preventive treatments had failed had a longer mean duration of migraine history at baseline than those who had never failed a preventive treatment.
Topiramate was the most frequently reported failed prior preventive medication category, followed by β-blockers and tricyclic antidepressants, across all treatment-failure subgroups.

The absolute magnitude of erenumab's long-term treatment effect appeared to decline with increasing number of prior preventive treatment failures, suggesting that patients with multiple failed treatments are increasingly difficult to treat.

Erenumab is a fully human monoclonal antibody that selectively binds to and inhibits the canonical calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) receptor, the mechanism underlying its migraine preventive effect.
Pooled analysis across rheumatic diseases showed a significant, small-effect decrease in gut microbial richness (observed species) in patients versus controls.
When stratified by disease, a significant decrease in observed-species richness was found only in rheumatoid arthritis, not other rheumatic diseases.
Pooled Chao1 index was significantly decreased overall in rheumatic disease patients versus controls, with the disease-specific decrease driven mainly by systemic lupus erythematosus.
Shannon diversity index was significantly decreased overall across rheumatic diseases compared with controls.
Shannon index was significantly decreased in both rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus when examined by specific disease.
In contrast to most diseases, Shannon diversity was significantly increased in systemic sclerosis patients compared with controls.
Simpson index was significantly decreased overall in rheumatic disease patients compared with controls.
A significant decrease in Simpson index (richness/evenness) was found specifically in rheumatoid arthritis patients versus controls.
Simpson index was also significantly decreased specifically in gout patients versus controls.
Simpson index was significantly decreased in fibromyalgia patients versus controls, with low heterogeneity, suggesting reduced gut microbial evenness/richness in fibromyalgia.
Among seven rheumatic diseases with frequently reported beta-diversity differences, consistent differences across all studies were found only for ankylosing spondylitis and IgG4-related disease.

Streptococcus was the most consistently enriched genus, reported as increased in ankylosing spondylitis, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren's syndrome, systemic lupus erythematosus and systemic sclerosis in nearly all studies reporting it.
Lactobacillus, typically considered a beneficial commensal, was consistently enriched in ankylosing spondylitis, systemic lupus erythematosus and systemic sclerosis across all reporting studies.

The anti-inflammatory, butyrate-producing genus Faecalibacterium was consistently depleted in rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren's syndrome and systemic lupus erythematosus in nearly all reporting studies.

Decreases in alpha-diversity were mainly observed in medication-free/treatment-naïve patient studies, with the Simpson index effect size not varying significantly and heterogeneity dropping substantially in studies where ≥80% of patients were on antirheumatic treatment.
Regional subgroup analysis showed that most alpha-diversity indices were decreased only in patients from Eastern countries, not those from Western countries.

Gut dysbiosis is proposed to breach gut epithelial barrier integrity via zonulin-mediated disassembly of tight junction proteins, a phenomenon reported in rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, systemic lupus erythematosus and other rheumatic diseases.

Faecalibacterium's anti-inflammatory properties are thought to be mediated via its role in butyrate production, a short-chain fatty acid important for mucosal integrity and reducing inflammation; its depletion parallels findings in Crohn's disease and inflammatory bowel disease.

Streptococcus metabolites and membrane vesicles are proposed to cross the gut-blood barrier and activate pro-inflammatory macrophages, triggering low-grade systemic inflammation that may cause or exacerbate tissue damage in rheumatic disease.
At night, RMSSD was significantly lower in vestibular migraine patients compared to healthy controls.
At night, high-frequency (HF) HRV power was significantly lower in vestibular migraine patients compared to healthy controls, indicating reduced vagal tone.
At night, the LF/HF ratio was significantly elevated in vestibular migraine patients compared to healthy controls, indicating sympathetic predominance.
At night, low-frequency (LF) HRV power was significantly elevated in vestibular migraine patients compared to healthy controls, consistent with increased sympathetic activity.
At night, RMSSD was significantly lower in migraine (non-vestibular) patients compared to healthy controls.
At night, HF HRV power was significantly lower in migraine patients compared to healthy controls.
At night, RMSSD was significantly lower in the migraine group compared to healthy controls, indicating reduced vagal (parasympathetic) activity.
At night, high frequency (HF) power was significantly lower in the migraine group compared to healthy controls, reflecting reduced parasympathetic tone.
At night, the LF/HF ratio was significantly elevated in the migraine group compared to healthy controls, indicating a shift toward sympathetic predominance.

Overall, patients with vestibular migraine show autonomic dysfunction marked by sympathetic hyperfunction and vagal hypofunction that is more pronounced at night, and this dysfunction appears more severe than in migraine patients without vestibular symptoms.
Half of the patients tested with autonomic nervous system testing fulfilled clinical criteria for POTS after SARS-CoV-2 vaccination.
More than half of tested patients had reduced length-dependent sweat production consistent with small fiber neuropathy after vaccination.
A subset of patients had overlapping POTS and abnormal sudomotor testing after vaccination.
The vast majority of patients undergoing formal autonomic nervous system testing had abnormal findings.
About a third of patients undergoing skin biopsy had nerve fiber density below pathological thresholds for small fiber neuropathy.
Skin biopsies from post-vaccination neuropathy patients showed increased C4d complement deposition on cutaneous endothelial cells compared to age/sex matched healthy controls.
Two of five patients with CSF evaluation had oligoclonal bands despite otherwise normal CSF parameters.
Most patients receiving a standard-dose, slow-taper corticosteroid regimen reported significant symptom improvement within two weeks.
A short course of corticosteroid with rapid taper failed to produce improvement in any of the three patients who received it.
Patients with persistent post-vaccination small fiber neuropathy and dysautonomia who received a single cycle of IVIg showed dramatic symptom improvement within two weeks.
Among patients who never received immunotherapy, most had partial recovery by 12 weeks, some had none, and one had complete recovery.
The overwhelming majority of patients in this post-vaccination neuropathy series were women.
A subset of patients developed mild transient symptoms after the first vaccine dose with full symptom onset after the second dose, suggesting immune priming to the spike protein.
A minority of skin biopsies showed axonal swellings in nerve fibers, consistent with an active axonal process.
A minority of skin biopsies showed borderline low nerve fiber density at the distal leg site.
Nerve conduction studies were consistent with pure small-fiber axonal neuropathy without large-fiber involvement in all patients tested.
Brain and spinal cord MRI scans were unremarkable in all patients evaluated, arguing against central structural causes of the neuropathic symptoms.

Prior mouse studies showing preferential ACE2 receptor expression on small-fiber sensory neurons are cited as a possible mechanistic explanation for the predominance of small fiber neuropathy after SARS-CoV-2 vaccination.
Meningeal mast cell density showed a non-significant trend toward increase in K14 mice (lacking meningeal lymphatics) compared to WT controls.
Mast cell spatial distribution in meninges was equally random and normally distributed in both K14 and WT mice, indicating no spatial association between mast cells and lymphatic vessel location.
Basal MCP-1 release from meninges was significantly higher in K14 mice (lacking meningeal lymphatics) than in WT controls.
Basal IL-12p70 release from meninges was significantly decreased in K14 mice compared to WT littermates.
Basal levels of IL-6, IL-10, TNFα, and IFNγ released from meninges did not differ between K14 and WT mice.
Stimulation of meninges with the P2X7 agonist BzATP significantly increased IL-10 release in both WT and K14 mice.
Stimulation of meninges with the P2X7 agonist BzATP significantly increased TNFα release in both WT and K14 mice.
The BzATP-induced increase in IL-10 and TNFα release did not differ between WT and K14 mice, suggesting lack of mLVs does not alter sensitization to purinergic stimulation.
Basal CGRP release from meningeal preparations was similar between K14 and WT mice.
KCl-stimulated CGRP release from meningeal trigeminal nerve endings was significantly lower in K14 mice lacking meningeal lymphatics than in WT controls.
Basal (spontaneous) nociceptive spiking activity in meningeal trigeminal nerve afferents did not differ significantly between WT and K14 mice.

ATP-induced nociceptive spiking activity increased identically in both WT and K14 mice, indicating that developmental meningeal lymphatic dysfunction does not alter basal or triggered trigeminal nociception.
In adult mice with AAV-mediated ablation of meningeal lymphatics, basal nociceptive spiking activity did not differ from control mice, replicating the K14 model result.

ATP-induced nociceptive spiking was significantly increased over baseline in both control and lymphatic-ablated mice, with a non-significant trend toward greater ATP-induced firing in ablated animals.

Meningeal trigeminal innervation density, complexity, endpoint number, coverage area, and fluorescence intensity did not differ between K14 and WT mice, indicating meningeal lymphatic deficiency does not affect trigeminal innervation.
In the questionnaire-based population sample, 57% of migraineurs reported at least one cranial autonomic symptom and 31% reported two or more.
Interview-based validation in a subsample of 302 migraineurs found lower prevalences of cranial autonomic symptoms than the questionnaire: 44% for one symptom and 22% for two or more.
Facial/forehead sweating was the most common cranial autonomic symptom reported by migraineurs, at 39% prevalence.
Lacrimation was the second most common cranial autonomic symptom reported by migraineurs, at 24% prevalence.
The migraine diagnostic questionnaire showed 80% specificity and 68% sensitivity for cranial autonomic symptoms when validated against a semi-structured interview.
Cranial autonomic symptoms showed only weak intercorrelation with each other and did not form clear clusters, arguing against a single unifying pattern.
The migraine diagnostic questionnaire's cranial autonomic symptom items showed 80% specificity and 68% sensitivity when validated against a semi-structured interview.
Correlation analysis between individual cranial autonomic symptoms in migraine patients showed only weak correlations, with no clear clustering of symptoms detected.

The authors propose the first diagnostic appendix criteria for cranial autonomic symptoms in migraine, intended for genetic and epidemiological research, with tighter criteria suggested for clinical and pathophysiological studies of this possible endophenotype.

Hemodynamic changes during straining (Valsalva maneuver) while bearing down for a bowel movement led to an MCA stroke in a patient with a history of migraines who harbored an undiagnosed arachnoid cyst that had elevated his baseline intracranial pressure.
Arachnoid cysts are found in about 1% of adults and are frequently asymptomatic, typically discovered incidentally.
The most common symptom produced by mass effect from an arachnoid cyst is headache, though neurovascular compression can cause a range of symptoms.
The patient's presentation and timing met criteria for tPA treatment for the MCA stroke, but he was not considered a good candidate for thrombectomy given the large stroke size.

Due to concern for subclinical increased intracranial pressure from the large stroke, the patient was treated with 3% hypertonic saline and mannitol, but his physical examination did not improve despite this intervention.
The patient had a history of migraines with a flare-up on the morning of the event, prior to collapsing while straining during defecation.

The authors suggest patients with migraines and/or arachnoid cysts be counseled to avoid straining during bowel movements, use laxatives during constipation, and promote gut health via fiber, diet, and hydration to reduce risk of hemodynamically triggered neurovascular events.
During the Valsalva maneuver, decreased vagal nerve influence via baroreceptor activation triggers a transient increase in heart rate and restoration of blood pressure in healthy individuals.

High-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation to the primary motor cortex has the strongest literature support for reducing pain intensity and associated symptoms in peripheral neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia, and migraine.
Repeated daily rTMS sessions produce effects that can be prolonged through spaced maintenance stimulation sessions, though some individuals do not respond to M1-targeted rTMS.

Among the 24 participants with self-reported chronic pain, specific diagnoses included joint hypermobility syndrome (n=6), chronic headache and/or migraine (n=4), fibromyalgia (n=3), Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes (n=2), endometriosis (n=1) and rheumatoid arthritis (n=1), with five participants presenting more than one pain type.

One participant described fibromyalgia and irritable bowel syndrome as strongly interlinked with each other and with stress, sleep and activity levels, a connection they reported learning about online.

Young people with chronic pain reported feeling dismissed by healthcare professionals and misunderstood by family and friends, which contributed to their turning to online communities for validation and empathetic support.

Citing prior research, the authors note that diagnostic uncertainty is experienced by nearly one third of adolescents with chronic pain, and that diagnoses of idiopathic chronic pain are often not accepted by patients.

Participants, particularly those with fibromyalgia, felt the NHS website provided only generic, outdated treatment information ('missing a lot out') and did not offer novel pain management options, prompting them to seek alternative online resources.

Young people described an Instagram-based 'online chronic pain community' as the most helpful resource for managing chronic pain, providing empathetic support, validation and practical advice from peers with lived experience.

Young people used free YouTube yoga videos and mindfulness apps (Calm, Headspace) to self-manage pain-related mood, sleep and physical activity, favoring YouTube once the free content of paid apps was exhausted, partly due to COVID-19 lockdown restrictions.

In unadjusted analyses, the Fibromyalgia Survey Questionnaire (FSQ) was weakly but statistically significantly correlated with pressure pain threshold (PPT) at all tested sites among patients with active RA.
In unadjusted analyses, FSQ was weakly but statistically significantly correlated with temporal summation (TS) at all tested sites among patients with active RA.

After adjusting for demographic factors, study site, disease characteristics, and pain catastrophizing, the correlation between FSQ and QST remained statistically significant only for temporal summation at the wrist and pressure pain threshold at all sites except the thumb.
Sensitivity analysis stratified by sex found no differences in the association between FSQ and QST measures.
Sensitivity analysis of individual FSQ components did not reveal differences in association with QST measures.
The authors concluded that FSQ and QST were only weakly correlated among RA patients and should not be considered interchangeable measures of pain sensitization.

Conditioned pain modulation (CPM), unlike pressure pain threshold and temporal summation, was not reported among the QST measures showing statistically significant correlation with the Fibromyalgia Survey Questionnaire.

Despite statistically significant correlations, the overall strength of association between FSQ and QST was weak, leading the authors to conclude the two measures are not interchangeable for assessing pain sensitization in RA.

In the intention-to-treat analysis, high-load progressive shoulder strengthening exercise (HEAVY) led to a significantly greater reduction (improvement) in WOSI total score than low-load exercise (LIGHT) at 16 weeks.

In the per-protocol population (patients adhering to at least two-thirds of sessions), the benefit of high-load exercise over low-load exercise on WOSI total score was even larger and reached the predefined minimal important difference.

A greater proportion of patients receiving high-load exercise achieved a clinically relevant improvement in shoulder function than those receiving low-load exercise, both in ITT and per-protocol analyses.
Patients receiving high-load exercise were significantly less likely to have a positive shoulder rotation test postintervention compared with low-load exercise.
Patients receiving high-load exercise had significantly higher odds of rating an important improvement in physical symptoms on Global Perceived Effect compared with low-load exercise.
High-load shoulder strengthening exercise was associated with significantly more transient muscle soreness and headaches than low-load exercise, though no serious adverse events occurred.
High-load exercise showed a non-significant trend toward greater improvement in shoulder muscle strength (scaption and external rotation) compared with low-load exercise.
Approximately four out of five people with hypermobility spectrum disorder experience symptoms in the shoulder joint, with significant impact on daily life.

More than two-thirds of patients receiving high-load strengthening exercise improved shoulder function above the minimal important difference threshold, and 64% reported an important improvement in physical symptoms after treatment.
There were no significant differences in painkiller use or concomitant treatment between the high-load and low-load exercise groups at baseline or postintervention.
48 of 153 patients (31%) were classified as headache frequency responders, achieving at least a 30% reduction in monthly headache days at month 3.
45 of 153 patients (29%) were classified as headache disability responders, achieving at least a 4-point reduction in HIT-6 score at month 3.
Across all 153 patients, the median monthly headache days fell by 5.0 days from baseline to month 3.
Across all 153 patients, the median monthly migraine days fell by 4.0 days from baseline to month 3.
32 patients (21%) achieved at least a 50% reduction in monthly headache days, and 3 patients (2%) became migraine-free with a 100% reduction in MHD at month 3.
Overall HIT-6 score decreased by a median of 4 points from baseline to month 3 across all patients.
The proportion of patients with medication overuse headache fell from 52% at baseline to 19% at month 3.
69 of 153 patients (45%) remained treatment responders and continued sTMS use at 12 months, corresponding to 74% of the month-3 responders.
In patients continuing treatment, the reduction in monthly headache days was sustained and remained significant compared to baseline at month 12.
In patients continuing treatment, the reduction in monthly migraine days increased further from month 3 to month 12 and remained significant versus baseline.
Number of headache-free days significantly increased from baseline to month 12 in patients continuing sTMS treatment.
Number of days using abortive treatment significantly decreased from baseline to month 12 in patients continuing sTMS.
Medication overuse headache prevalence continued to fall to 8% at month 12 among patients continuing sTMS.
The proportion of patients with severe headache-related disability decreased from 93% at baseline to 63% at both month 3 and month 12.
Treatment response (change in MHD) did not significantly differ between patients with migraine with aura and those with migraine without aura at month 3 or month 12.
Change in MHD from baseline did not significantly differ between chronic migraine and high-frequency episodic migraine patients at month 3 or month 12.
Treatment response did not significantly differ between patients who had previously failed BoNT/A and those who had not, at month 3 or month 12.
Treatment response did not significantly differ between patients with and without medication overuse headache at month 3 or month 12.
During the 3-month sTMS trial, 35 adverse events were reported by 15% (23/153) of patients, mostly mild or moderate and transient.
The most frequent adverse events with sTMS use were discomfort at the stimulation site (34%), worsening of headache (28%), and nausea (11%).

Treatment discontinuation due to adverse events was rare, with only one patient stopping sTMS due to scalp sensitivity, while six responders discontinued due to dissatisfaction rather than side effects.
In animal models, occipital sTMS has been shown to interfere with mechanically and chemically induced cortical spreading depression, considered the pathophysiological substrate of migraine aura.
Preclinical evidence suggests that sTMS modulation of cortical activity in animal models may occur through interaction with GABAergic circuits.
sTMS may modulate spontaneous and C-fibre evoked trigeminovascular activity of third order thalamic neurons, suggesting a mechanism for migraine pain modulation.
The paper notes that about 40% of chronic migraine patients treated with onabotulinumtoxinA do not achieve a satisfactory treatment response, based on cited literature.
Response rates for CGRP monoclonal antibodies in chronic migraine are reported to vary between 27% and 41% across cited studies.
Erenumab is cited as a potentially effective treatment for refractory chronic migraine, although long-term data were lacking at the time.
In properly phenotyped refractory chronic migraine patients, open-label studies of occipital nerve stimulation showed long-term beneficial response in about a third of patients.
Vagus nerve stimulation, another non-invasive neuromodulation approach, was shown to be ineffective in refractory migraine patients in cited literature.
An open-label extension of pivotal topiramate trials showed an 8.6% discontinuation rate among patients who had already received topiramate.
In a 5-year extension of a randomised trial of erenumab for episodic migraine prevention, 34% of 383 followed-up patients discontinued the drug.
In the current audit, only 16% of patients discontinued sTMS treatment, a comparatively low rate versus other preventive migraine treatments discussed.
Recent anti-CGRP monoclonal antibody trials reported placebo response rates ranging between 15% and 39%.

The 16% reduction in sTMS responders between month 3 and month 12 in this audit was similar in magnitude to the 14% placebo response reported in a refractory chronic migraine study, suggesting the long-term sTMS effect is unlikely to be explained by placebo alone.
A prior sham-controlled clinical trial found sTMS delivered over the occipital cortex superior to sham as an abortive treatment in migraine with aura patients.
Prior open-label evidence testing three-month sTMS efficacy in episodic migraine suggested that almost half of patients obtained at least a 50% reduction in headache days.

A company-sponsored UK post-market audit of sTMS in 449 predominantly chronic migraine patients showed good short-term tolerability and effectiveness, but analysis was conducted in only 190 of 449 patients (42%), warranting cautious interpretation.
In animal migraine models, occipital sTMS interferes with mechanically and chemically induced cortical spreading depression, considered the pathophysiological substrate of migraine aura.
Pre-clinical evidence suggests sTMS modulation of cortical activity in animal migraine models may occur through interaction with GABAergic circuits.
sTMS may modulate spontaneous and C-fibre evoked trigeminovascular activity of third order thalamic neurons, suggesting a mechanism for migraine pain modulation.
NLRP3 expression was significantly reduced in PBMCs of cluster headache patients, both during attacks and during headache-free periods.
IL-1β levels in PBMCs were higher during CH attacks compared with headache-free CH periods, though the difference did not reach statistical significance.
NF-κB levels in PBMCs were higher during CH attacks compared with headache-free CH periods, though not statistically significant.
NLRP1 levels were significantly lower in CH patients with three or more autonomic manifestations compared with those with fewer autonomic symptoms.
HMGB1 levels were significantly lower in CH patients with three or more autonomic manifestations.
Patients with three or more autonomic manifestations of cluster headache had significantly lower S100b levels than those with fewer autonomic features.
Neuron-specific enolase (NSE) levels were significantly lower in cluster headache patients with three or more autonomic manifestations compared to those with fewer.
Neuronal nitric oxide synthase (nNOS) levels were significantly lower in cluster headache patients with three or more autonomic manifestations compared to those with fewer.
Endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) levels were significantly lower in cluster headache patients with three or more autonomic manifestations compared to those with fewer.
No correlation was found between any of the measured inflammation-related factors and the clinical parameters of cluster headache.
10 mg of atogepant produced a significantly higher rate of ≥50% reduction in 12-week mean monthly migraine-days than placebo, with nearly 3-fold greater odds of response.
30 mg of atogepant produced a significantly higher rate of ≥50% reduction in 12-week mean monthly migraine-days than placebo, with 3.5-fold greater odds of response.
60 mg of atogepant produced a significantly higher rate of ≥50% reduction in 12-week mean monthly migraine-days than placebo, with 3.8-fold greater odds of response.
All atogepant doses significantly increased the proportion of participants achieving a ≥25% reduction in 12-week mean migraine-days compared with placebo.
All atogepant doses significantly increased the proportion of participants achieving a ≥75% reduction in 12-week mean migraine-days compared with placebo.
All atogepant doses significantly increased the proportion of participants achieving complete (100%) elimination of migraine-days over 12 weeks compared with placebo.
A prespecified sensitivity analysis excluding day-1 eDiary data confirmed the robustness of the 100% responder rate findings.
All atogepant doses showed higher ≥50% responder rates than placebo within each 4-week interval, with response rates increasing over the 12-week treatment period.
For the ≥25% responder threshold, 10 mg of atogepant did not significantly differ from placebo specifically during weeks 5 through 8, though all other dose/interval comparisons were significant.
All atogepant doses showed higher ≥75% responder rates than placebo within each 4-week interval, increasing progressively over the treatment course.
All atogepant doses showed higher 100% responder rates (complete migraine-day elimination) than placebo within each 4-week interval, increasing progressively over the treatment course.

A significantly greater proportion of atogepant-treated participants than placebo-treated participants reported feeling much better or very much better on the Patient Global Impression of Change scale at week 12.
A significantly greater proportion of atogepant-treated participants reported being satisfied or extremely satisfied with treatment at week 12 compared with placebo.
Overall treatment-emergent adverse event rates were similar across all atogepant dose groups and placebo, indicating no new safety signal.
Constipation was more frequently reported with atogepant than placebo, representing the most common treatment-emergent adverse effect.
Nausea was more frequently reported with atogepant than placebo, representing one of the most common treatment-emergent adverse effects.
Responder rates trended higher with increasing atogepant dose, although the study was not formally designed or powered to test dose-response.
Generalized joint hypermobility (Beighton score ≥5) was significantly more common among female than male ACL reconstruction patients.
Before ACL reconstruction, patients with generalized joint hypermobility had a lower knee extension limb symmetry index than patients without hypermobility.
Before ACL reconstruction, patients with generalized joint hypermobility had a lower knee flexion limb symmetry index than patients without hypermobility.
One year after ACL reconstruction, the primary outcome (KOOS sports and recreation function) did not differ between patients with and without generalized joint hypermobility.
No significant differences were found between GJH and non-GJH patients in the other KOOS subscales or postoperative physical activity level (Tegner Activity Scale) at 1 year.

At 1 year, hop test performance (vertical hop, single-leg hop for distance, side hop) did not differ between patients with and without GJH, and mean LSI exceeded the 90% acceptable threshold in both groups.
The preoperative knee flexion and extension strength deficits seen in GJH patients did not persist at 1-year postoperative follow-up.
Within 1 year, ACL re-injury occurred numerically more often in patients with GJH than without, but the difference was not statistically significant and the study was underpowered for this analysis.

Adjusted linear regression analysis (controlling for sex, age, and graft type) showed generalized joint hypermobility did not significantly influence any of the investigated patient-reported, functional, or strength outcomes.
At baseline, patients with and without GJH did not differ in age, weight, height, BMI, concomitant meniscus/cartilage injury, graft type, or preoperative KOOS and hop-test scores.
Chronic intermittent nitroglycerin administration significantly decreased basal cephalic mechanical thresholds relative to vehicle, producing cephalic allodynia in the chronic migraine model.
Chronic NTG treatment significantly increased the number of dendritic branch points in VPM neurons compared to vehicle.
Total neuronal length in the VPM was not significantly altered by chronic NTG treatment.
Sholl analysis showed no significant change in dendritic intersections in the VPM following chronic NTG.
Chronic NTG did not significantly alter branch points, total neuronal length, or Sholl complexity of central amygdala neurons.
Chronic NTG did not significantly alter branch points, total neuronal length, or Sholl complexity of caudate putamen neurons.
Repeated cortical spreading depression (CSD) events significantly decreased the number of dendritic branch points in vlPAG neurons compared to sham.
CSD also significantly decreased total neuronal length in the vlPAG compared to sham.
Sholl analysis showed no statistically significant change in dendritic intersections in the vlPAG following CSD, despite a numerical decrease.
CRPS (tibial fracture/casting model) significantly decreased the total number of dendritic branches in dorsal hippocampal neurons compared to uninjured controls.
CRPS significantly decreased total neuronal length in the dorsal hippocampus compared to controls.
Sholl analysis revealed significantly decreased dendritic intersections in the hippocampus following CRPS.
CRPS did not significantly change the number of branch points in PAG neurons, in contrast to the increases seen in other PAG morphology measures.
CRPS significantly increased total neuronal length in the PAG compared to control, contrasting with the decreased complexity seen after chronic NTG or CSD.
Sholl analysis revealed a significant increase in dendritic intersections in the PAG following CRPS, opposite to the direction seen in migraine models.
CRPS did not significantly alter branching, length, or Sholl complexity of pyramidal neurons in the somatosensory cortex, unlike the decreases seen there following chronic NTG or CSD.
Seven days of morphine treatment (hyperalgesic priming) significantly decreased hind paw withdrawal thresholds compared to saline-treated rats, indicating mechanical hypersensitivity.

Morphine-induced mechanical hypersensitivity resolved by day 21, with thresholds no longer significantly different from saline controls, demonstrating the transient/reversible nature of priming alone.

In morphine-primed rats whose hypersensitivity had resolved, repeated restraint stress on days 20 and 21 reinstated and progressively worsened mechanical hypersensitivity, modeling the stress-triggered transition from episodic to chronic functional pain.

Intra-CeA microdialysis of the KOR antagonist nor-BNI significantly increased paw withdrawal thresholds (reduced mechanical hypersensitivity) compared to vehicle in the functional pain model, restoring thresholds to pre-priming baseline.
After stress, intra-CeA nor-BNI significantly decreased duration of audible vocalizations evoked by noxious hindpaw compression, indicating reduced affective/aversive pain response.
Nor-BNI decreased ultrasonic vocalization duration but this effect did not reach statistical significance.

Nor-BNI had no significant effect on withdrawal thresholds evoked by tonic hindpaw compression (paw pressure test), in contrast to its effect on dynamic von Frey mechanosensitivity, suggesting selective action on averse-affective rather than tonic sensory pain.
Intra-CeA nor-BNI decreased anxiety-like behavior in the elevated plus maze, increasing both time spent and entries into the open arms, without affecting locomotor activity.

Intra-CeA nor-BNI decreased both background firing activity and stimulus-evoked (innocuous and noxious) responses of CeA multireceptive neurons recorded extracellularly in vivo in the functional pain model.

In brain slices from the functional pain model, nor-BNI application decreased the excitability (frequency-current relationship) of genetically identified CeA-CRF neurons, without altering resting membrane potential.

Nor-BNI did not affect optically or electrically evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) in CeA-CRF neurons driven by parabrachial glutamatergic input, indicating KOR blockade does not act on excitatory transmission.

Nor-BNI significantly increased parabrachial-evoked feedforward inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) in CeA-CRF neurons, restoring synaptic inhibition that is impaired in the functional pain model.
Nor-BNI increased the frequency, but not amplitude, of spontaneous IPSCs in CeA-CRF neurons, suggesting a presynaptic site of action for KOR-mediated disinhibition in the functional pain model.

The study concludes that inhibitory (GABAergic feedforward) control of CeA-CRF neurons is impaired in the functional pain syndrome model, and that endogenous KOR activation in the amygdala drives this disinhibition to produce pain-like and aversive-affective behaviors.
The modified composite estrogen score (mCES), reflecting cumulative endogenous/exogenous estrogen exposure, was not significantly associated with risk of Sjögren's disease after adjustment.
Use of estrogen replacement therapy was associated with an increased risk of developing Sjögren's disease.
A history of polycystic ovarian syndrome was associated with increased risk of Sjögren's disease.
Hysterectomy without bilateral oophorectomy was associated with increased risk of Sjögren's disease.
Fibromyalgia preceding diagnosis was the strongest comorbid predictor of subsequently developing Sjögren's disease.
Osteoporosis preceding diagnosis was associated with increased risk of developing Sjögren's disease in a predictive model.
Use of hormone replacement therapy (HRT) was associated with increased risk of developing Sjögren's disease in the predictive model.
Prior diabetes was associated with a decreased risk of developing Sjögren's disease, suggesting a possible protective effect.
Higher body mass index (BMI) was associated with a slightly decreased risk of developing Sjögren's disease per unit increase.
Lymphoma was identified as a comorbidity preceding Sjögren's disease diagnosis and associated with increased risk.
Pulmonary disease was identified as a comorbidity preceding Sjögren's disease diagnosis.
The authors developed a multivariable predictive model for Sjögren's disease risk incorporating fibromyalgia, osteoporosis, hormone replacement therapy, diabetes, and body mass index.
In the predictive model, prior fibromyalgia was associated with a 2.50-fold increased risk ratio for later Sjögren's disease diagnosis.
In the predictive model, prior osteoporosis was associated with an 84% increased risk ratio for later Sjögren's disease diagnosis.
In the predictive model, hormone replacement therapy use was associated with a 61% increased risk ratio for later Sjögren's disease diagnosis.
In the predictive model, prior diabetes was associated with a substantially reduced risk ratio for later Sjögren's disease diagnosis, suggesting a possible protective effect.
Across 14 studies and 465 patients, cardioneuroablation was associated with an overall freedom from syncope rate of 91.9%.
Ablation restricted to the right atrium produced a significantly lower freedom from syncope than left atrial-only or biatrial ablation.

The technique used to localize ganglionated plexi (fractionated electrogram mapping, spectral method, high-frequency stimulation, anatomic, or combined) did not significantly affect freedom from syncope after cardioneuroablation.
Adolescents with generalised joint hypermobility (GJH) showed a greater risk of temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disc displacement on MRI compared with adolescents without GJH.
The association between GJH and TMJ disc displacement was particularly pronounced for disc displacement without reduction, a more severe TMD phenotype.
The KIT D816V somatic mutation is present in approximately 95% of patients with advanced systemic mastocytosis.
Additional somatic mutations in SRSF2, ASXL1, and RUNX1 occur in 60% to 70% of patients with advanced systemic mastocytosis.
60% to 80% of patients with advanced systemic mastocytosis have multilineage involvement including an associated hematologic neoplasm.
Serum tryptase levels are elevated in patients with advanced systemic mastocytosis as a consequence of mast cell burden.
Midostaurin, a multikinase/KIT inhibitor, has changed the treatment landscape for advanced systemic mastocytosis.
Avapritinib, a selective KIT D816V inhibitor, has changed the treatment landscape for advanced systemic mastocytosis.

The authors propose refined ECNM-AIM response criteria using a tiered approach combining histopathologic (bone marrow mast cell burden, tryptase), molecular (KIT D816V variant allele frequency), clinical (C-findings), and symptom response measures to better capture clinical benefit and long-term outcomes in advanced systemic mastocytosis.
Activating point mutations in the KIT gene are one of the WHO minor diagnostic criteria for systemic mastocytosis that can be assessed by the pathologist.
Aberrant expression of CD25, and/or CD2, and/or CD30 on mast cells is a WHO minor diagnostic criterion for systemic mastocytosis.

The morphologic hallmark of systemic mastocytosis is the accumulation of spindle-shaped, hypogranulated mast cells forming compact aggregates in bone marrow and other extracutaneous tissues, which constitutes the WHO major diagnostic criterion.

Final subclassification of systemic mastocytosis into bone marrow mastocytosis, indolent SM, smoldering SM, aggressive SM, SM with an associated hematologic neoplasm, or mast cell leukemia carries prognostic significance and requires integrating morphologic, clinical, radiologic, and biochemical B- and C-findings.

Cutaneous, gastrointestinal, and neurological complaints, musculoskeletal pain, skin lesions, anaphylaxis, and osteoporosis are the main mast cell mediator-related symptoms and signs affecting quality of life in indolent systemic mastocytosis.
Serum tryptase is recommended as a secondary outcome parameter that indirectly reflects mast cell burden but does not correlate with the severity of signs, symptoms, or quality-of-life impairment.
KIT D816V allele burden is recommended as a secondary outcome parameter that indirectly reflects mast cell burden but does not correlate with symptom severity or quality-of-life impairment.

The consortium proposes categorical treatment response thresholds based on percent change from baseline in patient-reported outcome measures: complete response >90%, major response 60-90%, partial response 30-60%, and no response <30%.

The consortium recommends using validated mastocytosis-specific patient-reported outcome measures as the primary outcome parameters to define treatment response in indolent systemic mastocytosis, in both clinical trials and everyday practice.
This case report describes central nervous system involvement of multiple myeloma presenting as SUNCT-type headache, a clinical presentation not previously reported in the literature.

In central nervous system involvement of multiple myeloma, reported symptom frequencies are visual changes in 36%, radiculopathy in 27%, headache in 25%, confusion in 21%, dizziness in 7%, and seizures in 6% of cases.
Secondary SUNCT, caused by an identifiable underlying pathology rather than occurring as a primary headache disorder, has been sparsely described, with fewer than 60 cases reported in the literature.
Risk factors suggesting a secondary etiology for SUNCT-like headache, as illustrated by this case, include new-onset autonomic features, older age, and a history of malignancy.
In a Norwegian population study, the one-year prevalence of secondary headaches was 2.14%, and in 80% of these cases the cause could be diagnosed from the patient's history alone.

In a UK tertiary headache service using red-flag screening of 3655 consecutive patients over five years, 14.5% underwent imaging and only 11 patients (2.1% of those scanned, 0.3% of the whole clinic population) had a significant imaging finding.
Medication-overuse headache may occur in more than 70% of patients with chronic daily headache.

Patients who use opioid or triptan analgesia for more than 10 days/month, or simple analgesia for more than 15 days/month, are at risk of increased neuronal hyperexcitability and peripheral/central sensitisation that potentiates their headaches.

Incidental findings on brain MRI occur in about 2% of the general population, including neoplasia (0.7%), aneurysm (0.35%), arachnoid cysts (0.5%), Chiari I malformations (0.24%) and demyelination (0.06%).
In population studies, women with migraine have an increased risk of white matter lesions on brain MRI compared with women without migraine.
Women with migraine show a higher prevalence of hyperintense lesions in the brainstem compared with women without migraine (4.4% vs 0.7%).
White matter and brainstem lesions seen on MRI in migraine patients are not believed to be associated with cognitive changes, although the clinical significance remains an area of ongoing research.

In a study of patients ultimately diagnosed with primary or metastatic brain tumours, 77% had presented with a headache phenotype resembling tension-type headache, illustrating that a benign-appearing phenotype should not provide false reassurance in the presence of red flags.

Among 376 patients with cluster headache, the rate of pituitary adenomas was similar to that in the general population, supporting that dedicated pituitary MRI is only needed when suggestive symptoms are present.
Non-contrast CT performed within six hours of thunderclap headache onset has a sensitivity of 98.7% for detecting subarachnoid haemorrhage, but this sensitivity drops considerably after six hours.

In the derivation sample, one or more daytime ambulatory SBP drops below 90 mmHg were significantly more frequent in reflex syncope patients than in matched controls, with 91% specificity and 32% sensitivity.
Two or more daytime SBP drops below 100 mmHg were more common in reflex syncope patients than controls in the derivation sample, achieving 84% specificity and 40% sensitivity.

Night-time SBP drops below 90 and 100 mmHg were significantly more frequent in syncope patients than controls, but had lower diagnostic yield than daytime drops and were excluded from subsequent diagnostic analyses.
In an independent validation sample, one or more daytime SBP drops below 90 mmHg again identified reflex syncope patients with high specificity, confirming the derivation sample findings.
In the validation sample, two or more daytime SBP drops below 100 mmHg identified syncope patients with 83% specificity and 35% sensitivity, replicating derivation sample results.

The specificity of daytime SBP drops below 90 mmHg for diagnosing hypotensive susceptibility exceeded 90% only in patients whose average 24-hour SBP was 125 mmHg or higher, decreasing in patients with lower baseline SBP.

In the validation subgroup with average 24-hour SBP below 125 mmHg, requiring two or more daytime SBP drops below 90 mmHg achieved 100% specificity for reflex syncope, at the cost of lower sensitivity.

Eleven syncope patients with normal office BP were found on ABPM to have constitutional hypotension (low 24-hour average SBP), and were excluded from the main analysis, illustrating that ABPM can uncover a hypotensive predisposition missed by office BP measurement.

The authors cite a prior study reporting that reflex syncope is associated with a distinct hemodynamic profile of lower systolic BP, higher diastolic BP, and higher heart rate compared with the general population.
Over a 6-year period, 10.4% of elective pediatric referrals to the practice were related to functional somatic symptoms (FSS).
The incidence of pediatric FSS referrals did not show a significant upward trend over the 6-year study period, contrary to prior suggestions that FSS incidence is increasing.
Referrals for pediatric FSS showed clear seasonal variation, peaking in March and November and reaching a nadir around August.
The overall prevalence of generalized joint hypermobility (Beighton score ≥4/9) among Thai physical therapy students was 21.18%, with 20.00% in females and 1.18% in males.
The elbow joint showed the highest frequency of hypermobility among all Beighton score joints assessed in both GJH and non-GJH groups.
Non-dominant leg resting quadriceps angle (QArelax) was significantly higher in the GJH group compared with the non-GJH group.

The between-group difference in quadriceps angle seen at rest disappeared when measured during quadriceps muscle contraction (QAcon), suggesting GJH affects musculotendinous tone rather than bony alignment.
There was no significant difference in the rate of lower limb joint pain/injury within the past year between GJH and non-GJH groups at any joint.
In multivariable logistic regression, age was not significantly associated with lower limb joint pain/injury in the GJH group.
In multivariable logistic regression, navicular drop of the dominant leg was not significantly associated with lower limb joint pain/injury in the GJH group.
No difference in tibiofemoral angle was found between GJH and non-GJH groups in either quadriceps contraction state, indicating GJH did not alter bony frontal-plane knee alignment.
The ankle and foot were the joints most commonly reported with pain/injury in the past year for both GJH and non-GJH groups.
Among 83 adult patients managed by an integrated specialty pharmacy team, 72% (60 patients) remained persistent on droxidopa therapy over the study period.
Patients managed by the integrated specialty pharmacy showed high medication adherence to droxidopa, with a median proportion of days covered of 0.98.
Over 36 months, specialty pharmacists performed 60 interventions after droxidopa initiation, most involving dose changes, drug-drug interaction management, and medication reconciliation.
In migraine patients, NRS pain scores were significantly reduced from preoperative levels at every postoperative timepoint from 1 day to 24 months after CT-guided SPG RFTA.
In cluster headache patients, NRS pain scores were significantly reduced from preoperative levels at every postoperative timepoint from 1 day to 24 months after CT-guided SPG RFTA.

At 24 months post-surgery, NRS scores differed significantly between the migraine and CH groups, with CH showing greater long-term improvement, whereas no significant difference was seen at earlier timepoints.
The effective rate of SPG RFTA for migraine declined progressively from 100% at 1 day to 71.42% at 24 months post-surgery.
The effective rate of SPG RFTA for cluster headache remained high (90-100%) across all follow-up timepoints up to 24 months.
The difference in effective rate between migraine and CH groups became statistically significant at 24 months, with CH showing a higher effective rate than migraine.
In migraine patients, facial numbness incidence following SPG RFTA declined from 100% at 1 day to 7.14% at 24 months.
In cluster headache patients, facial numbness incidence following SPG RFTA declined from 100% at 1 day to 0% at 24 months.
The rate of facial numbness did not significantly differ between migraine and cluster headache patients at any postoperative timepoint.
In migraine patients, the frequency of headache attacks per 90 days was significantly reduced after SPG RFTA compared with before treatment.
The duration of individual headache attacks in migraine patients did not significantly change after SPG RFTA compared with before treatment.
After SPG RFTA, cluster headache patients showed a significant decrease in duration of the remission phase and a significant increase in duration of the cluster phase compared with before treatment.
In migraine patients, combined pain frequency and intensity scores on the modified 2D-VAS improved from a range of 2-6 before RFTC treatment to 1-2 after treatment.

The sphenopalatine ganglion, located in the pterygopalatine fossa and containing parasympathetic, sympathetic, and trigeminal sensory fibers, is proposed to play a key role in the pathophysiology of migraine, cluster headache, and trigeminal autonomic headache.
CT-guided RFTA of the SPG caused facial numbness as an adverse effect in most patients that was generally reversible and considered an acceptable trade-off given the pain relief achieved.
The author proposes that migraine nociception occurs within a perivascular unit composed of endothelial cells, vascular smooth muscle cells, perivascular nerve fibers, and mast cells.

The author states that migraine attacks may originate peripherally via humoral or neurogenic release of nociceptive substances around blood vessels, or centrally via brain-generated efferent activity in autonomic and somatic nerves.
POTS patients showed higher somatic vigilance than matched controls.
POTS patients reported significantly more anxiety than matched controls.
Patients exhibited a more pronounced anticipatory tachycardia just before standing on tilt-table testing, interpreted as a physiological marker of fear conditioning to orthostasis.
While standing, POTS patients had a faster heart rate than controls.
Plasma catecholamine levels were higher in POTS patients than controls while standing.
End-tidal CO2 was lower in POTS patients than controls while standing, consistent with hyperventilation.
Patients with postural tachycardia syndrome had reduced middle cerebral artery blood flow velocity while standing compared to controls.
Multi-linear logistic regression showed that epinephrine secretion predicted the magnitude of tachycardia and hyperventilation upon standing in POTS patients.
Excessive somatic vigilance predicted the magnitude of tachycardia and hyperventilation on standing in POTS patients, alongside epinephrine secretion.

The authors propose that POTS is a functional disorder in which standing acquires a frightful quality, such that a fear-conditioned response is elicited even when standing occurs alone, and heightened somatic anxiety may predispose to this fear-conditioned hyperadrenergic state.
KCl-induced cortical spreading depression significantly inhibited dural-evoked firing in a subset of trigeminocervical complex neurons, reaching a maximum reduction to 65% of baseline at 15 minutes.
In the majority of neurons (21 of 30), dural-evoked responses did not change significantly over 90 minutes after KCl-induced CSD compared with baseline.
Spontaneous background firing in the TCC was not significantly altered by CSD in either the unaffected or inhibited neuron groups.
The selective 5-HT1B/1D receptor antagonist GR127935 significantly reversed the CSD-induced inhibition of dural-evoked TCC neuronal firing.
The non-selective opioid receptor antagonist naloxone significantly reversed the CSD-induced inhibition of dural-evoked TCC neuronal firing, with effect apparent 20 minutes after injection.
Intravenous vehicle injection had no effect on either spontaneous or dural-evoked TCC neuronal firing, confirming the specificity of drug effects.

Microinjection of the sodium channel blocker lidocaine into the nucleus raphe magnus (NRM) did not reverse CSD-induced inhibition of TCC neuronal firing, indicating the NRM is not required for this effect.
Microinjection of the GABAA receptor agonist muscimol into the nucleus raphe magnus (NRM) did not reverse CSD-induced inhibition of TCC neuronal firing.
Among inhibited neurons, animals treated with naloxone showed a greater number of CSD events than the control group.
The number of KCl-induced CSD events over 90 minutes did not differ significantly between the group of neurons unaffected by CSD and the group whose firing was inhibited.
Among the 35 reviewed pediatric paroxysmal hemicrania (PH) cases, boys were slightly more affected than girls.
Onset of pediatric PH occurred across a broad age range with a mean onset age of 6.5 years.
There was a lag between symptom onset and diagnosis, with a mean diagnosis age of 8.2 years compared to a mean onset age of 6.5 years.
Left-sided head pain occurred twice as frequently as right-sided pain among pediatric PH cases.
Nearly all pediatric PH cases were accompanied by ipsilateral cranial autonomic features during attacks.
Physical examination, EEG, and brain MRI were normal in pediatric paroxysmal hemicrania cases.
Some pediatric PH patients required combination therapy of indomethacin with other medications to achieve response.
Concomitant migrainous features in pediatric paroxysmal hemicrania can cause diagnostic confusion with migraine.
While most paroxysmal hemicrania attacks in children occurred spontaneously, some common triggers were identified.
Orthostatic hypotension is defined by an unusually large drop in blood pressure upon standing, which raises the risk of adverse outcomes even in patients without symptoms.

Continuous blood pressure monitoring has revealed four major subtypes of orthostatic hypotension: initial orthostatic hypotension, delayed blood pressure recovery, classic orthostatic hypotension, and delayed orthostatic hypotension.
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension may represent the earliest clinical manifestation of Parkinson's disease or related synucleinopathies.
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension often co-occurs with supine hypertension.

Management of orthostatic hypotension is recommended to be stepwise and individualised, favouring non-pharmacological measures such as stopping blood-pressure-lowering drugs and using counterpressure manoeuvres before pharmacological treatment.
Chronic use of toothpaste containing pro-convulsant essential oils was associated with new-onset or worsening cluster headache in five patients.
Discontinuing the causative essential-oil-containing toothpaste led to complete resolution of cluster headache attacks within 5 to 10 days in all five patients.
Re-challenge with the same toothpaste in one patient led to recurrence of a cluster headache attack after two months, supporting a causal relationship.
None of the five patients experienced recurrence of cluster headache attacks during follow-up of 1 to 2 years after discontinuing the essential-oil-containing toothpaste.
At 2 years of follow-up, mean total cost per participant was significantly lower in the empiric pacemaker (PM) arm than the implantable cardiac monitor (ICM) arm.
There was no statistically significant difference in QALYs gained between participants randomized to pacemaker insertion versus implantable cardiac monitor at 2 years.
In the 3-year decision-analytic model, empiric pacemaker insertion dominated (lower cost and higher QALYs than) the implantable cardiac monitor strategy.
A large majority of participants randomized to the ICM arm ultimately crossed over to receive a pacemaker due to documented bradycardia.
Bootstrapped resampling confirmed pacemaker insertion was almost always less costly than implantable cardiac monitor insertion and yielded more QALYs in the majority of replicates.

Probabilistic sensitivity analysis of 40,000 iterations showed the pacemaker strategy was cost-saving and either more or less effective than the ICM strategy in the vast majority of iterations, with ICM cost-saving in only a tiny fraction.

The pacemaker strategy was found to be cost-effective relative to the implantable cardiac monitor strategy at a willingness-to-pay threshold of $50,000 per QALY in the large majority of simulation iterations.

Empiric pacemaker insertion was clinically superior to implantable cardiac monitor use, with a much higher proportion of participants remaining free of the composite clinical outcome (death, syncope, bradycardia, device complications) over 2 years.

In a scenario analysis assuming more intensive cardiologist-led follow-up for pacemaker patients, both strategies' costs increased, but the pacemaker strategy remained less costly than the implantable cardiac monitor strategy.

The baseline per-participant device insertion cost was substantially lower for implantable cardiac monitor than for pacemaker, though this was offset by later pacemaker crossover costs in the ICM arm.
In a cohort of 15 migraine patients followed for 20 weeks, migraine onset occurred 3.3 times more frequently between 06:00 and 12:00 than during other 6-hour periods.
In a large study of 1698 patients experiencing 3582 migraine attacks, 48% of attacks occurred between 04:00 and 09:00.
In a prospective cohort of 58 female migraine patients recording 2314 attacks over 12 months, pain intensity peaked around 13:40 with a peak-to-trough ratio of 25.6.
In 115 pediatric migraine patients aged 5-18 years, pain showed a bimodal pattern with a peak in the afternoon (16:48) and a second peak in the early morning (06:35).
A large cohort of 786 migraine patients found attack frequency was higher throughout the day with peaks at 10:00 and 22:00, and lower frequency at night (03:00).

A cohort of 100 migraine patients found that 42% experienced more than 75% of their attacks at night or in the early morning (3:00-7:00), contrasting with the predominantly morning pattern seen in other cohorts.
A recent RCT of 61 migraine patients found no significant difference in mean pain levels between morning and afternoon.

In a cohort of 82 migraine patients, migrainous headache characteristics occurred most frequently between 06:00 and 12:00 and least frequently between 18:00 and 06:00, with the same pattern observed for all headache types.
In a very large cross-sectional study of 2389 patients, migraine attacks most often began between 04:00-06:00 (15.4% of attacks) or 06:00-08:00 (11.8% of attacks).
In a crossover trial of 85 patients with diabetic neuropathy (DN) or postherpetic neuralgia (PHN), pain worsened from 08:00 to 20:00 in the majority of patients (34/55 DN, 26/30 PHN).
The diurnal worsening of neuropathic pain (DN/PHN) throughout the day was maintained even when patients were treated with analgesics such as gabapentin and morphine.

In a separate crossover trial of 56 patients with DN or PHN treated with gabapentin, nortriptyline, or their combination, pain scores increased throughout the day both at baseline and during drug treatment.
