Pooled analysis of baseline data from two neuropathic pain crossover trials found that diurnal variation in pain was more prominent in females than males and more prominent in diabetic neuropathy than postherpetic neuralgia.

In 21 female fibromyalgia patients, those with low dolorimetry scores (<2.25 kg) showed a diurnal pain pattern with maximum pain in the morning, while patients with high dolorimetry scores (>2.25 kg) showed no diurnal variation.

Fibromyalgia patients secreted a greater proportion of their daily urinary melatonin metabolite (aMT6s) during daytime hours compared to healthy controls, indicating disrupted circadian melatonin secretion.

In fibromyalgia patients, higher nighttime aMT6s secretion correlated with lower depressive symptoms, while higher daytime aMT6s secretion correlated with more tender/trigger points and poorer sleep quality.

In fibromyalgia patients, a negative correlation was found between pain pressure threshold and daytime aMT6s levels, while a positive correlation was found between tender point count and daytime aMT6s levels.

In 21 patients with hand osteoarthritis who recorded pain six times daily for 10 days, a significant circadian rhythm in pain severity was identified, with the lowest pain point occurring at or after 16:10.
In 241 patients with knee osteoarthritis, pain intensity was significantly lower in the early afternoon compared with early and late morning testing sessions.
In 157 patients with hand, hip, or knee osteoarthritis, pain severity was increased during the morning and early afternoon and declined during the evening.

In a double-blind crossover trial of 66 patients with hip or knee osteoarthritis, about half showed a unimodal circadian pain profile with a single peak at varying times of day, 23 showed a bimodal profile with morning and evening peaks, and 4 showed little diurnal variation.

Cortisol is proposed to play an anti-inflammatory role in rheumatoid arthritis by reducing proinflammatory cytokine levels, while melatonin is proposed to play a proinflammatory role by inhibiting matrix metalloproteinase-9, an enzyme protecting against joint damage.
Rheumatoid arthritis patients had significantly increased melatonin levels at midnight compared to healthy subjects.
Melatonin-treated subjects showed an increase in inflammatory indicators compared to placebo-treated subjects.

Rheumatoid arthritis increased circadian rhythmicity through chronic inflammation, altering expression/pathways of peripheral blood mononuclear leukocyte genes, phospho-STAT3/ATF2 signaling, and hepatic ceramide synthases, with 104 genes differentially expressed morning-to-evening in RA subjects compared to 25 in healthy controls.
In a collagen-induced arthritis mouse model, the rhythmic gene expression trends seen in human RA subjects were consistent across most cases of inflammatory arthritis.

In a 4-period crossover trial, 34 of 55 patients with diabetic neuropathy and 26 of 30 with postherpetic neuralgia showed a temporal pattern of pain worsening throughout the day from 08:00 to 20:00, which persisted even when patients were on analgesic treatment.

In a separate 3-period crossover trial of 56 patients with diabetic neuropathy or postherpetic neuralgia, pain scores increased throughout the day both during pretrial baseline and during treatment with gabapentin, nortriptyline, or their combination.
In seven patients with idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia on carbamazepine, the frequency of pain attacks was lowest during night hours (23:00–5:00) and highest during the morning (8:00–11:00).
In a cohort of 15 migraine patients followed over 20 weeks (211 migraines documented), the incidence of migraine onset from 06:00 to 12:00 was 3.3 times greater than during other 6-hour periods.
In a large study of 1698 patients with 3582 migraine attacks, 48% of attacks occurred from 04:00 to 09:00, significantly more frequent than the rate during the remaining hours.
In 58 female patients who prospectively recorded 2314 migraine attacks over 12 months, pain peaked around 13:40 with a peak-to-low ratio of 25.6.
In 115 pediatric migraine patients aged 5-18 years, pain showed a peak in the afternoon (16:48) and a secondary peak in the early morning (06:35).
In a large cohort of 786 migraine patients, attack frequency was higher throughout the day with peaks at 10:00 and 22:00, and less frequent at night (03:00).
In a cohort of 100 migraine patients, 42% experienced more than 75% of their attacks at night and in the early morning hours (3:00-7:00).
A more recent RCT of 61 migraine patients found no significant difference in mean pain levels between morning and afternoon.

In a cohort of 82 migraine patients, migrainous headache characteristics presented most frequently at 06:00-12:00 and least frequently at 18:00-00:00 and 00:00-06:00, a pattern also seen for all headache types combined.
In a large cross-sectional study of 2389 patients, migraine attacks most often began between 04:00-06:00 (15.4% of attacks) or 06:00-08:00 (11.8% of attacks).
In 31 patients assessed via computerized ecological momentary assessment, tension headache intensity was significantly lower in the morning and peaked in the late afternoon (16:00).
In a study of 1134 cluster headache patients, 58% had attacks between 19:00 and 07:00, with a peak between 24:00 and 03:00, and 41% of responders showing a peak at 02:00.
In a cross-sectional study of 147 episodic and chronic cluster headache patients and controls, attacks occurred most often between 00:00-4:00 and least often between 12:00-16:00.

In a multicenter study of 175 cluster headache patients, the circadian pattern of attacks changed with disease progression: nighttime attacks predominated early in the disease course, while daytime attacks increased with progression and decreased in the most advanced disease.

In a cohort of 475 patients (421 episodic, 54 chronic cluster headache), the most commonly reported attack interval was nighttime (2:00-4:00), and the lowest rates occurred at 10:00-14:00; a third of patients reported no rhythmicity.
In 123 cancer patients on chronic opioid therapy, breakthrough pain peaked at 10:00, with distinct acrophases for bony metastases (9:45) versus visceral metastases (10:30).

In 92 hospice/home-care cancer patients with limited life expectancy, cosinor analysis showed a breakthrough pain acrophase of 12:30 overall, with differences by metastasis site and ECOG performance status.

In 104 cancer patients, the circadian pattern of breakthrough analgesia need differed by delirium status: patients without delirium required more analgesia in the morning, while patients with delirium required more in the evening and at night.

In a randomized double-blind crossover trial of 42 advanced cancer patients, sustained-release morphine sulfate dosed in the morning versus evening showed no statistically significant difference in pain scores.
A 1976 study of 41 patients with intractable cancer pain reported that pain intensity increased linearly throughout the day, reaching maximum at 22:00.

Pooled analysis of baseline data from two crossover trials found that the degree of diurnal variation in neuropathic pain intensity was significantly greater in female patients than male patients, and greater in diabetic neuropathy than postherpetic neuralgia.
In mice, whole-brain metenkephalin levels followed a circadian rhythm, being twice as high at the end of the resting phase compared to the beginning of the resting phase.
In rats, beta-endorphin levels in the pituitary gland, pons, medulla, and cerebellum showed circadian variation, peaking at the beginning of the activity phase.

In a murine tibia fracture model, NSAIDs were most effective for postoperative pain, healing, and recovery when administered during the active circadian phase, and clock genes Per2, Nr1d1, and Nr1d2 were upregulated in mice receiving NSAIDs during the active phase compared to the resting phase.
In seven male volunteers, plasma endogenous opioid levels showed a circadian rhythm, with a peak in the morning and a nadir in the late evening.
In six healthy adult volunteers, plasma beta-endorphin levels showed a circadian pattern with a peak in the morning and a trough in the evening.
In 17 neonates, blood beta-endorphin levels were significantly higher in the morning than in the afternoon.
In rats, opiate receptor binding in the forebrain showed circadian variation, with a peak during the activity period and a trough overnight.

In a mouse sciatic nerve ligation neuropathic pain model, the circadian rhythm of thermal withdrawal latency was reversed compared to sham-operated mice, and this shift correlated with altered mu-opioid receptor mRNA expression in the periaqueductal gray matter.

RNA sequencing in mice with chronic morphine exposure showed that circadian rhythm gene networks were enriched among genes overexpressed in mice with opioid-induced hyperalgesia relative to control mice.
In rats, substance P levels in the substantia nigra and central gray matter showed a circadian rhythm, peaking between 20:00 and 04:00.
The Tac1 gene, which encodes substance P, was found to oscillate under transcriptional regulation by CLOCK genes, affecting the persistence and period of circadian rhythms in pain-related signaling.

In a mouse formalin pain model, blocking melatonin receptors with luzindole abolished the normally heightened dark-phase pain-related behavior seen with saline pretreatment, and pinealectomy reduced nocturnal tonic nociceptive responses, indicating a proalgesic role for endogenous melatonin in tonic pain.

In mice with sciatic nerve ligation-induced neuropathic pain, hypothalamic melatonin receptor mRNA expression was altered, and these mice showed thermal hyperalgesia with increased wakefulness and decreased NREM sleep at night compared to sham-operated mice.

In a post-marketing surveillance study of 61 patients with chronic tension headaches, 30 days of melatonin supplementation was associated with a significant decrease in the number of headaches per month and in VAS pain intensity.
Concomitant fibromyalgia diagnosis was about eight times more common in females than males among patients with rheumatoid arthritis.
Fibromyalgia comorbidity prevalence ranged from 3% in male SLE patients to 15% in female PsA patients, varying by sex and rheumatic disease.
IBS diagnosis in rheumatic disease patients ranged from 7% (SLE) to 16% (SSc) and was more common in females, with male-to-female ratios varying from 1.4 to about 5.
Urologic chronic pelvic pain syndrome diagnosis prevalence (about 1-2%) did not appear to differ by sex across rheumatic diseases.
Migraine diagnosis was present in 11-20% of patients with rheumatic diseases and was substantially higher in females (>20% in PsA, SjS, SLE) than males (6-7%).
Chronic tension-type headache diagnosis prevalence (2-3%) showed no apparent sex differences among patients with rheumatic diseases.
Chronic low back pain was the most common COPC comorbidity in rheumatic diseases, ranging from 13% in SSc to 40% in RA and SjS, with sex patterns differing by disease (higher in males with PsA).
CFS diagnosis ranged from 4% in SSc to 12% in SLE and SjS, with a male-to-female ratio between 1.5 and 2, indicating relatively higher male prevalence compared with other COPCs.
Endometriosis diagnosis was found in 2-4% of female patients with rheumatic diseases, with a notable burden in Sjögren syndrome.
Vulvodynia and temporomandibular disorder diagnoses were rare (0.2-1%) but present among patients with rheumatic diseases.
Black patients with rheumatic diseases had the highest prevalence of one or more COPCs (52-66%), while Asian patients had the lowest (26-49%).
Patients with public insurance had a higher prevalence of one or more COPCs than those with private insurance, exemplified by 66% vs 58% in Sjögren syndrome.
Divorced/separated patients had the highest prevalence of one or more COPC diagnoses across rheumatic diseases.
Former smokers had the highest prevalence of one or more COPC diagnoses among patients with rheumatic diseases.
Patients with one or more COPCs were older at first recorded rheumatic disease visit and had higher current BMI than those without COPCs.
Receipt of specialty pain clinic care was higher among patients with one or more COPCs, ranging from 18% in RA to 29% in SSc, yet the majority of patients with COPCs did not receive such care.

Depression and anxiety diagnoses were more prevalent among patients with one or more COPCs, with depression prevalence ranging from 30% (RA) to 41% (SSc) and a prevalence ratio of 2 to 4 compared with patients without COPCs.
Patients with SSc and one or more COPCs were four times as likely to have a concomitant substance use disorder diagnosis compared with those without COPCs (12% vs 3%).
Patients with one or more COPCs had two to three times more emergency department visits and twice as many surgeries and hospitalizations on average than those without COPCs.

Using a stricter case definition (≥2 diagnoses at least 30 days apart) reduced the estimated prevalence of chronic low back pain, e.g., from 30% to 18% in PsA and from 27% to 15% in SLE, though associations with sex, race, and health care use patterns remained consistent.
More than half of patients with RA, SjS, and SLE had a concomitant COPC diagnosis, with SjS having the highest overall COPC prevalence (62%), followed by PsA (44%) and SSc (36%).
The observed fibromyalgia prevalence in RA and PsA (9-11%) was lower than a prior meta-analysis's pooled estimate (18-24% in RA, 18% in PsA), a discrepancy the authors could not fully explain.

In vasovagal syncope patients, older age was independently associated with lower cerebral tissue oxygenation (SctO2) during the presyncopal phase, after adjusting for concurrent systolic blood pressure and sex.
The decrease in SctO2 from supine to presyncopal phase (delta presyncope) was not significantly associated with age in vasovagal syncope patients after adjustment for sex and concurrent SBP.
In orthostatic hypotension patients, increasing age was associated with lower SctO2 in the supine position, after 3 and 10 minutes of tilt, during the presyncopal phase, and at minimum SctO2.

After adjusting for sex and concurrent SBP, the decrease in SctO2 from supine to presyncopal phase (delta SctO2 presyncope) showed only a borderline non-significant association with age in orthostatic hypotension patients.
Among patients with a negative head-up-tilt test, supine SctO2 was inversely associated with age.
Apart from the supine timepoint, no other associations between SctO2 and age were found among patients with a negative head-up-tilt test.
When vasovagal syncope patients were divided into age groups (<30, 30-60, >60 years), presyncopal SctO2 was significantly lower in older patients.
The decrease in SctO2 from supine to presyncopal phase (delta presyncope) was significantly greater in older vasovagal syncope patients compared with younger patients.
Mean systolic blood pressure during the presyncopal phase did not differ across age groups in vasovagal syncope patients, in contrast to SctO2.
Among orthostatic hypotension patients divided by age group, SctO2 was significantly lower in older subjects after 10 minutes of head-up tilt, during the presyncopal phase, and at minimum SctO2.
Systolic blood pressure during the presyncopal phase did not differ according to age among orthostatic hypotension patients, despite SctO2 differing by age.
There was no significant difference in supine cerebral tissue oxygenation levels between smokers and non-smokers, suggesting smoking status did not substantially confound the age-related findings.

An earlier, smaller SYSTEMA-cohort study (n=54, combining VVS, OH and negative HUT patients) found no effect of age on baseline SctO2 or on the change in SctO2 during tilt, contrasting with the current larger study, which found significant age effects when the groups were analyzed separately.
Clinically relevant depression (PHQ-9 ≥10) was most frequent in patients with comorbid fibromyalgia and migraine, followed by fibromyalgia alone, and least frequent in migraine alone.
Positive suicidal ideation (PHQ-9 item 9) was most common in the fibromyalgia+migraine group and least common in the migraine-only group.
Clinically relevant insomnia (ISI ≥10) was most prevalent in the fibromyalgia+migraine group and least prevalent in the migraine-only group.
Health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-5L index) was significantly lower in the fibromyalgia and fibromyalgia+migraine groups than in the migraine-only group.
EQ-5D-5L VAS self-rated health scores were lowest in the fibromyalgia+migraine group among the three groups.
Patients with fibromyalgia and with comorbid fibromyalgia+migraine reported a significantly higher number of associated pathologies than migraine-only patients.
Osteoarthritis was the most commonly reported comorbid pathology among patients with fibromyalgia and fibromyalgia+migraine.
Thyroid disease (hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism) was the most frequent comorbidity reported among migraine-only patients.
Irritable bowel syndrome was especially frequent among patients with comorbid fibromyalgia and migraine compared with the other groups.
Healthcare resource utilization differed significantly among all three groups for every resource assessed, with the migraine group showing lowest overall use except for emergency room visits.
Compared with fibromyalgia alone, patients with comorbid fibromyalgia and migraine used significantly more emergency room visits, radiographies, MRI and other medical tests.

After adjusting for pain intensity and number of pathologies, the depression score difference between migraine and fibromyalgia groups was no longer statistically significant, although both groups still differed significantly from the fibromyalgia+migraine group.
Suicidal ideation severity differences between the groups were no longer statistically significant after controlling for pain intensity and number of pathologies.

After covariate adjustment, insomnia score differences between migraine and fibromyalgia, and between fibromyalgia and fibromyalgia+migraine, were no longer significant, but the difference between migraine and fibromyalgia+migraine persisted.
After covariate adjustment, the EQ-5D-5L VAS difference between fibromyalgia and fibromyalgia+migraine was no longer significant, while differences involving the migraine group remained significant.
Among patients with comorbid fibromyalgia and migraine, reported migraine duration was much longer than fibromyalgia duration, suggesting migraine onset preceded fibromyalgia onset.
Among outpatients with mild COVID-19, roughly a third had at least one persistent symptom 3-9 months after illness onset, per a cited external study.
Among those who received inpatient COVID care, the large majority reported at least one persistent symptom an average of 60 days after onset, per a cited external study.
Long COVID is projected to impose a massive economic burden in the USA, including a large workforce reduction, per cited estimates.
In a Louisiana integrated health system, Black patients were disproportionately represented among COVID-19 hospitalizations and deaths relative to their share of the overall patient population.
Physicians are reported to more often underestimate pain in Black patients than in White patients, reducing treatment recommendation accuracy.
Black patients presenting to emergency departments for abdominal pain experience longer wait times and lower admission rates than White patients.

In this sample of 15 Black long COVID patients, at least two participants each reported fatigue/insomnia, brain fog, anosmia, dyspnea, headache, chest pain/palpitations, worsening of pre-existing conditions, joint/muscle pain, paresthesia, anxiety, depression, dermatologic changes, fever/diarrhea, lymphadenopathy, blurry vision, and weight changes.

One participant described substantial difficulty obtaining a formal POTS diagnosis despite seeing two cardiologists and a neurologist repeatedly, contributing to frustration and lack of care resolution.

Several participants reported that physicians dismissed or minimized their long COVID symptoms, sometimes attributing them to psychiatric causes, which led participants to doubt their own perceptions.
A participant reported being repeatedly denied short-term disability benefits for long COVID despite advocating for herself, due to lack of documentation showing COVID affected her ability to work.
In a study of COVID patients discharged from 38 Michigan hospitals, Black patients had lower rates of primary care follow-up visits and higher hospital readmission rates than White patients.
Black patients are more likely to be uninsured, which reduces their capacity to seek specialist care for long COVID.

Long COVID has been conceptually likened to other chronic pain and fatigue conditions—fibromyalgia, myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome, post-intensive care syndrome, and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome—suggesting these may represent overlapping subsets of long COVID patients.

Participants described hesitancy toward COVID testing driven by fear that personal health information would be stored in databases, reflecting broader distrust of medical systems within Black communities.
A hospitalized participant described confusing hospital discharge instructions that placed a COVID-negative family member at risk of exposure during transport home.
Dysautonomia was reported in 4 of 19 (21%) ITPR1-IgG/anti-Sj-seropositive patients across the pooled literature.

One ITPR1-IgG/anti-Sj-seropositive patient had subacute pandysautonomia confirmed by thermoregulatory sweat test and autonomic reflex test before later developing dementia, encephalopathy, and seizures.
A patient with ITPR1-IgG/anti-Sj-associated polyradiculoneuropathy showed pathologically reduced heart rate variability, indicating cardiac autonomic neuropathy.

ITPR1 is expressed in sympathetic ganglia and in smooth muscle cells of the bowel and bladder, and ITPR1-IgG/anti-Sj has been shown to bind smooth muscle cells in the enteric wall, suggesting a mechanism for autonomic enteropathy.
One patient with ITPR1-IgG/anti-Sj-associated dysautonomia had repeated stroke episodes attributed to intermittent atrial fibrillation.
ITPR1 is expressed in human and murine cardiac myocytes and has been implicated in modulating the propensity of human myocardium to develop arrhythmias.
Among ITPR1-IgG/anti-Sj-seropositive patients with peripheral neuropathy, 6 of 7 were male, despite an overall female predominance (M:F 1:1.5) in the full cohort.

ITPR1 dysregulation has been shown in animal studies to contribute to hyperalgesia and allodynia, consistent with its expression in dorsal root ganglia, trigeminal ganglia, and the substantia gelatinosa where C-fibre pain-transmitting neurons synapse.

A prospective study of paraneoplastic autoantibody evaluation specimens found ITPR1-IgG/anti-Sj at a frequency of 15 per 100,000 specimens per year, higher than anti-Tr/DNER but lower than anti-Hu, anti-Ri, and anti-Yo.

A tumour was identified in 9 of 20 (45%) ITPR1-IgG/anti-Sj-seropositive patients with available data, most commonly breast and lung cancers, supporting classification as a facultative paraneoplastic neurological syndrome.
Patients with exclusively IgG2-subclass ITPR1-IgG/anti-Sj antibodies had a milder clinical course than patients with predominantly IgG1 antibodies, who were severely disabled at follow-up.
Across the pooled cases, immunotherapy (PLEX, IVIG, IVMP/steroids, rituximab, or cyclophosphamide) produced no significant improvement in most ITPR1-IgG/anti-Sj-seropositive patients.

In the new index case, high-dose IVMP alone or combined with PLEX and IVIG repeatedly produced significant and prompt clinical improvement, sometimes with complete recovery of cognitive and psychiatric symptoms.
In the two patients in whom it was assessed, the ITPR1-specific antibody index was below 4, indicating an extrathecal (peripheral) rather than intrathecal origin of CSF ITPR1-IgG.

ITPR1-IgG/anti-Sj was absent in 250 healthy individuals and 105 patients with non-neurological disorders, and was not detected in almost 52,000 samples from patients with putative autoimmune neurological disease, supporting high assay specificity.

ITPR1-specific CD4+ T cells and CD8+ CD45RO+ T cells, alongside B cells, were demonstrated by proliferation assay in an ITPR1-IgG/anti-Sj-seropositive patient, supporting a possible T-cell-mediated component of pathogenesis.
Monoclonal antibodies against CGRP significantly reduce migraine frequency and allodynia in nearly half of treated patients.
Functional coupling between the hypothalamus and the spinal trigeminal nucleus/dorsal rostral pons is significantly increased during the migraine prodromal phase.
A longitudinal fMRI study found cyclic changes in brain perfusion in hypothalamic and limbic regions (insula, accumbens, hippocampus) with highest perfusion occurring during the headache attack.
Functional connectivity of the hypothalamus with sensory and frontal cortices, basal ganglia, and cerebellum progressively increases before headache onset and then drops suddenly at attack onset.
Resting-state analysis showed decreased functional connectivity between the hypothalamus and medial prefrontal cortex in chronic migraine patients.

Interictal imaging in episodic migraineurs showed altered functional connectivity between the hypothalamus and subcortical structures including locus coeruleus, pontine nuclei, caudate, cerebellar Crus I/II, temporal lobe and hippocampus, suggesting stronger autonomic nervous system influence.
A study found ictal versus interictal differences in activity of the brainstem/pons, cerebellum, thalamus, insular, and cingulate cortices associated with allodynia in migraine.
Imaging studies have shown increased prevalence of white matter lesions and cerebellar structural/functional alterations in patients with migraine, associated with prognosis and chronification.

Three familial hemiplegic migraine (FHM) genes have been identified: CACNA1A (voltage-gated calcium channel), ATP1A2 (Na-K+ ATPase), and SCN1A (voltage-gated sodium channel), all with significantly higher expression in the cerebellum.
A GWAS identified three lead variants associated with migraine with aura, one located in CACNA1A, providing a gene-based link between monogenic and polygenic forms of migraine.
GWAS identified migraine risk loci containing CALCA and CALCB genes, which encode CGRP and represent targets for migraine-specific therapeutics.

Migraineurs, particularly those with aura, show hypermetric reaching movements that become more pronounced with increased inertial load, suggesting subclinical cerebellar (lateral hemisphere) dysfunction.

Migraine patients with and without aura showed altered results on a neurotologic test of oculomotor function and posture despite only 25% reporting vertigo or dizziness, indicating subclinical vestibulo-cerebellar dysfunction.
A recent study found that up to 85% of women with migraine with aura and chronic migraine had vestibular symptoms that worsened during headache attacks.

MRI comparison of healthy individuals, vestibular migraine, and migraine with or without aura patients found increased volume of the red nucleus, thalamus and occipital regions, and decreased cerebellar volume, indicating cerebellar network involvement across migraine phenotypes.

A case report described visual snow syndrome evolving from episodic to chronic without headache following an infarction affecting the cerebellar Crus I and Lobule VI, illustrating cerebellar influence on high-level visual processing.

The cerebellum and anterior insular cortex were implicated in altered affective pain perception in children with tumors in the posterior cerebellum, and similar altered pain perception has been reported in cerebellar infarction cases.
Vertigo or dizziness occurs in about 50% of migraine patients, with lifetime prevalence of 16% for migraine and 7% for vertigo in the general population, and 1% for vestibular migraine.
Cervical muscles were found to be weaker in migraine patients with concurrent neck pain, and this weakness was associated with severity of cutaneous allodynia and disease chronification.

Migraine is more common in patients with cervical dystonia, a movement disorder thought to originate from abnormal basal ganglia and cerebellar processing, possibly due to shared genetic mutations affecting ion channels/pumps.
MELAS, a mitochondrial disorder, is linked to migraine and produces recurrent headaches along with muscle weakness and exercise intolerance.

Antioxidant supplementation with riboflavin and coenzyme Q10 may improve migraine frequency, severity, and fatigue levels, supporting a role of impaired oxidative mitochondrial metabolism in migraine-related fatigue.
Proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy showed that creatine was significantly increased in the pons of migraine without aura patients interictally, proposed as a biomarker for migraine without aura.
Systemic lactate levels were found to be increased in patients with migraine and fibromyalgia compared to healthy controls.

Population-based imaging studies found significantly higher prevalence of white matter hyperintense and infarct-like lesions in the deep cerebellum of migraineurs, particularly those with aura, likely due to hypoperfusion and embolism in small vasculature.
A recent study found that migraineurs with clinically silent cerebellar infarctions showed no or minimal cerebellar dysfunction, despite the higher prevalence of these lesions.
The risk and prevalence of essential tremor are substantially higher in migraineurs, and prevalence of migraine is higher in patients with essential tremor.
The locus coeruleus has been shown to simultaneously inhibit trigeminovascular neurons in the spinal trigeminal nucleus caudalis and increase cortical spreading depolarization susceptibility.

fMRI mapping of trigeminal nociception in the nostril of healthy individuals showed activation of the ipsilateral posterior cerebellar lobules VI, VIIIa, and Crus I, with intensity and unpleasantness processed mainly in lobule VI, alongside functional connectivity to rostral pons, PAG, and thalamus.
Low serum vitamin D levels have previously been associated with several highly prevalent pain-related conditions, including fibromyalgia, migraine, and chronic widespread pain.
Low serum vitamin D was found to be associated with tension-type headache, mainly the chronic subtype, but the causal nature of this relationship remains unclear.

The reported association between tension-type headache and low vitamin D may be a secondary by-product of comorbid diseases/conditions that are independently linked to both low vitamin D and tension-type headache, particularly generalized musculoskeletal compromise, rather than a direct causal link.

No evidence-based indication currently exists for vitamin D supplementation in the prevention of tension-type headache, and only one ongoing trial specifically evaluating vitamin D efficacy in chronic TTH in adults was identified.
Subcutaneous nitroglycerin injection markedly increased head-scratching frequency in rats compared to controls, validating the migraine-like behavioral model.
Rizatriptan and low-dose XZR significantly reduced head-scratching frequency relative to the NTG group, while intermediate and high doses of XZR showed a non-significant reduction.
NTG injection produced strong periorbital and plantar mechanical allodynia, reflected by markedly lower withdrawal thresholds than controls.
Rizatriptan and all XZR doses significantly increased periorbital withdrawal thresholds compared with NTG group, indicating reduced periorbital allodynia.
XZR treatment at all doses significantly increased plantar withdrawal thresholds compared with the NTG group, indicating reduced extracephalic allodynia.
NTG-injected rats spent 1.4-fold more time in the dark chamber than controls, indicating light-aversive (photophobic) behavior.
Rizatriptan and high-dose XZR significantly reduced photophobic behavior compared with the NTG group.
Serum CGRP was significantly elevated in NTG-induced migraine rats compared to controls.
XZR decreased elevated serum CGRP levels in a dose-dependent manner, with the high dose returning CGRP to normal levels; rizatriptan also decreased CGRP.
Plasma 5-HT concentration was significantly decreased in NTG-induced migraine rats compared with controls.
XZR treatment, most notably at the intermediate dose, increased plasma 5-HT concentrations compared to the NTG group.
Serum substance P levels did not change significantly with any intervention, though a downward trend was observed in the XZR low-dose group.
The percentage of degranulated dural mast cells was much higher in NTG-induced migraine rats than in controls, indicating local neurogenic inflammation.
Rizatriptan and XZR (low and high doses) significantly decreased the percentage of degranulated dural mast cells compared with the NTG group.
Brain TNF-α and serum IL-1β and IL-6 were significantly elevated in NTG-induced migraine rats compared to controls.
Intermediate-dose XZR reversed the elevated levels of TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 in migraine rats, similarly to rizatriptan.
Plasma NO levels were significantly elevated in NTG-induced migraine rats compared to controls.
All doses of XZR significantly reduced plasma NO levels compared with the NTG group.
NOS activity was nearly 3-fold higher in NTG-induced migraine rats than in controls.
Imperatorin, a coumarin absorbed into serum after XZR administration, directly bound recombinant neuronal nitric oxide synthase with high affinity in a concentration-dependent manner.
Xanthotoxin, a coumarin absorbed into serum after XZR administration, directly bound recombinant neuronal nitric oxide synthase with high affinity in a concentration-dependent manner.
LPS stimulation significantly increased nNOS protein expression in PC12 cells compared with untreated cells, modeling neuroinflammation in vitro.
XZR treatment dose-dependently reduced nNOS expression in LPS-stimulated PC12 cells, reaching statistical significance at the highest dose tested.
Imperatorin dose-dependently inhibited nNOS expression in LPS-stimulated PC12 cells.
Xanthotoxin dose-dependently inhibited nNOS expression in LPS-stimulated PC12 cells.
LPS stimulation increased iNOS protein expression roughly 1.7-fold in PC12 cells compared with untreated cells, and high-dose XZR reversed this to near-normal levels.
Unlike xanthotoxin, imperatorin had little effect on iNOS expression in LPS-stimulated PC12 cells, while xanthotoxin inhibited iNOS in a dose-dependent manner.
LPS stimulation activated the NF-κB signaling pathway in PC12 cells, increasing phosphorylated IKKβ and NF-κB and decreasing IκBα.
XZR at 50 and 100 μg/ml significantly inhibited NF-κB pathway activation in LPS-stimulated PC12 cells, reducing p-IKKβ/IKKβ and p-NF-κB/NF-κB and increasing IκBα.
Imperatorin dose-dependently downregulated p-NF-κB/NF-κB expression, and at the highest dose also reduced p-IKKβ/IKKβ, in LPS-stimulated PC12 cells.
Xanthotoxin dose-dependently downregulated p-NF-κB/NF-κB expression in LPS-stimulated PC12 cells.
The nonselective NOS inhibitor L-NAME decreased phosphorylated IKK/IKK and NF-κB/NF-κB levels in PC12 cells, supporting that NO produced via NOS promotes NF-κB signaling.
XZR exhibited an analgesic effect in the acetic-acid-induced writhing model, significantly decreasing the frequency of writhing behavior.

In a preliminary experiment testing both sexes, XZR showed a more pronounced therapeutic effect on NTG-induced migraine-like behavior in male rats than in female rats, with male rats showing fewer individual differences.
The majority of participants with chronic low back pain reported poor sleep quality.
Participants with CLBP and central sensitization had significantly higher (worse) PSQI scores than CLBP participants without central sensitization and healthy controls.
Scores on the 2011 Fibromyalgia Survey (a surrogate measure of central sensitization) were significantly positively correlated with sleep quality scores.

A composite quantitative sensory testing-based central sensitization index (pressure pain thresholds and conditioned pain modulation) was significantly, though weakly, negatively correlated with sleep quality.
Logistic regression showed that classification as having fibromyalgia by the 2011 FM survey was significantly associated with poor sleep quality (PSQI), with an odds ratio of 6.00.
The quantitative sensory testing-based central sensitization index was not significantly associated with PSQI-measured sleep quality in logistic regression.
After adjusting for covariates, the association between FM status and sleep quality became non-significant, though the direction of effect remained similar.

A German telephone survey found that migraine prevalence and probable migraine differ by sex, with more women than men meeting full diagnostic criteria and additional probable migraine cases in both sexes.

In an 18-year observational case series of 1000 atypical migraine patients, attacks often had shorter duration or fewer episodes and lacked the full complement of typical migraine symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, phonophobia, or photophobia, with some patients experiencing only phonophobia without photophobia.
Vestibular migraine, a common subtype in clinical practice, is easily missed because triggers produce vestibular symptoms rather than headache.

The diagnostic criteria for migraine without aura and episodic/chronic tension-type headache overlap substantially (similar episode number, duration, intensity, phonophobia, photophobia, and mild nausea), causing diagnostic confusion in clinical practice.
Alice in Wonderland syndrome is a rare migraine-related disorder characterized by distorted perceptions of time, space, vision (micropsia/macropsia), hearing, and somesthetic sensations.
Migraine can transform into a mild-to-moderate, more tolerable headache pattern in elderly patients, a phenomenon not addressed by ICHD-3.

The author proposes clinical indicators for diagnosing atypical migraine, including prodromal symptoms, autonomic symptoms, interictal normality between recurrent attacks, known migraine triggers, family history of migraine or vestibular migraine, sleep-aborting attacks, and past history of episodic syndromes.

Many atypical migraine patients are treated symptomatically without a formal migraine diagnosis, missing opportunities for targeted non-pharmacological measures such as trigger avoidance and lifestyle modification, as well as appropriate abortive/preventive migraine drugs.
A dose-response relationship was found between K. brevis bloom intensity and the reporting of upper respiratory tract symptoms among southwest Florida residents.
A dose-response relationship was found between K. brevis bloom intensity and reporting of neurotoxic shellfish poisoning (NSP)-like symptoms.
A dose-response relationship was found between K. brevis bloom intensity and reporting of headaches.
Reporting of neurotoxic shellfish poisoning-like symptoms during K. brevis blooms was higher among participants with a past medical history of migraines compared to those without.
Reporting of neurotoxic shellfish poisoning-like symptoms during K. brevis blooms was higher among participants with a past medical history of chronic fatigue syndrome compared to those without.
Reporting of neurotoxic shellfish poisoning-like symptoms during K. brevis blooms was higher among participants with a past medical history of mild memory loss compared to those without.
The association between headache reporting and K. brevis bloom intensity was stronger among individuals with a prior medical history of migraines compared to those without.

Autonomic nervous system dysfunction, including nausea, vomiting, photophobia, palpitations and facial flushing, commonly occurs before or during migraine attacks and is proposed as an important pathophysiological mechanism of migraine.
During a migraine attack, sympathetic nervous system activity increases while parasympathetic activity is suppressed.
During a migraine attack, parasympathetic nervous system activity is suppressed while sympathetic activity increases.

The authors cite prior research finding that both sympathetic and parasympathetic nerve activity are lower in migraine patients than in healthy individuals, and that acupuncture can improve autonomic nerve function.

Acupuncture at the Fengchi (GB20) acupoint has been shown to beneficially influence the autonomic nervous system in migraine patients, reducing the low-frequency power of heart rate variability in association with clinical improvement.
Acupuncture at the Neiguan (PC6) acupoint significantly enhances vagus nerve activity and has a relatively specific effect on heart rate variability.

The Tianrong (SI17) acupoint lies near the cervical ganglia of the sympathetic trunk, and acupuncture there is proposed to regulate cervical sympathetic plexus activity and bidirectionally modulate cerebral artery blood flow velocity in migraine treatment.

A previous study by the authors reported an 80% effective rate for the autonomic-regulating acupuncture regimen compared with 67% for a control regimen, and these figures were used to power the sample size calculation for this trial.
Migraine prevalence is higher in women than men, affecting approximately 17% of women and 8% of men in Europe.
Body awareness, measured by the Body Awareness Questionnaire, did not differ significantly between young adults with and without HSD.
Fatigue levels, measured by the Fatigue Severity Scale, were similar between individuals with and without HSD.
Individuals with HSD performed significantly better (greater flexibility) on the Sit and Reach test compared to those without HSD.
Dominant side grip strength was significantly lower in individuals with HSD than in those without HSD.
Neck musculoskeletal discomfort was significantly greater in individuals with HSD compared to those without HSD.
Back musculoskeletal discomfort was significantly greater in individuals with HSD compared to those without HSD.
Dominant wrist musculoskeletal discomfort was significantly greater in individuals with HSD compared to those without HSD.
Overall total musculoskeletal problems were significantly greater in individuals with HSD compared to those without HSD.
An active duty female with multiple prior fractures was found to have heterozygous CREB3L1, a rare genetic cause of osteogenesis imperfecta.
CREB3L1 codes for a transcription factor important for the differentiation of osteoblasts, and mutations in this gene represent an emerging recognized cause of osteogenesis imperfecta.
Patients with migraine with aura showed increased resting-state functional connectivity between the right antero-dorsal insula and a cerebellar/vermal/lingual cluster compared to healthy controls.
Patients with migraine with aura showed increased functional connectivity between the left antero-dorsal insula and a cerebellar/vermal/lingual cluster compared to healthy controls.
No significant connectivity differences were found between MA and HC for the other insular seeds (anterior, posterior, middle, ventral) besides the antero-dorsal ROI.
The overlapping cerebellar region functionally coupled to both right and left antero-dorsal insula clusters corresponded anatomically to vermis VI.
ROI-to-ROI analysis found no functional connectivity between the right or left lingual cortices and the right or left antero-dorsal insula, excluding lingual cortex involvement in the effect.
ROI-to-ROI analysis confirmed strong functional coupling between the right and left antero-dorsal insula and vermis VI.
The strength of functional connectivity between the antero-dorsal insula and vermis VI was not correlated with migraine duration, attack frequency, or time since last attack.
No difference in functional coupling between vermis VI and the antero-dorsal insula ROIs was found between patients with migraine without aura and healthy controls.

Compared with migraine without aura, migraine with aura showed increased functional coupling between the right antero-dorsal insula and vermis VI, but not between the left antero-dorsal insula and vermis VI, indicating specificity of the connectivity increase to migraine with aura.

The authors hypothesize that increased antero-dorsal insula-vermis VI connectivity in migraine with aura may reflect altered parasympathetic cardiovascular autonomic control, given both regions' known roles in ANS regulation, though this was not directly tested in the study.
Cited prior literature indicates migraine with aura specifically (unlike migraine without aura) is associated with increased risk of syncope after adjustment for confounders.

A cited review of cardiovascular autonomic function in migraine reported a trend toward greater autonomic dysfunction in migraine with aura than without aura, with sympathetic dysfunction more common than parasympathetic dysfunction.
The patient had elevated anti-VGKC complex antibodies targeting the LGI-1 protein, supporting an autoimmune paraneoplastic etiology for his Morvan syndrome.
Brain FDG-PET showed hypermetabolism in bilateral basal ganglia, hippocampus, amygdala, and mesial temporal lobe consistent with autoimmune encephalitis, despite a normal MRI.
FDG-PET demonstrated higher sensitivity than MRI for detecting autoimmune encephalitis, as this patient's brain MRI was negative despite PET showing a typical hypermetabolism pattern.
Whole-body FDG PET/CT identified a mildly hypermetabolic anterior mediastinal mass measuring 4.5 cm x 3 cm with SUVmax of 4, later confirmed as mixed thymoma.
Following total thymectomy for the pathologically confirmed mixed thymoma (Masaoka stage IIB), the patient showed clinical improvement in his Morvan syndrome manifestations.
Anti-CASPR-2 antibodies, though less common than anti-LGI-1, are reported to be predominant among VGKC-complex antibodies in Morvan syndrome and are consistently associated with thymoma.
The patient exhibited multiple autonomic dysfunction signs, including fluctuating blood pressure and decreased urine output, consistent with the dysautonomia seen in Morvan syndrome.
FIQR scores, reflecting fibromyalgia symptom burden and functional impact, were significantly lower at the 1-month follow-up compared with pretreatment baseline after peripheral nerve blockade.
FIQR scores continued to decrease from the first to the third month, indicating ongoing regression of fibromyalgia symptoms after nerve blockade.
VAS pain scores were significantly lower at both the first and third month follow-ups compared to pretreatment baseline.
There was no significant difference in VAS pain scores between the first month and third month follow-ups, suggesting a plateau in pain-reducing effect after the initial improvement.
MIDAS scores, reflecting migraine-related disability, were significantly lower at the third month follow-up compared to baseline.
The number of days in pain per month was significantly lower at both the first and third month follow-ups compared to baseline.
The number of analgesics taken in the last month was significantly lower at both the first and third month follow-ups compared to baseline.
The number of days in pain was significantly higher at the third month than at the first month, suggesting waning efficacy of the single early re-injection over time.
The number of analgesics taken was significantly higher at the third month than at the first month, indicating that the migraine-related benefit of the blockade may have begun to decrease.
A large epidemiology study reported that 55.8% of patients with fibromyalgia also had migraine.
In a study of 1466 patients, fibromyalgia was found in 24.3% of patients with migraine.
Fibromyalgia frequency was reported to be 17.4% among patients with episodic migraine.
Cerebrospinal fluid glutamate levels were reported to be high in patients with fibromyalgia, implicating excitatory neurotransmitter imbalance in central sensitization.
Cerebrospinal fluid substance P levels were reported to be high in patients with fibromyalgia, implicating excitatory neuropeptide signaling in central sensitization.
Cerebrospinal fluid serotonin levels were reported to be low in patients with fibromyalgia, implicating deficient inhibitory neurotransmission in central sensitization.
Cerebrospinal fluid noradrenaline levels were reported to be low in patients with fibromyalgia, implicating deficient inhibitory neurotransmission in central sensitization.
In a randomized controlled study cited by the authors, flunarizine treatment in patients with both migraine and fibromyalgia reduced both migraine attack frequency and fibromyalgia flares.
In the same cited study, fibromyalgia flares were more frequent in patients who had a higher frequency of migraine attacks.

A prior study (Yilmaz et al.) found that bilateral greater occipital nerve blockade in patients with episodic migraine and fibromyalgia significantly decreased VAS, MIDAS, and FIQR scores at the first and third months, with greater benefit at the third month.
Upslope walking increased anterior tibial translation more in GJH patients than in healthy controls during early and late gait cycle phases.
Upslope walking significantly increased knee flexion angle compared to level walking in both GJH patients and healthy controls.
40.4% of patients undergoing hip arthroscopy for FAIS with or without dysplasia had generalized joint hypermobility (BTS ≥4).
Female patients were significantly more likely than male patients to have a Beighton test score ≥4.
Patients with BTS ≥4 were on average younger than those with BTS <4.
Male patients had significantly greater BMI than female patients.
Female patients were significantly more likely to have had an injection before surgery than male patients.
Patients with BTS ≥4 had greater hip internal rotation at 90° of flexion than those with BTS <4, and this remained a significant univariable difference.
Hip internal rotation when prone was significantly greater in BTS≥4 patients univariably, but the difference was no longer significant after controlling for age and sex.
Female patients had significantly greater hip internal rotation at 90° of flexion than male patients.
Female patients had significantly greater hip internal rotation while prone than male patients.
Female patients had significantly greater hip internal rotation in extension univariably, but this was no longer significant after controlling for BTS.
Female patients were more likely to have a positive prone apprehension relocation test than male patients.
Radiographic alpha angle was significantly smaller in patients with BTS ≥4 compared to those without.
Presence of a posterior wall sign was significantly associated with BTS ≥4 status, even after controlling for sex and age.
Femoral version measured on CT was significantly greater in patients with BTS ≥4.
McKibben index measured on CT was reported to be significantly different between BTS ≥4 and BTS <4 groups.
CT alpha angle was univariably significantly smaller in BTS≥4 patients, but this was not significant after controlling for sex and age.
Male patients were more likely to have a Tönnis grade of 1 than female patients.
Male patients were more likely than female patients to have a positive posterior wall sign.
Male patients had a significantly greater radiographic alpha angle on modified Dunn view than female patients.
Male patients had significantly less femoral anteversion on CT than female patients.
Male patients had a significantly decreased McKibben index compared with female patients.

Superior hip joint capsule thickness showed a statistically significant negative correlation with hip internal rotation at 90° of flexion, meaning thinner capsules were associated with greater rotation.
Superior hip joint capsule thickness showed a statistically significant negative correlation with hip internal rotation in extension.
Superior hip joint capsule thickness showed a statistically significant negative correlation with hip internal rotation while prone.
Thinner superior hip capsule thickness on MRI was negatively correlated with hip internal rotation measured in extension.
Thinner superior hip capsule thickness on MRI was negatively correlated with hip internal rotation measured while prone.
Thinner superior hip capsule thickness on MRI was negatively correlated with hip external rotation at 90 degrees of flexion.
Male patients had a significantly thicker superior hip joint capsule than female patients, though this difference lost significance after controlling for Beighton test score.

Patients with a Beighton test score of 4 or higher had a significantly thinner superior hip capsule than those with a score below 4, but this difference lost significance after controlling for age and sex.
Superior hip capsule thickness showed a statistically significant positive correlation with hip internal rotation at 90 degrees of flexion, though the correlation was weak.
Superior hip capsule thickness showed a statistically significant positive correlation with hip internal rotation while prone, though the correlation was weak.
No significant associations were found between Beighton test score group or sex and the presence of labral tears, acetabular subchondral cysts, or femoral neck cysts on MRI.
Patients with fibromyalgia had a 3.69-fold increased risk of developing migraine compared to matched controls.
Unaffected siblings of fibromyalgia probands had a 1.51-fold increased risk of developing migraine compared to matched controls.
Patients with migraine had a 4.86-fold increased risk of developing fibromyalgia compared to matched controls.
Unaffected siblings of migraine probands had a 1.59-fold increased risk of developing fibromyalgia compared to matched controls.

The bidirectional risk pattern seen in both probands and their unaffected siblings suggests a familial coaggregation of fibromyalgia and migraine, implicating shared genetic or environmental etiology rather than direct causation.
Tension-type headache prevalence is markedly higher in females (about 45%) than males (about 25%), with associated reductions in quality of life and productivity.
A meta-analysis found tension-type headache patients have moderately lower heart rate variability (vmHRV) compared to controls.
The same meta-analytic effect size indicated moderately lower heart rate variability in migraine patients compared to controls.

A meta-analysis found low-to-moderate evidence of pressure pain hypersensitivity in the trigeminal and neck areas of tension-type headache patients compared with headache-free controls, widespread only in chronic (not episodic) TTH.
Dry needling of myofascial trigger points reduced headache index by 65% over 6 weeks, compared to a 33% increase with sham needling.
Needle EMG recordings showed dramatically more electrical activity in active myofascial trigger points than in nearby non-tender muscle.

Pharmacological blockade experiments showed the alpha-sympathetic antagonist phentolamine almost completely suppressed trigger point EMG activity, while the cholinergic antagonist curare had no effect, supporting alpha-sympathetic mediation of trigger points.

During a stressful mental arithmetic task, EMG activity at the trigger point rose to a mean of 28.31 microvolts versus 4.44 microvolts at the non-tender site, returning to a baseline of 15.99 microvolts during recovery.
Passive relaxation induction (autogenic training) reduced trigger point EMG activity down to the level of the adjacent non-tender site.

In a randomized trial of 137 adolescents with episodic and chronic TTH, non-drug HRV biofeedback therapy produced a more pronounced decrease in headache intensity, reactive anxiety, and depression, and improved quality of life compared with drug therapy alone.
In children with functional abdominal pain, longer periods of vagal withdrawal were seen versus asymptomatic children, and HRVB improved vagal tone while abdominal pain symptoms reduced.
Peroutka postulated that migraineurs show chronic sympathetic hypofunction based on overwhelming objective diagnostic and clinical data.
Migraine is associated with a complex pattern of ANS alterations reflecting an imbalance between sympathetic and parasympathetic tone.
Migraine patients have consistently been found to have lower heart rate variability during both interictal and ictal periods.
A meta-analysis reported that vagal nerve stimulation produced acute relief of cluster headache.
One study also reported acute relief of migraine using vagal nerve stimulation.

In a double-blind, sham-controlled multi-center trial, a non-invasive VNS device reduced headache days in both the sham and actual VNS groups, with adherent actual-VNS patients reporting fewer headache days.
A meta-analysis concluded that yoga therapy may reduce headache frequency in migraine patients despite methodological limitations.
A study comparing yoga intervention to care as usual in migraine patients found reduced symptoms and improved vagal tone in the yoga group.
A meta-analysis found that biofeedback modalities, alone or combined with other therapies, produced a medium effect-size treatment advantage over controls for migraine.
A pediatric meta-analysis of 5 studies (137 participants) found biofeedback reduced migraine frequency compared with waiting-list control.
The same pediatric meta-analysis found biofeedback reduced migraine attack duration compared with waiting-list control.
The same pediatric meta-analysis found biofeedback reduced headache intensity compared with waiting-list control.

A follow-up study of a smartphone-based biofeedback device found poor adherence and only a non-significant reduction of about one headache per month in the intervention group, possibly affected by COVID-19 pandemic conditions.

A randomized controlled trial of app-based HRV biofeedback for migraine found it feasible and acceptable, but the primary clinical outcome did not differ significantly from control; however, high app users reported more benefit than low users.
Headache disorders, including migraine, have been associated with dermatologic conditions such as ecchymoses, inflammatory skin conditions, and neurocutaneous disorders.
Proposed pathophysiology linking headache and skin manifestations includes activation of the trigeminal autonomic system alongside involvement of similar pro-inflammatory molecules.
In the original UMSARS clinimetric validation of 40 MSA patients, all UMSARS-I items showed substantial to excellent interrater agreement except item 9, orthostatic symptoms.
A subsequent analysis found that all UMSARS-II items had substantial or excellent intrarater reliability except oculomotor dysfunction (item 3), which showed only moderate intrarater agreement.

UMSARS-I items 8 (falling) and 9 (orthostatic symptoms), as well as UMSARS-II item 3 (oculomotor dysfunction), correlated poorly with their subscale's total sum score, indicating weaker internal consistency for these items.
Criterion-related validity analysis showed a strong correlation between UMSARS-I, UMSARS-II, and a three-point overall clinical severity scale categorizing disease as mild, moderate, or severe.

Content validity of the UMSARS was supported by strong correlations between the UMSARS and the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale, and between UMSARS-II and the International Cooperative Ataxia Rating Scale.
The UMSARS validation cohort consisted of moderately to severely disabled MSA patients, so it remains unclear whether the psychometric findings generalize to patients with mild disease severity.

An item-response theory analysis of 557 MSA patients with mean follow-up of 2.3 years found that most UMSARS items progressed with disease duration except UMSARS-I items 9 (orthostatic symptoms), 10 (urinary function), and 11 (sexual function) and UMSARS-II items 3 (oculomotor dysfunction) and 4 (tremor at rest), and that approximately 70% of scale information was carried by only 11 of the 26 items.

Analysis of annual change concluded that UMSARS-I items 9 (orthostatic symptoms) and 12 (bowel function) and UMSARS-II items 4 and 5 (tremor at rest and action tremor) show little ability to detect change, whereas items assessing dressing/hygiene and posture/gait showed good sensitivity to change.

A third analysis in two independent datasets (a clinical trial and a natural history study) found that items assessing key motor functions were most sensitive to change while items assessing autonomic symptoms were less sensitive to change, and that more UMSARS-I than UMSARS-II items impacted patients' quality of life.
Despite poor sensitivity to change of UMSARS items assessing autonomic symptoms, autonomic features are strongly correlated with quality of life and life satisfaction in patients with MSA.
The FDA did not accept the current UMSARS, particularly the UMSARS-II motor examination, as the primary outcome for registrational MSA trials and instead preferred modified versions of the scale.

A recently completed industry-sponsored randomized clinical trial (NCT03952806) used a modified UMSARS score consisting of a subset of the original UMSARS-I and UMSARS-II items as its primary endpoint.
5-week-old female oim mice weighed significantly less than wild-type littermates.
Avulsion fractures at high tendinous stress areas such as the calcaneus were observed exclusively in oim mice on CT imaging, not in wild-type mice.
On average, oim mice sustained more than one calcaneal fracture each, producing superior concavity bone deformation.
Bone mineral density in the ulna epiphysis measured by pQCT was significantly lower in oim than in WT mice.
The BV/TV ratio in the olecranon epiphysis (elbow) was significantly reduced in oim mice compared with WT.
There was a borderline, non-significant correlation between triceps brachii tendon thickness and BV/TV in the proximal ulna epiphysis, suggesting an osteotendinous unit relationship.
The mass of flexor digitorum longus tendons was significantly lower in oim mice than WT.
The length of flexor digitorum longus tendons was significantly shorter in oim mice than WT.
Flexor digitorum longus tendons from oim mice had significantly lower ultimate stress than WT tendons, indicating reduced tensile resistance.
Ultimate strain of oim tendons trended higher than WT but did not reach statistical significance.
Tendon toughness was not significantly different between oim and WT tendons, although the trend approached significance.
The elastic modulus (rigidity) of oim flexor digitorum longus tendons was significantly lower than WT tendons.
Femoral ultimate load from three-point bending was significantly lower in oim than WT mice.
Femoral stiffness was significantly lower in oim than WT mice.
Femoral yield load was significantly lower in oim than WT mice.
Femoral post-yield displacement was significantly lower in oim than WT mice, indicating reduced ductility.
Total work to fracture of the femur was markedly reduced in oim mice, consistent with all other reduced biomechanical parameters.
Femoral trabecular bone mass (BV/TV) was significantly reduced in oim mice on microCT.
Femoral trabecular number was significantly reduced in oim mice.
Femoral trabecular thickness was significantly, though modestly, reduced in oim mice.
Cortical bone thickness of the femur was significantly reduced in oim mice.
Total cross-sectional area of the femoral diaphysis was significantly reduced in oim mice.
Femoral marrow area was significantly reduced in oim mice.
Cross-sectional moment of inertia in the medio-lateral axis was markedly reduced in oim femurs, indicating impaired resistance to bending.
Cortical bone porosity in the femur was significantly higher in oim mice than in WT littermates.
Non-enzymatic collagen crosslinking, reflecting advanced glycation end-products such as pentosidine, was significantly higher in oim triceps brachii tendon than in WT tendon.
The β-sheet content of collagen secondary structure was significantly higher in oim tendons than in WT tendons.
Collagen NH stretch-bound water content was significantly lower in oim tendons than in WT tendons.
Collagen III protein expression was significantly lower in oim tail tendon than in WT tendon by Western blot.
Decorin protein expression in tail tendon did not differ significantly between oim and WT mice.
Tenomodulin protein expression in tail tendon did not differ significantly between oim and WT mice.
The phosphate/amide I ratio, reflecting the degree of bone mineralization, was significantly higher in oim femur than in WT femur.
HPO4 (acid phosphate) content of bone mineral was significantly higher in oim femur than in WT femur, suggesting lower hydroxyapatite maturation.
Mineral crystallinity of femoral bone was significantly lower in oim mice than in WT mice.
Collagen maturity of the organic bone matrix was significantly reduced in oim femur compared with WT femur.
About 9-11% of patients with chronic migraine achieved a ≥75% reduction in monthly headache days (percent-based excellent response) at each of the first three onabotulinumtoxinA treatment cycles.
Total responders (patients reporting zero headache days during a treatment cycle) were rare, comprising less than 1% of the sample in each of the first three cycles.

Using a stricter, frequency-based definition of excellent response (<4 monthly headache days), roughly 4-5% of patients qualified at each treatment cycle, a lower proportion than with the percent-based definition.
Medication overuse at baseline was significantly more prevalent among percent-based excellent responders than non-responders.
Baseline number of days per month with medication intake (MDs) was significantly higher among percent-based excellent responders than non-responders.

In multivariate logistic regression, presence of medication overuse at baseline and excellent responder status during the first and second BT-A cycles were independent predictors of percent-based excellent response at the third cycle, with good model fit and discrimination.

Patients who were percent-based excellent responders at 9 months (third cycle) were significantly more likely to have already been excellent responders at 3 and 6 months, indicating early response predicts sustained response.

Female sex was significantly less prevalent among frequency-based excellent responders than non-responders, and was the only variable significantly associated with this stricter response category at the third BT-A cycle.

Baseline headache days (HD) and medication days (MD) were significantly associated with responder status only in univariate, not multivariate, analysis, so they were not independent predictors of excellent response.

According to cited literature, calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) is linked to trigeminal-mediated pain and its peripheral blood levels are higher in patients with chronic migraine and medication overuse; onabotulinumtoxinA reduces inter-ictal CGRP levels.
OnabotulinumtoxinA is proposed to act by inhibiting the SNARE complex, thereby blocking exocytosis of CGRP from trigeminal C-fibers.

Animal model data cited in the discussion indicate that medication overuse is a risk factor for peripheral sensitization of the trigeminal pathway, with up-regulation of CGRP found in the trigeminal ganglion in rats.
Adolescents with symptomatic joint hypermobility (SJH) had nearly three-fold higher odds of low back pain compared to those without SJH.
SJH was associated with nearly three-fold higher odds of low back pain without objective clinical or imaging findings (LBPWF).
SJH was associated with nearly three-fold higher odds of low back pain with objective clinical or imaging findings (LBPOF), such as herniated disk or spinal stenosis.
Gender was not significantly associated with the presence of symptomatic joint hypermobility in this cohort.
Low back pain prevalence in the overall adolescent cohort was 3.7%.
Symptomatic joint hypermobility (confirmed by Beighton score and rheumatologist evaluation) had a prevalence of 0.11% in this adolescent cohort.
Among subjects with SJH, 10% had concomitant low back pain compared to only 3.7% in the non-SJH cohort.
Low back pain with objective imaging or clinical findings (LBPOF) was 2.5 times more prevalent among subjects with SJH than in the general cohort.
Meta-analysis of 29 studies (n=4874) found the pooled prevalence of large fiber peripheral neuropathy in nonselected pSS populations was 15.0%.
Meta-analysis of 11 studies (n=733) found the pooled prevalence of median nerve entrapment (carpal tunnel syndrome) in pSS patients was 12.8%.
Meta-analysis of 16 studies (n=1430) found the pooled prevalence of cranial nerve involvement in pSS patients was 5.4%.
Meta-analysis of 10 studies (n=935) found the pooled prevalence of trigeminal neuropathy in pSS patients was 3.9%, the commonest cranial mononeuropathy.
In the cohort by Sène et al., using laser-evoked potentials, quantitative sensory testing, and autonomic testing, the estimated prevalence of pure small fiber neuropathy in pSS was 9.2%.
Among pSS patients with large fiber peripheral neuropathy, 83% were female, mean age at diagnosis was 59 years, and neuropathic symptoms preceded or led to pSS diagnosis at a 2:1 ratio.
Distal axonal (length-dependent) polyneuropathy was the most common type of pSS-related large fiber PN, accounting for almost 80% of cases.

Sensory ganglionopathy (neuronopathy) was the second most common pSS-related PN type, accounting for 20% of cases, characterized by asymmetrical, non-length-dependent pure sensory loss and sensory ataxia.
Among pSS patients with large fiber PN, 50% had sensorimotor distal axonal PN and 50% had sensory-only neuropathy, while less than 1% had pure motor neuropathy.
Among eight studies distinguishing pure sensory PN subtypes, sensory neuronopathies/ganglionopathies versus distal sensory axonal polyneuropathy occurred at a 2:3 ratio.
Among cases of pure SFN in pSS, presentations were distal/symmetrical versus diffuse/asymmetrical at a 2:3 ratio.
Among pSS patients with pure SFN, 89% were female, and neuropathic symptoms preceded or led to pSS diagnosis at a 4:1 ratio.

Patients with neurophysiologically confirmed small fiber dysfunction showed more intense squeezing/pressure sensations, more frequent dynamic mechanical allodynia, and higher prevalence of restless leg syndrome, suggesting sensitization of spared large Aβ fibers and second-order nociceptive neurons.
Patients with pSS-related small fiber neuropathy had reduced electrochemical skin conductance, indicating sympathetic small fiber dysfunction.
Increasing age was identified as a risk factor for developing polyneuropathy in pSS patients, possibly via microangiopathic changes in endoneurial vessels.

Font et al. reported that presence of ANA and anti-Ro/SSA antibodies was associated with development of pure sensory neuropathy in pSS patients, but this was not confirmed by a later study by Gono et al.
Giordano et al. found no significant association between either antiglycosphingolipid or anti-ganglioside-GM1 antibodies and development of peripheral neuropathy in pSS.
Hsu et al. showed that anti-β2-glycoprotein-I antibody and perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (p-ANCA) levels might carry a risk for developing neuropathy in pSS patients.
Jamilloux et al. found cryoglobulinemia to be a unique predictive factor for neurological manifestations in pSS, particularly sensorimotor neuropathies and mononeuritis multiplex.
Sène et al. found a strong association between sensorimotor neuropathies and presence of mixed cryoglobulins, supporting vasculitis as a pathogenetic mechanism.
Increasing age is associated with greater risk of developing polyneuropathy in pSS patients, possibly due to microangiopathic changes in endoneurial vessels.

Font et al. reported that presence of antinuclear antibodies and anti-Ro/SSA antibodies is associated with development of pure sensory neuropathy in pSS patients, though this association was not confirmed by a subsequent study by Gono et al.
Giordano et al. found no significant association between antiglycosphingolipid antibodies or anti-ganglioside-GM1 antibodies and the development of peripheral neuropathy in pSS patients.
Hsu et al. showed that anti-β2-glycoprotein-I antibody and perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody levels might carry increased risk for developing neuropathy in pSS patients.

Jamilloux et al. demonstrated in a retrospective cohort that cryoglobulinemia is a unique predictive factor for developing neurological manifestations, particularly sensorimotor neuropathies and mononeuritis multiplex, in pSS.

Sène et al. found a strong association between sensorimotor neuropathies and the presence of mixed cryoglobulins, suggesting vasculitis as a pathogenic mechanism for pSS-related peripheral neuropathy.
Sène et al. demonstrated an association between sensorimotor pSS-related neuropathy and a higher prevalence of B-cell monoclonal proliferation markers and chronic B-cell activation.

Presence of B-cell activation markers (ANA, anti-SSA/Ro, anti-SSB/La, rheumatoid factor, hypergammaglobulinemia) is lower in nonataxic sensory neuropathies, suggesting these patients belong to a distinct pSS subgroup with peripheral sensory neurotropism.

In a retrospective cohort, Terrier et al. found pSS patients with vasculitis-associated neuropathy treated with oral glucocorticoids had significantly better response at 6 months than those without vasculitis.
Mori et al. found that among pSS patients treated with prednisone for neuropathy, those with mononeuritis multiplex had the greatest benefit, suggesting PNS vasculitis in this subgroup.

In a prospective cohort, oral prednisone alone or combined with cyclophosphamide or IVIG resulted in clinical stabilization or improvement in most patients with pure sensory neuropathy over a mean 10-year follow-up.
Delalande et al. found no beneficial effect of steroids in pSS patients with axonal polyneuropathy or ganglionopathy.
Cyclophosphamide combined with corticosteroids in a small group of pSS patients with multiple mononeuropathy (n=7) led to partial recovery or stabilization in all patients.
Mycophenolate mofetil added to glucocorticoids showed good results in a small group of pSS patients (n=7) with sensory ganglionopathy.

In a retrospective multicenter study of 19 pSS patients with neuropathy without necrotizing vasculitis, monthly IVIG (2 g/kg body weight) was well tolerated and half of patients improved, with the best response in sensorimotor or nonataxic sensory neuropathy.

In a cross-sectional study, Mori et al. treated 13 pSS patients with IVIG (2 g/kg over 5 days); those with polyradiculoneuropathy and painful sensory neuropathy responded best, while sensory ataxic neuropathy responded less favorably.
Pereira et al. reported poor results with IVIG (as monotherapy or add-on) in a small number of pSS patients with sensory ganglionopathy (n=6).

Pindi Sala et al. reported that IVIG in 12 pSS patients with pure small fiber neuropathy allowed 75% to discontinue analgesics and 25% to reduce analgesic use, with benefit sustained for a mean follow-up of 25 months after treatment completion.
In a small retrospective series, mycophenolate mofetil added to glucocorticoids produced good results in pSS patients with sensory ganglionopathy.

A retrospective multicenter study of IVIG in pSS-related neuropathy without necrotizing vasculitis found that about half of patients improved, with the best response in sensorimotor or nonataxic sensory neuropathy.

Mori et al. treated 13 pSS-related neuropathy patients with IVIG; those with polyradiculoneuropathy and painful sensory neuropathy responded most favorably, while sensory ataxic neuropathy patients responded less well.
In a retrospective cohort by Pereira et al., IVIG given to a small number of pSS patients with sensory ganglionopathy produced poor results.

Pindi Sala et al. reported that IVIG treatment in pSS patients with pure small fiber neuropathy allowed analgesics to be discontinued in most patients and reduced in the remainder, with benefit persisting long after treatment completion.
In a longitudinal cohort, 11% of pSS patients without baseline peripheral neuropathy developed it after a median follow-up of 89 months.
Among 10 pSS patients with pure small fiber neuropathy followed for a mean of 37 months, one patient progressed to develop peripheral neuropathy.
Presence of vasculitis, the mononeuritis multiplex subtype, acute onset, and high CRP levels were associated with a better prognosis in pSS-related peripheral neuropathy.
A chronic and insidious course of neuropathic symptoms was linked to poorer treatment response, although the neuropathy overall tends to be slowly progressive.
Overall survival is reduced in pSS patients with peripheral neuropathy compared with those without, particularly among those with mononeuropathy multiplex and axonal polyneuropathy.
Women veterans with a headache diagnosis were significantly younger, more often non-White, and more often unmarried than men veterans with headache.
Men with headache had a higher rate of traumatic brain injury than women with headache.
Men with headache had a higher rate of PTSD than women with headache.
Women with headache had a substantially higher rate of military sexual trauma than men with headache.
Men with headache had a higher rate of overweight/obesity than women with headache.
Age-adjusted incidence rates of medically diagnosed headache disorders were higher among women veterans than men in every year observed.
Age-adjusted 1-year period prevalence rates of headache were consistently higher in women veterans than men across the study period.
A higher proportion of men than women veterans with headache received a diagnosis of headache not otherwise specified (NOS).
Women veterans were far more likely than men veterans to be diagnosed with migraine, including all migraine subtypes.
Women veterans were somewhat more likely than men to be diagnosed with tension-type headache.
Men veterans were more likely than women veterans to be diagnosed with cluster headache.
Men veterans were more likely than women to be diagnosed with post-traumatic headache, plausibly reflecting men's higher rate of TBI.
More men than women veterans had only a single headache type documented over the 12-year cohort period.
Women veterans with headache had significantly more annual headache-related encounters and were evaluated by more provider types than men.
Women veterans with headache had significantly higher rates of Primary Care Plus, Emergency Department, Neurology, and other specialty visits than men.
Men with headache were more likely to see Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (PM&R) specialists but less likely to see Pain Clinic Specialists or Psychiatrists compared with women.
Women veterans with headache received interdisciplinary care combining primary care with neurology or pain specialists significantly more often than men.
Black veterans were overrepresented among those diagnosed with headache relative to their overall representation in the VHA population.
Unlike other headache types, there was no statistically significant gender difference in diagnosis of hemicrania continua.
