Individuals with post-traumatic headache who reported bilateral symptoms during sustained neck rotation (Bi-Symp) had significantly lower sub-occipital pressure pain thresholds on both sides compared to those with no symptoms (Asymptomatic), with no side-to-side difference within either group.

In the Uni-Symp group (symptoms in only one rotation direction), sub-occipital pressure pain thresholds were significantly lower on the side corresponding to the symptomatic sustained neck rotation direction compared to the asymptomatic side.
Scalene muscle pressure pain thresholds did not differ within or between the Asymptomatic, Uni-Symp, and Bi-Symp groups.
During the loading response and terminal swing phases of gait, proximal displacement of the ankle was significantly greater in the GJH group than in controls.
The GJH group showed greater proximal/distal range of motion at the ankle throughout the gait cycle than controls.
The GJH group showed greater internal/external rotation range of motion at the ankle than controls.
The GJH group showed greater plantarflexion/dorsiflexion range of motion at the ankle than controls.

Vasovagal syncope is not associated with mortality but causes injuries, reduces quality of life, and is associated with anxiety and depression.
Physical counterpressure maneuvers may help prevent vasovagal syncope but have limited efficacy in older patients and those with short or absent prodromal symptoms.
Orthostatic training lacks long-term efficacy for vasovagal syncope and is limited by poor patient compliance.
Yoga might help reduce vasovagal syncope, although the underlying biomedical mechanism is unknown.
Yoga may help reduce vasovagal syncope recurrence, though the biological mechanism behind this effect is unknown.
About a third of vasovagal syncope patients continue to experience fainting despite conservative treatment measures such as hydration, salt intake, and counterpressure maneuvers.
Metoprolol did not reduce syncope recurrence in a pivotal randomized clinical trial of vasovagal syncope patients.
Fludrocortisone significantly reduces syncope recurrences in vasovagal syncope patients when titrated to target doses, with tolerable side effects.
Fludrocortisone, when titrated to target doses, significantly reduces syncope recurrences in patients with vasovagal syncope and has tolerable side effects.

Cardioneuroablation may help patients with vasovagal syncope but has not yet been evaluated in a formal clinical trial.
A systematic literature review found that hearing loss occurred in 63% of Stickler syndrome patients overall.
In type 1 Stickler syndrome (COL2A1), 52% of patients had hearing loss, mostly sensorineural, mild, and affecting higher frequencies, resembling early-onset presbycusis.
In STL1 patients, DPOAE amplitude was significantly decreased, more than expected from the pure tone audiogram, indicating outer hair cell dysfunction.

In type 2 and 3 Stickler syndrome (COL11A1/COL11A2), hearing loss prevalence is estimated at 69-83%, generally more severe than in STL1, mild-to-moderate at low/mid frequencies and moderate-to-severe at high frequencies.

Heterozygous COL11A1 mutations causing haploinsufficiency are associated with milder or absent Stickler syndrome symptoms, with parental carriers of homozygous/compound heterozygous families often asymptomatic.
Biallelic dominant-negative non-glycine COL11A2 substitutions have been described causing non-syndromic prelingual profound deafness.
Profound sensorineural hearing loss has been observed in the rare autosomal recessive form of type 2 Stickler syndrome caused by biallelic COL11A1 mutations.
STL3 (COL11A2) patients lack ocular symptoms because Col11a2 is not expressed in the eyes, unlike Col11a1.
Mice with targeted Col11a2 disruption showed frequency-independent moderate cochlear hearing loss with impaired collagen fibrillar configuration in the tectorial membrane.
Heterozygous Col11a1 haploinsufficiency in mice did not result in significant hearing loss, mirroring the human phenotype.

In recessive STL4, STL5, and STL6 (COL9A1/2/3 mutations), sensorineural hearing loss was consistently present in all patients, typically a downsloping audiogram from mild-moderate low-frequency to severe/profound high-frequency loss.
Recessive Stickler syndrome (COL9 gene mutations) exhibits more frequent and more severe hearing loss than dominant Stickler syndrome (COL2A1/COL11A1/COL11A2).
Col9 knock-out mice showed progressive hearing loss apparent at a young age with morphological tectorial membrane changes starting in the basal cochlear turn and progressing apically.
Two siblings with a homozygous LRP2 mutation and a Stickler-like ocular phenotype showed no significant hearing loss at a young age apart from temporary conductive hearing loss.
Lrp2-deficient mice showed progressive hearing impairment, which may explain why hearing was still normal in the two young human LRP2-mutation carriers.

In patients with biallelic LOXL3 mutations causing a Stickler-like phenotype, hearing was not formally tested in all cases, but no hearing loss was reported apart from conductive loss in one young patient.

Tissue-specific ablation of Loxl3 in the inner ear of mice resulted in progressively elevated hearing thresholds across all frequencies, with hair cell and secondary spiral ganglion neuron degeneration.

A family with a heterozygous BMP4 mutation and a Stickler-like ocular phenotype showed high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss more pronounced with older age than expected from typical age-related decline.
Bmp4 heterozygous null mice showed elevated hearing thresholds and circling behavior, with significantly reduced neuronal processes in the organ of Corti and reduced vestibular stereocilia.
Otosclerosis and stapedial fixation have been reported sporadically in type 1 Stickler syndrome, likely a coincidental occurrence given the high prevalence of otosclerosis in Caucasians.

Hypermobility of the tympanic membrane has been reported across different types of Stickler syndrome, possibly related to prior middle ear problems or type II collagen involvement, though not all cases link to middle ear disease.
Glycine substitutions disrupting the triple helical structure of type II collagen are associated with a higher risk of hearing loss in STL1 compared to loss-of-function mutations.
Most STL1-causing mutations are loss-of-function mutations predicted to result in nonsense-mediated decay of COL2A1 mRNA.
Among 71 patients with genetically confirmed RFC1-CANVAS, six female patients had also been diagnosed with primary Sjögren syndrome by their clinicians.

All six patients presented with a sicca syndrome, but only four met confirmed primary Sjögren syndrome diagnosis per 2016 ACR-EULAR classification criteria, suggesting sicca symptoms in CANVAS patients may lead to pSS misdiagnosis.
Five of the six patients had a history of chronic cough.
Examination of the six patients revealed cerebellar syndrome in three, vestibulopathy in two, pes cavus in three, and dysautonomia in two, consistent with the multisystem CANVAS phenotype.
Two of the six patients with RFC1-CANVAS misdiagnosed or co-diagnosed with pSS had vestibulopathy on examination.
Pes cavus was observed in three of the six patients with CANVAS suspected of or diagnosed with pSS.
Dysautonomia was present in two of the six CANVAS patients suspected of or diagnosed with pSS.
Neurophysiological examination showed that the sensory ganglionopathy was generally severe and symmetrical in these CANVAS patients.
Only four of the six suspected pSS patients actually met the 2016 ACR-EULAR classification criteria for confirmed primary Sjögren syndrome, despite all having sicca syndrome.
Four of the six patients were treated with immunosuppressive therapy but did not respond, and one experienced side effects.

The authors recommend that suspicion or diagnosis of pSS in a patient with sensory ganglionopathy should not exclude RFC1 expansion analysis, since a CANVAS diagnosis may deter clinicians from initiating or continuing immunosuppressive therapy in unconfirmed pSS patients.
The authors note that a sicca syndrome in RFC1-CANVAS patients may lead to misdiagnosis of primary Sjögren syndrome.

Serum TNF-alpha is elevated in individuals who suffer from migraine.
Serum interleukin-1 is elevated in individuals who suffer from migraine.
CGRP is secreted during migraine attacks and is found in over half of the neurons in the trigeminal ganglion, a region influenced by pro-inflammatory cytokines.
Elevated interferon-gamma and TNF-alpha, which regulate CGRP synthesis, are hypothesized to explain the link between migraine and celiac disease via a systemic inflammatory response.
CGRP exhibits antimicrobial effects against several gut bacterial strains including Escherichia coli, Enterococcus faecalis, and Lactobacillus acidophilus.
The presence or absence of gluten in the diet changes the diversity and number of gut microbial populations, potentially producing dysbiosis.
In celiac disease, undegraded gluten peptides serve as a food source for various duodenal bacteria, contributing to dysbiosis.
The number of bacterial species, diversity, and proportions in the gut is altered in celiac disease due to activation of the immunological cascade causing the inflammatory response.
Interleukin-6, along with IL-1, IL-8, and TNF-alpha, is linked to migraine pain and is elevated during migraine episodes.
Interleukin-8, along with IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha, is linked to migraine pain and is elevated during migraine episodes.
Gut bacteria produce neurotransmitters such as serotonin, GABA, and CGRP, which are exchanged between cell types and participate in gut-brain axis signaling relevant to migraine.
Intestinal cells in the gut produce large amounts of 5-hydroxytryptamine (serotonin), impacting the nervous system.

Physical and mental stressors cause hypothalamic release of corticotrophin-releasing hormone, triggering adrenal cortisol release, which can alter the gut microbiota profile and intestinal permeability, resulting in dysbiosis.
Immune inflammatory mediators including IL-1, IL-6, IL-18, TNF-alpha, and interferon-gamma sensitize afferent nerve terminals and elicit visceral pain in the gut.

Increased gut permeability can trigger inflammatory and immunological responses through lipopolysaccharide leakage, and pro-inflammatory cytokines can in turn further increase gut permeability, forming a bidirectional loop.
Gluten may impact nociceptive responses in the trigeminal pathway and contribute to the onset of migraine pain, mediated by pro-inflammatory cytokines including TNF-alpha, IL-1, and IL-6.

The panel defines an exaggerated orthostatic pressor response as a sustained rise in systolic blood pressure of at least 20 mmHg upon standing from supine, regardless of the absolute standing blood pressure value.
Orthostatic hypertension is defined as an exaggerated orthostatic pressor response combined with a standing systolic blood pressure of at least 140 mmHg.
In a large general-population cohort, systolic blood pressure decreased slightly on average from supine to standing, providing normative data underlying the 20 mmHg cutoff.
In the Malmö Offspring Study, systolic blood pressure rose slightly on average after 3 minutes of standing, corroborating the earlier Malmö Preventive Project normative data.
Plasma norepinephrine rises more during standing in patients with orthostatic hypertension than in others, implicating excessive sympathetic activation in its pathogenesis.
Pharmacological blockade of alpha-adrenoreceptors attenuates the exaggerated orthostatic blood pressure rise seen in orthostatic hypertension.
Patients with orthostatic hypertension frequently show an extreme nocturnal blood pressure dipping pattern and an exaggerated early-morning blood pressure surge on 24-hour ambulatory monitoring.
Depending on the diagnostic criteria applied, orthostatic hypertension prevalence ranged from 5% to 30% across epidemiological surveys and clinical trials.
Age, adiposity, arterial hypertension, and diabetes mellitus are reported risk factors for developing orthostatic hypertension.
An exaggerated orthostatic pressor response with normal office blood pressure may precede development of arterial hypertension in younger individuals.
Among people with arterial hypertension, those with an exaggerated orthostatic pressor response are more likely to show subclinical cerebrovascular disease and peripheral arterial disease.
Orthostatic hypertension is associated with increased all-cause and cardiovascular mortality.
Small-scale studies suggest orthostatic hypertension results from an excessive increase in vascular resistance upon standing, though the underlying mechanism may vary with age.
UMSARS-I and UMSARS-II scores correlated positively with scores on the MSA Quality of Life (QOL) scale in a longitudinal MSA clinic cohort.
UMSARS-I scores increased at a rate of 3.12 points per year in this MSA cohort followed longitudinally.
UMSARS-II scores increased at a rate of 5.55 points per year, faster than UMSARS-I, over the study period.
Individual UMSARS subquestions varied in how strongly they contributed to the overall rate of change on the scale.

A curated/optimized version of UMSARS retaining 8 of 12 UMSARS-I subquestions and 10 of 14 UMSARS-II subquestions, selected based on correlation with QOL, appeared more responsive to change than the full original scale.

Familial synucleinopathy caused by alpha-synuclein locus triplication or certain point mutations can manifest with an MSA-like clinical phenotype.
Somatic copy number variations of the SNCA gene have been associated with MSA.
Neurofilament light chain is increased in MSA compared to Parkinson's disease in both CSF and blood during early-stage disease.
Skin biopsy shows alpha-synuclein deposition predominating in somatosensory nerve fibers in MSA versus sympathetic adrenergic fibers in Parkinson's disease, aiding differential diagnosis.
[18F]PBR06 TSPO-PET imaging showed markedly increased radiotracer accumulation in the basis pontis and cerebellar white matter of an MSA-C patient compared to a healthy control.

Among 406 patients with parkinsonism-ataxia spectrum disorders evaluated at the multidisciplinary clinic over 5 years, 127 were classified as having possible or probable MSA, of whom 71 were alive as of January 2022 and 51 had died, with 30 of the deaths neuropathologically confirmed as MSA.

The program generated 38 iPSC lines from MSA and related disorders, including 22 lines matched to postmortem brain tissue, of which 15 derived from neuropathologically confirmed MSA cases.

iPSC lines were prioritized from familial synucleinopathy patients including two with alpha-synuclein triplication, one with duplication, and one carrying the alpha-synuclein A53T mutation, who present with aggressive diffuse synucleinopathy including MSA-like presentations.

Rapid recruitment into an investigator-initiated observational-to-treatment clinical trial was feasible: all 4 patients already in early observational follow-up were recruited and completed 6 months of drug treatment, and 16 additional patients were recruited within 9 months despite pandemic-related disruptions.

[18F]PBR06 TSPO-PET uptake tracked closely with the expected regional distribution of neuropathology across the clinic's MSA patients, consistent with other TSPO ligands.

The clinic's brain bank has stored 37 postmortem brains from MSA and related neurodegenerative diseases (including familial PD, DLB, SCA, and PSP) over a 5-year period, targeting a postmortem interval of less than 4 hours.

A cited study found that the ability versus inability to amplify amyloidogenic alpha-synuclein conformers from olfactory mucosa using seed amplification assay differentiates probable MSAp from MSAc, respectively.

Patients with chronic migraine showed decreased resting-state oscillatory functional connectivity compared with healthy controls, predominantly in beta and gamma bands within salience (insula, anterior cingulate cortex), sensorimotor (primary motor, primary and secondary somatosensory cortex), and default mode (posterior cingulate cortex) networks.

An SVM classifier using MEG oscillatory connectivity features distinguished chronic migraine patients from healthy controls in the training data set, with the Fine Gaussian kernel performing best (accuracy 86.8%, AUC 0.9, sensitivity 1.0, specificity 0.68).
In an independent testing data set, the trained SVM model generalised well to distinguish CM from HC, with Fine Gaussian and Linear kernels both achieving 94.1% accuracy.
The MEG-based SVM classification model distinguished chronic migraine from episodic migraine with high accuracy using the Fine Gaussian kernel.

The classification model also differentiated chronic migraine from fibromyalgia with favourable accuracy, supporting specificity of the MEG connectivity signature to migraine rather than chronic pain generally.

148 of 200 (74%) migraine patients reported at least one cranial autonomic symptom during headache episodes, higher than previously assumed.
Lacrimation was the most common cranial autonomic symptom, occurring in 45.5% of migraine patients.
Conjunctival injection was present in 34.5% of migraine patients as a cranial autonomic symptom.
Eyelid edema was reported in 34% of migraine patients as a cranial autonomic symptom.
Aural fullness/pressure was observed in 27.5% (55/200) of migraine patients, supporting its inclusion as a CAS in ICHD-3 beta.
Facial sweating, a sympathetic sign, was present in 25% of migraine patients.
Facial flushing, a parasympathetic sign, was present in 17.5% of migraine patients.
Nasal congestion was present in only 9% of migraine patients, making nasal CAS considerably less common than ocular CAS.
Rhinorrhea was present in 5% of migraine patients, one of the least frequent CAS.
Ptosis was the least common cranial autonomic symptom, observed in only 4% of migraine patients.
Ocular CAS were far more common (84.5%) than nasal CAS (12%) in migraineurs, suggesting predominant activation of the ophthalmic trigeminal division.
Two or more cranial autonomic symptoms co-occurred in 70% of migraineurs, with symptom counts ranging from one to seven CAS per patient.
Bilateral CAS was present in 87% (129/148) of affected migraine patients, contradicting earlier assumptions that CAS is predominantly unilateral.
Unilateral or ipsilateral CAS occurred in only 13% (19/148) of affected patients, including one rare case of contralateral CAS.

No demographic or headache characteristic (age, gender, family history, frequency/intensity of headache, duration of illness, nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, aura, or aggravating factors) was significantly associated with the presence of cranial autonomic symptoms.
Sunlight was reported as a headache-aggravating factor in 100% of CAS-positive migraine patients, suggesting a possible predisposition for pure cranial autonomic activation triggered by light.

Migraine-with-CAS patients had a higher frequency of associated symptoms (nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia) compared to migraine-without-CAS patients, although this was not statistically significant.
Chronic migraine patients were more represented in the CAS-positive group than the CAS-negative group.
Headache severity was greater in CAS-positive patients than CAS-negative patients.
A previous study cited in this paper found that migraine patients with cranial autonomic symptoms have higher CGRP levels in external jugular blood during attacks than those without such symptoms.
Nearly two-thirds of migraine patients treated with monoclonal antibodies reported at least one cranial autonomic symptom.
The proportion of patients reporting CAS was significantly higher among those treated before the July 2020 national reimbursement criteria change than after.
Monoclonal antibodies targeting the CGRP pathway significantly reduced monthly headache days from baseline to 12 weeks of treatment.
Patients with cranial autonomic symptoms showed a significantly greater reduction in monthly headache days with monoclonal antibody treatment than those without CAS.
The proportion of patients achieving higher response-rate categories was numerically greater in CAS+ patients but did not reach statistical significance compared with CAS- patients.
Baseline monthly headache days did not differ significantly between patients with and without cranial autonomic symptoms.
Treatment response to monoclonal antibodies did not differ according to the frequency or number of cranial autonomic symptoms reported by patients.
No patients discontinued monoclonal antibody treatment due to severe adverse events, while two stopped early due to perceived ineffectiveness.
Treatment with IVIg markedly reduced COMPASS-31 autonomic symptom score from 51 at baseline to 11 after approximately 1.5 years.
The patient's functional ability score improved from 10% at baseline to 80% after IVIg immunotherapy.
Following IVIg therapy, heart rate variability parameters (SDNN and RMSSD) significantly improved, indicating electrophysiological recovery of cardiovagal function.
Neurophysiologic testing in this Sjogren's syndrome patient demonstrated both cardiovagal and sudomotor autonomic impairment.
Neurological examination of the patient revealed tonic pupils, consistent with parasympathetic autonomic involvement.
After 6 months of IVIg therapy, the patient could walk long distances unsupported and had significantly fewer gastrointestinal complaints and syncopal episodes.
After approximately 1.5 years of IVIg immunotherapy, the patient's functional ability score improved from a baseline of 10% to 80%.
Control heart rate variability analysis after immunotherapy showed significant improvement in SD of the RR interval (SDNN) and root mean square of successive RR interval differences (RMSSD).
Women with fibromyalgia scored significantly higher on the Toronto Alexithymia Scale (TAS-20) than women with chronic migraine and healthy controls.
Women with fibromyalgia scored significantly higher on the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) than women with chronic migraine and healthy controls.

The relationship between alexithymia severity and psychological distress was significantly stronger in the fibromyalgia and chronic migraine patient groups than in healthy controls, indicating group moderation of this association.

A study of nearly 154,000 US veterans found increased risk of multiple cardiovascular problems (myocarditis, arrhythmia, stroke, blood clots, myocardial infarction, heart failure) within a year of recovering from acute COVID-19, including in previously healthy, non-obese, non-smoking individuals without kidney disease or diabetes.

In the veterans cohort, increased risk of post-COVID cardiovascular complications was observed regardless of age, race, sex, obesity, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, hyperlipidemia, or pre-existing cardiovascular disease.
Patients with more severe acute COVID-19 (home recovery vs hospitalization vs ICU admission) had progressively higher risk of post-COVID cardiovascular complications in the veterans cohort.

Over 12 months, COVID-19 was associated with an excess of 45.29 cardiovascular incidents per 1000 people versus controls, comprising major adverse cardiovascular events, dysrhythmias, other cardiovascular disorders, thromboembolic disorders, ischemic heart disease, cerebrovascular disorders, and inflammatory heart/pericardial disease.

Cardiovascular MRI of 100 recently recovered COVID-19 patients found detectable high-sensitivity troponin T in 71%, significantly elevated troponin T in 5%, cardiac abnormality in 78%, and ongoing myocardial inflammation in 60% (some asymptomatic), about two months after infection.
In an early Wuhan case series of 41 COVID-19 patients, 5 (12%) had myocardial injury with elevated high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I.
A meta-analysis of six published studies from China found that 8% of patients with COVID-19 had associated cardiac injury.

One study suggested that up to 7% of deaths in COVID-19 patients were caused by myocarditis.

Plasma from Long COVID/PASC and acute COVID-19 patients contained anomalous amyloid micro clots resistant to fibrinolysis (requiring two rounds of trypsinization to solubilize), with markedly elevated α2-antiplasmin, fibrinogen chains, and serum amyloid A compared to healthy controls and T2DM controls.

A UK sample-based study found persistent symptoms lasting 4 weeks or longer in 1.7% of children overall during the second and third UK COVID-19 waves, rising to 4.6% among children with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Among nearly 154,000 US veterans, COVID-19 was associated with an extra 45.29 cardiovascular events per 1000 people over 12 months compared to controls.
Post-COVID patients had an extra 23.48 major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), including myocardial infarction and stroke, per 1000 people compared to controls.

Post-COVID patients had an extra 11.61 incidents of heart failure per 1000 people compared to controls.
Post-COVID patients had an extra 3.56 incidents of non-ischemic cardiomyopathy per 1000 people compared to controls.
Post-COVID patients had an extra 9.88 incidents of thromboembolic disorders per 1000 people compared to controls.
Post-COVID patients had an extra 5.47 incidents of pulmonary embolism per 1000 people compared to controls.

A 10-year follow-up of pneumonia patients found that over a third developed cardiovascular disease events, with the highest risk in the first year after hospitalization, remaining elevated compared with controls throughout follow-up.
A Danish nationwide survey found SARS-CoV-2-positive children aged 0-14 had higher odds of reporting a symptom lasting more than two months than matched controls across all age groups.

A German matched cohort study of over 150,000 individuals found significantly higher incidence rates of combined health outcomes in the COVID-19 cohort than controls in both children/adolescents and adults.
A UK sample-based study found persistent symptoms lasting four or more weeks in children were more common among those with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection than overall.
In an analysis of 1.2 million UK smartphone users, two doses of a COVID-19 vaccine halved the risk of developing long COVID.

A large-scale study of more than 13 million people found vaccination against SARS-CoV-2 lowers the risk of long COVID after infection by only about 15%, a much smaller effect than an earlier smaller study suggested.
The 13-million-person study found no difference in the type or severity of long COVID symptoms between unvaccinated SARS-CoV-2 infected patients and those with breakthrough infections.
A German autopsy study detected SARS-CoV-2 viral copies in the heart tissue of the majority of patients who died of COVID-19.
A 39-patient autopsy series found SARS-CoV-2 in cardiac tissue in the majority of patients, with about a third showing viral loads above 1000 copies.

Human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes exposed to SARS-CoV-2 showed active infection with marked transcriptomic disruption of structural proteins, myofibrillar fragmentation, and loss of nuclear DNA, mirroring changes seen in human autopsy specimens.

A systematic review of 316 cardiac autopsy cases across 41 studies found myocyte/ventricular hypertrophy, fibrosis, acute ischemia, microvascular thrombi, and SARS-CoV-2 detectable in nearly half of examined hearts.
A 50-case cardiac autopsy study by Sang J C et al. found high rates of myocardial fibrosis, hypertrophy, and microthrombi.

A review of 50 studies covering 548 hearts found myocardial necrosis and oedema as the most prevalent acute findings, with hypertrophy, fibrosis, and detectable SARS-CoV-2 common chronic/persistent findings.
SARS-CoV-2 binds to ACE2 receptors with greater affinity than SARS-CoV, which may partly explain its increased tropism for organs including the heart.
Unlike SARS-CoV-2, the four common-cold human coronaviruses (HCoV-229E, HCoV-NL63, HCoV-OC43, HCoV-HKU1) have not shown any involvement in the heart.

Micro clots in acute COVID-19 and Long COVID/PASC plasma were resistant to fibrinolysis and required a second round of trypsinization before the persistent pellet deposits could be solubilized, unlike controls or T2DM plasma.
An early Wuhan case series found that 12% of 41 COVID-19 patients had myocardial injury with elevated high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I.
A meta-analysis of six published Chinese studies found that 8% of COVID-19 patients had associated cardiac injury.
A retrospective study of 416 hospitalized COVID-19 patients found 20% had underlying myocardial injury, which was associated with a tenfold higher mortality rate than patients without cardiac injury.
One study suggested that myocarditis accounted for up to 7% of deaths among COVID-19 patients.

Cardiovascular MRI in recently recovered COVID-19 patients found detectable hsTnT in the majority and significantly elevated levels in 5%, with the majority showing some cardiac irregularity and over half showing ongoing myocardial inflammation around two months post-infection.
An international cohort study of more than 3500 people by Athena Akrami's team identified 205 different symptoms associated with long COVID.
A review of nine studies on long COVID prevalence found that between 32.6% and 87.4% of patients reported at least one symptom persisting after several months.
The PHOSP-COVID study led by Evans found little relationship between the severity of the acute COVID-19 phase or organ damage and the subsequent severity of long COVID.

A study published in Nature found that the frequency of long COVID showed a graded increase corresponding to the severity of the initial acute COVID-19 phase, from asymptomatic/non-hospitalized through hospitalized to ICU-admitted patients.

The case report describes an adolescent presenting with right-sided headache and periorbital changes, illustrating a trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia as a differential diagnosis distinct from migraine.
Patients who developed PDPH (Group P) had a significantly greater increase in headache rate from before to after cesarean section than the spinal-no-PDPH or general anesthesia groups.
The proportion of patients developing a new-onset headache after cesarean section was much higher in the PDPH group than in the spinal-no-PDPH group, with none in the general anesthesia group.
The number of painful days per month increased significantly after cesarean section only in the PDPH group, not in the spinal-no-PDPH or general anesthesia groups.

Among patients with pre-existing headaches, worsening after cesarean section was significantly more common in the PDPH group than in the spinal-no-PDPH group, with none in the general anesthesia group.
Overall, 5.5% of patients with pre-existing headaches experienced worsening of their headache after cesarean section, most of whom were in the PDPH or spinal-no-PDPH groups.
In multiple logistic regression, each 1-unit increase in pre-gestational NRS headache pain score was associated with a 1.51-fold increased risk of headache worsening after cesarean section.
Headache location, presence of aura, and allodynia were not significant predictors of headache worsening in the regression model.
Allodynia rates increased substantially after cesarean section in the PDPH group, while remaining stable in the spinal-no-PDPH and general anesthesia groups.

After excluding patients with new-onset headache, the increase in allodynia rate in the PDPH group was no longer statistically significant, suggesting the increase was driven mainly by new-onset headache cases.
The presence of orthostatic symptoms did not significantly differ between pre-gestational and post-cesarean periods in any of the three groups.
All three patients in the PDPH group who developed new-onset headache also showed persistent orthostatic symptoms in the post-cesarean period.
In the PDPH group, aura tended to be more frequent before cesarean section than after, but this trend was not statistically significant.
Headaches were predominantly unilateral in all groups in both periods, with no significant differences in laterality between the PDPH, spinal-no-PDPH, and general anesthesia groups.
Rates of nausea-vomiting and photophobia-phonophobia did not significantly change between pre-gestational and post-cesarean periods in any group.
Mean headache pain intensity (NRS) did not significantly change from before to after cesarean section within any of the three groups.
Baseline (pre-gestational) chronic headache prevalence was similar across the PDPH, spinal-no-PDPH, and general anesthesia groups before cesarean section.
Oncogenic activity from mutant KIT is described as a key driver of mast cell expansion and disease progression in mastocytosis.
Patients with systemic mastocytosis may experience mediator-related symptoms and can develop a co-occurring mast cell activation syndrome.
Anti-CASPR2 antibody encephalitis is described as often presenting with autonomic nerve damage in addition to epilepsy, cognitive dysfunction, peripheral neuropathy, and ataxia.

All three reported patients with CASPR2 antibody-associated rapidly progressive parkinsonism improved after treatment with anti-epileptic drugs plus intravenous steroid pulse therapy followed by oral steroid therapy.
Among 116 sleep syncope patients pooled across studies, the mean age was 46.9 years and 61.4% were female.
Nearly all sleep syncope patients (96.5%) also had a history of typical daytime vasovagal syncope.
More than half of sleep syncope patients (54.3%) reported syncopal episodes during childhood.
About half (52.5%) of sleep syncope patients were supine at the moment of syncope onset, while the rest fainted shortly after standing.
In two studies, 67.6% of sleep syncope patients had a history of phobias.
Head-up tilt testing was positive in 90.9% of sleep syncope patients tested across five studies.
Upper gastrointestinal symptoms were common in sleep syncope, with 65.6% experiencing nausea and 42.9% experiencing vomiting.
When restricted to studies specifying symptom timing, 90.0% of sleep syncope patients had nausea occurring prior to syncope.
There was a non-significant trend toward higher prevalence of gastrointestinal medical conditions in sleep syncope patients compared to controls (11.6% vs 3.4%, p=0.06), reported in Jardine et al.
Lower gastrointestinal symptoms (urge to defecate or abdominal pain) were present in 86.0% of sleep syncope patients across six studies.
In studies specifying symptom timing, all 8 patients (100%) reported urge to defecate or abdominal pain occurring before syncope.
Profuse sweating or diaphoresis was reported in 64.2% of sleep syncope patients with available data.
Significant bradycardia (<30 bpm) or asystole (>3s) during witnessed/monitored episodes occurred in 53.8% of the small subset of patients with such monitoring.
Vagotonia, defined as clustered vasovagal episodes over a few hours, was present in 30.4% of patients in the Jardine et al. cohort.
Sleep syncope prevalence among vasovagal syncope patients in retrospective studies ranged widely from 2.5% to 21.3%.
In long-term follow-up of the Jardine et al. cohort, only 24.2% of sleep syncope patients had recurrence and just 8.1% continued to have a high burden of sleep syncope after clinical assessment.
Only 2.9% of sleep syncope patients in the Jardine et al. cohort underwent permanent pacemaker insertion during follow-up, suggesting pacemakers are rarely required.
Gastrointestinal symptom prevalence in sleep syncope patients was notably higher than reported in general vasovagal syncope populations, particularly for lower abdominal discomfort.
In a general vasovagal syncope population reported by Sheldon et al., nausea or vomiting prior to syncope occurred in only 36.8% of patients, substantially lower than the rates seen in sleep syncope.

Gastrointestinal prodromal symptoms in sleep syncope are believed to result from exaggerated vagal activity mediated by the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus nerve, which regulates subdiaphragmatic organs.

The authors hypothesize that the hypothalamus may play a crucial role in initiating sleep syncope events, potentially triggered by sleep/wake transitions or nightmares, linking gastrointestinal symptoms (via dorsal motor vagal nucleus) with the cardioinhibitory vasovagal cascade (via nucleus ambiguus).
Patients with orthostatic hypotension hospitalized for hypertensive crises had over three times the odds of 30-day readmission with falls compared to those without orthostatic hypotension.
Orthostatic hypotension was not significantly associated with 30-day readmission for hypertensive crises.
Rates of acute kidney injury during hypertensive crisis hospitalization did not differ significantly between OH and non-OH groups.
Rates of stroke or transient ischemic attack did not differ significantly between OH and non-OH groups.
Rates of aortic dissection did not differ significantly between OH and non-OH groups.
Patients with orthostatic hypotension were less likely to develop acute heart failure during hypertensive crisis hospitalization than those without orthostatic hypotension.
Patients with orthostatic hypotension were less likely to develop acute coronary syndrome during hypertensive crisis hospitalization than those without orthostatic hypotension.
Patients with orthostatic hypotension hospitalized for hypertensive crises had longer hospital length of stay than those without orthostatic hypotension.
Patients with orthostatic hypotension hospitalized for hypertensive crises incurred higher hospitalization costs than those without orthostatic hypotension.
Over a third of patients with migraine received a prescription opioid during the 12-month follow-up period.
Patients with chronic migraine and those with certain comorbidities had higher opioid dosages than other migraine patients.
Patients with chronic migraine were twice as likely as those with episodic migraine to receive at least 20 morphine milligram equivalents per day.
Patients with chronic migraine had a longer median duration of opioid day supply than patients with episodic migraine.
About 7% of chronic migraine patients receiving opioids reached high-dose exposure (at least 50 MME/day) within a 90-day window during follow-up.
Younger age was a significant risk factor associated with new-onset chronic migraine in a Cox proportional hazards model.
Female sex was a significant risk factor for new-onset chronic migraine.
Residence in the South and West US regions was significantly associated with increased risk of new-onset chronic migraine.
A diagnosis of medication overuse headache was a significant risk factor for new-onset chronic migraine.
A diagnosis of depression was a significant risk factor for new-onset chronic migraine.
A diagnosis of back pain was a significant risk factor for new-onset chronic migraine.
A diagnosis of fibromyalgia was a significant risk factor for new-onset chronic migraine.
In a cohort of 179 hospitalized COVID-19 pneumonia patients, those presenting with headache had markedly higher mortality than those without headache.

A 28-year-old female with COVID-19 developed unusual intermittent intranasal burning pain followed by intense short-lasting facial pain, phenotypically suggestive of trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia possibly triggered by the virus.
A 45-year-old male with COVID-19 developed an evolving bifrontal-to-holocranial postural headache and had laboratory findings of thrombocytopenia and mild hyponatremia.

Despite IL-6 cytokine storm being implicated in neuroinflammation in migraineurs, COVID-19 headache patients surprisingly show stable or lower IL-6 levels, possibly reflecting a protective, localized neuroinflammatory response.
TNF-alpha, known to be elevated at neuropathic pain sites and to contribute to peripheral and central pain sensitization, has an unknown role in COVID-19 headache physiology.

SARS-CoV-2 binding causes ACE2 to downregulate itself, disrupting the AngI-ACE-AngII-AT1R axis and raising AT1R and CGRP levels, which may contribute to headache and its chronification even after pathogen clearance.
Olfactory and gustatory dysfunction occur in a substantial proportion of COVID-19 patients and are associated with a shorter disease course/hospital stay, suggesting prognostic value.

Cortical spreading depression, a slow cortical depolarization wave, is proposed as a central mechanism producing peripheral and delayed central sensitization that may explain COVID-19 headache without aura, analogous to migraine without aura.

A cited study found reduced conditioned pain modulation in episodic migraineurs and absent CPM in chronic migraineurs, indicating loss of descending pain inhibition that could facilitate trigeminovascular activation and explain increased headache frequency in COVID patients with prior primary headache disorders.
COVID-19-related headache prevalence varies widely across studies globally, ranging from 8% to 70.3%.

Fever in COVID-19 escalates pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1 and IL-6, which agitate the hypothalamus and contribute to headache, although fever-free headaches also occur, suggesting additional pathways.

Hypothalamic nuclei (supraoptic, paraventricular, infundibular) contain the highest density of CGRP neurons, particularly at RAMP1 loci, implicating them in cluster headache pathophysiology based on prior mouse experiments.

Tocilizumab (used for giant cell arteritis, an IL-6 pathway modulator) and intranasal Vazegepant (a CGRP receptor antagonist for acute migraine with an ongoing trial for COVID-19 lung infection) suggest a possible therapeutic link between headache pathophysiology and COVID-19 treatment.

In Case 2, multiple analgesic and abortive treatments (paracetamol, naproxen, topiramate, paracetamol-caffeine, ibuprofen, tramadol, ketorolac) provided almost no complete symptomatic relief for the post-COVID headache, although the headache gradually diminished and resolved over two months.

The cohort consisted of 52 patients identified as CASPR2 antibody-positive in CSF between 2006 and 2020, of whom 48 had sufficient data for analysis; CSF positivity (rather than serum-only) was used to select limbic encephalitis cases.
The cohort was overwhelmingly male with older median age at onset, consistent with prior descriptions of CASPR2-encephalitis demographics.

About a third of patients had a history of cancer at last visit, but the diversity of tumor types and their timing relative to disease onset suggested the association was fortuitous rather than paraneoplastic.
At disease onset, most patients had at least one neurologic symptom, distributed among limbic (54%), PNH (21%), and cerebellar (17%) categories, but usually only one category was present at a time.
Seizures were the most common limbic symptom at onset and were usually isolated, without accompanying cognitive or behavioral changes.
No patient presented at onset with the full classic triad of limbic encephalitis (seizures, amnesia, and behavioral change), highlighting the difficulty of early recognition.

Nonspecific symptoms such as asthenia, mood disorders, insomnia, weight loss, and hyperhidrosis were common at onset, and in some patients (19%) were the only presenting features, without limbic, PNH, or cerebellar symptoms.
Only 10% of patients had at least 3 of the core CASPR2 symptoms (as defined by van Sonderen et al.) at disease onset, suggesting these core criteria are insensitive for early diagnosis.
CASPR2-encephalitis progresses slowly, with the disease peak reached at a median of nearly 17 months after onset, substantially longer than reported for NMDA-receptor and LGI1-encephalitis.
Fewer than half of the patients fulfilled the Graus criteria for definite autoimmune limbic encephalitis over the disease course, largely due to low fulfillment of the subacute-onset criterion.

On expert re-reading, EEG abnormalities (slow waves, interictal epileptiform discharges, ictal events) were found in about a third of recorded patients, mostly in temporal regions, with ictal events consistently triggered by hyperpnea.

Immunotherapy (steroids, IV immunoglobulins, rituximab, cyclophosphamide, and other agents) was initiated in all patients but was started, on average, almost a year after disease onset, substantially later than reported for other autoimmune encephalitides.
About a third of patients relapsed, typically about two years after onset, and most relapses occurred within three months of full or partial immunotherapy withdrawal.
Mortality during follow-up was 17%, occurring in the oldest patients years after onset, mostly unrelated to the neurologic disease itself.
Long-term functional outcome was good in most survivors, and no correlation was found between delay to first immunotherapy and functional outcome (mRS score).
Dysautonomia was a frequent nonlimbic symptom in CASPR2-encephalitis, present in over a third of patients at the peak of disease and in nearly half of patients over the entire disease course.
Persistent cerebellar ataxia at long-term follow-up was significantly more common among functionally dependent patients than among independent patients.
Long-term quality of life in survivors was largely similar to a normative population, except for a moderate reduction in the vitality subscore of the SF-36.
Continuous 1-Hz taVNS increased static functional connectivity between the nucleus tractus solitarius and occipital cortex compared with the pre-stimulation resting state.
Continuous 1-Hz taVNS increased static functional connectivity between the locus coeruleus and occipital cortex compared with the pre-stimulation resting state.
Continuous 1-Hz taVNS decreased static functional connectivity between the nucleus tractus solitarius and thalamus compared with the pre-stimulation resting state.
Continuous 20-Hz taVNS increased static functional connectivity between the locus coeruleus and anterior cingulate cortex compared with the pre-stimulation resting state.
1-Hz taVNS produced greater locus coeruleus-precuneus static functional connectivity than 20-Hz taVNS.
1-Hz taVNS produced greater locus coeruleus-inferior parietal cortex static functional connectivity than 20-Hz taVNS.
20-Hz taVNS increased locus coeruleus-anterior cingulate cortex functional connectivity compared with 1-Hz taVNS.
The strength of NTS-thalamus static functional connectivity during the pre-taVNS resting state was positively correlated with the number of migraine attacks patients had in the past four weeks.

In high-frequency episodic migraine (HFEM), the combination of unilateral pain and unilateral cranial autonomic symptoms (UP+UAs) independently predicted ≥50% response to anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies at 24 weeks.
In HFEM, UP+UAs also independently predicted ≥75% (super-response) to anti-CGRP mAbs at 24 weeks, though this association was only borderline significant after correction for multiple comparisons.
In chronic migraine (CM), presence of unilateral pain alone was independently and positively associated with ≥50% response to antiCGRP mAbs.
In CM, presence of unilateral cranial autonomic symptoms (UAs) alone was independently associated with ≥50% response to antiCGRP mAbs.
In CM, the combination UP+UAs was independently associated with ≥50% response to antiCGRP mAbs, and models combining UP+UAs fit significantly better than models with the two variables separated.
In CM, the combination of unilateral pain and allodynia was independently associated with ≥50% response to antiCGRP mAbs, reflecting combined peripheral and central sensitization.
In CM, obesity was a negative independent predictor of ≥50% response to antiCGRP mAbs.
In CM, UP+UAs also independently predicted ≥75% (super-)response to antiCGRP mAbs.
In CM, the combination of unilateral pain and allodynia independently predicted ≥75% (super-)response to antiCGRP mAbs.
At 24 weeks, anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies produced ≥50%, ≥75%, and 100% response rates of 64.9%, 30.8%, and 1% respectively in HFEM, and 61.4%, 30.2%, and 2.4% respectively in CM.
No clinical or demographic predictor of 100% response (complete responders) to antiCGRP mAbs was identified in either HFEM or CM, likely due to the small number of complete responders.

Chronic migraine patients showed a distinct clinical profile compared to high-frequency episodic migraine patients, with higher obesity prevalence, pain intensity, unilateral cranial autonomic symptoms, allodynia, prior treatment failures, and psychiatric comorbidities, but lower rates of unilateral pain, triptan response, and botulinum toxin response.
In univariate analysis of HFEM patients, UP+UAs was associated with higher rates of both ≥50% and ≥75% response, and UP+allodynia showed a trend toward higher ≥75% response.
In univariate analysis of CM patients, ≥50% response was associated with lower BMI and lower baseline monthly headache days, in addition to UP+UAs, UP+allodynia, and UP+UAs+allodynia combinations.

Genetic testing revealed an abnormal expansion of 101 GGC repeats in the NOTCH2NLC gene, confirming the diagnosis of neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease (NIID) in a patient presenting mainly with migraine-aura-like symptoms.
Skin biopsy showed neuronal eosinophilic hyaline intranuclear inclusions in sweat gland epithelial cells and fibroblasts that were immunoreactive to p62, supporting the diagnosis of NIID.
Skin biopsy showed that the neuronal eosinophilic hyaline intranuclear inclusions were also immunoreactive to ubiquitin, consistent with NIID pathology.
Brain MRI DWI showed persistent hyperintense signals in the corpus callosum and corticomedullary junction, together with early-onset brain atrophy, in this NIID patient.
Oral administration of sibelium (flunarizine hydrochloride) prevented recurrence of the patient's migraine-aura-like headache and visual symptoms after they reappeared following a cold.
A previously reported 20-year-old man with NIID had an 81 GGC repeat expansion in the NOTCH2NLC 5'UTR and presented with hemiplegic migraine and seizure.

A previously reported 86-year-old man with NIID had vestibular migraine-like attacks for over 30 years followed by essential tremor and dementia, and genetic testing revealed a mutation in the SCN5A gene.

The authors hypothesize that cerebral hypoperfusion and vascular dysfunction may contribute to accumulation of eosinophilic inclusions, causing ischemic/hypoxic neuronal changes that lead to migraine attacks and NIID progression.
Diffuse vasospasm without ischemia and blood–brain-barrier disruption have been proposed as mechanisms explaining the brain atrophy that accompanies NIID.

A patient with migraine and cranial autonomic dysregulation developed a persisting unilateral corneal arcus, likely linked to vascular dysregulation.
The same migraine patient exhibited persisting alterations of conjunctival vessels attributed to autonomic vascular dysregulation.

Cranial autonomic dysregulation, common in cluster headache or migraine, is described as causing peripheral vascular dysfunction that may raise risk of ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke, myocardial infarction, retinal vasculopathy, cardiovascular mortality, and peripheral artery disease, and can manifest with ocular symptoms such as increased lacrimation, conjunctival injection, and facial swelling.
Erenumab treatment reduced mean monthly migraine days by 6.0 days at month 3 compared to baseline.
At month 6, mean MMD reduction was 7.5 days versus baseline, with 48% of patients (n=76) achieving at least 30% reduction and continuing treatment.
At month 3, 49%, 35% and 13% of patients achieved at least 30%, 50% and 75% reductions in MMD respectively.
At month 6, 31.3% of patients achieved at least a 50% reduction in MMD and 15.6% achieved at least a 75% reduction.
Erenumab treatment reduced HIT-6 (migraine-related disability) scores by 7.7 points at month 3 and 7.5 points at month 6 compared to baseline.
The proportion of patients with medication overuse headache decreased from 54% at baseline to 20% at month 3 and 25% at month 6 with erenumab treatment.
At month 12, 38% of patients maintained at least a 30% MMD reduction, 26% maintained at least 50%, and 13% maintained at least 75% reduction.
At month 18, 33% of patients maintained at least 30% MMD reduction, 24% maintained at least 50%, and 13% maintained at least 75%.

At month 24, only 23% of patients maintained at least a 30% MMD reduction, 16% maintained at least 50%, and 8% maintained at least 75%, indicating a marked decline in sustained response over two years.
Over the 24-month follow-up, 54% of the 160 patients discontinued erenumab treatment.
By month 6, four patients discontinued erenumab due to lack of efficacy while 21 discontinued due to side effects, including one pregnancy.
Constipation was the most frequent adverse event reported with erenumab, occurring in 21.2% of patients, followed by flu-like symptoms in 15.6%.

Severe adverse events leading to discontinuation in the first six months included constipation (n=11), headache worsening after injection (n=5), flu-like symptoms (n=2), whole body itchiness (n=1), severe mood deterioration (n=1) and new onset hypertension (n=1).

The proportion of patients reporting adverse events declined over time on erenumab, from 28.8% at month 12 to 20.5% at month 18 and 5.4% at month 24, with constipation remaining the most common side effect.
Three female patients became pregnant during erenumab treatment (discontinuing treatment upon discovery), with no reported complications in the pregnancies, newborns, or postpartum mothers.
The proportion of patients in the severe HIT-6 impact category decreased from 95% at baseline to 46% at month 6, 29% at month 12, and 16% at month 24 among those continuing treatment.

The audited resistant chronic migraine population had failed prior treatments extensively: 91.9% had failed BoNT/A injections and all patients had failed greater occipital nerve blocks, with an average of 8.3 failed preventive treatment classes.
The article describes overlap in pathophysiology between migraine and gastroparesis involving interplay of the central, autonomic, and enteric nervous systems.
Gastroparesis (delayed gastric emptying) can occur both during acute migraine attacks and in between attacks, requiring modification of migraine management.
Delayed gastric emptying in migraine patients can impair absorption of oral migraine medications, so alternate drug formulations should be considered for some patients.

Noninvasive vagus nerve stimulation, already FDA cleared for migraine treatment, is also being studied as a treatment for gastroparesis, motivated by the shared role of autonomic dysfunction in both conditions.
Autonomic nervous system dysfunction is highlighted as a significant shared feature in the pathophysiology of both gut motility disorders and migraine.
Migraine shows high comorbidity with fibromyalgia syndrome, consistent with shared etiological and psychophysiological mechanisms among symptom disorders.
Migraine is highly comorbid with irritable bowel syndrome as part of a broader spectrum of chronic overlapping pain and functional somatic disorders.
Migraine shows comorbidity with functional non-epileptic seizures, depression, anxiety, and posttraumatic stress disorder, framed under integrative concepts such as functional somatic disorders.

Symptom disorders including migraine share etiological factors such as female preponderance and psychological vulnerability, and psychophysiological mechanisms such as altered sensory processing and pain expectancy.

Migraine management is increasingly moving toward addressing total symptom burden using both centrally acting pharmacological treatments and non-pharmacological psychological and behavioral approaches.
A recent survey found that dry eye symptoms occur in 95-98% of patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome, making it one of the most disabling and prevalent symptoms of the disease.

The authors note that, unlike the well-characterized dysfunction of the salivary gland in pSS (including invading 'innately activated' B cells, lymphoepithelial lesion formation, and epithelial contribution to inflammation), understanding of how the lacrimal gland becomes dysfunctional in pSS remains minimal.
Offspring of parents with PTSD had approximately twice the risk of migraine compared to matched controls whose parents had no PTSD or major psychiatric disorder.
Offspring of parents with PTSD had a higher risk of irritable bowel syndrome compared to matched controls.
Offspring of parents with PTSD had a substantially higher risk of depressive disorder compared to matched controls, after adjusting for demographics and family psychiatric history.

The 44-year-old patient's fibromyalgia was diagnosed alongside underlying cervical spondylosis, with 13 of 18 ACR-defined tender points positive, suggesting spondylosis as a peripheral contributing factor to her fibromyalgia symptoms.
After one month of multimodal chiropractic care, the patient's back pain rating dropped from 6/10 to 2/10 with improved cervical and lumbar mobility.
At initial presentation, surface EMG showed high muscle tension across the patient's cervical and all spinal segments.
After 16 months of chiropractic therapy, sEMG signals and EP stress score normalized, corresponding with the patient's symptom relief.

NSAIDs, muscle relaxants, antidepressants, anti-epileptics, aqua-therapy, and acupuncture failed to relieve the patient's symptoms after 6 months, prompting her to seek chiropractic care instead.
Cited literature indicates that roughly 20-35% of fibromyalgia patients have a peripheral neuropathic origin to their pain.
In a cited case, caudal epidural blocks temporarily relieved a fibromyalgia patient's back pain and laryngopharyngeal paresthesia for about 3 weeks after each of four monthly blocks.

In a cited study of 18 patients with chronic whiplash-related disorders, cervical medial branch blocks reduced familiar neck pain intensity by at least 80% and altered pressure and cold pain thresholds at remote sites.

In a cited survey of 367 Japanese chronic pain patients, psychiatric disorder co-occurrence was similarly high in those with fibromyalgia (96.9%) and without fibromyalgia (93.5%), with no statistically significant difference between groups.

A cited fMRI study found that depression symptom severity corresponded to the magnitude of pain-evoked neuronal activation in the amygdala and contralateral anterior insula, brain regions involved in affective pain processing.
A cited qualitative study of 40 adults with fibromyalgia found that 77.5% reported persistent tiredness/fatigue that did not resolve even after sleep or rest.

Cited microdialysis studies of muscle interstitial fluid showed increased concentrations of glutamate, pyruvate, lactate, and serotonin in fibromyalgia patients, indicative of increased anaerobic muscle metabolism.

Cited fMRI studies demonstrated reduced functional connectivity in the descending pain-modulating system alongside hyperexcitability in the pain matrix in fibromyalgia, consistent with central sensitization.
The EULAR guideline update did not recommend NSAIDs, monoamine oxidase inhibitors, SSRIs, growth hormone, or corticosteroids for fibromyalgia due to lack of effectiveness.

EULAR guidelines gave exercise therapy (aerobic and strengthening) the only 'strong for' recommendation for fibromyalgia management, proposed to work by increasing anti-nociceptive neurotransmitters and reducing glutamate.
Atomoxetine treatment reduced annualized vasovagal syncope frequency from a median of 5.5 episodes per year to 0 episodes per year.
Most patients on atomoxetine showed subjective improvement, and over half remained free of syncope during follow-up.

A Poisson-distribution-based individual patient analysis found that 7 of 12 subjects achieved statistically significant improvement, 3 of 12 had no recurrent syncope but insufficient follow-up time to reach significance, and 2 of 12 did not improve significantly.
